Shoji Kawamori
Mamoru Oshii
context: Tomino's Gundam was canceled mid-run for poor ratings. The model-kit company Bandai saved it — kit sales drove a re-edit into theatrical films, and the franchise became sustainable.

question: The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles first appeared in a 1984 black-and-white comic from Mirage Studios by two friends with a single staple in the cover. In what year did the first issue arrive?
context: Eastman and Laird printed about 3,000 copies of TMNT #1 in May 1984 — meant as a one-shot parody of Frank Miller's Daredevil. A copy now sells for tens of thousands.

question: The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles' obsession with pizza was not in Eastman and Laird's 1984 comic — it was added when the property went mainstream. In what medium did the pizza obsession debut?
answer: The 1987 animated series
choices: The 1987 animated series
The 1984 original comic
The 1990 live-action film
Playmates action figures
context: The 1987 Murakami-Wolf-Swenson cartoon softened the Turtles for kids, added pizza, color-coded the masks, and made April O'Neil a redhead reporter. The comic Turtles all wore red.

question: The animated series ThunderCats, about a band of feline humanoids who fled the destruction of Thundera, debuted in syndication in what year?
context: ThunderCats aired 130 episodes between 1985 and 1989, animated by Japan's Pacific Animation. The first episode, 'Exodus,' showed the cats fleeing Thundera in suspended animation.

question: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe, the Filmation cartoon based on Mattel's action figures, debuted in syndication in what year?
context: He-Man ran 130 episodes in two seasons. Filmation reused animation cycles aggressively to make it on budget. Each episode ended with a moral lesson direct-to-camera.

question: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero — the Hasbro-tied cartoon featuring Cobra Commander, Destro, and the Baroness — premiered in 1983 as a five-part miniseries. In what year did the regular daily series begin?
context: Two miniseries (1983 and 1984) preceded the daily syndicated run that started in September 1985. Larry Hama wrote the Marvel tie-in comic, where most of the character bibles originated.

question: The Transformers animated series, debuting alongside the Hasbro toyline, ran in daily syndication. Optimus Prime, Megatron, and the rallying cry 'More than meets the eye' all date to that first season. In what year did it premiere?
context: Hasbro licensed Takara's Diaclone and Microman toy lines and asked Marvel for a story. Bob Budiansky and the Marvel team wrote names and bios for every character — Hasbro had only sent visuals.

question: The animated Transformers: The Movie — known for its rock-opera soundtrack and the death of several main characters — released in what year?
context: The 1986 film was scored by Vince DiCola with Stan Bush's 'The Touch.' It also gave Orson Welles his final voice role as Unicron. Generations of kids cried in theaters.

question: The animated series Voltron: Defender of the Universe — five lions that combined into a giant robot — debuted in U.S. syndication in what year?
context: Voltron was a heavily-edited dub of two unrelated Japanese shows: Beast King GoLion (the lions) and Armored Fleet Dairugger XV (the vehicle team). U.S. producers spliced them into one franchise.

question: X-Men: The Animated Series, with its kinetic guitar-driven theme song and Bryan Singer-influencing art style, debuted on Fox Kids in what year?
context: The X-Men cartoon ran 76 episodes through 1997. It adapted Dark Phoenix, Days of Future Past, and the Phalanx Covenant straight from the comics — unusually faithful for Saturday morning.

question: Batman: The Animated Series, the Bruce Timm and Paul Dini production famous for its dark deco art style, premiered on Fox Kids in what year?
context: Timm and Dini's BTAS painted on black paper instead of white — a technique borrowed from Max Fleischer's Superman cartoons. Mark Hamill's Joker debuted in the fourth-aired episode.

question: Spider-Man: The Animated Series, the Fox Kids show that adapted decades of Marvel storylines including the Symbiote saga and Six Arms, premiered in what year?
context: The 1994 Spider-Man series ran five seasons through 1998. It was famously censored — no Mary Jane being kidnapped 'in a sack,' no fists striking faces. Christopher Daniel Barnes voiced Peter.

question: The 1977 film originally titled simply Star Wars — later subtitled Episode IV: A New Hope — was written and directed by a filmmaker who founded both Lucasfilm and Industrial Light & Magic to make it. Who?
answer: George Lucas
choices: George Lucas
Steven Spielberg
Francis Coppola
Brian De Palma
context: Lucas's working title was 'The Star Wars.' Studio heads thought it would flop. He took back-end deals on toys and sequel rights instead of salary — and ended up owning everything.

question: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, the prequel set in 1935, released in 1984 with Kate Capshaw and Ke Huy Quan opposite Harrison Ford. What was its year of release?
context: Temple of Doom's dark tone — heart-ripping, child slavery — directly led the MPAA to create the PG-13 rating later that year. Spielberg called it his least favorite of the four.

question: Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial — a boy named Elliott hides an alien in his California suburb — released in what year?
context: E.T. opened June 11, 1982. It overtook Star Wars as the highest-grossing film ever and held that record until Jurassic Park. The candy that lured E.T. was Reese's Pieces; M&M's passed.

question: Ghostbusters, the Ivan Reitman film about parapsychologists who go into business catching ghosts in Manhattan, released in what year?
context: Aykroyd's original script was a much more cosmic affair — set in the future, with multiple ghostbusting teams across realities. Harold Ramis grounded it in present-day New York.

question: The 1984 film The Terminator — a cyborg from 2029 hunting Sarah Connor in 1984 Los Angeles — launched the careers of its director and its star. Who directed it?
answer: James Cameron
choices: James Cameron
Ridley Scott
John Carpenter
Walter Hill
context: Cameron sold the script for one dollar on the condition he could direct it. He wrote much of it during a fever-dream in a Rome hotel. Schwarzenegger had been considered for Reese, not the Terminator.

question: Aliens, the 1986 sequel to Ridley Scott's Alien, was directed by the man fresh off The Terminator. Sigourney Weaver returned as Ripley to fight not one xenomorph but an infestation. Who directed?
answer: James Cameron
choices: James Cameron
Ridley Scott
David Fincher
Joe Dante
context: Cameron pitched Aliens to Fox by writing 'ALIEN' on a whiteboard, adding an 'S,' then drawing dollar signs through the S. The film cost 18 million and made over 130 million.

question: Rankin/Bass's stop-motion holiday special Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, narrated by a snowman based on the singer Burl Ives, first aired on NBC in what year?
context: Rudolph aired December 6, 1964. It is the longest continuously-running holiday special in U.S. television history. The original puppets were lost for decades and only resurfaced in 2005.

question: A Charlie Brown Christmas, the first Peanuts television special — featuring Vince Guaraldi's piano score and Linus reading from the Gospel of Luke — first aired in what year?
context: CBS executives hated everything about it: real children voicing the characters, jazz score, religious text, no laugh track. It aired December 9, 1965, drew 50 percent of all U.S. TV viewers, and won an Emmy.

question: The 1983 film A Christmas Story, based on the writing of Jean Shepherd and featuring Ralphie's desperate quest for a Red Ryder BB gun, first released in what year?
context: A Christmas Story was directed by Bob Clark, also responsible for Porky's and Black Christmas. It flopped on release. TBS's 24-hour Christmas Day marathons starting in 1997 turned it into a tradition.

question: The 1990 film Home Alone, in which Macaulay Culkin's Kevin McCallister is left behind by his family and fends off two burglars in suburban Chicago, was directed by whom?
answer: Chris Columbus
choices: Chris Columbus
John Hughes
Joe Dante
Howard Deutch
context: John Hughes wrote and produced. Columbus directed. Home Alone was the highest-grossing live-action comedy ever made at the time and held that record for 21 years.

question: Die Hard, the action film that put Bruce Willis in a Christmas-Eve siege of a Los Angeles skyscraper, released in what year?
context: Die Hard was based on Roderick Thorp's 1979 novel Nothing Lasts Forever. Sylvester Stallone, Burt Reynolds, and Clint Eastwood all turned down John McClane. Willis was a TV guy on Moonlighting.

question: The 1966 Western The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, starring Clint Eastwood as the Man With No Name and Eli Wallach as Tuco, was directed by an Italian filmmaker who shot all three Dollars films. Who?
answer: Sergio Leone
choices: Sergio Leone
Sergio Corbucci
Federico Fellini
Mario Bava
context: Leone shot the climactic graveyard standoff with three Panavision cameras and held single eye-and-pistol close-ups for minutes. Ennio Morricone scored it; the soundtrack outsold the film.

question: Sergio Leone's first Western, A Fistful of Dollars, brought Clint Eastwood to international stardom and remade Kurosawa's Yojimbo without permission. In what year did it release?
context: Kurosawa's lawyers sued. Leone settled for distribution rights in Asia. Eastwood took the part for fifteen thousand dollars after every American TV cowboy he competed with — including Charles Bronson — turned it down.

question: Clint Eastwood's Unforgiven, his elegiac Western that won Best Picture and Best Director at the Oscars, released in what year?
context: Eastwood had owned David Webb Peoples's script for fifteen years before he felt old enough to play William Munny. The film won four Oscars and was the third Western ever to win Best Picture.

question: Dances with Wolves, the Kevin Costner Western that won seven Academy Awards including Best Picture and Best Director, released in what year?
context: Costner directed Dances with Wolves with no prior directing experience. Industry insiders called it 'Kevin's Gate.' It made over 400 million worldwide and beat Goodfellas for Best Picture.

question: Young Guns — the brat-pack Western about Billy the Kid and the Lincoln County War, starring Emilio Estevez, Charlie Sheen, and Kiefer Sutherland — released in what year?
context: Young Guns made Bon Jovi's 'Blaze of Glory' soundtrack into a #1 hit for the 1990 sequel. The first film grossed over 45 million on a modest budget and reignited the late-80s Western.

question: Duck Tales, the Disney Afternoon cartoon featuring Scrooge McDuck and his nephews diving through a money bin, premiered in syndication in what year?
context: Duck Tales adapted Carl Barks's Donald Duck comics. Its theme song was so catchy that Mark Mothersbaugh later cited it as a high point of 80s TV theme writing. 100 episodes ran through 1990.

question: The Warner Bros. animated series Animaniacs, executive-produced by Steven Spielberg, premiered with the Warner siblings, Pinky and the Brain, and the Goodfeathers. In what year?
context: Animaniacs ran 99 episodes through 1998. Its writers slipped jokes past Standards & Practices for years — 'Fingerprints' and 'Hello Nurse' are referenced still. Pinky and the Brain got their own series in 1995.

question: Tiny Toon Adventures, the WB cartoon starring Buster, Babs, Plucky, and Hamton at Acme Looniversity, premiered in 1990 with Spielberg producing. What network first aired it?
answer: Syndication and Fox Kids
choices: Syndication and Fox Kids
Cartoon Network
Nickelodeon
ABC Saturday Morning
context: Tiny Toons aired first in syndication, then moved to Fox Kids. It led directly to Animaniacs and helped revive WB animation. Spielberg's deal with WB had been signed years earlier.

question: Rugrats, Nickelodeon's groundbreaking animated series about a band of toddlers, was produced by a Hungarian-Armenian American studio also responsible for The Simpsons' early seasons. Which studio?
answer: Klasky Csupo
choices: Klasky Csupo
Hanna-Barbera
Filmation
DiC Entertainment
context: Klasky Csupo also produced Aaahh!!! Real Monsters and the first three seasons of The Simpsons. Rugrats premiered in August 1991. Tommy Pickles is one year old in series — for all 172 episodes.

question: Disney's Darkwing Duck, the masked-mallard parody of pulp heroes — 'I am the terror that flaps in the night' — premiered as part of the Disney Afternoon. In what year?
context: Darkwing was originally pitched as a Duck Tales spinoff with Launchpad McQuack — who indeed became his sidekick. The show ran 91 episodes through 1992 between syndication and ABC Saturday morning.

question: The Ren & Stimpy Show, Nickelodeon's John Kricfalusi-created cartoon about a Chihuahua and a cat that broke every Saturday-morning rule, premiered in what year?
context: Ren & Stimpy premiered August 11, 1991, alongside Rugrats and Doug as Nick's first Nicktoons. Kricfalusi's micromanagement and missed deadlines led to his firing in 1992. The show kept going without him.

question: Disney's Gargoyles, the surprisingly dark afternoon cartoon about stone warriors guarding modern Manhattan, premiered in syndication in what year?
context: Gargoyles ran 78 episodes through 1997 — most as part of the Disney Afternoon. Greg Weisman's show featured Shakespeare quotes, Macbeth as an actual character, and Star Trek alumni in nearly every role.

question: Disney's TaleSpin, the air-pirate-adventure cartoon that re-imagined Jungle Book characters as 1930s aviators, premiered in syndication in what year?
context: TaleSpin aired 65 episodes as part of the original Disney Afternoon block. Baloo flew the Sea Duck for the air-freight company Higher for Hire, alongside Kit Cloudkicker and Rebecca Cunningham.

question: Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers, the Disney Afternoon cartoon that turned the chipmunks into pint-sized detectives with Gadget and Monterey Jack, premiered in what year?
context: Rescue Rangers' theme song became one of the most recognized 80s/90s TV themes. It ran 65 episodes through 1990 and was a Disney Afternoon flagship. A 2022 live-action film revived it.

question: Freakazoid!, the Warner Bros. cartoon about a teen turned into a manic superhero by a corrupted internet packet, was developed by Bruce Timm and Paul Dini and premiered in 1995. Which network ran it?
answer: Kids' WB
choices: Kids' WB
Fox Kids
Saturday CBS
Saturday ABC
context: Freakazoid! was originally planned as a Batman: TAS-style serious hero. Timm pitched a parody route instead. It ran 24 episodes on Kids' WB and earned a cult following on Cartoon Network.

question: Captain Planet and the Planeteers — an environmental superhero show with five teens whose rings (earth, fire, wind, water, heart) summoned a green-mulleted hero — premiered in what year?
context: Ted Turner funded Captain Planet personally. Whoopi Goldberg, LeVar Burton, and Meg Ryan voiced characters. Captain Planet himself was voiced by David Coburn. Six seasons aired through 1996.

question: Inspector Gadget, the cartoon about a bumbling cyborg detective whose niece Penny and dog Brain do the actual sleuthing, premiered in syndication in what year?
context: Inspector Gadget was animated by France's DiC studios. The villain Dr. Claw was never shown above the hands — only his gauntlet, his cat Madcat, and his menacing voice. The face was finally revealed in a 1999 live-action film.

question: Garfield's Halloween Adventure — the prime-time special where Garfield and Odie dress as pirates trick-or-treating — first aired on CBS in what year?
context: The special won an Emmy. Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield through 12 of these prime-time specials. The pirate ghosts haunting the old man's cabin gave nineties kids nightmares.

question: The Smurfs animated series, based on Peyo's Belgian comics, premiered on NBC Saturday morning in what year?
context: Hanna-Barbera produced The Smurfs from 1981 to 1989 — nine seasons, 256 episodes. Papa Smurf was voiced by Don Messick, who also did Scooby-Doo. The Smurfs originated in Belgium in 1958.

question: Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! — the original Hanna-Barbera mystery cartoon featuring Fred, Daphne, Velma, Shaggy, and a Great Dane — premiered on CBS Saturday morning in what year?
context: Scooby debuted September 13, 1969. The show was created in response to parental backlash against violent Saturday cartoons. The franchise has run almost continuously since — over 50 years.

question: The Flintstones, Hanna-Barbera's prime-time animated sitcom about a Stone Age family in Bedrock, premiered on ABC in what year?
context: The Flintstones was the first prime-time animated series with original content. It ran six seasons. Fred's voice (Alan Reed) and Barney's (Mel Blanc) became as recognizable as live-action TV stars.

question: The Simpsons, the Fox prime-time animated series originating as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show, debuted as its own half-hour series in what year?
context: Matt Groening pitched the family — names borrowed from his own — minutes before the Ullman meeting. The first half-hour 'Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire' aired December 17, 1989. The show is still running.

question: South Park, Trey Parker and Matt Stone's animated series about four foul-mouthed Colorado mountain-town kids, premiered on Comedy Central in what year?
context: The pilot 'Cartman Gets an Anal Probe' aired August 13, 1997. The show originated as a 1995 video Christmas card — Jesus vs. Santa — that Brian Graden circulated as a forwarded VHS.

question: The Muppet Show, Jim Henson's syndicated variety-show vehicle for Kermit, Miss Piggy, Fozzie, and Gonzo, premiered in what year?
context: Henson and his team produced The Muppet Show at ATV in England — no American network would touch it. Five seasons aired in syndication. The show won three Emmys and produced a still-massive theatrical career.

question: Sesame Street, the public-television show built around Children's Television Workshop research, premiered on PBS in what year?
context: Sesame Street debuted November 10, 1969. Joan Ganz Cooney founded the Workshop. The show's mix of street-level skits and Henson Muppets — Big Bird, Bert and Ernie, Cookie Monster — reshaped children's TV.

question: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, the gentle PBS show built around Fred Rogers's slow tempo and direct address, premiered nationally in what year?
context: Rogers had hosted regional versions since 1963. The national PBS premiere was February 19, 1968. The show ran through 2001 — nearly 900 episodes — and Rogers personally answered fan letters.

question: The Twilight Zone, Rod Serling's anthology series whose theme music is shorthand for the uncanny, first premiered on CBS in what year?
context: Serling created, wrote much of, and narrated the show. Five original seasons aired through 1964. 'To Serve Man,' 'Time Enough at Last,' and 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet' became cultural shorthand.

question: The Outer Limits, the 1960s anthology series often confused with The Twilight Zone but distinct in its sci-fi-monster focus, premiered on ABC in what year?
context: The Outer Limits opened with the iconic 'We will control the horizontal. We will control the vertical' narration. Two original seasons aired through 1965. Harlan Ellison's 'Demon with a Glass Hand' aired in season two.

question: Star Trek, Gene Roddenberry's space-Western about Captain Kirk's Enterprise crew, premiered on NBC in what year?
context: Star Trek debuted September 8, 1966. NBC nearly canceled it after season two; a write-in campaign saved it for one more year before cancellation. Reruns turned it into a juggernaut.

question: Star Trek: The Next Generation, the syndicated successor with Patrick Stewart as Captain Picard, premiered in what year?
context: TNG ran seven seasons through 1994. Paramount put it directly into syndication to bypass network notes. Rick Berman and Michael Piller took over from Roddenberry by season three.

question: Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the darker spinoff set on a Bajoran-Cardassian space station with Avery Brooks as Commander Sisko, premiered in what year?
context: DS9 ran seven seasons through 1999. Ronald D. Moore and Ira Steven Behr leaned into long-form serialized storytelling years before it was fashionable on broadcast TV.

question: Star Trek: First Contact, the second TNG-cast film and a fan favorite featuring the Borg invading Earth's past, released in what year?
context: Jonathan Frakes directed; Brent Spiner co-wrote. The film hit theaters November 1996 and remains the highest-grossing TNG-cast Star Trek film. Cameos by Star Wars actor James Cromwell as Zefram Cochrane.

question: Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, the second original-cast film and widely considered the best Star Trek film, released in what year?
context: Khan opened June 4, 1982. Director Nicholas Meyer reframed Trek as Horatio Hornblower in space — submarine warfare, naval lines of command. Ricardo Montalban returned from the 1967 TV episode 'Space Seed.'

question: The X-Files, the Fox conspiracy-procedural created by Chris Carter and starring David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson as FBI agents Mulder and Scully, premiered in what year?
context: The X-Files premiered September 10, 1993, with a Pacific Northwest pilot directed by Robert Mandel. It ran nine seasons through 2002, returned for two more in 2016-18, and turned 'I want to believe' into a poster.

question: Buffy the Vampire Slayer, the Joss Whedon series spun off from his 1992 film, premiered as a TV show on the WB in what year?
context: Buffy premiered March 10, 1997, on the WB. It moved to UPN in 2001 for its final two seasons. Sarah Michelle Gellar played Buffy across all 144 episodes — and Anthony Stewart Head played Giles.

question: Xena: Warrior Princess, the Lucy Lawless-led action series spun off from Hercules: The Legendary Journeys, premiered in syndication in what year?
context: Xena debuted September 4, 1995. The show ran six seasons and 134 episodes through 2001, shot in New Zealand by the production team that would later expand into Lord of the Rings.

question: Highlander, the Russell Mulcahy film about immortal sword-fighters with Christopher Lambert and Sean Connery and a Queen soundtrack, released in what year?
context: Highlander opened in March 1986. The Queen songs were written specifically for the film — 'Princes of the Universe,' 'Who Wants to Live Forever,' and 'A Kind of Magic' all appeared. The film spawned a TV series in 1992.

question: Labyrinth, the Jim Henson film starring David Bowie as the Goblin King and Jennifer Connelly as the teenager Sarah, released in what year?
context: Labyrinth came out June 1986 and tanked at the box office. Henson, devastated, did not direct another feature. The film grew into a midnight-movie staple — Bowie's 'Magic Dance' became eternal.

question: The Dark Crystal, Jim Henson and Frank Oz's animatronic fantasy with not a single human on screen, released in what year?
context: The Dark Crystal opened in December 1982. Brian Froud designed the creatures. The film's failure with audiences pushed Henson toward the gentler Labyrinth four years later.

question: Willow, the Ron Howard fantasy film produced by George Lucas with Warwick Davis as a Nelwyn farmer and Val Kilmer as the swordsman Madmartigan, released in what year?
context: Willow opened May 1988. Lucas conceived the story years earlier; the title character was named for Warwick Davis when Davis joined as the lead. James Horner scored. A Disney+ revival followed decades later.

question: The NeverEnding Story, the Wolfgang Petersen film adapting Michael Ende's German fantasy novel and featuring a luckdragon named Falkor, released in what year?
context: The NeverEnding Story was the most expensive non-American film of its time. Limahl's title track was a Top 10 hit worldwide. Ende hated the adaptation and tried to have his name removed from the credits.

question: Alien, Ridley Scott's space-haunted-house film about a Nostromo crew and a single xenomorph, released in what year?
context: Alien opened May 25, 1979. Sigourney Weaver was relatively unknown. H.R. Giger designed the creature; the chestburster scene was filmed in one take with the cast not fully briefed on what would happen.

question: John Carpenter's The Thing, his Antarctic-research-station body-horror remake starring Kurt Russell as helicopter pilot R.J. MacReady, released in what year?
context: The Thing opened June 25, 1982 — two weeks after E.T. It bombed in part because audiences wanted the warm alien, not the paranoid one. Critical reappraisal made it a horror canon staple.

question: Halloween, John Carpenter's slasher film featuring Michael Myers stalking Jamie Lee Curtis's Laurie Strode in Haddonfield, Illinois, released in what year?
context: Halloween opened October 25, 1978. Carpenter scored it himself on a tight schedule — the now-iconic 5/4 piano motif was written in three days. Made on a 300,000-dollar budget, it made 70 million.

question: The Evil Dead, Sam Raimi's debut film featuring Bruce Campbell as Ash fighting deadites in a Tennessee cabin, released theatrically in what year?
context: Raimi shot The Evil Dead in Tennessee on a low budget assembled from family and dentists' investments. Stephen King championed the film publicly, calling it the most ferociously original horror film of the year.

question: Evil Dead II, Sam Raimi's tone-shifting horror-comedy sequel with Bruce Campbell's Ash and the chainsaw hand, released in what year?
context: Evil Dead II opened March 13, 1987. Raimi treated it partly as a remake — the prologue recaps the first film in five minutes. The chainsaw-hand-and-boomstick combo became Ash's defining iconography.

question: Army of Darkness, Sam Raimi's third Ash film sending Bruce Campbell back to medieval times with a 1973 Oldsmobile, released in what year?
context: Army of Darkness opened February 19, 1993. Universal Studios cut Raimi's original ending and forced a happier one in for U.S. release. The director's cut restores Raimi's bleaker post-apocalyptic intent.

question: John Carpenter's They Live, the cult sci-fi film starring wrestler Roddy Piper as a drifter who finds sunglasses that reveal aliens posing as the wealthy elite, released in what year?
context: They Live opened November 4, 1988. Carpenter co-wrote it under the pen name Frank Armitage. The six-minute fight scene between Piper and Keith David was Piper's pro-wrestling choreography brought to film.

question: Big Trouble in Little China, John Carpenter's kung-fu fantasy film starring Kurt Russell as truck driver Jack Burton lost in Chinatown's hidden underworld, released in what year?
context: Big Trouble in Little China opened July 2, 1986 and tanked. Carpenter and Russell believed Fox marketed it as an action film when it was a screwball comedy. It became a cult favorite in the VHS years.

question: Rocky, the boxing film starring and written by Sylvester Stallone as a Philadelphia club fighter who gets a shot at the heavyweight title, released in what year?
context: Rocky opened November 21, 1976. Stallone wrote the script in three days and refused all offers unless he could star. The film won Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing.

question: Rocky IV, the Cold War-themed sequel pitting Stallone's Balboa against Dolph Lundgren's Ivan Drago, released in what year?
context: Rocky IV opened November 27, 1985 and was the highest-grossing sports film for decades. Apollo Creed's death in the ring set up Balboa's revenge match in Moscow on Christmas Day.

question: First Blood, the first Rambo film starring Stallone as a Vietnam vet pursued through Pacific Northwest woods by a small-town sheriff, released in what year?
context: First Blood opened October 22, 1982. Director Ted Kotcheff and Stallone reshaped David Morrell's 1972 novel into a kinder film — Rambo lives, where the novel kills him. The Rambo sequels followed in 1985 and 1988.

question: Rurouni Kenshin, the Meiji-era manga about a wandering swordsman with a reverse-edge blade trying to atone for his past as an assassin, was created by whom?
answer: Nobuhiro Watsuki
choices: Nobuhiro Watsuki
Kentaro Miura
Eiichiro Oda
Yasuhiro Nightow
context: Watsuki began Kenshin in 1994. The Kyoto arc — Shishio Makoto's coup — was animated faithfully in the 1996-99 anime. A 2012 live-action film starring Takeru Satoh kicked off a five-film series.

question: Koyoharu Gotouge's manga Demon Slayer began serialization in Weekly Shonen Jump in what year?
context: Demon Slayer ran from February 2016 to May 2020 in Jump — 205 chapters. The 2019 anime by Ufotable made it a phenomenon. Gotouge retired from serial manga right after the series concluded.

question: Studio Ghibli's Grave of the Fireflies — released double-billed with My Neighbor Totoro in 1988 — was directed not by Miyazaki but by Ghibli's other co-founder. Who?
answer: Isao Takahata
choices: Isao Takahata
Hayao Miyazaki
Yoshifumi Kondo
Goro Miyazaki
context: Takahata adapted Akiyuki Nosaka's 1967 semi-autobiographical novel. The film was offered to schools paired with Totoro and devastated audiences. Takahata died in 2018.

question: Hideaki Anno's anime Neon Genesis Evangelion premiered on Japanese television in what year?
context: NGE premiered October 4, 1995, on TV Tokyo. The original 26-episode run ended with two famously experimental final episodes. The 1997 theatrical film End of Evangelion gave the finale a different form.

question: Akira director Katsuhiro Otomo serialized the manga in Young Magazine for nearly a decade before completing the 1988 film. In what year did he begin the Akira manga?
context: Otomo began the Akira manga in December 1982. He concluded it in June 1990 — two years after the film. The manga and film diverge significantly past the halfway point.

question: Nobuhiro Watsuki's manga Rurouni Kenshin is set during a specific era of Japanese history — the period of rapid Westernization after the Tokugawa shogunate fell. What era?
answer: Meiji era
choices: Meiji era
Edo era
Heian era
Taisho era
context: The Meiji Restoration began in 1868. Kenshin is set roughly a decade later. Kenshin himself is a former Bakumatsu assassin trying to atone in peacetime. The Kyoto arc focuses on enemies from his old life.

question: Dragon Ball, the 1984 manga that became the Dragon Ball Z anime juggernaut, was created by an artist whose style would influence a generation of mangaka. Who?
answer: Akira Toriyama
choices: Akira Toriyama
Yoshihiro Togashi
Hirohiko Araki
Hiromu Arakawa
context: Toriyama loosely adapted the Chinese classic Journey to the West for Dragon Ball's opening arc. Goku began as a tail-wagging boy with a magic staff. Toriyama died in March 2024.

question: Dragon Ball Z, the anime adaptation that adapted the Saiyan, Namek, Cell, and Buu sagas, first aired on Japanese TV in what year?
context: DBZ premiered April 26, 1989, on Fuji TV — 291 episodes through 1996. Funimation's dubbed version with Sean Schemmel as Goku reached U.S. cable in the late 1990s.

question: Hunter x Hunter, the 1998 manga famous as much for its hiatuses as its plotting, was created by a mangaka also responsible for Yu Yu Hakusho. Who?
answer: Yoshihiro Togashi
choices: Yoshihiro Togashi
Eiichiro Oda
Tite Kubo
Hirohiko Araki
context: Togashi's chronic back problems and high standards led to hiatuses lasting years. The 2011 Madhouse anime adaptation animated most of the major arcs. He is married to Sailor Moon creator Naoko Takeuchi.

question: Yu Yu Hakusho, the 1990 manga about a delinquent named Yusuke Urameshi who becomes a Spirit Detective, was created by whom?
answer: Yoshihiro Togashi
choices: Yoshihiro Togashi
Akira Toriyama
Masashi Kishimoto
Hirohiko Araki
context: Togashi began Yu Yu Hakusho the same year he married Naoko Takeuchi. The Dark Tournament arc is widely cited as one of the genre's high points. The anime ran 1992-94 in Japan.

question: Captain N: The Game Master, the NBC Saturday-morning cartoon starring a teen pulled into a video-game world to lead Mega Man, Simon Belmont, and Pit, premiered in what year?
context: Captain N premiered September 9, 1989. Kevin Keene piloted a Zapper light gun and wore a NES controller as a belt buckle. Three seasons aired through 1991. Nintendo Power magazine published companion comics.

question: WarGames, the John Badham film starring Matthew Broderick as a teenager who hacks a military supercomputer thinking it's a game, released in what year?
context: WarGames opened June 3, 1983. The WOPR supercomputer's question 'Shall we play a game?' joined the cultural lexicon. The film helped shape U.S. computer-security legislation in the late 1980s.

question: The Wizard, the Universal film starring Fred Savage and produced as essentially a feature-length Nintendo commercial — including the on-screen reveal of Super Mario Bros. 3 — released in what year?
context: The Wizard opened December 15, 1989. Power Glove sales briefly spiked despite the device's notorious uselessness. The film's Mario 3 unveiling was timed weeks before the game's North American launch.

question: Ready Player One, the 2018 film adapting Ernest Cline's 2011 novel about a teenager hunting Easter eggs in a 1980s-pop-culture virtual world, was directed by whom?
answer: Steven Spielberg
choices: Steven Spielberg
Robert Zemeckis
J.J. Abrams
Joe Cornish
context: Spielberg directed despite many of the novel's references being to his own films. Several Spielberg-specific bits — Back to the Future's DeLorean prominent, the Shining hotel — appeared in the film.

question: Stranger Things, the Netflix series steeped in 1980s pop culture with a band of kids in Hawkins, Indiana investigating a parallel dimension, premiered in what year?
context: Stranger Things premiered July 15, 2016. The Duffer Brothers initially pitched it as a feature film. Its first season's marketing leaned heavily on Stephen King and Spielberg comparisons.

question: Wreck-It Ralph, the Disney animated film starring an arcade-game villain who longs to be a hero and cameos by Bowser, M. Bison, and other classic-game characters, released in what year?
context: Wreck-It Ralph opened November 2, 2012, with John C. Reilly voicing Ralph and Sarah Silverman as Vanellope. Director Rich Moore pulled cameos from Capcom, Sega, and Nintendo through painstaking licensing.

question: The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters, the documentary about Steve Wiebe's pursuit of the Donkey Kong record held by Billy Mitchell, released in what year?
context: The King of Kong was directed by Seth Gordon. The film made Twin Galaxies' Walter Day and the rivalry between Mitchell and Wiebe famous beyond the arcade-record-keeping subculture.

question: The Last Starfighter, the 1984 sci-fi film about a teenager recruited by aliens to fight an interstellar war after mastering an arcade game in his trailer-park courtyard, released in what year?
context: The Last Starfighter pioneered photorealistic CG spaceships years before Toy Story. The arcade cabinet itself — built only as a prop — has been replicated by fans seeking to play it.

question: Tron, Disney's 1982 sci-fi film about a programmer sucked into a digital world by a corporate AI, released in what year?
context: Tron opened July 9, 1982. Steven Lisberger directed; Jeff Bridges starred as Kevin Flynn. Disney built the film as a showcase for early computer graphics. Years later it became foundational to digital-aesthetic cyberpunk.

question: The Matrix, the Wachowski sci-fi film starring Keanu Reeves as a hacker who learns reality is a simulation, released in what year?
context: The Matrix opened March 31, 1999. Bullet-time was a custom rig of 122 still cameras. The film famously cited Ghost in the Shell, Plato's allegory of the cave, and Lewis Carroll as direct inspirations.

question: Pac-Man, the Namco arcade game whose iconic yellow circle eats dots and ghosts, was designed in Japan by Toru Iwatani. In what year did it release?
context: Pac-Man hit Japanese arcades May 22, 1980. Iwatani designed it to attract women players to the male-dominated arcade. The pizza-with-a-slice-missing origin story was Iwatani's own anecdote.

question: Pac-Man's creator was a Namco designer who said he was inspired by a pizza with a slice missing. Who was he?
answer: Toru Iwatani
choices: Toru Iwatani
Shigeru Miyamoto
Hideo Kojima
Yu Suzuki
context: Iwatani also designed Libble Rabble. He never received royalties — Japanese company policy of the time. Namco gave him an internal-promotion bonus and a desk.

question: Donkey Kong, the Nintendo arcade game that introduced Mario (as Jumpman) climbing girders to save a girl from an ape, released in what year?
context: Donkey Kong released July 1981. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto sketched the levels by hand. Nintendo had unsold Radar Scope cabinets in the U.S.; converting them to Donkey Kong saved the company's American operation.

question: Donkey Kong was designed by Nintendo's then-young artist who would go on to create The Legend of Zelda and Super Mario Bros. Who?
answer: Shigeru Miyamoto
choices: Shigeru Miyamoto
Gunpei Yokoi
Satoru Iwata
Hiroshi Yamauchi
context: Miyamoto was an industrial designer Yamauchi hired without much technical background. Donkey Kong was his first leading game design. He had to teach himself enough programming to communicate with engineers.

question: Galaga, the Namco arcade shooter whose Boss Galaga ships abduct your fighter and create dual-fighter combo runs, released in what year?
context: Galaga released September 1981, succeeding Galaxian (1979) and Moon Cresta. The 'shoot the captured ship to free your fighter and combine' mechanic became one of the most copied in arcade history.

question: Asteroids, the Atari vector-graphics arcade game where a triangular ship shoots increasingly small space rocks, released in what year?
context: Asteroids released November 1979. Designed by Lyle Rains and Ed Logg. Players abused the difficulty curve by 'lurking' — staying in one safe spot and picking off UFOs forever. Atari patched it later.

question: Defender, the Williams Electronics arcade game by Eugene Jarvis featuring a side-scrolling planet with humanoids to rescue and aliens to shoot, released in what year?
context: Defender released February 1981. Its complex controls — joystick plus five buttons — were notorious. The game grossed over a billion dollars in quarters. Jarvis went on to design Robotron 2084.

question: Robotron: 2084, the Eugene Jarvis arcade game with twin-stick controls and waves of robotic enemies, released in what year?
context: Robotron premiered April 1982. The twin-stick scheme — left stick to move, right stick to shoot — became a standard. Jarvis credits a car accident layoff with giving him time to design it.

question: Centipede, the Atari arcade game where a player at the bottom shoots a descending centipede through a mushroom field, was co-designed by one of the first women credited on a major arcade game. Who was she?
answer: Dona Bailey
choices: Dona Bailey
Carol Shaw
Roberta Williams
Sierra Adams
context: Bailey co-designed Centipede with Ed Logg at Atari and led the development team. The trackball control was unusual for 1981; the game's bright color palette was deliberately marketed at women players.

question: Joust, the Williams arcade game where players ride mounted-bird warriors and joust by flapping into enemies, released in what year?
context: Joust released July 1982. Designed by John Newcomer. The cooperative-or-competitive two-player mode was unusual — players could choose to help or hurt each other in real time, decades before that became standard.

question: Q*bert, the Gottlieb arcade game featuring an orange creature hopping across an isometric pyramid while swearing in a speech bubble, released in what year?
context: Q*bert released October 1982. Designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee. The 'curse word' bubble was a placeholder for synthesized speech — they kept it. The game spawned cereals, lunchboxes, and a Saturday morning cartoon.

question: Dig Dug, the Namco arcade game where the player digs underground tunnels and pumps up monsters until they explode, released in what year?
context: Dig Dug released March 1982. Designed by Masahisa Ikegami. The two enemies — Pookas and Fygars — became fixtures of Namco's character roster, reappearing in Pac-Land and Mr. Driller decades later.

question: Frogger, the Konami arcade game requiring a player to hop a frog across a busy road and river to safety, released in what year?
context: Frogger released October 1981. Konami licensed it widely; Sega and Atari distributed versions worldwide. The game's premise was simple, but its 'cars then logs then turtles' difficulty curve became a teaching example.

question: Space Invaders, the Taito arcade game that allegedly caused a coin shortage in Japan when it launched, released in what year?
context: Space Invaders released July 1978. Designed by Tomohiro Nishikado. The Japanese 100-yen coin shortage was likely apocryphal — but real revenue records confirm the game's massive cultural impact.

question: Street Fighter II, the Capcom arcade fighting game that revolutionized the genre with eight selectable world warriors, released in what year?
context: Street Fighter II released February 1991. Designed by Akira Nishitani and Akira Yasuda. The game's success singlehandedly revived arcades in the early 1990s. Capcom updated and re-released it for over a decade.

question: Mortal Kombat, the Midway arcade fighting game famous for digitized actors and fatalities, released in what year?
context: Mortal Kombat released October 1992. Designed by Ed Boon and John Tobias. The game's graphic violence drove the formation of the ESRB rating system in 1994 — directly leading to today's M-for-Mature ratings.

question: NBA Jam, the Midway arcade basketball game by Mark Turmell that introduced 'BOOMSHAKALAKA' and 'HE'S ON FIRE' to the lexicon, released in what year?
context: NBA Jam released April 1993. The game's two-on-two fast-arcade style departed from realistic basketball games. Tim Kitzrow's announcer voice became iconic — kids quoted his lines decades later.

question: OutRun, the Sega arcade racing game by Yu Suzuki featuring a Ferrari Testarossa, branching paths, and a tropical synthwave soundtrack, released in what year?
context: OutRun released September 1986. The deluxe cabinet hydraulically tilted in response to corners. Yu Suzuki took a European road trip for inspiration; the game's pastel-coastal aesthetic prefigured the entire vaporwave movement.

question: After Burner, the Sega arcade flight game by Yu Suzuki featuring an F-14 Tomcat in a roll-cage motion cabinet, released in what year?
context: After Burner released July 1987. Suzuki designed the cabinet to physically rotate with the on-screen plane. The deluxe version sold for over $10,000 each — operators recouped costs through massive arcade revenue.

question: Killer Instinct, the Rare-developed Midway arcade fighting game famous for its 'C-C-C-COMBO BREAKER!' announcer and chained Ultra Combos, released in what year?
context: Killer Instinct released October 1994. Rare's pre-rendered 3D fighter sprites were generated by Silicon Graphics workstations. The home SNES version came on a special expanded ROM cartridge.

question: Tekken, the Namco arcade fighting game that competed with Virtua Fighter as one of the first true 3D fighters, released in what year?
context: Tekken released December 1994. Designed by Seiichi Ishii, who had previously worked on Virtua Fighter at Sega. Tekken's unique button layout (one button per limb) distinguished it from Capcom's six-button style.

question: Virtua Fighter, the Sega arcade game widely credited as the first true 3D polygonal fighting game, was designed by Yu Suzuki and released in what year?
context: Virtua Fighter released October 1993, on Sega's Model 1 board. The game's flat-shaded polygons looked crude even at launch — but the fluid martial-arts animation and depth-aware combat opened a new genre.

question: Dance Dance Revolution, the Konami rhythm-arcade game requiring players to step on a directional pad in time with music, released in Japanese arcades in what year?
context: DDR premiered November 1998. The Konami Bemani division also developed Beatmania and DrumMania. DDR became a global gym-and-arcade phenomenon; the U.S. version launched in 1999.

question: The House of the Dead, the Sega light-gun arcade game pitting players against zombie hordes with a 9mm pistol controller, released in what year?
context: The House of the Dead released March 1996. Sega's AM1 division designed it. The B-movie acting and chunky polygons aged into camp; the franchise spawned a 2003 Uwe Boll film widely regarded as among the worst ever made.

question: Crazy Taxi, the Sega arcade driving game ported as a Dreamcast launch title, putting players behind the wheel of a taxi grabbing fares in time-limited city sprints, released in arcades in what year?
context: Crazy Taxi released January 1999 in arcades. The licensed Offspring and Bad Religion soundtrack helped sell the Dreamcast port. A long-running lawsuit over its core mechanic was eventually dismissed.

question: The Atari 2600, the home console with the woodgrain plastic case and cartridge slots — the dominant home gaming hardware of the late 1970s — first released in what year?
context: The Atari 2600 (originally the Atari VCS) launched September 1977. It dominated the home market for years and helped trigger — then helped recover from — the 1983 video game crash through its E.T. fiasco.

question: Atari's commercial failure E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) for the 2600 was the most infamous bad-game story until its mythical fate was confirmed in 2014. What happened to the unsold cartridges?
answer: Buried in a New Mexico landfill
choices: Buried in a New Mexico landfill
Melted down at a Texas plant
Returned to Spielberg's company
Stored in an Arizona warehouse
context: Atari trucked unsold E.T. cartridges to the Alamogordo landfill in 1983. A 2014 dig confirmed the urban legend — diggers actually found the cartridges. The film Atari: Game Over documents the excavation.

question: The North American video game crash, when retailers abandoned cartridge sales, Atari and Coleco lost massive revenue, and the home market collapsed before Nintendo revived it, occurred in what year?
context: The crash bottomed in 1983-84. U.S. game industry revenue fell from 3 billion to 100 million within two years. Nintendo's NES launch in 1985 used the term 'Entertainment System' specifically to avoid retailer skittishness about 'video games.'

question: The Nintendo Entertainment System launched in the United States with Super Mario Bros. as its pack-in title in what year?
context: Nintendo launched the NES in New York and Los Angeles in October 1985, then nationwide in 1986. The console was sold as a 'toy' (with R.O.B. the robot) to dodge the post-crash retailer freeze on video games.

question: Nintendo's Famicom, the Japanese predecessor to the NES, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The Famicom (Family Computer) launched July 15, 1983 in Japan. Early hardware issues forced Nintendo to recall and replace defective units. Donkey Kong was a launch title.

question: Super Mario Bros., the Shigeru Miyamoto Famicom and NES game that defined the platform-genre, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Mario Bros. released September 13, 1985 in Japan, October 1985 in North America. Sold over 40 million copies. The game's world 1-1 has been studied as an example of unspoken design teaching.

question: Super Mario World, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System launch title that introduced Yoshi as a rideable companion, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Mario World released November 21, 1990 in Japan, August 1991 in North America. Miyamoto and team had wanted Yoshi to appear in earlier Mario games — the SNES was the first hardware able to handle him.

question: Super Mario 64, the Nintendo 64 launch title that established conventions of 3D platforming and camera control, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Mario 64 released June 23, 1996. Miyamoto and his team built the open-world Peach's Castle hub specifically to teach players to control a 3D character — a problem no one had solved before.

question: The Legend of Zelda, Shigeru Miyamoto's open-overworld dungeon adventure that introduced Link, Princess Zelda, and Hyrule, released in Japan in what year?
context: The Legend of Zelda released February 21, 1986 in Japan on the Famicom Disk System, August 1987 in North America. The gold-plated cartridge case became iconic. The series has sold over 150 million copies.

question: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, the Super Nintendo entry widely considered one of the best games ever made, released in Japan in what year?
context: A Link to the Past released November 21, 1991. Miyamoto's team returned to top-down 2D after the side-scrolling Zelda II experiment. The Light World / Dark World mechanic established a template Zelda would use for decades.

question: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the Nintendo 64 entry that established 3D action-adventure conventions, released in what year?
context: Ocarina of Time released November 21, 1998 in Japan, days later worldwide. Z-targeting reshaped 3D combat across the industry. Reviewers gave the game perfect scores nearly universally — Nintendo's gold standard.

question: Metroid, the Famicom and NES game that introduced Samus Aran's mission to Planet Zebes — and whose ending famously revealed something about its protagonist — released in Japan in what year?
context: Metroid released August 6, 1986 in Japan on the Famicom Disk System. Yoshio Sakamoto and Gunpei Yokoi designed it. The interlinked map encouraged exploration in a way few platformers had attempted before.

question: Super Metroid, the Super Nintendo follow-up considered by many fans the best in the series, released in what year?
context: Super Metroid released March 19, 1994 in Japan. The game's 'show, don't tell' design — animals teaching shinespark techniques, environments hinting at progression — became a touchstone for the 'metroidvania' genre.

question: Final Fantasy VII, Square's PlayStation breakthrough that brought JRPGs to mass Western audiences with prerendered 3D backgrounds and a controversial mid-game moment, released in Japan in what year?
context: Final Fantasy VII released January 31, 1997 in Japan. The North American release was September 7. Tetsuya Nomura designed the characters; Nobuo Uematsu scored. Sales over 14 million.

question: Chrono Trigger, the Super Nintendo RPG produced by a 'dream team' of Square's veterans plus Dragon Ball's Akira Toriyama doing character art, released in Japan in what year?
context: Chrono Trigger released March 11, 1995. Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest), and Toriyama led the team. Yasunori Mitsuda scored — his work on this game launched his career.

question: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid, the PlayStation game that took the stealth-action genre mainstream with cinematic cutscenes and Snake's mission to Shadow Moses, released in Japan in what year?
context: Metal Gear Solid released September 3, 1998 in Japan. Kojima had been making Metal Gear games since 1987; MGS was the first 3D entry. The Psycho Mantis fight remains one of gaming's most famous fourth-wall moments.

question: Resident Evil, the Capcom survival-horror PlayStation game by Shinji Mikami that introduced fixed-camera mansion exploration and limited inventory survival, released in Japan in what year?
context: Resident Evil released March 22, 1996 in Japan. The Japanese title 'Biohazard' was changed to avoid a trademark conflict with a New York band. The Western voice acting became infamously memed for decades.

question: Resident Evil 4, the Shinji Mikami GameCube entry that revolutionized over-the-shoulder shooter cameras and inspired Gears of War, released in what year?
context: Resident Evil 4 released January 11, 2005 on GameCube. Mikami went through multiple cancelled prototypes before settling on the village setting. The Ada Wong sequence was added late and recycled across releases.

question: Silent Hill, the Konami PlayStation psychological-horror game by Team Silent featuring foggy-town exploration and a guitar-and-pipe-clanging Akira Yamaoka score, released in what year?
context: Silent Hill released February 23, 1999 in Japan. Team Silent — Konami's internal Tokyo studio — designed the fog initially to mask the PS1's draw distance, then made it a defining aesthetic.

question: GoldenEye 007, the Rare-developed Nintendo 64 first-person shooter that defined console multiplayer with split-screen Stack and Complex matches, released in what year?
context: GoldenEye released August 1997. Designed by Martin Hollis and Karl Hilton. Originally an on-rails shooter, the team shifted to free-roaming FPS late in development. The pause-buffer-throwing-grenades trick was a multiplayer staple.

question: Super Smash Bros., the Nintendo 64 four-player fighting game by Masahiro Sakurai mixing Nintendo characters into a free-for-all platform brawl, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Smash Bros. released January 21, 1999 in Japan. Sakurai pitched it as 'Dragon King: The Fighting Game' before Nintendo licensed its mascots. Pikachu, Mario, Link, and Kirby joined the original 12-fighter roster.

question: Super Smash Bros. Melee, the GameCube sequel that became the dominant competitive Smash title with twenty-plus years of professional play, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Smash Bros. Melee released November 21, 2001 in Japan. Sakurai had only 13 months to develop it. The team worked through holidays. Competitive techniques like wavedashing emerged from unintended physics.

question: Pocket Monsters Red and Green — the original Game Boy releases that launched the Pokemon phenomenon — released in Japan in what year?
context: Red and Green released February 27, 1996 in Japan. The Western Red and Blue release adapted Green's roster. Satoshi Tajiri and Game Freak developed the games over six years. Ken Sugimori did the original character art.

question: Pokemon Red and Blue, the Western Game Boy release that launched Pokemon outside Japan with Pikachu's English-language anime, released in North America in what year?
context: Pokemon Red and Blue released September 28, 1998 in North America. Nintendo of America's launch marketing made Pikachu the franchise face; the anime had been dubbed earlier in 1998 to prime the U.S. market.

question: Pokemon Gold and Silver, the Game Boy Color sequels that introduced the Johto region, day/night cycles, and breeding, released in Japan in what year?
context: Gold and Silver released November 21, 1999 in Japan. The games included a complete return trip to the original Kanto region in their endgame — a feat of cartridge engineering Game Freak said they'd never repeat.

question: Crash Bandicoot, the orange-marsupial PlayStation platformer by Naughty Dog that became Sony's unofficial mascot, released in North America in what year?
context: Crash Bandicoot released September 9, 1996. Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin designed Naughty Dog's hit at a time when 3D platforming was still wide open. Crash's 'wumpa fruit' chase scenes were a technical showpiece.

question: Spyro the Dragon, the Insomniac Games PlayStation platformer about a small purple dragon, released in what year?
context: Spyro the Dragon released September 9, 1998 in North America. Stewart Copeland of The Police scored the soundtrack — an unusual choice for a platformer. Insomniac would later pivot to Ratchet & Clank.

question: Tomb Raider, the Core Design game that put Lara Croft in jungles, ancient ruins, and a baseline of player-character iconography, released in what year?
context: Tomb Raider released October 25, 1996 on Saturn, PlayStation, and PC. Toby Gard designed Lara. Despite the iconic polygonal form, original animation came from a single dedicated animator — Heather Gibson.

question: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, the Neversoft skateboarding game whose punk-and-ska soundtrack became as iconic as its mechanics, released in what year?
context: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater released August 1999. The Goldfinger 'Superman' track became the franchise anthem. Hawk himself landed the 900 on July 27, 1999 — weeks before the game shipped.

question: Gran Turismo, the Polyphony Digital PlayStation racing simulator by Kazunori Yamauchi setting a new bar for car physics and licensed vehicles, released in Japan in what year?
context: Gran Turismo released December 23, 1997 in Japan. Yamauchi's team licensed over 100 cars. The game sold 10.85 million copies — the best-selling PlayStation 1 game of all time.

question: Castlevania, the Konami platformer about Simon Belmont entering Dracula's castle with a whip and sub-weapons, released in Japan in what year?
context: Castlevania released September 26, 1986 on the Famicom Disk System. Hitoshi Akamatsu directed. The game's gothic horror tone and orchestral 8-bit soundtrack established a franchise still active today.

question: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, the Koji Igarashi PlayStation entry that inverted the castle, introduced exploration progression, and gave the genre its name 'metroidvania,' released in what year?
context: Symphony of the Night released March 20, 1997 in Japan, October 1997 in North America. Igarashi's design rebooted Castlevania's structure. Michiru Yamane's soundtrack became one of gaming's most celebrated.

question: Mega Man, the Capcom NES game where the blue robot defeats six 'Robot Master' bosses (and gains their weapons), released in Japan in what year?
context: Mega Man released December 17, 1987 in Japan. Designed by Akira Kitamura. The 'rock paper scissors' weapon-vulnerability system became a series staple. Sales were modest; Mega Man 2 (1988) was the franchise breakout.

question: Mega Man 2, widely considered the franchise's pinnacle and home of 'Dr. Wily's Castle Stage 1' — one of the most-covered videogame compositions ever — released in Japan in what year?
context: Mega Man 2 released December 24, 1988 in Japan. Capcom let the small team produce it on their own time after the first game underperformed. Sales over 1.5 million on NES.

question: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!, the Nintendo NES boxing game with sprite-based opponents and a pattern-recognition combat system, released in North America in what year?
context: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! released October 1987. Tyson's licensing deal expired in 1990; later prints replaced him with the fictional Mr. Dream. Glass Joe — the perpetually weeping French boxer — was the first opponent.

question: Shadow of the Colossus, the Fumito Ueda PlayStation 2 game where a lone wanderer fights only sixteen massive bosses in a vast empty landscape, released in what year?
context: Shadow of the Colossus released October 18, 2005 in Japan. The minimalist storytelling and the lack of conventional combat-tutorial enemies set it apart. Ueda's prior game Ico (2001) shared the design lineage.

question: God of War, the Santa Monica Studios PS2 game starring Kratos in a brutal Greek-mythology revenge story, released in what year?
context: God of War released March 22, 2005. David Jaffe directed. The game's Quick Time Event finishers became a console-action staple. Sales exceeded 4.6 million on PS2 alone.

question: Kingdom Hearts, the Square-Disney crossover PS2 RPG mixing Final Fantasy characters with Disney heroes, released in Japan in what year?
context: Kingdom Hearts released March 28, 2002 in Japan. Tetsuya Nomura directed; the deal between Square and Disney reportedly happened in an elevator. Sora's spiky hair and chunky shoes became as iconic as any Square hero's.

question: Dragon Quest, the Yuji Horii Enix RPG that established many JRPG conventions and dominated Japanese sales for years, released on the Famicom in what year?
context: Dragon Quest released May 27, 1986 in Japan. Horii designed; Akira Toriyama did character art. The series's later releases were so culturally important Japan reportedly banned weekday launches to prevent students cutting class.

question: Phantasy Star, the Sega Master System RPG by Yuji Naka featuring first-person dungeons and a female protagonist Alis Landale, released in Japan in what year?
context: Phantasy Star released December 20, 1987 in Japan on the Master System. The game's first-person 3D dungeons were technically ambitious for the hardware. Naka would later create Sonic the Hedgehog.

question: Shenmue, the Yu Suzuki Dreamcast adventure famous for being the most expensive game ever made at its time and for inventing 'Quick Time Events,' released in Japan in what year?
context: Shenmue released December 29, 1999 in Japan. Yu Suzuki spent over 47 million dollars producing it. The detailed city of Yokosuka and full day-night NPC schedules were unprecedented in 1999.

question: Sonic the Hedgehog, the Sega Genesis game by Yuji Naka and Naoto Ohshima that gave Sega its mascot answer to Mario, released in what year?
context: Sonic the Hedgehog released June 23, 1991 in North America. Sega briefly pack-in-bundled Sonic with new Genesis consoles to drive hardware sales — a move that helped Sega dominate the early 1990s console war.

question: Sonic the Hedgehog 2, introducing Miles 'Tails' Prower as a sidekick and the Spin Dash mechanic, released in what year?
context: Sonic 2 released November 21, 1992. Sega coordinated worldwide launches the same day — 'Sonic 2sday' was one of the first international synchronized game releases.

question: Streets of Rage 2, the Sega Genesis beat-em-up with Yuzo Koshiro's still-celebrated dance-rock soundtrack, released in what year?
context: Streets of Rage 2 released December 20, 1992 in Japan. Koshiro's soundtrack — composed on a Commodore Amiga — anticipated jungle and drum-and-bass music years before those genres mainstreamed.

question: Golden Axe, the Sega arcade and Genesis beat-em-up featuring three warriors (a barbarian, a dwarf, and an Amazon) battling a giant skeleton sorcerer, released in what year?
context: Golden Axe released June 1989 in arcades. Designed by Makoto Uchida, who had previously made Altered Beast. The 'Rise from your grave' line of Altered Beast was the franchise's most-quoted moment.

question: Earthworm Jim, the Doug TenNapel-created Sega Genesis and SNES platformer about a worm in a robot suit, released in what year?
context: Earthworm Jim released October 1994. TenNapel's animation studio Shiny Entertainment built it. The Saturday-morning cartoon adaptation followed in 1995, but the game was the franchise's high point.

question: The Sony PlayStation, the CD-based console that displaced Nintendo as Japan's market leader and gave us Final Fantasy VII, Metal Gear Solid, and Crash Bandicoot, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The PlayStation launched December 3, 1994 in Japan, September 1995 in North America. Sony had been jilted by Nintendo on a CD add-on partnership. Their pivot to standalone console reshaped the entire industry.

question: The Sega Saturn, the 32-bit Sega console with a famously disastrous American launch ('Surprise! It's on sale now'), launched in Japan in what year?
context: The Saturn launched November 22, 1994 in Japan. The Western launch four months early caught retailers off-guard. The hardware's dual-CPU design made development notoriously difficult; Sega's market share collapsed.

question: The Sega Dreamcast, Sega's final console launch and home to Crazy Taxi, Shenmue, Jet Set Radio, and Phantasy Star Online, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The Dreamcast launched November 27, 1998 in Japan, September 9, 1999 in North America (9-9-99). Despite a strong launch, internal Sega politics and PlayStation 2 anticipation killed the console by 2001.

question: The Nintendo Game Boy, the Gunpei Yokoi-designed handheld with a green-tinted LCD and Tetris pack-in, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The Game Boy launched April 21, 1989 in Japan, August 1989 in North America. Tetris drove sales among adults. Yokoi's 'lateral thinking with seasoned technology' philosophy chose battery life over color.

question: The Game Boy Color, Nintendo's belated color upgrade to the original Game Boy and home of Pokemon Gold and Silver, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The Game Boy Color launched October 21, 1998 in Japan. It was backward-compatible with all original Game Boy games — recoloring them on the fly using a palette. The hardware bridged Game Boy and Game Boy Advance.

question: The Nintendo 64, Nintendo's third home console and home to Super Mario 64, GoldenEye, and Ocarina of Time, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The N64 launched June 23, 1996 in Japan, September 29, 1996 in North America. Nintendo stayed with cartridges over CDs, which capped game sizes but kept load times short. Sony's PlayStation eventually outsold it three-to-one.

question: The Nintendo Wii, the motion-control console that brought casual players into gaming with bowling, tennis, and golf in a single pack-in title, launched in North America in what year?
context: The Wii launched November 19, 2006 in North America. Wii Sports — packaged with the console in most markets — became the best-selling video game of all time at over 80 million units sold.

question: Microsoft's original Xbox console, home of Halo: Combat Evolved and arrival of the 'Xbox Live' online service, launched in North America in what year?
context: The Xbox launched November 15, 2001 in North America. Bill Gates pitched it as the box that would dominate the living room. Halo, originally a Bungie Mac game, became the launch killer app.

question: Halo: Combat Evolved, the Bungie first-person shooter that defined the Xbox launch and built Master Chief into Microsoft's premier mascot, released in what year?
context: Halo launched November 15, 2001 alongside the Xbox. Originally a Mac strategy game, then a third-person shooter, then a first-person shooter — Bungie's design pivoted under Microsoft's acquisition.

question: Halo 2, the Bungie sequel that established Xbox Live multiplayer as the standard for console online play, released in what year?
context: Halo 2 launched November 9, 2004 — the largest entertainment launch of the year. Its online matchmaking and party system became templates the industry copied. Bungie crunched brutally to finish it.

question: Sony's PlayStation Portable, the company's first handheld and the first portable system to play UMD movie discs, launched in Japan in what year?
context: The PSP launched December 12, 2004 in Japan, March 2005 in North America. The UMD movie format failed commercially. Modders cracked PSP firmware almost immediately, opening homebrew on a level the DS never matched.

question: Nintendo's DS handheld, the dual-screened touch-and-stylus device that sold over 150 million units worldwide, launched in North America in what year?
context: The DS launched November 21, 2004 in North America. Nintendo positioned it as an experimental third pillar alongside the Game Boy line. Brain Age, Nintendogs, and a strong RPG library drove sales.

question: The Final Fantasy series's main theme, crystal theme, and 'One-Winged Angel' (the FF7 finale music) were all composed by Square's longtime musical director. Who?
answer: Nobuo Uematsu
choices: Nobuo Uematsu
Yasunori Mitsuda
Koji Kondo
Akira Yamaoka
context: Uematsu scored every mainline Final Fantasy from I (1987) to X (2001) plus much of XII (2006). 'One-Winged Angel' was the first JRPG track to use Latin-text choir vocals.

question: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night's celebrated soundtrack — fusion of gothic organ, jazz piano, and Bach motifs — was composed by a Konami veteran who would score Castlevania entries for two decades. Who?
answer: Michiru Yamane
choices: Michiru Yamane
Akira Yamaoka
Yuzo Koshiro
Motoi Sakuraba
context: Yamane joined Konami in 1988 and scored fourteen Castlevania titles. Her Symphony of the Night soundtrack borrows heavily from baroque counterpoint — Bach by way of Castlevania.

question: Silent Hill 1 through 4's distinctive industrial-and-acoustic-guitar soundtracks were all composed by one Konami sound designer with a love of trip-hop and reverb. Who?
answer: Akira Yamaoka
choices: Akira Yamaoka
Michiru Yamane
Yuzo Koshiro
Yasunori Mitsuda
context: Yamaoka had freedom rare for a game composer — Team Silent let him score every Silent Hill from 1 (1999) to Shattered Memories (2009). He played the guitar and engineered the recordings himself.

question: Katamari Damacy, the Keita Takahashi PlayStation 2 game where the player rolls a sticky ball through household objects to build a celestial body for the King of All Cosmos, released in Japan in what year?
context: Katamari Damacy released March 18, 2004 in Japan. The shockingly low budget and bright color palette made it a sleeper hit. Takahashi quit Namco after the third entry — he disliked sequels.

question: Mario Kart 64, the Nintendo 64 sequel to Super Mario Kart, introduced four-player split-screen and the Battle Mode arenas in what year?
context: Mario Kart 64 released December 14, 1996 in Japan. The Rainbow Road track ran 6:45 in single-player and remains one of the longest courses in series history. Star Cup remains a benchmark of difficulty.

question: Mario Party, the Nintendo 64 multiplayer party game whose minigames famously destroyed control sticks, released in Japan in what year?
context: Mario Party released December 18, 1998 in Japan. Hudson Soft developed the original entries. The palm-rotating minigame 'Tug o' War' triggered enough hand injuries that Nintendo briefly offered free protective gloves.

question: Diablo, the Blizzard PC isometric action-RPG that defined click-loot dungeon gameplay, released in what year?
context: Diablo released December 31, 1996. Blizzard's small Condor team — soon Blizzard North — built it as a turn-based game before pivoting to real-time clicks. The randomized dungeons and items started a genre.

question: StarCraft, the Blizzard real-time strategy game whose three asymmetric factions (Terran, Zerg, Protoss) became Korean national esports, released in what year?
context: StarCraft released March 31, 1998. The original tournament scene exploded in South Korea by 1999. Two professional leagues — OnGameNet and MBCGame — ran televised StarCraft matches for over a decade.

question: Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness, the Blizzard real-time strategy sequel with Humans and Orcs on naval-and-aerial campaigns, released in what year?
context: Warcraft II released December 9, 1995. The Edition with Beyond the Dark Portal expansion shipped in 1996. Warcraft III followed in 2002. World of Warcraft launched 2004 — Blizzard's longest-running franchise.

question: Doom, the id Software shareware FPS by John Romero and John Carmack that codified the first-person shooter, released in what year?
context: Doom released December 10, 1993. Carmack pioneered the BSP rendering tech. Romero designed levels. The shareware first episode (Knee-Deep in the Dead) spread the game across BBSes faster than any commercial product could.

question: Quake, id Software's true 3D follow-up to Doom with full polygonal levels and a Trent Reznor industrial soundtrack, released in what year?
context: Quake released June 22, 1996. Carmack rewrote the entire engine. The community-made tooling — QuakeC scripting, custom maps — kicked off modern modding culture.

question: Wolfenstein 3D, the id Software shareware game that established the first-person shooter template with B.J. Blazkowicz fighting Nazis in a castle, released in what year?
context: Wolfenstein 3D released May 5, 1992. The game's title built on the 1981 Castle Wolfenstein from Muse Software. Apogee published it as shareware — leading to id Software's flush 1993 and Doom.

question: Duke Nukem 3D, the 3D Realms first-person shooter with Duke's quips and destructible toilets, released in what year?
context: Duke Nukem 3D released January 29, 1996. The Build engine by Ken Silverman allowed interactive environments far beyond Doom's. Duke Nukem Forever began development immediately and shipped fifteen years later in 2011.

question: Half-Life, the Valve PC FPS featuring Gordon Freeman in the Black Mesa research facility — a game that abolished cutscenes in favor of scripted gameplay sequences — released in what year?
context: Half-Life released November 19, 1998. Gabe Newell's Valve, founded by former Microsoft employees, debuted with one of the most influential FPS of all time. Marc Laidlaw wrote the story.

question: Counter-Strike, originally a Half-Life mod by Minh Le and Jess Cliffe before Valve bought it, released as a Steam version in what year?
context: Counter-Strike 1.0 released November 9, 2000 as a standalone product. The mod itself had launched June 1999. By 2003 it was the dominant competitive FPS, played in LAN cafés worldwide for a decade.

question: World of Warcraft, Blizzard's massively multiplayer online game set in the Warcraft universe, launched in North America in what year?
context: World of Warcraft launched November 23, 2004. By 2010 it had over 12 million subscribers. Designed by Rob Pardo, Jeff Kaplan, and Tom Chilton, it built on EverQuest and Ultima Online but smoothed out their rough edges.

question: EverQuest, Sony Online Entertainment's MMORPG that established the genre in the West before World of Warcraft, released in what year?
context: EverQuest released March 16, 1999. Brad McQuaid and the 989 Studios team built it. The game's brutal death penalty (corpse runs) and 'Camp the spawn' mechanics became culture-defining for late-1990s gamer communities.

question: Ultima Online, the Origin Systems and Richard Garriott MMORPG that pioneered persistent online worlds with full PvP and player housing, released in what year?
context: Ultima Online released September 24, 1997. Garriott built on the Ultima single-player tradition. The game's robust economy and player-housing system became templates the genre would borrow for decades.

question: Ico, the Fumito Ueda PlayStation 2 game about a horned boy escaping a castle hand-in-hand with a luminous girl, released in Japan in what year?
context: Ico released December 6, 2001 in Japan, September 2002 in North America. Ueda's minimalist storytelling and Kenji Kawai's score made it an art-house critical darling. Its commercial sales were modest.

question: Secret of Mana, the Square SNES action-RPG with real-time three-player simultaneous combat, released in Japan in what year?
context: Secret of Mana released August 6, 1993 in Japan as Seiken Densetsu 2. Hiromichi Tanaka directed. The ring-menu interface was one of the genre's first attempts at smooth real-time menus.

question: Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars, the Square-developed SNES collaboration with Nintendo, released in Japan in what year?
context: Super Mario RPG released March 9, 1996 in Japan. Chihiro Fujioka and Yoshihiko Maekawa directed. The game's odd Geno-Mallow ensemble and Yoko Shimomura score became cult favorites. Toby Fox cited it as Undertale's inspiration.

question: EarthBound, the Shigesato Itoi Super Nintendo cult RPG set in a present-day Eagleland, released in North America in what year?
context: EarthBound released June 5, 1995 in North America (Mother 2 in Japan, 1994). Sales were modest. The game's eccentric humor, real-world settings, and final boss sequence have made it a touchstone for indie developers.

question: F-Zero, the Super Nintendo launch-title futuristic racing game whose Mode 7 pseudo-3D track scaling impressed early SNES owners, released in what year?
context: F-Zero released November 21, 1990 in Japan as a launch title. Designed by Kazunobu Shimizu. The series' GameCube entry F-Zero GX (2003) was developed by Sega's Amusement Vision team — a rare Nintendo-Sega collaboration.

question: Star Fox, the Nintendo SNES rail-shooter using the Super FX chip for polygonal graphics on the SNES, released in what year?
context: Star Fox released February 21, 1993 in Japan. The Super FX chip — designed by Argonaut for the SNES — let the cartridge calculate 3D math the SNES couldn't. The next Star Fox would be N64-native in 1997.

question: Donkey Kong Country, the Rare-developed Super Nintendo platformer with pre-rendered 3D graphics that wowed 1994 audiences, released in what year?
context: Donkey Kong Country released November 21, 1994. Tim Stamper and the Rare team rendered the graphics on Silicon Graphics workstations and compressed the textures into the SNES cartridge. Sales exceeded 9 million.

question: Banjo-Kazooie, Rare's Nintendo 64 collect-a-thon platformer about a bear and a bird in a backpack, released in what year?
context: Banjo-Kazooie released June 29, 1998. Designed by Gregg Mayles. The game's musical wit (Grant Kirkhope's compositions adapt to each level's atmosphere) became Rare's calling card.

question: Perfect Dark, Rare's spiritual successor to GoldenEye 007 with Joanna Dark fighting an alien corporate conspiracy, released in what year?
context: Perfect Dark released May 22, 2000. The single-player needed the N64 Expansion Pak. The 'simulants' AI in multiplayer became the gold standard for offline shooter bots through the entire generation.

question: Conker's Bad Fur Day, Rare's wildly adult Nintendo 64 platformer about an alcoholic squirrel, released in what year?
context: Conker's Bad Fur Day released March 5, 2001. Rare reworked the kid-friendly Twelve Tales: Conker 64 after a backlash from sites complaining about saccharine platformers. The pivot was complete — Conker swore, drank, and parodied The Matrix.

question: When Mortal Kombat came to home consoles in 1993, only one version included the gore by default. Players on the other had to enter a code. Which console got the gore by default?
answer: Sega Genesis
choices: Sega Genesis
Super Nintendo
Atari Jaguar
Game Boy
context: Sega's Genesis included full blood and fatalities. The SNES version replaced blood with gray sweat and toned down fatalities. The Genesis version outsold the SNES version three-to-one — and triggered the U.S. Senate's 1993 hearings on video game violence.

question: On July 4, 1982, a 16-year-old in Hollywood, Florida named Billy Mitchell played Donkey Kong at his family's pizza restaurant and achieved the first publicly verified high score. What was his eventual score that year?
context: Mitchell's 1,047,200 stood for over 25 years as the Donkey Kong world record. The score sparked decades of arcade-record disputes and was central to The King of Kong (2007). Twin Galaxies later disqualified the score in 2018.

question: Pong, the Atari arcade game often (inaccurately) called the first video game, was designed by Allan Alcorn as a training assignment and became Atari's first hit. In what year did it release?
context: Pong released November 1972 in arcades. Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney had founded Atari that summer. Alcorn — a recently-hired engineer — built the prototype as a learning exercise. They installed it in Andy Capp's Tavern.

question: The Twin Galaxies arcade in Ottumwa, Iowa became the unofficial high-score record-keeping authority for classic arcade games starting in 1981. Who founded it?
answer: Walter Day
choices: Walter Day
