Billy Mitchell
Steve Wiebe
Tim Brown
context: Day, a former arcade operator, founded Twin Galaxies in 1981. He cataloged high scores from arcades worldwide and certified records. The King of Kong documentary featured the Twin Galaxies arbitration of the Mitchell-Wiebe dispute.

question: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (1994) and its sequel Sonic & Knuckles (1994) used a unique hardware feature on the Sonic & Knuckles cartridge — a pass-through slot. What was the official name of this feature?
answer: Lock-On Technology
choices: Lock-On Technology
Cartridge Stack
Genesis Combo
Power Pak
context: Sonic & Knuckles's Lock-On Technology pass-through cartridge let players plug Sonic 1, 2, or 3 into the top. The combined game gave players Knuckles in Sonic 2 or a longer Sonic 3 & Knuckles campaign.

question: The Metal Gear series — and Metal Gear Solid in particular — was the creation of a Konami auteur known for blurring film and video game conventions. Who?
answer: Hideo Kojima
choices: Hideo Kojima
Yoshiyuki Tomino
Yu Suzuki
Shinji Mikami
context: Kojima joined Konami in 1986. The original Metal Gear shipped in 1987 for the MSX2. He directed every mainline Metal Gear entry until his split from Konami in 2015.

question: In Stranger Things season 1 (2016), Dustin and his friends play a tabletop game in Mike's basement — and one player's reference to a specific game-mechanic creature becomes a season-long metaphor. What game are they playing?
answer: Dungeons and Dragons
choices: Dungeons and Dragons
Magic the Gathering
Risk
Stratego
context: Mike's red box D&D set is visible. The 'demogorgon' from the campaign becomes Will's shorthand for the season's monster. The 1980s setting accurately depicted the Satanic Panic-adjacent paranoia around D&D.

question: The Atari 2600 (1977-1992) had a famously controversial label promising 'Video Chess' — a game whose absence triggered a real legal threat from a young programmer. What was his name?
answer: Warren Robinett
choices: Warren Robinett
Steve Bristow
Bob Whitehead
Larry Kaplan
context: Robinett's Adventure (1980) contained the first known video game Easter egg — his name hidden in a room. Atari's no-credits policy frustrated him and other programmers, leading to the founding of Activision in 1979.

question: Atari programmer dissatisfaction over no credits led four 1979 defectors to found the first third-party publisher of console games. What did they call the new company?
answer: Activision
choices: Activision
Imagic Inc.
Coleco Games
Mattel Games
context: David Crane, Larry Kaplan, Alan Miller, and Bob Whitehead founded Activision October 1979. Their pitch: name developers, pay royalties. They released Boxing, Skiing, and Dragster in 1980 — paving the way for the entire third-party industry.

question: Super Smash Bros. — across all five games — was led by one Sakurai-named director, originally a HAL Laboratory employee. Who?
answer: Masahiro Sakurai
choices: Masahiro Sakurai
Hideki Kamiya
Shigeru Miyamoto
Yu Suzuki
context: Sakurai also created Kirby (1992). His Smash directorial vision balanced casual fun with deep mechanical depth — a tightrope few designers attempt. He left HAL in 2003 to run Smash from his own studio.

question: The original Metal Gear, Hideo Kojima's first project at Konami, released for the MSX2 platform in what year?
context: Metal Gear released July 7, 1987 on the MSX2 in Japan. The U.S. NES port came later (and added a final-level twist Kojima disliked). The Metal Gear 2 sequel on MSX2 (1990) cemented the franchise's identity.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto joined Nintendo as an industrial designer (not a programmer) in what year?
context: Miyamoto joined Nintendo in 1977 at age 24. His father knew Hiroshi Yamauchi personally. His first major design assignment was Radar Scope (1980), which flopped — leading him to Donkey Kong.

question: The Tron arcade game, released alongside the 1982 Disney film and featuring four minigames on its iconic blue-and-orange cabinet, hit arcades in what year?
context: The Tron arcade game outgrossed the film at the U.S. box office in 1982. Bally Midway built it. Light Cycles, Tanks, Grid Bugs, and the MCP cone were the four programs players competed in.

question: Dragon's Lair, the Don Bluth laserdisc arcade game where Dirk the Daring rescued Princess Daphne through animated quick-time prompts, released in what year?
context: Dragon's Lair released June 1983. Bluth's defection from Disney funded the animation. Quarters cost 50 cents — double standard arcade rate — and players still lined up. The Cinematronics laserdisc tech kept the game in repair shops constantly.

question: Konami's 1991 four-player arcade beat-em-up based on a Fox prime-time animated family was a quarter-eater that featured each family member as a playable character. What was the game?
answer: The Simpsons Arcade Game
choices: The Simpsons Arcade Game
Family Guy Arcade
King of Hill Arcade
Bobby's World Arcade
context: The Simpsons Arcade Game released April 1991. Homer, Marge, Bart, and Lisa took down Mr. Burns's plot. The four-player cabinet became a quarter-eating standby of every mall arcade for years.

question: Konami's 1989 four-player beat-em-up based on the 1987 TMNT cartoon let four kids each pick their own turtle and brawl through the streets of New York. The NES port appeared with which subtitle?
answer: II: The Arcade Game
choices: II: The Arcade Game
Manhattan Project
Sewer Slaughter
Heroes in Time
context: TMNT II: The Arcade Game (1990 NES) brought the arcade game home. The arcade version ate quarters through 1989-91. Konami also produced TMNT III: The Manhattan Project and Turtles in Time for SNES.

question: Atari Inc. was acquired in 1976 by a much larger company that owned Warner Bros. studios and DC Comics. Which corporation bought Atari from Nolan Bushnell?
answer: Warner Communications
choices: Warner Communications
Universal Studios
Disney Entertainment
Paramount Studios
context: Warner Communications bought Atari in 1976 for 28 million dollars. The acquisition funded Atari's growth and eventually the 2600 launch. After the 1983 crash, Warner split Atari and sold pieces — to Jack Tramiel and others.

question: Nintendo's transformation from a 19th-century Kyoto playing-card company into a global gaming giant was led by its third-generation president, who ran the company from 1949 to 2002. Who?
answer: Hiroshi Yamauchi
choices: Hiroshi Yamauchi
Satoru Iwata
Mitsuhiro Aoki
Tatsumi Kimishima
context: Yamauchi took over Nintendo from his grandfather in 1949 at age 21. He hired Miyamoto and gave Yokoi creative latitude. He retired in 2002, handed the presidency to Satoru Iwata, and died in 2013 at 85.

question: Wreck-It Ralph, the 2012 Disney animated film whose 1980s arcade-game world featured cameos from Bowser, M. Bison, and other classic-game villains in a 'Bad-Anon' support group, released in what year?
context: Wreck-It Ralph released November 2, 2012. Director Rich Moore secured cameo rights from Capcom, Sega, Nintendo, Namco, and more. Q*bert, Pac-Man ghosts, Sonic, Zangief — all in one Disney film.

question: The Pokemon franchise was conceived by a Japanese designer obsessed with bug-collecting as a child. He pitched the concept of trading creatures via the Game Boy link cable to Game Freak. Who?
answer: Satoshi Tajiri
choices: Satoshi Tajiri
Junichi Masuda
Shigeru Miyamoto
Hidetaka Suehiro
context: Tajiri co-founded Game Freak in 1989. The Pokemon concept took six years to develop with Nintendo's backing. He named the protagonist Satoshi (Ash in English) after himself and rival Shigeru after Miyamoto.

question: Ms. Pac-Man, the 1982 arcade sequel widely considered superior to its predecessor, was originally developed by an unauthorized group — a Boston-area company called General Computer Corporation — before Bally Midway licensed it. What was the original name they used?
answer: Crazy Otto
choices: Crazy Otto
Ms. Otto
Super Pac
Pac-Maze
context: GCC's Crazy Otto was originally a Pac-Man enhancement kit. Bally Midway purchased the rights, added the Ms. Pac-Man theme, and shipped it without Namco's full blessing. Iwatani himself later complained about it.

question: On the 1993 Sega Genesis Mortal Kombat home release, a specific code unlocked the full arcade-quality blood and fatalities that were absent by default. What was the famous code?
answer: ABACABB
choices: ABACABB
ABBABAC
UDLRSEL
BABABAA
context: ABACABB enabled blood on the Genesis version. The code became one of the most famous in gaming history. Genesis sold three times more copies than the censored SNES Mortal Kombat, helping trigger the 1993 Senate hearings.

question: In Stranger Things season 2 (2017), Dustin tries to identify an unfamiliar creature using a tabletop reference book. The creature, he eventually concludes, is a 'D'Artagnan' — though the book name doesn't match the show's setting. What book is he consulting?
answer: Dungeons and Dragons Monster Manual
choices: Dungeons and Dragons Monster Manual
Pathfinder Bestiary
Necronomicon Excerpts
Forgotten Realms Bestiary
context: Dustin's Monster Manual reference is era-appropriate. The Duffer Brothers consulted with D&D experts to keep the references authentic — though they took some liberties on which specific edition characters used.

question: Mattel's Intellivision, the Atari 2600's main competitor with sharper graphics and a controller numeric keypad, launched in what year?
context: The Intellivision launched in 1979 nationally after a test market in 1978. Mattel's George Plimpton ads pitted Intellivision against the 2600 for years. The console's keypad let players use overlay strips for each game.

question: Coleco's ColecoVision, a third major home console launched in 1982 with Donkey Kong as its pack-in, offered hardware closer to arcade quality than its competitors. In what year did it launch?
context: ColecoVision launched August 1982. The Donkey Kong pack-in was a coup — Coleco licensed it from Nintendo before Atari could. The console's Expansion Module #1 made it backward-compatible with Atari 2600 games.

question: Ms. Pac-Man, the 1982 arcade sequel introducing four mazes and randomized ghost behavior, released in what year?
context: Ms. Pac-Man released February 3, 1982 in arcades. The four maze variants and randomized ghost AI made it more replayable than the original. Critics often rate it as the better game in retrospective rankings.

question: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!, the licensed NES boxing game where players faced fighters culminating in Tyson himself, released in what year?
context: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! released October 1987 in North America. Tyson's likeness rights expired in 1990; subsequent reprints replaced him with the fictional Mr. Dream. Original cartridges with Tyson now sell for premiums.

question: Yoshi, the green dinosaur companion who eats enemies and lays eggs, first appeared in a Mario game when?
answer: Super Mario World (1990)
choices: Super Mario World (1990)
Super Mario Bros 2 (1988)
Mario Paint (1992)
Super Mario 64 (1996)
context: Miyamoto wanted Mario to have a dinosaur sidekick in Super Mario Bros. 1 (1985) but the NES hardware couldn't handle it. The SNES enabled Yoshi's debut in Super Mario World — the SNES launch title.

question: Metroid (1986) ended with a reveal about its protagonist that became one of gaming's first famous twists. What was the surprise?
answer: Samus Aran is a woman beneath the suit
choices: Samus Aran is a woman beneath the suit
The Mother Brain is the player
Zebes is actually Earth
Samus is a Chozo
context: Sakamoto and Yokoi added the helmet-off ending sequence as a joke that became iconic. Speedrunners who beat the game under 5 hours got a swimsuit ending — sub 3 hours, a bikini. The reveal became a series defining feature.

question: Superman first appeared in Action Comics #1, the issue that effectively created the superhero genre. In what year was it published?
context: Action Comics #1 hit newsstands April 18, 1938. Cover-dated June 1938. Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster sold the rights for $130 — a deal they spent the rest of their lives trying to renegotiate.

question: Batman first appeared in Detective Comics #27, the issue that gave DC its second iconic superhero. In what year was it published?
context: Detective Comics #27 was cover-dated May 1939, hitting stands March 30. Bob Kane signed it; Bill Finger ghost-wrote most of the early Batman material. Finger received no credit until 2015.

question: Captain America Comics #1, with its famous cover of Cap punching Adolf Hitler, was published in what year?
context: Cap #1 was cover-dated March 1941 — before U.S. entry into WWII. Joe Simon and Jack Kirby created him. Timely Comics, the publisher, would eventually become Marvel.

question: Spider-Man's first appearance in Amazing Fantasy #15 — the famous bargain-rate try-out issue — came in what year?
context: Amazing Fantasy #15 was cover-dated August 1962. Lee wrote; Steve Ditko drew. Amazing Fantasy was being canceled — Spider-Man was a Hail Mary that became a sales sensation. His own title launched March 1963.

question: The Incredible Hulk first appeared in his own self-titled issue #1, originally green-and-gray (no, gray-and-not-green) due to a printing complication. In what year?
context: Hulk #1 was cover-dated May 1962. Lee wrote; Kirby drew. The Hulk was originally gray; printing made his color inconsistent, so Lee switched him to green starting in issue #2. The gray cancer didn't kill the launch.

question: Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83 — a Marvel anthology title — in what year?
context: Journey into Mystery #83 was cover-dated August 1962. Lee wrote, Larry Lieber scripted, Kirby drew. Thor's series replaced JIM in 1966 — when the lightning-pun god got his own banner.

question: Iron Man first appeared in Tales of Suspense #39 — a Marvel monster-and-suspense anthology — in what year?
context: Tales of Suspense #39 was cover-dated March 1963. Larry Lieber scripted. Don Heck and Jack Kirby drew. Lee co-credited Heck for the gray armor — Iron Man went red-and-gold within months.

question: The Avengers #1 — the Marvel team comprising Thor, Iron Man, Hulk, Wasp, and Ant-Man — was published in what year?
context: Avengers #1 was cover-dated September 1963. Lee wrote, Kirby drew. Captain America joined in #4 (March 1964) and became the team's leader. The Avengers helped fuse Marvel's separate solo titles into one universe.

question: Wolverine first appeared as a hostile cameo in Incredible Hulk #181 — a last-page cliffhanger that became Marvel's most influential character debut. In what year?
context: Hulk #181 was cover-dated November 1974. Len Wein wrote; Herb Trimpe drew. John Romita Sr. designed the costume. Wolverine joined the X-Men in Giant-Size X-Men #1 (1975) and never let go.

question: Chris Claremont wrote X-Men continuously for an unprecedented span, defining the team and its core characters from the Bronze Age through the early 1990s. How long was his initial run?
answer: Sixteen years (1975-1991)
choices: Sixteen years (1975-1991)
Ten years (1975-1985)
Twenty years (1971-1991)
Twelve years (1979-1991)
context: Claremont took over X-Men #94 in 1975 and stayed through Uncanny #279 and X-Men v2 #3 in 1991. His tenure is widely considered the longest, most influential run in mainstream comics history.

question: Chris Claremont and John Byrne's most celebrated X-Men arc ran through Uncanny X-Men #129-137 in 1980 and forced editor Jim Shooter to demand a final-act change. What was the arc called?
answer: The Dark Phoenix Saga
choices: The Dark Phoenix Saga
Days of Future Past
God Loves Man Kills
Inferno Saga
context: The Dark Phoenix Saga centered on Jean Grey. Shooter's last-minute editorial intervention famously reshaped the ending. Claremont and Byrne disagreed about the change for decades.

question: Watchmen, the 1986-87 twelve-issue DC limited series widely considered the most important superhero comic ever published, was written by whom?
answer: Alan Moore
choices: Alan Moore
Frank Miller
Neil Gaiman
Garth Ennis
context: Moore conceived the series as a deconstruction of the superhero genre. Dave Gibbons illustrated. John Higgins colored. The smiley face pin with a single drop of blood became one of comics's most recognized images.

question: The artist who illustrated Alan Moore's 1986 Watchmen — drawing the rigid 9-panel grids that became a structural language of the medium — was who?
answer: Dave Gibbons
choices: Dave Gibbons
John Higgins
Brian Bolland
Jim Lee
context: Gibbons worked closely with Moore on the layouts. The strict grids enforced reading discipline. Issue 5 ('Fearful Symmetry') had a panel structure that mirrored from beginning to end — pages 1 and 28 visually identical.

question: Frank Miller's The Dark Knight Returns, the four-issue 1986 prestige-format DC limited series featuring a 55-year-old Bruce Wayne returning to crimefighting in a dystopian Gotham, released in what year?
context: TDKR's first issue hit stands February 1986. Miller wrote and drew it; Klaus Janson inked; Lynn Varley colored. Together with Watchmen and Maus, it triggered the 'comics for adults' wave of the late 1980s.

question: The Sandman, Neil Gaiman's seventy-five-issue DC/Vertigo series running from 1988 to 1996 about Dream of the Endless, was written by whom?
answer: Neil Gaiman
choices: Neil Gaiman
Alan Moore
Grant Morrison
Frank Miller
context: Gaiman pitched The Sandman based loosely on a 1930s Sandman character. The series's literary aspirations and fantasy-anthology structure made it the definitive Vertigo title and Gaiman's career-defining work.

question: Hellboy, the right-handed-doom paranormal investigator and Big Red since 1993, was created by an artist-writer who was inspired by Lovecraft, Howard, and folklore. Who?
answer: Mike Mignola
choices: Mike Mignola
Frank Miller
Bernie Wrightson
Mike Allred
context: Mignola began Hellboy at Dark Horse Comics in 1993. The character — half-demon, half-occult-detective — gave Mignola the platform for stark, shadow-driven storytelling. The BPRD spinoff branched off in 2003.

question: Preacher, the 1995-2000 Vertigo series about a Texas pastor, his hitman girlfriend, and an Irish vampire on a quest to find God, was written by whom?
answer: Garth Ennis
choices: Garth Ennis
Warren Ellis
Neil Gaiman
Grant Morrison
context: Ennis wrote all 66 issues. Steve Dillon drew. The series ran in floppies and would later become AMC's Preacher TV show (2016-2019). Jesse Custer, Tulip O'Hare, and Cassidy are gospel-American characters at this point.

question: Frank Miller's Sin City — the noir black-and-white series that became the visual template for the 2005 Robert Rodriguez film — began at Dark Horse Comics in what year?
context: Sin City began in Dark Horse Presents in April 1991 as 'Sin City' serial. The first hardcover collection appeared in 1992. Miller's stark white-on-black style influenced an entire generation of black-and-white indie comics.

question: Frank Miller's 300, the five-issue 1998 Dark Horse limited series about Leonidas and the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae, released in what year?
context: 300 published May-September 1998. Lynn Varley colored it. Zack Snyder's 2007 film adapted it nearly panel-for-panel. The book won Eisner Awards for Best Limited Series and Best Writer/Artist.

question: V for Vendetta, the Alan Moore and David Lloyd Warrior magazine serial (later finished at DC) about a Guy Fawkes-masked anarchist in fascist Britain, began in what year?
context: V began in Warrior #1 (March 1982). The series was incomplete when Warrior folded; Moore and Lloyd finished it at DC's Vertigo line in 1988-89. The Wachowskis adapted it as a 2005 film.

question: Alan Moore took over DC's Saga of the Swamp Thing in 1983 and ran on it through 1987, fundamentally redefining the character. What was the issue number of his first?
answer: Issue 20
choices: Issue 20
Issue 21
Issue 19
Issue 25
context: Moore's run began with Saga of the Swamp Thing #20 (January 1984). Issue 21 ('The Anatomy Lesson') was the famous redefinition — turning Alec Holland into a plant elemental. The series became one of DC's most acclaimed.

question: Marvel's 1991 six-issue limited series Infinity Gauntlet, written by Jim Starlin with art by George Pérez and Ron Lim, established Thanos's grand cosmic threat. In what year did it release?
context: Infinity Gauntlet ran July-December 1991. Thanos's quest for the gauntlet directly inspired the Avengers films' Infinity Saga. Pérez left after issue 4 due to health issues; Lim finished out the run.

question: DC's 1992 'The Death of Superman' arc, where Doomsday brought down the Man of Steel, was published in what year?
context: The arc culminated in Superman v2 #75 (January 1993). Newsstands sold out instantly. Dan Jurgens and Brett Breeding drew the death issue. The arc was followed by 'Funeral for a Friend' and 'Reign of the Supermen.'

question: DC's Batman 'Knightfall' arc, where Bane systematically broke Batman, ran in what year?
context: Knightfall ran April-November 1993. Doug Moench, Chuck Dixon, and Alan Grant wrote. The arc concluded in Batman #500 with Bruce Wayne replacing himself with Azrael as Batman temporarily.

question: DC's 1985-86 twelve-issue Crisis on Infinite Earths — the line-wide reboot that streamlined fifty years of continuity into a single Earth — was written by whom?
answer: Marv Wolfman
choices: Marv Wolfman
Roy Thomas
Cary Bates
Mike W. Barr
context: Wolfman and George Pérez had been pitching the idea since 1981. The series ran April 1985 - March 1986. The Earth-Two characters (the original Flash, the Justice Society) were retired or restructured.

question: Marvel's Civil War, the 2006 seven-issue Mark Millar event series pitting Captain America against Iron Man over a superhero registration act, released in what year?
context: Civil War ran May 2006 - January 2007. Steve McNiven drew. Mark Millar's premise — heroes registering with the government — split the Marvel Universe in two. The 2016 film loosely adapted it.

question: Kingdom Come, the 1996 four-issue Elseworlds DC series by Mark Waid and Alex Ross depicting an aging Justice League and a new generation of unprincipled heroes, released in what year?
context: Kingdom Come ran May-August 1996. Alex Ross's photorealistic painted art remained unmatched in superhero comics. Waid based much of the theology on the Book of Revelation. A 2007 sequel by Waid alone followed.

question: Marvels, the 1994 four-issue Marvel mini-series by Kurt Busiek and Alex Ross showing the Marvel Universe through a single photojournalist's eyes, released in what year?
context: Marvels ran January-April 1994. Alex Ross painted; Busiek wrote. The series's ground-level perspective on classic Marvel moments — the Fantastic Four's first appearance, X-Men, etc. — won Busiek and Ross critical acclaim.

question: Bone, Jeff Smith's self-published 55-issue series about the Bone cousins fleeing Boneville into a valley of dragons, rat creatures, and a Locust Queen, began publication in what year?
context: Bone began in 1991 from Smith's own Cartoon Books. The series ran 55 issues through 2004. Smith took inspiration from Carl Barks, Walt Kelly, and Tolkien — Bone became the gold standard for indie comics craft.

question: Usagi Yojimbo, the long-running comic about a rabbit samurai wandering Edo-period Japan, has been created and drawn by a single creator since 1984. Who?
answer: Stan Sakai
choices: Stan Sakai
Jeff Smith
Frank Miller
Mike Mignola
context: Sakai began Usagi Yojimbo in 1984 in Albedo Anthropomorphics #2. The series has run through Fantagraphics, Mirage, Dark Horse, and IDW. Sakai has won numerous Eisners — he draws every panel himself.

question: Weird Tales, the pulp magazine that published Robert E. Howard's Conan, H.P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos, and Clark Ashton Smith's Zothique stories, was founded in what year?
context: Weird Tales launched March 1923. Founded by J.C. Henneberger and J.M. Lansinger in Chicago. Its early issues were rough; under editor Farnsworth Wright (1924-1940) the magazine became the foundational pulp of horror and weird fiction.

question: Robert E. Howard, creator of Conan the Cimmerian and Solomon Kane, spent his entire life in one small Texas town. What town?
answer: Cross Plains, Texas
choices: Cross Plains, Texas
Marfa, Texas
Hondo, Texas
Brackettville, Texas
context: Howard lived in Cross Plains from 1919 (age 13) until his suicide in 1936. The Howard House Museum still stands there. Lovecraft corresponded with him for years, never having met. Howard wrote at a relentless rate.

question: Clark Ashton Smith, the third pillar of the Weird Tales triumvirate alongside Howard and Lovecraft, was a poet and weird-fiction writer based in which state?
answer: California
choices: California
Massachusetts
New York
Texas
context: Smith spent his life in Auburn, California — a recluse in a cabin he built himself. He wrote prose for the pulps only between 1929 and 1935 but his Zothique, Hyperborea, and Xiccarph stories defined the dying-earth subgenre.

question: H.P. Lovecraft invented a fictional grimoire that became central to his Mythos — a book of dread knowledge supposedly written by the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred. What did Lovecraft name it?
answer: The Necronomicon
choices: The Necronomicon
The Pnakotic Manuscripts
The Book of Eibon
The Cultes des Goules
context: Lovecraft invented the Necronomicon in 'The Hound' (1924). The fictional book became part of his Mythos's fabric. Lovecraft repeatedly insisted in letters that it didn't exist — yet libraries get inquiries to this day.

question: Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd and Gray Mouser stories — about a tall barbarian and his crafty thief partner adventuring through Lankhmar — coined a literary term for the entire genre. What term did Leiber name?
answer: Sword and Sorcery
choices: Sword and Sorcery
Heroic Fantasy
Pulp Adventure
Weird Romance
context: Leiber proposed 'sword and sorcery' in a 1961 letter to a fanzine, in conversation with Michael Moorcock. The term stuck. The first Fafhrd and Mouser story 'Two Sought Adventure' ran in Unknown in 1939.

question: Tarzan of the Apes, Edgar Rice Burroughs's 1912 novel about a British nobleman raised by apes, first appeared in what magazine?
answer: All-Story Magazine
choices: All-Story Magazine
Argosy Magazine
Weird Tales
Saturday Evening Post
context: Tarzan of the Apes was serialized in All-Story Magazine October 1912. Burroughs had already serialized A Princess of Mars there earlier the same year. Tarzan would generate twenty-four novels and a film franchise across decades.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's A Princess of Mars, the first John Carter novel introducing Dejah Thoris and Barsoom, was serialized in All-Story Magazine in what year?
context: A Princess of Mars (originally 'Under the Moons of Mars') ran February-July 1912. John Carter inspired comic-book heroes from Buck Rogers to Superman. Disney's 2012 film John Carter was a famously expensive flop.

question: Philip Marlowe, the Los Angeles private detective who anchored eight novels including The Big Sleep, Farewell My Lovely, and The Long Goodbye, was created by whom?
answer: Raymond Chandler
choices: Raymond Chandler
Dashiell Hammett
James M. Cain
Mickey Spillane
context: Chandler wrote his first Marlowe novel The Big Sleep (1939) at age 50. His prose style — wisecracking similes layered over sentimentality — defined American hardboiled detective fiction.

question: Doc Savage, the bronze-skinned superman of the 1930s pulps and direct inspiration for Superman, debuted in his own magazine in what year?
context: Doc Savage Magazine launched March 1933. Lester Dent wrote most stories under the house name Kenneth Robeson. Doc and his Fabulous Five — Renny, Ham, Long Tom, Monk, and Johnny — ran 181 issues through 1949.

question: Flash Gordon, Alex Raymond's iconic adventure comic strip pitting Yale-grad-turned-spaceman Flash against Ming the Merciless, debuted in what year?
context: Flash Gordon debuted January 7, 1934 as a Sunday strip. King Features Syndicate launched it as competition for Buck Rogers (1929). Raymond's lush brushwork influenced comics art for the next half-century.

question: Isaac Asimov's Foundation, the saga of psychohistory and a galactic Empire's decline, began as a short story in Astounding Stories in what year?
context: 'Foundation' (later renamed 'The Encyclopedists') ran in Astounding May 1942. Asimov wrote it at age 22, inspired by Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. The eventual Foundation trilogy was assembled from the magazine serials in 1951-53.

question: Robert Heinlein's Starship Troopers, the 1959 novel about Mobile Infantry and military citizenship that later inspired Paul Verhoeven's 1997 film, released in what year?
context: Starship Troopers released December 1959. Heinlein won his second Hugo for it. The novel triggered a long-running argument about whether it was satirical, advocating, or both. Verhoeven's film took the satirical reading.

question: Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451, the novel about a society where firemen burn books, released in what year?
context: Fahrenheit 451 released October 1953. Bradbury wrote the original novella ('The Fireman') in 1951. The novel was expanded from there. Bradbury's title is the temperature at which paper auto-ignites — chosen for ominous specificity.

question: Ray Bradbury's The Martian Chronicles, the linked short-story collection about humans colonizing Mars, was published in what year?
context: The Martian Chronicles released May 1950. Bradbury assembled it from stories he'd previously sold to Planet Stories, Thrilling Wonder Stories, and Maclean's. The book established him as one of science fiction's premier prose stylists.

question: Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the prose compilation that gave us the modern Arthurian canon, was first printed by William Caxton in what year?
context: Caxton printed Le Morte d'Arthur July 31, 1485. Malory wrote it in prison, completed around 1469. Caxton's printing made it the foundational Arthurian text. Tennyson, T.H. White, and countless modern authors drew directly from it.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley's The Mists of Avalon, a feminist retelling of the Arthurian cycle from Morgaine's perspective, released in what year?
context: Mists of Avalon released January 1983. Bradley's seven-hundred-page reimagining became a major bestseller. Its retelling of Camelot through Morgaine, Vivian, and Igraine's eyes brought new audiences to Arthurian fantasy.

question: DC's 1996 Elseworlds limited series Kingdom Come — Mark Waid's elegiac dystopian Justice League future — was painted in fully realized photorealistic art. Who painted it?
answer: Alex Ross
choices: Alex Ross
George Pérez
Jim Lee
Curt Swan
context: Ross's painted style — meticulously researched real models posing as superheroes — set Kingdom Come apart from any other comic of the 1990s. He'd previously painted Marvels (1994) with Kurt Busiek.

question: Astro Boy, the 1952 manga that established post-war Japanese comics as their own form, was created by an artist often called the 'God of Manga.' Who?
answer: Osamu Tezuka
choices: Osamu Tezuka
Eiichiro Oda
Akira Toriyama
Hayao Miyazaki
context: Tezuka (1928-1989) trained as a medical doctor before turning to manga full-time. Astro Boy (Mighty Atom in Japan) ran 1952-1968. Tezuka also created Phoenix, Black Jack, Buddha, and dozens of foundational manga titles.

question: Spider-Man's first appearance was illustrated by an artist whose distinctive angular style made Peter Parker and the original Spidey costume iconic. Who?
answer: Steve Ditko
choices: Steve Ditko
Jack Kirby
John Romita Sr.
Don Heck
context: Ditko co-created Spider-Man with Stan Lee in 1962. He left Marvel in 1966 over creative disputes. His Spider-Man design — the eye lenses, the web-pattern — set the visual standard.

question: The Adventures of Tintin, the Belgian comics series about a young reporter and his fox terrier Snowy, was created by whom?
answer: Herge
choices: Herge
Edgar P. Jacobs
Andre Franquin
Morris
context: Herge (Georges Remi) created Tintin in 1929 in the children's supplement Le Petit Vingtieme. The series ran through 1976. 24 albums in total — translated into over 70 languages.

question: Bill Watterson's comic strip Calvin and Hobbes began in newspaper syndication in what year?
context: Calvin and Hobbes debuted November 18, 1985 in 35 newspapers. By the time Watterson retired ten years later, it ran in over 2,400 papers worldwide. Watterson refused all merchandising offers throughout.

question: Alan Moore's V for Vendetta was illustrated by a British artist who developed a heavily-shadowed style perfect for the noir-fascist setting. Who?
answer: David Lloyd
choices: David Lloyd
Eddie Campbell
Brian Bolland
Steve Yeowell
context: Lloyd drew V's serialized run in Warrior magazine (1982-85) and finished it for DC (1988-89). His use of stark blacks and minimal dialogue tracking gave the series its distinct visual identity.

question: Weird Tales magazine, the foundational pulp magazine of horror and weird fiction, was founded in 1923 by an entrepreneur in Indianapolis. Who?
answer: J.C. Henneberger
choices: J.C. Henneberger
Farnsworth Wright
Hugo Gernsback
Howard Hill
context: Henneberger and J.M. Lansinger founded Weird Tales in March 1923. Edwin Baird edited the first eighteen issues. Farnsworth Wright took over in 1924 and ran the magazine until 1940 — the period that established its canonical contributors.

question: Garth Ennis's Punisher MAX run — a Marvel Max imprint take on Frank Castle through a stark, brutalist lens — released its first issue in what year?
context: Punisher MAX #1 released March 2004. Ennis wrote sixty issues through 2008. The Max imprint allowed Frank Castle to be the broken Vietnam-vet vigilante Ennis envisioned — without superhero universe distractions.

question: Mark Millar's Kick-Ass — the Marvel Icon series about a teenager who decides to be a superhero with no powers — published its first issue in what year?
context: Kick-Ass #1 released February 2008. John Romita Jr. drew. The series was creator-owned. Matthew Vaughn directed the 2010 film while the comic series was still being published.

question: Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd and Gray Mouser stories are set in a fictional city of thieves, beggars, sorcerers, and merchants on a fantasy world called Nehwon. What is the city called?
answer: Lankhmar
choices: Lankhmar
Sanctuary
Cynosure
Yondering
context: Lankhmar — built on a fog-blanketed peninsula at the mouth of the Hlal River — became one of fantasy's most influential settings. TSR adapted it as an official D&D setting in 1985 with Leiber's blessing.

question: Michael Moorcock's Elric of Melnibone, the albino sorcerer-prince and wielder of the soul-drinking Stormbringer sword, first appeared in 1961 in what magazine?
answer: Science Fantasy
choices: Science Fantasy
Weird Tales
Astounding
Amazing Stories
context: 'The Dreaming City' (June 1961, Science Fantasy) introduced Elric. Moorcock was 21. The character was a deliberate inverse of Howard's Conan — frail, decadent, doomed — and launched the multiverse-spanning Eternal Champion saga.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's narrative poem 'The Raven,' the ones with the raven on the bust of Pallas saying 'nevermore,' was first published in what year?
context: The Raven was first published January 29, 1845 in the New York Evening Mirror. Poe was paid nine dollars. The poem made him immediately famous. He died four years later under mysterious circumstances in Baltimore.

question: Stan Lee and Steve Ditko's Amazing Spider-Man issues #96-98 (1971) were published without the Comics Code seal because they dealt with what topic?
answer: Drug abuse
choices: Drug abuse
Sexual assault
Suicide
Vietnam War
context: The Comics Code prohibited any depiction of drug use, even cautionary. Lee was asked by the Department of Health to address the topic. The three issues — about Harry Osborn's pill addiction — ran sans Code. The CMAA changed the rules months later.

question: Steve Ditko, co-creator of Spider-Man and Doctor Strange, left Marvel Comics over creative disagreements with Stan Lee in what year?
context: Ditko quit Marvel in 1966 — over differences with Lee about the Spider-Man villain Green Goblin's identity, and over rising tensions about Ayn Rand-influenced philosophy. He spent the next decades at DC and Charlton.

question: Fritz Leiber's first Fafhrd and Gray Mouser story 'Two Sought Adventure' (later retitled 'The Jewels in the Forest') appeared in what magazine?
answer: Unknown
choices: Unknown
Weird Tales
Astounding
Amazing Stories
context: 'Two Sought Adventure' ran in Unknown magazine August 1939. Editor John W. Campbell published it. The pair would appear in over forty stories through 1991 — one of fantasy's longest character runs.

question: Mike Mignola's Hellboy first appeared in print in what year?
context: Hellboy first appeared in San Diego Comic-Con Comics #2, August 1993. The character then debuted in his own four-issue Hellboy: Seed of Destruction in March 1994. Mignola wrote and drew both.

question: The Comics Code Authority, the comics industry's self-censorship body that forbade depictions of monsters, drug use, and graphic violence, was established in what year?
context: The CCA was formed in late 1954 in response to Senate subcommittee hearings on juvenile delinquency. Frederic Wertham's Seduction of the Innocent prompted the hearings. EC Comics's horror line was decimated; the code stood through the 2010s.

question: Black Panther, T'Challa of Wakanda, first appeared as a Fantastic Four guest character in what year — making him the first major Black superhero in mainstream American comics?
context: Black Panther debuted in Fantastic Four #52 (July 1966) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. He predated the Black Panther Party (formed October 1966) by months. T'Challa got his own series in Jungle Action in 1973.

question: The Silver Surfer first appeared as a herald in Fantastic Four #48 — the first chapter of the Galactus trilogy — in what year?
context: FF #48 was cover-dated March 1966. Jack Kirby created the Silver Surfer without telling Lee; he just added the character to the pages he drew. Lee wrote in dialogue. The Surfer became Lee's favorite Marvel character.

question: Frank Miller took over Daredevil and reshaped the title from forgettable filler into one of Marvel's hottest books. His writing run began in what year?
context: Miller began writing Daredevil with issue #168 (January 1981). He'd been drawing since #158 (1979). He introduced Elektra in #168. His run reshaped the entire street-level corner of the Marvel Universe.

question: Elektra Natchios, the Greek assassin and Daredevil's ex-girlfriend, was created by Frank Miller and first appeared in Daredevil #168 in what year?
context: Elektra debuted in Daredevil #168 (January 1981). Miller created her with input from his then-girlfriend. Her arc through the series — and her eventual sai-wielding return — established the assassin-archetype Marvel would reuse for decades.

question: Marv Wolfman and George Pérez's New Teen Titans, the DC team revival that made Robin/Nightwing, Starfire, Raven, and Cyborg into household names, launched in what year?
context: The New Teen Titans #1 was cover-dated November 1980. The series became DC's best-selling title of the early 1980s, rivaling the X-Men. Wolfman and Pérez's collaboration ran throughout the decade.

question: Wolverine joined the X-Men as part of an 'All-New, All-Different' lineup introduced in a 1975 oversized issue. What was the issue called?
answer: Giant-Size X-Men #1
choices: Giant-Size X-Men #1
Uncanny X-Men #94
X-Men: First Class
All-New X-Men
context: Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) introduced Storm, Colossus, Nightcrawler, Banshee, and Sunfire — joining returning members Wolverine and Cyclops. Len Wein wrote, Dave Cockrum drew. The Claremont era began with #94.

question: Jim Lee's X-Men #1, the 1991 relaunch with multiple variant covers, set a record for highest-selling single comic issue ever — eight million copies — that still stands. In what year?
context: X-Men #1 by Lee and Claremont released October 1991 in four variant covers (plus a fifth gatefold). The combined eight million copies were never broken. Lee left Marvel months later to co-found Image Comics.

question: Image Comics, the creator-owned publisher founded by seven Marvel defectors including Jim Lee, Todd McFarlane, and Rob Liefeld, was founded in what year?
context: Image launched February 1992. The 'Image Seven' — Lee, McFarlane, Liefeld, Marc Silvestri, Erik Larsen, Jim Valentino, and Whilce Portacio — left Marvel over royalty disputes. Their pitch: creator ownership. The model reshaped the industry.

question: Spawn, Todd McFarlane's Image Comics signature character about a hellbound special-forces operative, debuted in what year?
context: Spawn #1 released May 1992. McFarlane self-published — the issue sold 1.7 million copies, then a record for an independent comic. The series has run continuously since, making McFarlane one of comics's longest-active creator-owners.

question: Lone Wolf and Cub, the epic samurai manga about a wandering executioner pushing his infant son in a wooden cart, was first serialized in Japan in what year?
context: Kazuo Koike wrote and Goseki Kojima drew Lone Wolf and Cub from September 1970 to 1976. The series is widely considered one of the masterpieces of the medium. Frank Miller cited its influence on his work directly.

question: Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira manga began serialization in Young Magazine in what year — preceding the 1988 anime film by years?
context: Akira began in Young Magazine December 1982. The manga ran until 1990 and totaled six volumes. The film was made before the manga concluded — the manga and film diverge significantly past the halfway point.

question: Doc Savage Magazine's primary author — who wrote most of the 181 issues under the house pseudonym Kenneth Robeson — was who?
answer: Lester Dent
choices: Lester Dent
Walter Gibson
Theodore Tinsley
Frank Belknap Long
context: Dent wrote 159 of the 181 Doc Savage stories from 1933 to 1949. His 'Master Plot' template — six chapters, problem stated, complication, twist, resolution — became a teaching example for pulp writers.

question: Masamune Shirow's Ghost in the Shell, the manga adapted by Mamoru Oshii in 1995, began serialization in Japan in what year?
context: Ghost in the Shell began serialization in Young Magazine April 1989. Shirow finished the manga in 1990. The 1995 anime film by Mamoru Oshii was a relatively spare adaptation; the 2002 Stand Alone Complex series went broader.

question: Kentaro Miura's manga Berserk began serialization in 1988 in a magazine outside the usual shonen-focused outlets. Which magazine?
answer: Young Animal
choices: Young Animal
Shonen Jump
Young Magazine
Big Comic Spirits
context: Berserk began in Hakusensha's seinen magazine Young Animal in 1989 (after a 1988 prototype). The mature focus allowed Miura to push the grotesque imagery and operatic tragedy that defined the work.

question: Casper the Friendly Ghost, the cute spectral character who'd become Harvey Comics's enduring property, first appeared in what year?
context: Casper began life in a 1939 Seymour Reit and Joe Oriolo children's book. Paramount's animation studio made him a star with 1945 short cartoons. The Harvey Comics title began in 1949. The 1995 film returned him to brief fame.

question: Archie Andrews, the eternally-teenaged Riverdale High School student in the love triangle with Betty and Veronica, first appeared in what year?
context: Archie first appeared in Pep Comics #22 (December 1941). MLJ Magazines published him; the company eventually renamed itself Archie Comics in 1946. The series has run continuously for 80+ years.

question: EC Comics — Tales from the Crypt, The Vault of Horror, The Haunt of Fear — the company that defined American horror comics in the early 1950s, began its horror line in what year?
context: EC Comics relaunched its line with the 'New Trend' titles in April 1950. William Gaines published; Al Feldstein and Gaines wrote much of the line. The Comics Code shut down EC's horror titles in 1954.

question: MAD Magazine, the EC Comics title that survived the Comics Code shutdown by switching to magazine format, was first published in what year?
context: MAD launched as a comic in October 1952. Editor Harvey Kurtzman led the satire focus. When the CCA threatened EC's other titles, Gaines converted MAD to magazine format in 1955 — bypassing the comics-specific Code.

question: Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics — the ethical framework governing fictional robot behavior — first appeared in his short story 'Runaround' in what year?
context: 'Runaround' ran in Astounding March 1942. The Three Laws shaped how science fiction discussed robotics for the next 80 years. Asimov spent his career writing stories that exposed loopholes in the Laws.

question: Before Conan, Robert E. Howard created another barbarian-king character — a former exile from a doomed island civilization who becomes king of Valusia. What was the character's name?
answer: Kull of Atlantis
choices: Kull of Atlantis
Bran Mak Morn
Solomon Kane
Cormac Mac Art
context: Kull's first story 'The Shadow Kingdom' ran in Weird Tales August 1929. Howard wrote fewer Kull stories than Conan — fourteen total, only three of which sold to Weird Tales during his lifetime. Howard's Kull was Conan's blueprint.

question: Raymond Chandler's first Philip Marlowe novel — adapted by Howard Hawks in 1946 with Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall — was published in what year?
context: The Big Sleep released February 1939. Chandler was 50. Marlowe had already appeared in the Black Mask short stories that Chandler 'cannibalized' to assemble the novel. The 1946 Hawks film became the noir gold standard.

question: Raymond Chandler's most personal and longest Marlowe novel, widely regarded as his finest work, was published in what year?
context: The Long Goodbye released March 1953. Chandler had just lost his wife Cissy; the novel's themes of grief and friendship reflect that. Robert Altman's 1973 film adaptation was famously contemporary in setting.

question: Amazing Stories, the first English-language pulp magazine devoted entirely to science fiction, was founded by Hugo Gernsback in what year?
context: Amazing Stories launched April 1926. Gernsback coined 'scientifiction' (later 'science fiction') as a genre label. The magazine's annual Hugo Awards are named for him. He died in 1967.

question: John W. Campbell took over editing of Astounding Stories (later Astounding Science Fiction) in 1937, beginning what is now called the Golden Age of Science Fiction. In what year did he start?
context: Campbell became editor of Astounding October 1937. He nurtured Asimov, Heinlein, Sturgeon, van Vogt, and Clarke. Astounding renamed itself Analog in 1960. Campbell's editorial style — and pseudoscience flirtations later — left a long shadow.

question: Edgar Allan Poe — the American writer who invented modern detective fiction with 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' and shaped horror with 'The Tell-Tale Heart' — was born in what year?
context: Poe was born January 19, 1809 in Boston. He died October 7, 1849 in Baltimore under mysterious circumstances. His parents were traveling actors; both died before he was three.

question: Lord Dunsany — the Irish writer whose The Gods of Pegana directly inspired Lovecraft's Mythos and Tolkien's mythology — was born in what year?
context: Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany, was born July 24, 1878 in London. He published The Gods of Pegana at his own expense in 1905. Yeats championed his work. Dunsany died in 1957 — still writing.

question: R.A. Salvatore's drow ranger Drizzt Do'Urden — the dark elf renegade with the white panther Guenhwyvar — first appeared in what year?
context: Drizzt debuted in The Crystal Shard (TSR, 1988) — Salvatore's first published novel. The Forgotten Realms editor Mary Kirchoff asked Salvatore for an 'unusual companion'; he proposed a drow. Drizzt became Forgotten Realms's biggest character.

question: Alan Moore's Saga of the Swamp Thing run (1984-1987) was drawn primarily by two collaborators who alternated. Who were they?
answer: Stephen Bissette and John Totleben
choices: Stephen Bissette and John Totleben
Brian Bolland and Dave Gibbons
Dave McKean and Bill Sienkiewicz
George Pérez and Jerry Ordway
context: Bissette and Totleben drew most of Moore's Swamp Thing. Rick Veitch took over later in the run. The team's organic ink-and-watercolor style perfectly matched Moore's horror-naturalism stories.

question: Alex Ross — DC and Marvel's premier painted-realism artist of the 1990s — broke through with what Marvel limited series?
answer: Marvels (1994)
choices: Marvels (1994)
Kingdom Come (1996)
Earth X (1999)
Universe X (2000)
context: Marvels (1994) — written by Kurt Busiek — was Ross's first major work. The series's photographic-realism approach to classic Marvel moments became influential. Kingdom Come (1996) at DC was the follow-up.

question: Jack Kirby — co-creator of Captain America, the Fantastic Four, X-Men, Hulk, Thor, and dozens of other characters — was born in what year?
context: Kirby was born Jacob Kurtzberg August 28, 1917 in Manhattan. His prolific career began in the 1930s and continued until his death in 1994. He drew faster than anyone in the industry and reshaped American comics's visual vocabulary.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin film, the most-analyzed footage of an alleged Bigfoot ever shot, was filmed at Bluff Creek, California in what year?
context: Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed the 59.5-second 16mm reel on October 20, 1967. The female-coded subject — nicknamed 'Patty' — has been analyzed for decades. Both Patterson and Gimlin maintained authenticity until their deaths.

question: The word 'Bigfoot' as the name for the Pacific Northwest hominid cryptid was coined by a newspaper reporter responding to footprint sightings in Humboldt County, California. In what year?
context: Andrew Genzoli of the Humboldt Times coined the term October 5, 1958, after a road construction crew worker named Jerry Crew reported giant footprints. The native Salish term 'sasquatch' predates 'Bigfoot' by decades.

question: The most famous Loch Ness Monster photograph — the 'surgeon's photograph' showing a long-necked creature with a head emerging from the water — was published in the Daily Mail in what year?
context: The surgeon's photograph appeared in the Daily Mail April 21, 1934. Robert Kenneth Wilson, the photographer, was a London gynecologist. In 1994, Marmaduke Wetherell's stepson Christian Spurling confessed it was a hoax — a toy submarine with a sculpted head.

question: Mothman, the cryptid sightings around Point Pleasant, West Virginia that culminated in the Silver Bridge collapse a year later, were first reported in what year?
context: Mothman sightings began November 12, 1966. The Silver Bridge collapsed December 15, 1967 killing 46 people. John Keel's 1975 book and Richard Gere's 2002 film made the legend famous internationally.

question: The Silver Bridge connecting Point Pleasant, West Virginia to Ohio collapsed during rush hour, killing 46 people. Mothman lore attributes a warning to the cryptid's appearances. In what year did the bridge collapse?
context: The Silver Bridge fell December 15, 1967. The cause was a defective eye-bar in the suspension chain. The disaster, occurring 13 months after the first Mothman sighting, fed John Keel's later book.

question: The Jersey Devil — the cryptid of the New Jersey Pine Barrens supposedly born of an 18th-century mother's curse — has been reported since which century?
answer: Eighteenth century
choices: Eighteenth century
Seventeenth century
Nineteenth century
Twentieth century
context: The Jersey Devil legend dates to the 1730s — Mrs. Leeds's cursed 13th child became the creature. Sightings spiked in 1909, with reports across multiple New Jersey and Pennsylvania towns over a single week.

question: The chupacabra — the goat-blood-draining cryptid that became one of Latin American cryptozoology's defining figures — was first reported in Puerto Rico in what year?
context: Chupacabra sightings began in Canovanas, Puerto Rico in March 1995. Madelyne Tolentino's vivid description launched the legend. The creature has since been reported across Latin America, Mexico, and the southwestern U.S.

question: Amelia Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan disappeared on a flight across the Pacific in what year?
context: Earhart disappeared July 2, 1937 between Lae, New Guinea and Howland Island. Her Lockheed Electra was never definitively found. The TIGHAR expedition's Nikumaroro theory — that she crashed and survived briefly on an atoll — remains the leading speculative explanation.

question: The Dyatlov Pass incident, in which nine experienced Soviet hikers died under circumstances that fueled decades of speculation, occurred in what year?
context: The hikers died the night of February 1-2, 1959 in the northern Ural Mountains. A 2019-2021 Russian investigation concluded an avalanche, with conditions matching a 'slab' phenomenon — the most plausible explanation to date.

question: Flight 19, the U.S. Navy training flight of five TBM Avenger torpedo bombers that vanished over the Atlantic and gave rise to Bermuda Triangle legends, disappeared in what year?
context: Flight 19 vanished December 5, 1945, off the Florida coast. A PBM Mariner rescue aircraft also disappeared during the search, increasing the mystery. No wreckage was ever conclusively identified.

question: The term 'Bermuda Triangle' was coined in a 1964 magazine article by Vincent Gaddis, building on earlier writings about regional disappearances. Which magazine?
answer: Argosy
choices: Argosy
Reader's Digest
Esquire
Saturday Evening Post
context: Gaddis's article 'The Deadly Bermuda Triangle' ran in Argosy magazine February 1964. He expanded it into the 1965 book Invisible Horizons. Larry Kusche's 1975 The Bermuda Triangle Mystery — Solved demolished most of the original claims.

question: The Mary Celeste, the American merchant brigantine found drifting and abandoned in the Atlantic with all hands missing, was discovered in what year?
context: The Mary Celeste was found drifting December 5, 1872 by the British ship Dei Gratia. Captain Briggs, his wife and daughter, and seven crew were never found. The lifeboat was missing — but the ship was seaworthy.

question: The Flannan Isles lighthouse off Scotland was found abandoned by its three keepers — no log entries, no signs of violence, no bodies recovered — in what year?
context: The Flannan Isles incident happened December 15, 1900. The relief vessel found the lighthouse empty. Two oilskin coats were missing. Storm waves were the leading theory — but no one ever recovered the bodies.

question: The Roanoke Colony — the English settlement on present-day North Carolina that vanished with only the word 'CROATOAN' carved on a tree — disappeared in what year?
context: John White left Roanoke for England in 1587. When he returned in 1590, the colony was abandoned. The word 'CROATOAN' was carved on a tree. Theories range from absorption into nearby Native tribes to disease and famine.

question: D.B. Cooper hijacked Northwest Orient Flight 305 on Thanksgiving Eve, extorted 200,000 dollars, and parachuted from the plane somewhere over Washington or Oregon. In what year?
context: D.B. Cooper hijacked the 727 November 24, 1971. He parachuted from the rear stairs somewhere over the Pacific Northwest. 5,800 dollars of the marked bills were found by an eight-year-old on the Columbia River in 1980. Cooper has never been identified.

question: The Somerton Man case — an unidentified body found on Somerton Beach in Adelaide, Australia with a torn slip from a copy of the Rubaiyat reading 'Tamam Shud' — occurred in what year?
context: The Somerton Man was found December 1, 1948. The 'Tamam Shud' ('it is ended') phrase came from a Rubaiyat copy connected through a coded message. In 2022, DNA testing identified him as Carl Webb — but no motive emerged.

question: The Lead Masks Case — two Brazilian electronic technicians found dead on a hill near Niteroi with lead eye-masks and a coded note — happened in what year?
context: Manoel Pereira da Cruz and Miguel José Viana were found August 20, 1966. Their lead masks, expensive raincoats, and cryptic notebook entries (about UFOs) remain unexplained. The case is one of South America's most famous unsolved deaths.

question: The Black Dahlia — Elizabeth Short, the 22-year-old aspiring actress whose mutilated body was found in a Los Angeles vacant lot — was killed in what year?
context: Short's body was found January 15, 1947. Over 150 suspects have been investigated; the case remains unsolved. Her nickname 'Black Dahlia' was apparently a play on the 1946 film The Blue Dahlia.

question: Jack the Ripper, the Whitechapel killer of the late Victorian period, murdered his five 'canonical' victims in what year?
context: The five canonical Ripper victims were killed August-November 1888 in Whitechapel, London. The killer was never identified. Over 100 names have been proposed as suspects across the 130-plus years since.

question: The Voynich Manuscript — the illustrated codex written in an undeciphered language with strange botanical and astronomical diagrams — was created in which century, according to carbon dating?
answer: Fifteenth century
choices: Fifteenth century
Thirteenth century
Sixteenth century
Twelfth century
context: Carbon dating in 2009 placed the parchment at 1404-1438 CE. The manuscript was acquired by Wilfrid Voynich in 1912. Despite teams of professional cryptographers, no one has ever decoded it. It rests at Yale's Beinecke Library.

question: The Antikythera mechanism — the ancient Greek bronze geared device that calculates astronomical positions and eclipses — was discovered in what year?
context: Greek sponge divers found the Antikythera shipwreck in 1900. The mechanism was recovered May 17, 1901. Centuries of corrosion concealed its complexity. X-ray and CT scanning in the 2000s revealed its 30-plus gears.

question: Gobekli Tepe, the Turkish archaeological site whose megalithic enclosures predate Stonehenge by 6,000 years, dates to roughly what age?
answer: 11,500 years ago
choices: 11,500 years ago
8,500 years ago
13,500 years ago
9,500 years ago
context: Gobekli Tepe's earliest structures date to about 9500 BCE — pre-pottery, pre-agriculture. The site was discovered in 1963 but not excavated systematically until the 1990s by Klaus Schmidt. It rewrites the timeline of human civilization.

question: The Nazca Lines — geoglyphs visible only from above showing hummingbirds, monkeys, spiders, and other figures — are located in which country?
answer: Peru
choices: Peru
Mexico
Chile
Bolivia
context: The Nazca Lines were created by the Nazca culture between 500 BCE and 500 CE. They are located in southern Peru's Nazca Desert. The geometric and figurative geoglyphs cover over 50 square kilometers.

question: Easter Island's massive moai statues were 'walked' upright across the island by their builders, according to a 2012 experiment by archaeologist Carl Lipo and team. In what year was this physical demonstration?
context: Lipo and Terry Hunt's 2012 experiment successfully rocked a moai replica through coordinated rope-walking. The technique matched Rapa Nui oral tradition that the statues 'walked' to their platforms.

question: Stonehenge's interior 'bluestones' — the smaller, distinctively colored stones — were transported from a specific region. From where?
answer: Wales
choices: Wales
Scotland
Ireland
Cornwall
context: The bluestones were quarried from the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire, Wales — roughly 240 kilometers from Stonehenge. They were moved between 3000 and 2900 BCE. How they were transported remains debated.

question: Plato's account of Atlantis — the lost civilization that fell beneath the waves — appears in which of his dialogues?
answer: Timaeus and Critias
choices: Timaeus and Critias
Republic and Laws
Symposium and Phaedrus
Gorgias and Meno
context: Plato describes Atlantis in Timaeus (c. 360 BCE) and the unfinished Critias. The story was framed as told to Solon by Egyptian priests. Whether Plato intended the account as historical or allegorical is debated to this day.

question: Project MKUltra — the CIA's mind-control and chemical-interrogation program — officially operated under that name from when to when?
context: MKUltra ran from April 13, 1953 to 1973. The program tested LSD on civilians and military personnel, sometimes without consent. The Church Committee hearings in 1975 exposed the program after Director Helms ordered most files destroyed in 1973.

question: The Wow! signal — the 72-second narrowband radio signal received by Ohio State University's Big Ear telescope that has never been explained — was received in what year?
context: Jerry Ehman noted the signal August 15, 1977 and wrote 'Wow!' in the margin. The signal came from the direction of the Sagittarius constellation. No subsequent observation of the same coordinates has detected anything similar.

question: The Phoenix Lights — the V-formation of bright lights seen over Phoenix, Arizona and reported by thousands of witnesses including the state's governor — occurred in what year?
context: The Phoenix Lights appeared March 13, 1997. Governor Fife Symington publicly mocked the sightings, then revealed years later he had personally witnessed them. The U.S. Air Force ultimately identified them as illumination flares from a training mission.

question: Betty and Barney Hill, the New Hampshire couple whose alleged 1961 alien abduction became the first well-documented case of its kind, were reportedly abducted in what year?
context: The Hills reported their abduction September 19-20, 1961. Their hypnosis sessions with Benjamin Simon — recorded — became the template for hundreds of later abduction narratives. John Fuller's 1966 book made the case famous.

question: Travis Walton — the Arizona logger whose 1975 disappearance and five-day absence inspired the film Fire in the Sky — vanished from a logging crew encounter in what year?
context: Walton's disappearance happened November 5, 1975. He returned November 11. His coworkers' polygraph results were given mixed weight; the case became foundational for the abduction-claim genre. The 1993 film adaptation took liberties with his account.

question: Doug Bower and Dave Chorley confessed to creating crop circles in southern English fields starting in the late 1970s, using planks and ropes. In what year did they go public?
context: Bower and Chorley confessed in September 1991. They demonstrated their plank-and-rope technique on camera for British TV. Their confession explained the original wave of crop circles; copycats continued the practice after.

question: Skinwalker Ranch in Utah — the notorious paranormal site that became a media franchise — was purchased by the Sherman family in what year?
context: Terry and Gwen Sherman bought the ranch in 1994. Their reports of strange phenomena prompted Robert Bigelow to buy the property in 1996 for NIDS investigations. The ranch passed to Brandon Fugal in 2016 — and to the Skinwalker Ranch History Channel show.

question: Slender Man, the tall faceless internet horror figure that began as a Something Awful forum image post, was created in what year?
context: Eric Knudsen posted the first Slender Man images June 10, 2009 on Something Awful. The character became the template for modern internet folklore. The 2014 Wisconsin attempted murder case ('Slender Man stabbing') brought the meme into mainstream news.

question: The SCP Foundation — the collaborative-fiction wiki of fictional contained anomalies, with SCP-173 'The Sculpture' as the founding entry — began as a wiki in what year?
context: The SCP wiki began January 2008. Moto42's original SCP-173 image was a 2004 sculpture by Izumi Kato. The site has grown to host thousands of contained 'anomalies' written by anonymous and pseudonymous contributors.

question: The Backrooms — the internet horror concept of an endlessly nested, yellow-carpeted, fluorescent-lit liminal space — originated from a 4chan image post in what year?
context: The Backrooms image was posted on 4chan's /x/ board May 12, 2019. The concept spawned countless creepypasta entries, a YouTube series by Kane Pixels, and an A24 film deal. The 'Level 0' yellow office is the foundational image.

question: JonBenet Ramsey, the six-year-old child beauty queen whose unsolved Christmas-night murder gripped American media, was killed in what year in Colorado?
context: JonBenet was found December 26, 1996 in the family's Boulder, Colorado basement. The case remains formally unsolved despite multiple investigations and the family's vindication from the original 'umbrella of suspicion' decades later.

question: Madeleine McCann, the three-year-old British girl who vanished from a holiday resort in Portugal, disappeared in what year?
context: Madeleine vanished May 3, 2007 from Praia da Luz, Portugal. The case became one of the most heavily covered missing-persons stories of the 21st century. German police identified a primary suspect in 2020; the investigation remains open.

question: Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370, the Boeing 777 carrying 239 people that vanished without explanation, disappeared in what year?
context: MH370 disappeared March 8, 2014 between Kuala Lumpur and Beijing. Debris washed up on Indian Ocean beaches; the wreckage was never definitively located. The 2018 official report concluded with no definitive cause.

question: Oak Island, the Nova Scotia island where treasure hunters have searched for centuries for a rumored buried fortune — the original 'money pit' was dug in what year?
context: The Oak Island money pit was first reported in 1795 by Daniel McGinnis. Six men have died in subsequent excavations. The History Channel series The Curse of Oak Island (since 2014) has documented modern attempts.

question: Ogopogo, the Canadian lake monster cryptid, supposedly inhabits which lake?
answer: Okanagan
choices: Okanagan
Champlain
Geneva
Erie
context: Ogopogo lives in Lake Okanagan in British Columbia. The legend predates European contact — the local Syilx tradition includes N'ha-a-itk, a 'spirit of the lake.' Modern reports began in the 1860s.

question: Champ, the North American lake monster cryptid sometimes called 'America's Loch Ness,' inhabits which lake on the New York-Vermont border?
answer: Lake Champlain
choices: Lake Champlain
Lake George
Lake Sebago
Lake Memphremagog
context: Champ has been reported since the 1800s. Burlington, Vermont and Port Henry, New York both claim local 'protection' for the cryptid. Samuel de Champlain may have sighted something similar in 1609 — though his account is disputed.

question: The Bunyip, the lake-and-swamp-dwelling monster of indigenous Australian folklore, is associated with which country?
answer: Australia
choices: Australia
New Zealand
Papua New Guinea
Indonesia
context: The Bunyip features in Aboriginal storytelling across many Australian language groups. European settlers in the 19th century occasionally reported sightings. The creature is described variously as having a dog-like face, horns, flippers, or scales.

question: The Wendigo — the cannibal-spirit cryptid of the Great Lakes region — originates in the traditions of which First Nations people?
answer: Algonquin peoples
choices: Algonquin peoples
Iroquois Confederacy
Sioux nations
Cherokee Nation
context: The Wendigo appears in Algonquin oral tradition — Anishinaabe, Cree, Innu, Naskapi, and others. The being represents the spiritual danger of cannibalism, gluttony, and selfishness. 'Wendigo psychosis' was used by 19th-century outside observers to label related conditions.

question: The Skinwalker — the malevolent shapeshifting witch of southwestern Native American tradition — comes from which culture?
answer: Navajo
choices: Navajo
Hopi
Apache
Pueblo
context: The Skinwalker (yee naaldlooshii) is a powerful taboo subject in Navajo culture. Many Navajo people consider the name itself dangerous to speak. Skinwalker Ranch's name and lore drew on this tradition but does not represent traditional Navajo belief.

question: The female-coded Bigfoot subject in the Patterson-Gimlin film, nicknamed 'Patty,' was estimated by Patterson and analysts to be roughly how tall?
answer: Seven feet tall
choices: Seven feet tall
Five feet tall
Nine feet tall
Four feet tall
context: Patty was estimated at 7-7.5 feet tall by Patterson based on filmed ground distance markers. Subsequent analysts have ranged the estimate from 6'4 to 8'. The film remains the most-discussed piece of cryptid footage ever shot.

question: The Dover Demon — a creature reportedly seen briefly by teenagers in 1977 with a smooth orange-skinned body and tendril-like fingers — was sighted in which state?
answer: Massachusetts
choices: Massachusetts
Connecticut
Vermont
New Hampshire
context: The Dover Demon was reported in Dover, Massachusetts on April 21-22, 1977. Three separate witness groups described it independently. Loren Coleman, a cryptozoologist, named and publicized the case.

question: The Yowie — the alleged hairy hominid of Australia, similar to Bigfoot or the Yeti — is a cryptid of which country?
answer: Australia
choices: Australia
New Zealand
Papua New Guinea
Indonesia
context: Yowie reports trace back to early colonial Australia. Aboriginal traditions across multiple language groups feature hairy man-creatures by various names. The 'Yowie' name was popularized in the late 19th century.

question: John Keel's 1975 book about the Mothman sightings and related strange events around Point Pleasant, West Virginia, became the source for the 2002 film. What was Keel's book called?
answer: The Mothman Prophecies
choices: The Mothman Prophecies
Mothman Rising
Eyes in the Trees
Beneath the Bridge
context: Keel published The Mothman Prophecies in 1975. The book combined Keel's reporting on West Virginia sightings with broader UFO and paranormal claims. Mark Pellington's 2002 film starring Richard Gere followed Keel's narrative loosely.

question: Lizzie Borden — the famous Massachusetts woman acquitted of axe-murdering her father and stepmother in 1892 — was tried in what year?
context: Borden's trial began June 5, 1893 in New Bedford. She was acquitted June 20. Despite the verdict, public opinion never fully cleared her. The Andrew Borden house in Fall River is now a popular bed-and-breakfast.

question: The moai — the massive stone statues of Easter Island — are located on what is officially a territory of which country?
answer: Chile
choices: Chile
Argentina
Peru
Ecuador
context: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) became a Chilean territory in 1888. The 887 moai date from c. 1250-1500 CE. Most stand 4-5 meters tall. The largest, Paro, stood 10 meters and weighed 82 tons.

question: The Rake, one of the early creepypasta entities — a pale humanoid creature crouching at the foot of beds — originated on online forum posts in what year?
context: The Rake's foundational thread appeared in late 2005 on 4chan's /b/ board. The creature has since been featured in countless creepypasta stories, indie horror games, and the SCP Foundation universe.

question: The Popobawa — a one-eyed bat-demon cryptid that allegedly attacks people in their sleep — is part of folklore in which East African region?
answer: Zanzibar
choices: Zanzibar
Madagascar
Mozambique
Seychelles
context: Popobawa reports cluster in Zanzibar and Pemba. The legend has surfaced in waves through the 1970s, 1995, and 2007. Some scholars connect it to sleep paralysis combined with political-tension periods.

question: The Thunderbird — the giant bird cryptid whose wingbeats produce thunder and whose eye-flashes produce lightning — appears across which broad cultural region?
answer: North American Native traditions
choices: North American Native traditions
Polynesian seafaring tradition
Sub-Saharan African tradition
Aboriginal Australian tradition
context: The Thunderbird is central to many Plains, Northwest Coast, and Great Lakes Native traditions. Each nation has specific names and stories. The bird is often a heroic figure, occasionally a warning.

question: The 'Lincoln-Kennedy coincidences' — the list of supposed parallels between the two assassinated presidents — became a famous trivia item in American folklore. Roughly how many points did the original list contain?
answer: About a dozen
choices: About a dozen
About 50
About 30
About 100
context: The original Lincoln-Kennedy list circulated in newspapers and magazines from 1964 onward, growing over the years. The 'coincidences' (Lincoln elected 1860, Kennedy elected 1960; both shot in the head; etc.) range from genuine parallels to dubious ones.

question: The Vanishing Hitchhiker — the urban-legend ghost who climbs into a passing motorist's car and disappears before reaching her destination — is one of the most widely documented modern American legends. What folklorist documented it definitively?
answer: Jan Harold Brunvand
choices: Jan Harold Brunvand
John Keel
Loren Coleman
Bernard Mergen
context: Brunvand documented dozens of variants in The Vanishing Hitchhiker (1981). The legend predates automobile travel — earlier 'phantom traveler' versions appear in 19th-century folklore.

question: The 'Mandela Effect' — the term coined for shared false memories like the spelling of 'Berenstain Bears' — was popularized by paranormal researcher Fiona Broome in what year?
context: Broome coined the term in 2009 after discussing her false memory of Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s. The term spread through Reddit and conspiracy circles in the early 2010s. Internet phenomenon explanations followed.

question: The Black-Eyed Kids (or 'BEKs') — the modern American legend of pale children with all-black eyes who beg to be let into homes — began with Brian Bethel's 1996 internet post. In what year was the original story?
context: Bethel's Black-Eyed Kids encounter was posted to a Usenet newsgroup in 1996. The narrative — meeting two boys at a movie theater begging for a ride — gained massive online traction through the 2000s.

question: The Philadelphia Experiment — the urban legend claiming the U.S. Navy made the destroyer USS Eldridge invisible (and possibly teleportable) — supposedly took place in what year?
context: The Philadelphia Experiment was supposedly conducted October 28, 1943. The story originated from a 1955 series of cryptic letters to UFO researcher Morris Jessup. No Navy records support any 'invisibility' research. The 1984 film popularized the legend.

question: The 'Tartaria' theory — the modern internet conspiracy framework reinterpreting 19th-century architecture as evidence of a vanished super-civilization — emerged primarily on which platform?
answer: YouTube
choices: YouTube
Reddit
TikTok
4chan
context: Tartaria theories spread through YouTube documentaries in the late 2010s. The conspiracy mixes Russian historical revisionism (Anatoly Fomenko's New Chronology), architectural mysticism, and Atlantis-style mythologizing.

question: The Antikythera Mechanism, the ancient Greek geared calculator recovered from a 1901 shipwreck, dates to roughly which century BCE?
answer: Second century BCE
choices: Second century BCE
Fifth century BCE
Fourth century BCE
First century BCE
context: The mechanism dates to roughly 100-150 BCE. Its complexity was so advanced that nothing comparable would appear until the 14th century CE. Cicero's writings hint at similar devices made by Posidonius and Archimedes.

question: The Wendigo of Algonquin tradition is, in many tellings, associated with a specific extreme behavior — one so taboo that the creature embodies its punishment. What behavior?
answer: Cannibalism
choices: Cannibalism
Treachery
Cowardice
Adultery
context: The Wendigo's cannibalism connection runs deep in Algonquin oral tradition — it is what a person becomes if they eat human flesh under starvation. Modern horror has expanded the Wendigo's terror into broader supernatural threats.

question: The Atacama Giant — the largest prehistoric anthropomorphic geoglyph in the world, carved into the side of a hill — is located in which country?
answer: Chile
choices: Chile
Peru
Bolivia
Argentina
context: The Atacama Giant is 86 meters tall and was likely created between 1000 and 1400 CE. It served as an astronomical calendar marking solstices for the Atacameno people. The figure was rediscovered in modern times in the 1960s.

question: Robert Schoch — a Boston University geologist — proposed in 1991 that the Great Sphinx of Giza showed weathering from heavy rainfall, suggesting the monument is older than mainstream archaeology dates. Older by roughly how much?
answer: Several thousand years older
choices: Several thousand years older
About 500 years older
Tens of thousands of years older
Hundreds of thousands older
context: Schoch's water-erosion hypothesis dates the Sphinx to perhaps 7000 BCE or earlier — millennia before the Old Kingdom Egyptian civilization. Mainstream Egyptologists reject the hypothesis; the debate continues among geologists and archaeologists.

question: The Valley of the Kings — the burial site of New Kingdom Egyptian pharaohs including Tutankhamun and Ramses the Great — is in which modern country?
answer: Egypt
choices: Egypt
Sudan
Libya
Israel
context: The Valley of the Kings sits on the west bank of the Nile across from Luxor. Howard Carter's discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922 made the site world-famous. Sixty-three known tombs cluster in the Valley.

question: The Kraken — the legendary giant cephalopod of Norse seafaring tradition — is most commonly associated with the waters around which European country?
answer: Norway
choices: Norway
Greenland
Iceland
Faroe Islands
context: The Kraken legend dates to the 13th century Norse sagas. Erik Pontoppidan's 1752 Natural History of Norway provided the modern compilation. The legend likely reflects encounters with real giant squid (Architeuthis) found in deep Atlantic waters.

question: The Tikbalang — the horse-headed forest spirit of folklore — is part of which country's traditional storytelling?
answer: Philippines
choices: Philippines
Indonesia
Vietnam
Thailand
context: The Tikbalang is a tall trickster spirit in Filipino folklore. Travelers crossing forest paths at night were said to be lost in confusion if they offended one. The creature appears in pre-Hispanic Tagalog and Bicol traditions.

question: The Aluxes — small mischievous spirit beings of Yucatec Mayan folklore who must be appeased by farmers building little stone houses — are part of which country's tradition?
answer: Mexico
choices: Mexico
Guatemala
Belize
Honduras
context: Aluxes appear throughout Yucatec Mayan folklore in Mexico. Modern Yucatec farmers still build kahtal alux (alux houses) on field corners as offerings. The beings supposedly protect crops if treated well.

question: Zemis — the Taino ancestor and nature spirits represented in carved stone, wood, and bone figures — were central to which Caribbean culture?
answer: Taino people
choices: Taino people
Inca people
Aztec people
Maya people
