question: *Captain N: The Game Master* (1989-91) was an NBC Saturday-morning cartoon about a kid named Kevin Keene pulled into Videoland to lead a team of Nintendo game heroes — Mega Man, Simon Belmont, Pit, and an oddly-drawn Princess Lana. How many seasons did it run?

question: *X-Men: The Animated Series* aired on Fox Kids beginning in October 1992. Its bold theme song (composed by Ron Wasserman) and detailed adaptation of comics arcs — Dark Phoenix, Days of Future Past, the Phalanx — built a generation of fans. How many seasons did it run?

question: *Batman: The Animated Series* premiered in September 1992 on Fox Kids. Its 'dark deco' visual style — black paper backgrounds painted with light, Art Deco architecture, jazz horn cues — was developed by which pair of producer-artists?

question: *Spider-Man: The Animated Series* aired on Fox Kids from November 1994 to January 1998. Across five seasons (65 episodes) it adapted everything from the Symbiote saga to Madame Web. Who voiced the lead?

question: *DuckTales* — the Disney TV animated series with the famous 'Woo-oo!' theme song — premiered in syndicated daily reruns in September 1987. It was the first attempt at the now-vast Disney TV animation slate. What year did the original run end?

context: The original *DuckTales* ran 100 episodes plus the 1990 theatrical film *DuckTales: Treasure of the Lost Lamp*. Carl Barks's original Scrooge McDuck comics from the 1950s-60s were the primary source material for most plotlines.

question: *Tiny Toon Adventures* (1990) was a Warner Bros. animated TV series that introduced a younger generation of Looney Tunes-inspired characters: Buster, Babs, Plucky, Hampton, Fifi. It was produced by an unusual collaboration. Who was the executive producer?

question: *Animaniacs* (1993-98) — the variety-show animated series with the Warner siblings Yakko, Wakko and Dot, plus the Pinky-and-the-Brain segments — won eight Emmy Awards across its run. How many episodes did its original Fox Kids/WB era produce?

question: *The Ren & Stimpy Show* premiered on Nickelodeon in August 1991 as one of the network's first three 'Nicktoons' (alongside *Rugrats* and *Doug*). Its creator was a Canadian animator whose work pushed the limits of children's TV. Who?

context: Kricfalusi was fired from the show in 1992 over delivery problems. His company Spumco produced the early episodes; Nickelodeon Animation Studio took over after the firing, splitting fans on which era was 'real' *Ren & Stimpy*.

question: *Rugrats* premiered on Nickelodeon in August 1991, alongside *Ren & Stimpy* and *Doug*, as one of the network's first three 'Nicktoons'. question: Rankin/Bass Productions, a New York animation house, produced the Christmas-special staples of mid-20th-century American TV using stop-motion puppet animation (then called 'Animagic'). The first hit special, narrated by Burl Ives as Sam the Snowman, aired in what year?
answer: 1964, premiering *Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer* on NBC in December
choices: 1964, premiering *Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer* on NBC in December
1962, the same year as Rankin/Bass's first feature *The New Adventures of Pinocchio*
1969, the same year as *Frosty the Snowman* (which actually came that year)
1974, the same year as *The Year Without a Santa Claus* with the Miser brothers
context: *Rudolph* has aired every Christmas season since 1964 — over 60 consecutive years on American network TV as of 2024. The Animagic animation was done by Tadahito Mochinaga's studio MOM Production in Tokyo.

question: *A Charlie Brown Christmas* was the first animated Peanuts television special. It featured kid voice actors actually voicing the kids, a jazz score by pianist Vince Guaraldi, and a long climactic recitation from Luke 2 by Linus. What year did it first air?
answer: 1965, premiering on CBS on December 9 of that year
choices: 1965, premiering on CBS on December 9 of that year
1962, the same year Schulz's strip 'Peanuts' marked its 12th anniversary
1970, four years after the cartoon series 'Charlie Brown's All Stars' first aired
1968, the same year Schulz's animation contract was renewed
context: Charles Schulz reportedly insisted on the Linus speech and refused to cut it. CBS executives feared the special would flop. It drew 45 percent of the American TV audience and won an Emmy and a Peabody.

question: *Garfield's Halloween Adventure* (1985), the animated TV special based on Jim Davis's comic strip, featured an unusual voice cameo as the ghost-story-telling old pirate. The voice was the last work the actor recorded before his death the following year. Who?
answer: Orson Welles? No — actually Lorenzo Music & C. Lindsay Workman were main; for the OLD PIRATE the voice was C. Lindsay Workman
choices: Orson Welles? No — actually Lorenzo Music & C. Lindsay Workman were main; for the OLD PIRATE the voice was C. Lindsay Workman
Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield for the entire 1980s Halloween, Christmas and other specials
Mel Blanc voiced one of the trick-or-treaters in the kids' costumes
Don Knotts narrated the bedtime story sequence at the start of the show
context: Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield from 1982 to 1991. He was so identified with the character that Bill Murray, in the 2004 live-action film, recorded his lines partly imitating Music's cadence in tribute to his predecessor.

question: *The Nightmare Before Christmas* (1993) is often called 'Tim Burton's' film — but Burton wrote the original story and produced. The director (his collaborator on multiple stop-motion films afterward) was credited separately. Who actually directed?
answer: Henry Selick, who would later direct 'James and the Giant Peach' (1996)
choices: Henry Selick, who would later direct 'James and the Giant Peach' (1996)
Mike Johnson, who would later co-direct Burton's 'Corpse Bride' (2005)
Tim Burton himself, who has long been listed as director in marketing
Mark Romanek, the music-video director with a similar visual style
context: Selick's previous credit was the MTV pilot 'Slow Bob in the Lower Dimensions'. Burton had developed the story in the early 1980s while still at Disney — it sat unmade for almost a decade before Disney's Touchstone label agreed to produce.

question: *National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation* (1989) — Chevy Chase as Clark Griswold, the dying tree, the disastrous lights, Cousin Eddie's RV — was the third 'Vacation' film. Who wrote the screenplay (also based on a short story by the same author)?
answer: John Hughes, who had also written the prior two 'Vacation' films
choices: John Hughes, who had also written the prior two 'Vacation' films
Harold Ramis, who directed and wrote the 1983 original 'Vacation'
Jeremiah S. Chechik, who directed the 1989 film but wrote no draft
Chevy Chase himself, who has long been credited as a co-writer of 'Caddyshack'
context: Hughes's 1980 short story 'Christmas '59' was the basis. Chechik directed; Hughes wrote and produced. The shopping-mall opening, the squirrel-in-the-tree gag, the SWAT raid: all Hughes. The film flopped on release and grew into a perennial through home video.

question: *Home Alone* (1990) was directed by a young filmmaker who had previously directed *Adventures in Babysitting* (1987) and would later direct the first two *Harry Potter* films. Who?
answer: Chris Columbus, who had been mentored by John Hughes on his first features
choices: Chris Columbus, who had been mentored by John Hughes on his first features
John Hughes himself, who wrote the *Home Alone* screenplay but did not direct
Joe Dante, who directed 'Gremlins' (1984) for Spielberg's Amblin
Howard Deutch, who directed Hughes's 'Pretty in Pink' (1986)
context: Hughes wrote *Home Alone* in nine days. The film opened against major competition in November 1990 and stayed at number one for twelve weeks — a record at the time. Macaulay Culkin was ten years old.

question: *Die Hard* (1988), Bruce Willis as John McClane in Nakatomi Plaza, has been the subject of a recurring online debate: is it a Christmas movie? The film is set on Christmas Eve and features 'Let It Snow' over the closing credits. Who directed?
answer: John McTiernan, who would direct 'The Hunt for Red October' in 1990
choices: John McTiernan, who would direct 'The Hunt for Red October' in 1990
Renny Harlin, who would direct 'Die Hard 2' two years later
John Carpenter, who declined the project to make 'They Live' instead
James Cameron, who had finished 'The Abyss' just before *Die Hard*
context: *Die Hard* was based on a 1979 novel, *Nothing Lasts Forever* by Roderick Thorp — itself a sequel to a 1966 thriller. Cameron co-wrote a *Die Hard 2*-related project but neither directed nor produced the original 1988 film.

question: *Pokemon Red and Blue*, the launch Game Boy titles in the West, released in North America in September 1998. The Japanese version had launched two years earlier, in February 1996, on the Game Boy under a different name pairing. What was it?
answer: *Pokemon Red and Green* (with Blue added later as a Japan-only re-release)
choices: *Pokemon Red and Green* (with Blue added later as a Japan-only re-release)
*Pokemon Yellow and Crystal* (the launch pair on the Japanese Game Boy)
*Pokemon Gold and Silver* (the original 1996 Japanese launch pair)
*Pokemon Red and Yellow* (the only original 1996 Japanese launch versions)
context: Game Freak's Satoshi Tajiri pitched 'Capsule Monsters' to Nintendo in 1990. Development stretched six years on a tiny team. In Japan, Green replaced Blue at launch; Blue was a Japanese fanclub-distributed revision used as the US launch's basis.

question: The original *Pokemon* anime English dub featured an end-credits song called the Pokerap, which named every Pokemon currently in the franchise. The original Pokerap covered exactly one full generation of creatures. How many?
answer: 151 Pokemon, the original Kanto generation introduced in Red and Blue
choices: 151 Pokemon, the original Kanto generation introduced in Red and Blue
251 Pokemon, all the Pokemon from Kanto through the new Johto region
100 Pokemon, an abridged version sung over a faster instrumental
200 Pokemon, the version produced for the second North American season
context: The Pokerap aired during the Indigo League season (1998-99 dub run). When Generation 2 added new Pokemon, the song was redone as the Pokerap 'GS' to cover the new 251 — but most fans remember the original Kanto list.

question: The Pokemon Trading Card Game was released in English in January 1999. Its first set — known as Base Set — contained 102 cards, with the most iconic card (Charizard, holographic) instantly becoming a playground status symbol. Who localized it for the US?
answer: Wizards of the Coast, which held the license until late 2003
choices: Wizards of the Coast, which held the license until late 2003
Topps, which had handled most American card-game licensing of the era
Decipher, which had also held the 'Star Trek' card-game license
Upper Deck, the trading-card company best known for sports cards
context: Wizards of the Coast also held *Magic: the Gathering* at the time. A holographic Charizard from the unlimited Base Set could sell for tens of dollars on the schoolyard in 1999 — a first-edition shadowless holo went for over $400,000 at peak in 2021.

question: *Dragon Ball*, Akira Toriyama's manga about a boy raised in the mountains with a magic staff, began serialization in 'Weekly Shonen Jump' in 1984. The story's earliest framing was a comic re-imagining of an ancient Chinese novel. Which?
answer: *Journey to the West* (16th-century, attributed to Wu Cheng'en)
choices: *Journey to the West* (16th-century, attributed to Wu Cheng'en)
*Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (14th-century, attributed to Luo Guanzhong)
*Water Margin* (14th-century, attributed to Shi Nai'an)
*Dream of the Red Chamber* (18th-century, attributed to Cao Xueqin)
context: Goku was a clear analog to Sun Wukong the Monkey King. The early *Dragon Ball* manga had a far lighter, comedic tone than the famous Saiyan saga onward — Toriyama himself acknowledged he didn't expect the series to run as long as it did.

question: In *Dragon Ball Z*'s Namek arc, Goku transforms for the first time into the legendary Super Saiyan during a fight against the alien tyrant Frieza. The transformation was a fan-shocking moment because the legend had been treated as myth. About how many manga chapters were dedicated to the buildup before it occurs?
answer: Roughly twelve chapters into the Frieza arc, in chapter 317 of the manga overall
choices: Roughly twelve chapters into the Frieza arc, in chapter 317 of the manga overall
Roughly one or two chapters of dedicated buildup, in the middle of the saga
Around fifty chapters of buildup, starting at the beginning of the Saiyan saga
Around five chapters, immediately after the Saiyans arrive on Earth
context: Toriyama's pacing in the Frieza arc was famously slow on weekly serialization — a single fight could span ten weeks. The transformation became a template for the entire franchise; later arcs would repeat the structure with new tiers (Super Saiyan 2, 3, Blue).

question: *Blade Runner* (1982) opens on a test scene: Holden is interrogating Leon with rapid emotional questions while a strange device on the desk reads the subject's eye dilation, blush response and breathing. What is the test called?
answer: The Voight-Kampff test, used to distinguish replicants from humans
choices: The Voight-Kampff test, used to distinguish replicants from humans
The Turing test, the philosophical test of indistinguishable machine intelligence
The Bayesian test, a probabilistic interrogation method from the 1950s
The Rorschach test, the ink-blot inkblot interpretation diagnostic tool
context: The Voight-Kampff was Philip K. Dick's invention in *Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?*. Hampton Fancher's screenplay kept the test largely intact. The device on the desk in the film was a working physical prop — its eye-tracker lens visibly dilates on screen.

question: *Rurouni Kenshin* (1994-99), the manga by Nobuhiro Watsuki, follows Himura Kenshin, a former government assassin from the bakumatsu period, now wandering Japan a decade later with a reverse-blade sword and a vow against killing. What real Japanese historical era is its setting?
answer: The early Meiji era, roughly 1878-1882 in the manga's framing
choices: The early Meiji era, roughly 1878-1882 in the manga's framing
The late Sengoku period, the warring-states era of the late 1500s
The middle Edo period, around the time of the Tokugawa shogun Ieyoshi
The post-war Showa period, roughly 1947-1952 under American occupation
context: Kenshin's signature sakabato (reverse-blade katana) has its cutting edge on the inside. The Kyoto arc, considered the manga's peak, follows the assassin Shishio Makoto and his plan to overthrow the new Meiji government from the imperial city.

question: *Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba* (2019 onward), the anime adapting Koyoharu Gotouge's manga, became one of the most successful anime franchises of the late 2010s and 2020s. Its lush, theatrical animation was produced by a Tokyo studio known for its high-budget action work. Which one?
answer: ufotable, the studio founded in 2000 known for the 'Fate' adaptations
choices: ufotable, the studio founded in 2000 known for the 'Fate' adaptations
Bones, the studio known for 'Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood'
MAPPA, the studio of 'Attack on Titan' Final Season and 'Jujutsu Kaisen'
WIT Studio, the original 'Attack on Titan' animation house
context: ufotable's blending of 2D character animation with 3D backgrounds (a so-called 'digital composite' approach) became the *Demon Slayer* visual signature. The studio had previously gained recognition for the 'Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works' adaptation.

question: *Attack on Titan* (manga began 2009, anime began 2013) is set in a world where humanity lives behind three massive concentric walls to keep out giant humanoid creatures called Titans. The walls each have a real-world German-style name. What is the OUTERMOST of the three?
answer: Wall Maria — the outermost wall, named after a Christian female figure
choices: Wall Maria — the outermost wall, named after a Christian female figure
Wall Rose — the middle wall, the second of the three concentric defenses
Wall Sina — the innermost wall, where the royalty and nobility reside
Wall Hermes — actually does not exist in the series at any point
context: Mangaka Hajime Isayama based the walls on medieval European fortified cities. The opening battle of the manga (and the anime's first episode) involves the breach of Wall Maria — without spoiling who is responsible.

question: *JoJo's Bizarre Adventure*, Hirohiko Araki's manga from 1987 onward, was a fight-action series that took an unusual turn in its third arc: instead of pure martial arts, characters manifested 'Stands' — psychic spirit-projections with unique powers. What is the name of Part 3?
answer: Stardust Crusaders, which introduced Stands as a series mechanic in 1989
choices: Stardust Crusaders, which introduced Stands as a series mechanic in 1989
Phantom Blood, the original 1987 arc set in Victorian England
Battle Tendency, the 1987-88 arc starring Joseph Joestar against vampires
Diamond is Unbreakable, the 1992-95 arc set in the town of Morioh
context: Stands were named after rock songs (Star Platinum, Magician's Red, Hierophant Green). Araki has explained that Stands replaced the earlier 'Hamon' (Ripple) energy as a way to give each character a visually distinct fight-power without retreading martial-arts mechanics.

question: *Yu Yu Hakusho* (1990-94 manga, 1992-94 anime) follows a 14-year-old delinquent named Yusuke Urameshi, who becomes a Spirit World detective. Who are his three closest partners in the Dark Tournament arc?
answer: Kazuma Kuwabara (oaf), Kurama (kitsune mage), Hiei (sword demon)
choices: Kazuma Kuwabara (oaf), Kurama (kitsune mage), Hiei (sword demon)
Genkai (master), Botan (oar), and Koenma (Spirit World prince)
Toguro (older brother), Yomi (demon king), and Sensui (final boss)
Joey (paramedic), Jin (wind master), and Touya (ice master)
context: Yusuke's revival in the first arc — a near-death ordeal where he must prove he should be revived — earned him his Spirit World assignment. The Dark Tournament arc (volumes 8-13) is widely cited as one of the finest tournament arcs in manga history.

question: *Mobile Suit Gundam* (1979), the founding 'real robot' anime, was created by a director who treated war and mecha as inherently tragic — a departure from earlier super-robot anime. Who directed and largely wrote the original series?
answer: Yoshiyuki Tomino, who famously is nicknamed 'Kill 'Em All Tomino' by fans
choices: Yoshiyuki Tomino, who famously is nicknamed 'Kill 'Em All Tomino' by fans
Hayao Miyazaki, who would later direct 'Castle in the Sky' (1986)
Mamoru Oshii, who would later direct 'Patlabor' (1989) and GitS (1995)
Leiji Matsumoto, the creator of 'Space Battleship Yamato' (1974)
context: Tomino's storyboards reportedly drove down the show's toy sales in 1979 by killing off so many characters. The franchise nonetheless became Bandai's largest property. The Universal Century timeline (Amuro Ray, Char Aznable) is the original continuity.

question: *Naruto*'s Team 7 is led by jonin Kakashi Hatake. Its three twelve-year-old genin members are Naruto himself and two others — a stoic boy with a tragic backstory, and a pink-haired medic in training. Who are the other two?
answer: Sasuke Uchiha (rival) and Sakura Haruno (medic, pink hair)
choices: Sasuke Uchiha (rival) and Sakura Haruno (medic, pink hair)
Hinata Hyuga (introvert) and Shino Aburame (insect-user kekkei genkai)
Shikamaru Nara (strategist) and Choji Akimichi (giant)
Neji Hyuga (cousin) and Tenten (weapons specialist)
context: Team 7 is one of three Konoha rookie teams introduced in the manga's first arc. Sakura was originally written as the protagonist's first love interest; Kishimoto has spoken publicly about regretting how he wrote her arc in later volumes.

question: *Bleach* (manga 2001, anime 2004-12) follows Ichigo Kurosaki, a teenager who becomes a Soul Reaper. Soul Reapers wield blade-form spirits called zanpakuto, which have a sealed form, a 'released' form (Shikai), and a final form (Bankai). Who created the series?
answer: Tite Kubo, born Noriaki Kubo, who began the manga in 'Shonen Jump' in 2001
choices: Tite Kubo, born Noriaki Kubo, who began the manga in 'Shonen Jump' in 2001
Eiichiro Oda, the creator of 'One Piece' in 'Shonen Jump' from 1997
Kentaro Yabuki, the creator of 'Black Cat' in 'Shonen Jump' from 2000
Kazue Kato, the creator of 'Blue Exorcist' in 'Jump Square' from 2009
context: Kubo finished the manga's 686 chapters in August 2016. The 'Thousand-Year Blood War' final arc was not animated until 2022; Studio Pierrot returned to finish it after a decade gap, with most of the original Japanese voice cast.

question: Evangelion Unit 01, piloted by Shinji Ikari in *Neon Genesis Evangelion* (1995), is not a robot but a biological cyborg with a soul. The Eva Units are revealed across the series to derive in part from a particular source. Without spoiling the late-series reveal, what is the in-universe building they are housed in called?
answer: The Geofront — a massive subterranean cavern beneath Tokyo-3
choices: The Geofront — a massive subterranean cavern beneath Tokyo-3
The Citadel — a Berlin-modeled fortress in Hideaki Anno's working notes
The Pyramid — Gendo Ikari's private terminal in the original storyboards
The Magi — the supercomputer triad in NERV's command bunker
context: Tokyo-3 itself, the show's setting, is a deliberately ordinary modern city — the Geofront below it is the secret hidden by the surface. The series uses scale dramatically: the Evas are 50 meters tall, the Geofront kilometers across.

question: *My Hero Academia* (manga 2014, anime 2016) opens with Izuku Midoriya, a 'Quirkless' (powerless) boy in a world where 80% of humans have superpowers. The hero he idolizes — All Might — possesses a unique inheritable power. What is it called?
answer: One for All, an inheritable power passed from holder to holder
choices: One for All, an inheritable power passed from holder to holder
All for One, the rival villain's power to take and give other powers
Decay, the destructive power held by All Might's grandson
Permeation, the intangibility power held by Mirio Togata in 1-A
context: All Might is the eighth holder of One for All. The arc structure of MHA, with a heroic mentor passing power to a young protagonist, draws explicitly from American Spider-Man comics — Kohei Horikoshi has cited Spider-Man as a primary influence.

question: *Fist of the North Star* (Hokuto no Ken), the post-apocalyptic martial-arts manga, debuted in 'Weekly Shonen Jump' in 1983. Its protagonist Kenshiro uses pressure-point strikes to make his opponents explode from within. The manga ran for five years. What two creators worked on it?
answer: Buronson (writer) and Tetsuo Hara (artist), a manga writer-artist team
choices: Buronson (writer) and Tetsuo Hara (artist), a manga writer-artist team
Akira Toriyama (writer) and Eiichiro Oda (artist), an unlikely cross-Jump pair
Yoshiyuki Tomino (writer) and Yoshikazu Yasuhiko (artist), the Gundam duo
Buronson (writer) alone, as a self-illustrated solo manga creator
context: Hara's hyper-muscled art style and Buronson's pulpy plotting made *Fist of the North Star* a definitive 1980s 'macho' manga. Its anime ran 152 episodes from 1984 to 1988, with violence that pushed Japanese TV broadcast standards to their limit.

question: *Sailor Moon* — the manga that helped open Western audiences to magical-girl anime — began serialization in 'Nakayoshi' in 1991. Its creator, a young woman who had previously published *Codename: Sailor V* as a one-shot, has remained famous despite a long retirement from comics. Who?
answer: Naoko Takeuchi, who married Yoshihiro Togashi (the 'Hunter x Hunter' creator)
choices: Naoko Takeuchi, who married Yoshihiro Togashi (the 'Hunter x Hunter' creator)
Rumiko Takahashi, who created 'Urusei Yatsura' and 'Inuyasha'
CLAMP, the four-woman manga collective behind 'Cardcaptor Sakura'
Sui Ishida, the male artist who would later create 'Tokyo Ghoul' (2011)
context: Sailor V appeared in 'Run-Run' magazine in 1991, then her redesign became Sailor Moon at the same time. Takeuchi married Togashi in 1999. Their hiatuses-and-comebacks have made them an oddly synchronized manga power couple.

question: *Captain N: The Game Master* (1989), the NBC Saturday-morning cartoon, pulled a regular American teenager into the world of Videoland to lead a team of Nintendo heroes against Mother Brain. What was the teenager's name?
answer: Kevin Keene, transported through the 'Ultimate Warp Zone' on his TV
choices: Kevin Keene, transported through the 'Ultimate Warp Zone' on his TV
Justin Bailey, a name borrowed from a 'Metroid' password trick
Billy Lee, a name borrowed from a 'Double Dragon' character
Mario Cabrera, a name from an unrelated 1980s Mattel toy line
context: The 'Justin Bailey' password was a famous trick used in original *Metroid* (1986) to start Samus partly-equipped in her under-suit. The writers of *Captain N* nodded to it many times across the show's three NBC seasons without naming it directly.

question: In *The Transformers: The Movie* (1986), one of the most beloved characters dies on-screen in the film's opening third — a moment so wrenching to its target audience that it remains a notorious trauma reference for an entire generation. WITHOUT spoiling later TV-series outcomes, who delivered Optimus Prime's voice in 1986?
answer: Peter Cullen, who had voiced Optimus on the TV show since 1984
choices: Peter Cullen, who had voiced Optimus on the TV show since 1984
Frank Welker, who voiced Megatron and several other Decepticons
Casey Kasem, who voiced the original Cliffjumper and Bluestreak
Mel Blanc, who voiced characters across mid-1980s Hanna-Barbera
context: Cullen had been cast in 1984 partly because of his ability to voice a deeply paternal, decent-sounding leader. He returned to voice Optimus in the 2007 Michael Bay live-action films and most subsequent Hasbro adaptations, decades later.

question: After *Transformers* the original 'Generation 1' toy line and TV show ended in the late 1980s, Hasbro and Mainframe Entertainment relaunched the franchise in 1996 with one of the first fully computer-generated animated series. What was it called?
answer: *Beast Wars: Transformers*, an entirely CG-animated half-hour syndicated series
choices: *Beast Wars: Transformers*, an entirely CG-animated half-hour syndicated series
*Transformers Energon*, which actually aired in 2004 with very different CG work
*Transformers Cybertron*, which actually aired in 2005 from the same partnership
*Transformers Animated*, which was a 2D-animated 2007 series instead
context: *Beast Wars* used CG rendered on the Mainframe studio's SoftImage workflows. It is widely considered one of the most ambitious 1990s animated TV experiments — a serial sci-fi war story with character arcs that the original 1980s show had not attempted.

question: *Voltron: Defender of the Universe* (1984), the syndicated American TV show, was actually an edit-and-redub of two separate Japanese anime series — one of them a lion-themed mecha show, the other a vehicle-themed mecha show. What was the lion-themed Japanese original called?
answer: *Beast King GoLion*, a 1981 Toei Animation series
choices: *Beast King GoLion*, a 1981 Toei Animation series
*Mobile Suit Gundam*, the 1979 Yoshiyuki Tomino series
*Macross*, the 1982 Studio Nue and Tatsunoko production
*Mazinger Z*, the 1972 Go Nagai super-robot anime
context: *GoLion* originally featured frequent character deaths, romance subplots and a darker tone than American Saturday morning would allow. American producers Peter Keefe and his team at World Events Productions edited heavily to make the *Voltron* version kid-safe.

question: *SilverHawks* (1986) was Rankin/Bass's follow-up to *ThunderCats*: a team of part-metal, part-human heroes patrolling the galaxy of Limbo from villain Mon*Star and his Mob. The show's tagline described the team as 'partly metal, partly real'. What other key phrase appears in the title sequence?
answer: 'Wings of silver, nerves of steel' — said in the opening narration
choices: 'Wings of silver, nerves of steel' — said in the opening narration
'Half-metal, half-human, all hero' — actually 'GI Joe' style, never said in SilverHawks
'Faster than light, sharper than steel' — actually never said in the SilverHawks intro
'Sworn to defend the galaxy from Mon*Star' — not the literal phrasing used
context: SilverHawks reused Rankin/Bass's *ThunderCats* production pipeline — same studio (Pacific Animation Corporation), same character-designer-style influence. The show ran 65 episodes but never achieved *ThunderCats*'s level of toy-line success.

question: *Freakazoid!* (1995-97), the Warner Bros. animated comedy about a teenage boy turned into a manic blue super-hero by a glitch in a Pinnacle chip, was the creation of two TV writers who had previously written for *Tiny Toon Adventures* and *Animaniacs*. Who was the lead creator?
answer: Bruce Timm and Paul Dini, the same duo behind 'Batman: The Animated Series'
choices: Bruce Timm and Paul Dini, the same duo behind 'Batman: The Animated Series'
John Kricfalusi and Bob Camp, the team behind 'Ren & Stimpy'
Don Bluth and Gary Goldman, the team behind 'Anastasia' (1997)
Joe Murray and Christy Karacas, who would later make 'Camp Lazlo'
context: *Freakazoid!* was originally pitched by Timm as a more serious super-hero show; Dini pushed it toward parody. Tom Ruegger, the *Animaniacs* showrunner, came on as supervising producer. The show ran two seasons of 24 episodes before Kids' WB pulled it.

question: *Gargoyles* (1994-97) was a Disney Afternoon syndicated animated series about a clan of medieval stone gargoyles awakened in modern Manhattan. Its tone was darker and more serialized than most contemporaneous Disney TV animation. Who created and ran the series?
answer: Greg Weisman, who would later run 'Young Justice' on Cartoon Network
choices: Greg Weisman, who would later run 'Young Justice' on Cartoon Network
Bruce Timm, who at the time was running 'Batman: The Animated Series'
Genndy Tartakovsky, who would later create 'Samurai Jack' (2001)
Tom Ruegger, who was at the time running 'Animaniacs' for Warner
context: Weisman's writers' room included a number of comics writers; David Goyer was a story editor. Many of *Gargoyles*'s voice cast came from the *Star Trek: The Next Generation* roster: Jonathan Frakes, Marina Sirtis, Brent Spiner, Michael Dorn.

question: *Darkwing Duck* (1991-92), the Disney Afternoon parody of caped pulp heroes, was a spinoff of *DuckTales*. Its title hero — 'I am the terror that flaps in the night!' — was a pastiche of the 1930s pulp adventurer The Shadow. Who voiced Darkwing?
answer: Jim Cummings, who also voiced Pete and Winnie the Pooh in this era
choices: Jim Cummings, who also voiced Pete and Winnie the Pooh in this era
Dan Castellaneta, who voiced Homer Simpson at the same period
Rob Paulsen, who voiced Yakko Warner in 'Animaniacs' (1993)
Maurice LaMarche, who voiced the Brain in 'Pinky and the Brain'
context: *Darkwing*'s creator Tad Stones designed Drake Mallard partly as a parody of self-important superheroes. Launchpad McQuack crossed over from *DuckTales*. The show ran 91 episodes — a long run by Disney Afternoon standards.

question: *TaleSpin* (1990) was a Disney Afternoon adventure series about a bear bush pilot named Baloo running an air-cargo service in the South Pacific city of Cape Suzette. The characters were redrawn from a 1967 Disney animated film. Which?
answer: *The Jungle Book* (1967), which introduced Baloo, Louie, Shere Khan, etc.
choices: *The Jungle Book* (1967), which introduced Baloo, Louie, Shere Khan, etc.
*Robin Hood* (1973), which introduced Little John, who is also a bear
*The Aristocats* (1970), which Disney would have re-cast as cats
*The Rescuers* (1977), which already featured bush-pilot albatrosses
context: *TaleSpin* recast Baloo as an adult adventurer, Louie as a nightclub owner, and Shere Khan as a corporate mogul. The show was a deliberate 1930s adventure-pulp pastiche — Indiana Jones, Tail-Spin Tommy, Terry and the Pirates style.

question: *Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers* (1989-90), the Disney Afternoon detective animated series, reimagined the classic Disney chipmunks as members of a tiny mystery-solving team. Who were their teammates?
answer: Gadget Hackwrench (engineer mouse) and Monterey Jack (Australian mouse)
choices: Gadget Hackwrench (engineer mouse) and Monterey Jack (Australian mouse)
Roger Rabbit (detective) and Jessica Rabbit (his glamorous wife)
Scrooge McDuck (financier) and Launchpad McQuack (their bush pilot)
Pluto (the dog) and Pete (their occasional villain in some episodes)
context: The show's pilot 'To the Rescue' aired as a five-part TV movie. Gadget Hackwrench — voiced by Tress MacNeille — became something of an internet folklore figure decades later, in a way the original 1989 Disney team could not have predicted.

question: *Doug* (1991-94 Nickelodeon, 1996-99 ABC) was a low-key animated comedy about a 12-year-old kid named Doug Funnie writing in his journal about his crush, his bullied friend, and his dog Porkchop. Who created it?
answer: Jim Jinkins, who founded Jumbo Pictures and later did 'PB&J Otter'
choices: Jim Jinkins, who founded Jumbo Pictures and later did 'PB&J Otter'
Klasky-Csupo, the studio that did 'Rugrats' and 'The Wild Thornberrys'
John Kricfalusi, the controversial creator of 'Ren & Stimpy'
Joe Murray, the creator of 'Rocko's Modern Life' (1993)
context: Jinkins reportedly drew Doug as an autobiographical character based on his own Virginia childhood. Disney purchased Jumbo Pictures in 1996; the ABC run softened some Nickelodeon edges, a shift fans noticed and debated for years.

question: *Recess* (1997-2001) was a Disney/One Saturday Morning animated series about a Third Street School 4th-grade clique navigating playground politics. The show frequently treated elementary-school recess as a fully governed parallel society. Who created it?
answer: Paul Germain and Joe Ansolabehere, formerly of 'Rugrats' at Klasky-Csupo
choices: Paul Germain and Joe Ansolabehere, formerly of 'Rugrats' at Klasky-Csupo
Jim Jinkins, who had created 'Doug' a few years earlier for Nickelodeon
Steven Spielberg, who had executive-produced 'Animaniacs' (1993)
Genndy Tartakovsky, who had created 'Dexter's Laboratory' in 1996
context: Germain and Ansolabehere had left Klasky-Csupo over a 1992 royalty dispute about *Rugrats*. *Recess* ran 65 episodes on ABC Saturday morning, plus three theatrical/direct-to-video films through 2003.

question: *Hey Arnold!* (1996-2004) was a Nickelodeon animated series about a 4th-grader with an oblong head, living with his eccentric grandparents in an inner-city boardinghouse. Its tone — gentler, more pensive than most kids' TV — became its signature. Who created it?
answer: Craig Bartlett, an animator who had been part of Will Vinton Studios
choices: Craig Bartlett, an animator who had been part of Will Vinton Studios
Klasky-Csupo, the studio behind 'Rugrats' (1991) at Nickelodeon
Stephen Hillenburg, who would create 'SpongeBob SquarePants' (1999)
John Kricfalusi, the creator of 'Ren & Stimpy' (1991) for Nickelodeon
context: Bartlett was Matt Groening's brother-in-law; he had developed Arnold as a Claymation short for the 'Penny' shorts on Pee-wee's Playhouse (1986). Nickelodeon greenlit the animated series after Bartlett pitched it three times.

question: Before they were a Saturday-morning cartoon, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles were a black-and-white indie comic published by Mirage Studios in May 1984. Who were the two creators?
answer: Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, who self-published Mirage Studios that year
choices: Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, who self-published Mirage Studios that year
Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, who never had any involvement with the Turtles
Frank Miller and Klaus Janson, the Daredevil pair Eastman openly parodied
Bob Kane and Bill Finger, the Batman duo who predated TMNT by 45 years
context: Eastman and Laird wrote and drew the first TMNT issue as a parody of Frank Miller's *Daredevil* and *Ronin*, Dave Sim's *Cerebus*, and Marv Wolfman's *New Teen Titans*. The comic was a runaway hit; toy and TV deals followed within two years.

question: The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles entered most children's homes via the syndicated 1987 animated TV series — softer than the Mirage comic, lighter, with pizza obsessions and a different color-coded mask for each turtle to help kids tell them apart. Who produced this animated series?
answer: Fred Wolf Films, an American studio that produced for the Murakami-Wolf-Swenson label
choices: Fred Wolf Films, an American studio that produced for the Murakami-Wolf-Swenson label
Filmation, the studio that had made 'He-Man and the Masters of the Universe'
DIC Enterprises, the producer of 'Dennis the Menace' and many syndicated shows
Hanna-Barbera Productions, who had passed on TMNT at an earlier development stage
context: The 1987 cartoon ran 193 episodes through 1996. Eastman and Laird had veto power on adaptations; they reportedly insisted on the color-coded masks because they did not want kids confusing the brothers — the comics had used all-red masks.

question: The first live-action Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles film was released in March 1990. It used Jim Henson Creature Shop animatronics for the turtle suits — Henson's last big project before his death in May 1990. What was the film called?
answer: *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* (1990), directed by Steve Barron
choices: *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* (1990), directed by Steve Barron
*Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Secret of the Ooze*, the 1991 sequel
*Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III*, the 1993 third feature film
*TMNT* (2007), the CG-animated film produced by Imagi Animation Studios
context: Jim Henson reportedly considered the Turtles his most demanding suit work ever — actors inside, animatronics on the face, full-bodied martial arts and pratfalls. The film was the highest-grossing independent film of all time on release.

question: *Pac-Man* (1980) was designed by a 25-year-old engineer at Namco who wanted to create an arcade game that wouldn't intimidate women — most arcade games of the late 1970s were combat-themed. The game's eponymous yellow protagonist was reportedly designed from a pizza with a slice removed. Who designed it?
answer: Toru Iwatani, then a recent graduate of the Tokai University engineering program
choices: Toru Iwatani, then a recent graduate of the Tokai University engineering program
Shigeru Miyamoto, who would design 'Donkey Kong' for Nintendo a year later
Eugene Jarvis, the American designer of 'Defender' for Williams in 1981
Nolan Bushnell, the founder of Atari and designer of the original 'Pong'
context: Iwatani also designed the four ghosts with intentionally different personalities: Blinky (chaser), Pinky (ambusher), Inky (random), Clyde (shy). The fruit symbols on each board are real Namco interpretations of seasonal Japanese produce.

question: *Pac-Man* (1980) does not actually have a fail-state ending: it has a 'kill screen' caused by a memory overflow. Reach a certain level and the right half of the screen becomes a garbled mess of characters. What level is the kill screen?
answer: Level 256, where an 8-bit counter overflows and corrupts the maze rendering
choices: Level 256, where an 8-bit counter overflows and corrupts the maze rendering
Level 99, the standard top-level cap on most arcade-era counters
Level 22, which is actually the 'Donkey Kong' (1981) kill-screen level
Level 30, after which 'Donkey Kong' simply repeats Level 22 forever
context: Billy Mitchell was the first publicly verified player to perfect *Pac-Man* — clearing all 256 boards without dying. The achievement requires several days of continuous play. The kill screen is now considered the canonical endpoint of the original arcade *Pac-Man*.

question: *Donkey Kong* (1981) has its own kill screen: a glitched bonus timer that makes the level impossible to complete. The level itself can be reached only by clearing every preceding board. What level is the *Donkey Kong* kill screen?
answer: Level 22 (often called Level 22 by players, technically the L=22 internal counter)
choices: Level 22 (often called Level 22 by players, technically the L=22 internal counter)
Level 256, which is actually the 'Pac-Man' (1980) kill-screen level
Level 99, the standard top-level cap on early Williams arcade games
Level 19, after which 'Joust' has its own counter overflow issue
context: The L=22 kill screen kills the player about four seconds into the level no matter what — Jumpman can do nothing to escape. Billy Mitchell's famous July 1982 *Donkey Kong* score of 1,047,200 was set on the kill-screen level.

question: *Donkey Kong* (1981) became the centerpiece of a long-running arcade-record rivalry. In July 1982, a Florida pizzeria owner named Billy Mitchell set what was then the world record. The record stood for years before Steve Wiebe of Redmond, Washington, challenged it. What was Mitchell's 1982 score?
answer: 1,047,200 points, set in Hollywood, Florida — a famously cited number
choices: 1,047,200 points, set in Hollywood, Florida — a famously cited number
874,300 points, an earlier 1982 record set by a different player
1,062,800 points, Steve Wiebe's later 2004 record at a higher level
996,400 points, the second-highest verified score of all of 1982
context: Walter Day's Twin Galaxies arcade in Ottumwa, Iowa, was the official scoring authority. Mitchell submitted his 1982 score through Twin Galaxies. The 2007 documentary *The King of Kong* chronicled Wiebe's later challenges to Mitchell's record-keeping.

question: *The King of Kong* (2007) made the small town of Ottumwa, Iowa, mid-1980s 'Video Game Capital of the World' famous in retrospect. The official scoring authority based there was run by a former game-arcade owner who became the de facto arbiter of arcade records. Who?
answer: Walter Day, who founded Twin Galaxies in 1981 as a scoreboard service
choices: Walter Day, who founded Twin Galaxies in 1981 as a scoreboard service
Billy Mitchell, who later disputed and dissolved much of the early scoreboard
Steve Wiebe, who only entered the scene as a record challenger in 2003
Jeff Hansen, who in fact co-ran Twin Galaxies in the early 1990s era
context: Day's scoreboard issued plaques and certificates for verified records, and he traveled to events to officiate. Twin Galaxies later changed hands and went through corporate restructurings; the 1982 'Iowa' era remains its mythic moment.

question: *Galaga* (1981) was Namco's follow-up to the 1979 *Galaxian*. It added the now-iconic 'capture beam' mechanic where a Boss Galaga could abduct one of your ships, and you could rescue it for a dual-ship bonus. Who designed it?
answer: Shigeru Yokoyama, the lead Namco arcade designer for several early 1980s titles
choices: Shigeru Yokoyama, the lead Namco arcade designer for several early 1980s titles
Toru Iwatani, the designer of 'Pac-Man' (1980) at Namco
Eugene Jarvis, the Williams designer of 'Defender' (1981) and 'Robotron'
Yu Suzuki, the Sega designer of 'Out Run' (1986) and 'After Burner'
context: *Galaga* used Namco's 3-Z80 chip arcade board. The capture/rescue gimmick — risking your second-to-last ship to rescue an abducted ship — became a defining mechanic of arcade shoot-'em-ups. The game appears as a cameo in 'The Avengers' (2012) under SHIELD's helicarrier monitors.

question: *Defender* (1981), Williams Electronics' side-scrolling shooter, was famous for its punishing difficulty and the panel of buttons (no joystick — buttons did everything). It made a young Williams engineer's career. Who designed it?
answer: Eugene Jarvis, who would later design 'Robotron: 2084' (1982) for Williams
choices: Eugene Jarvis, who would later design 'Robotron: 2084' (1982) for Williams
Howard Scott Warshaw, the Atari designer of 'E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial' (1982)
Bill Budge, the early Apple II games programmer of 'Raster Blaster' (1981)
Jeff Minter, the British designer of 'Tempest 2000' (1994) and Llamasoft
context: Jarvis spent six months building *Defender* without a coherent design; the controls — five buttons plus a joystick, simultaneously — terrified arcade owners on the AMOA 1980 show floor. The game became Williams's biggest 1981 hit, earning over $1 billion in quarters by the mid-1980s.

question: *Robotron: 2084* (1982), Eugene Jarvis's twin-stick shooter masterpiece, was reportedly inspired by *Berzerk* and George Orwell's *1984*. Jarvis broke his wrist in a car crash during development and rewrote the controls during recovery. What year is the in-game setting?
answer: 2084, exactly 100 years after Orwell's '1984' setting
choices: 2084, exactly 100 years after Orwell's '1984' setting
2042, a closer-future setting in some 1980s arcade games
2199, the setting of 'Mass Effect' (2007) two decades later
1984, the exact title of Orwell's source novel published in 1949
context: *Robotron* was the first major twin-stick shooter — one stick for movement, one for firing direction. Jarvis followed it with *Stargate* (1981, the *Defender* sequel) and decades of work on pinball and arcade games at Williams and Midway.

question: *Joust* (1982), Williams's medieval ostrich-and-buzzard combat arcade game, gave players an unusual control: there was no jump button. Players flapped their bird's wings by repeatedly hitting a single button. Who designed it?
answer: John Newcomer, the Williams designer of 'Sinistar' (1983) shortly afterward
choices: John Newcomer, the Williams designer of 'Sinistar' (1983) shortly afterward
Eugene Jarvis, then designing 'Robotron: 2084' for Williams the same year
Larry DeMar, Jarvis's frequent design partner on 'Robotron' and 'Stargate'
Bill Pfutzenreuter, the Williams arcade engineer behind 'Bubbles' (1982)
context: *Joust* combined two-player simultaneous play with friendly-fire mechanics: each player could choose to fight the other or cooperate. Knights mounted on flying ostriches and storks (Players 1 and 2) battled buzzard-mounted enemies on a series of platforms.

question: *Centipede* (1981), Atari's trackball arcade game where players shot a descending centipede in a mushroom field, was designed by one of the only female arcade-game designers of the 1980s. Who?
answer: Dona Bailey, who left the games industry in the mid-1980s
choices: Dona Bailey, who left the games industry in the mid-1980s
Carol Shaw, who designed 'Polo' and 'River Raid' for Atari and Activision
Roberta Williams, who designed 'Mystery House' for Sierra On-Line
Brenda Romero, who designed AD&D modules at TSR in the 1980s
context: Bailey had worked at General Motors writing assembly code for car ECUs. She joined Atari Coin-Op in 1980 — the only woman among forty designers — and co-designed *Centipede* with Ed Logg. She left the games industry after seeing how badly women were treated in arcades.

question: *Asteroids* (1979), Atari's hit space-rock-shattering arcade game, used a special kind of display unlike the raster monitors used by 'Pac-Man' or 'Donkey Kong'. The display drew shapes by tracing line segments directly with the electron beam. What was it called?
answer: Vector graphics — XY-deflected monochrome line displays, not raster
choices: Vector graphics — XY-deflected monochrome line displays, not raster
Sprite-based graphics — actually used by 'Pac-Man' and 'Donkey Kong'
Pixel-art raster graphics — actually used by every other early arcade game
Holographic displays — never used in any actual 1970s arcade machine
context: Vector arcade displays gave a distinctive crisp white-line look. *Asteroids* used a XY monitor manufactured by Wells-Gardner or Electrohome. Other vector classics: *Battlezone* (1980), *Tempest* (1981), *Star Wars* (1983). All eventually replaced by cheaper raster.

question: *Tempest* (1981), Atari's vector-graphics shooter where you piloted a 'blaster' around the rim of a 3D well firing at enemies climbing up, was designed by an idiosyncratic engineer who later updated the game as *Tempest 2000* for the Atari Jaguar in 1994. Who?
answer: Dave Theurer (original 1981 version) and Jeff Minter (Tempest 2000 version)
choices: Dave Theurer (original 1981 version) and Jeff Minter (Tempest 2000 version)
Eugene Jarvis (original) and Larry DeMar (Tempest 2000 reskin)
Toru Iwatani (original) and Yu Suzuki (Tempest 2000 reskin)
Nolan Bushnell (original) and John Romero (Tempest 2000 reskin)
context: Theurer designed *Tempest* and *Missile Command* at Atari. Minter — the British 'Llamasoft' designer who put llamas and goats into his shooters — was given the Atari Jaguar 1994 update. His version was widely praised, including by Theurer himself in later interviews.

question: *Q*bert* (1982), Gottlieb's isometric arcade game about a long-snouted creature hopping on a pyramid of cubes, is famous for a particular sound effect: when Q*bert dies, he yells a comic-book obscenity. The pixel-art text 'curse word' appears in a speech bubble. What is the actual sound?
answer: A randomly synthesized babble triggered by a 'knock generator' chip
choices: A randomly synthesized babble triggered by a 'knock generator' chip
A pre-recorded sample of Warren Davis (designer) shouting profanity
A backwards-tape-loop sample of a Gottlieb engineer's actual swear
A live MIDI improvisation by Williams Sound's chief engineer Larry DeMar
context: Warren Davis and Jeff Lee designed *Q*bert*. The 'curse generator' was an unintended hardware feature; Gottlieb decided to keep it as a feature once they realized players found it hilarious. The original speech-bubble pixel art included '@!#?@!' as a placeholder, never changed.

question: *Dig Dug* (1982), Namco's tunneling arcade game where a digger pumps up underground monsters until they explode, was designed by an engineer who would later design 'Mappy' (1983) at the same company. Who designed it?
answer: Masahisa Ikegami, with Yoshio Hirai and Shouichi Fukatani at Namco
choices: Masahisa Ikegami, with Yoshio Hirai and Shouichi Fukatani at Namco
Toru Iwatani, the designer of 'Pac-Man' (1980) at Namco
Shigeru Yokoyama, the designer of 'Galaxian' (1979) at Namco
Tatsuo Sayama, the Atari engineer behind 'Crystal Castles' (1983)
context: *Dig Dug* introduced Pooka (red goggle creatures) and Fygar (green fire-breathing dragons). The pump-and-explode mechanic made it one of the most distinctive arcade games of the era — and Disney bought film rights at one point in the mid-1980s.

question: *Frogger* (1981), Konami's now-iconic arcade game about a frog crossing a busy highway and a log-strewn river, was a Japanese arcade hit before reaching America. What North American distributor handled it?
answer: Sega/Gremlin, which had distributed many Konami titles in North America
choices: Sega/Gremlin, which had distributed many Konami titles in North America
Atari Inc., which handled all Japanese arcade imports in the early 1980s
Nintendo of America, which had not yet been founded as a North American arm
Bally/Midway, the dominant North American arcade distributor of the era
context: *Frogger* sold over 20,000 cabinets in its first year. The Sega/Gremlin distribution partnership also handled *Carnival* (1980) and *Pengo* (1982). Konami remained primarily Japanese until *Castlevania* (1986) and *Contra* (1987) made it a Western brand.

question: *Space Invaders* (1978), Taito's hit alien-shooter arcade game, was so successful in Japan that an urban legend (long disputed by historians but widely repeated) claimed it caused a national shortage of a specific Japanese coin. Which?
answer: The 100-yen coin, with which Japanese arcades were operated
choices: The 100-yen coin, with which Japanese arcades were operated
The 10-yen coin, used at lower price points in convenience stores
The 50-yen coin, used in vending machines but not arcade cabinets
The 500-yen coin, only introduced years later in Japan in 1982
context: Historians have shown Japan's mint actually increased 100-yen production during *Space Invaders*' run; the legend is exaggerated but not invented. The game was designed by Tomohiro Nishikado and used a Z80 chip and discrete logic in a complex hybrid design.

question: *Street Fighter II: The World Warrior* (1991), Capcom's fighting game that single-handedly revived the arcade industry in the early 1990s, introduced eight selectable fighters and a six-button control scheme. Who designed it?
answer: Akira 'Akiman' Yasuda (visuals) and Yoshiki Okamoto (production)
choices: Akira 'Akiman' Yasuda (visuals) and Yoshiki Okamoto (production)
Tomohiro Nishikado, the Taito designer of 'Space Invaders'
Yuji Naka, the Sonic Team designer behind 'Sonic the Hedgehog'
Toshiyuki Takezaki, the Konami designer behind 'Castlevania III'
context: *Street Fighter II* spawned the entire one-on-one fighting game genre. It introduced E. Honda, Blanka, Guile, Dhalsim, Chun-Li, Zangief — and brought Ryu and Ken back from the 1987 original (designed by Takashi Nishiyama, who left for SNK).

question: *Mortal Kombat* (1992), Midway's hit arcade fighting game, used digitized photographs of real actors performing martial-arts moves instead of hand-drawn sprites. Who created it?
answer: Ed Boon (programmer) and John Tobias (artist), both at Midway
choices: Ed Boon (programmer) and John Tobias (artist), both at Midway
Yu Suzuki (programmer) and Shigeru Miyamoto (artist), both at Sega
Eugene Jarvis (programmer) and Sam Dicker (artist), both at Williams
John Romero (programmer) and Adrian Carmack (artist), both at id Software
context: Boon and Tobias hired local Chicago-area martial artists as motion-capture subjects — Daniel Pesina played Johnny Cage, Liu Kang, and Scorpion. The first game's digitization rig used a VHS camera and a green-screen wall in a Midway warehouse.

question: *The Simpsons* arcade game (1991), Konami's four-player beat-'em-up where Marge, Bart, Lisa, and Homer Simpson rescued Maggie from Mr. Burns and Smithers, was famously fun in arcades but troubled at home. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Hiroyuki Sakou, the Konami arcade designer also behind 'TMNT' (1989)
choices: Hiroyuki Sakou, the Konami arcade designer also behind 'TMNT' (1989)
Yu Suzuki, the Sega designer of 'Out Run' (1986) and 'Virtua Fighter'
Tomohiro Nishikado, the Taito designer of 'Space Invaders' (1978)
Shigeru Miyamoto, the Nintendo designer of 'Donkey Kong' (1981)
context: Konami's 1989 *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* arcade and 1991 *Simpsons* both used the same four-player beat-'em-up template — and were both rarely seen at home because Konami did not license console ports. *X-Men: The Arcade Game* (1992) was a third in the series.

question: *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* (1989), Konami's four-player arcade beat-'em-up based on the 1987 animated TV show, allowed all four turtles to play simultaneously on a single cabinet. Who, of the four turtles, fought with sai daggers as the player-2 character?
answer: Raphael, in the red mask, with twin sai (Player 2 on the cabinet)
choices: Raphael, in the red mask, with twin sai (Player 2 on the cabinet)
Leonardo, in the blue mask, with twin katana (Player 1 on the cabinet)
Michelangelo, in the orange mask, with nunchucks (Player 3 on the cabinet)
Donatello, in the purple mask, with a bo staff (Player 4 on the cabinet)
context: The arcade game's iconic moment is Shredder turning a defeated turtle back into a regular turtle; the game's 30-minute arcade run was the kind of long-form playthrough rare in 1989. A SNES port followed in 1991 (*Turtles in Time*).

question: *Out Run* (1986), Sega's arcade driving game, let players steer a red Ferrari Testarossa from California to a chosen destination while choosing between five different soundtracks. Who designed it?
answer: Yu Suzuki, who would later design 'After Burner' and 'Virtua Fighter' at Sega
choices: Yu Suzuki, who would later design 'After Burner' and 'Virtua Fighter' at Sega
Tomohiro Nishikado, the Taito designer behind 'Space Invaders' (1978)
Shigeru Miyamoto, the Nintendo designer behind 'Super Mario Bros.' (1985)
Toru Iwatani, the Namco designer behind 'Pac-Man' (1980)
context: Suzuki used a moving cabinet — the cockpit hydraulically tilted left and right as the player turned. The Ferrari brand was unlicensed; Sega added 'Ferrari' badging in later cabinet revisions. The three soundtracks: 'Splash Wave', 'Magical Sound Shower', 'Passing Breeze'.

question: *Daytona USA* (1994), Sega's hit polygonal arcade racing game, used the Model 2 arcade board to deliver real-time texture-mapped 3D graphics — a stunning leap over earlier sprite-based racers. The cabinets supported eight-player networked play. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Toshihiro Nagoshi, who would later create the 'Yakuza' series at Sega
choices: Toshihiro Nagoshi, who would later create the 'Yakuza' series at Sega
Yu Suzuki, who had designed 'Out Run' (1986) earlier in the same studio
Tetsuya Mizuguchi, who would later design 'Rez' (2001) at Sega
Yuji Naka, the Sonic Team designer behind 'Sonic the Hedgehog' (1991)
context: *Daytona USA* arcade cabinets used a four-cabinet linked setup as standard. The Saturn home port (1995) was widely criticized as a downgrade — Suzuki and his team had to scale back the 3D for the much weaker Saturn hardware.

question: *Killer Instinct* (1994), the Rare-developed Midway-published fighting game, was famous for its 'C-c-c-combo breaker!' announcer call and pre-rendered 3D graphics. The arcade cabinet's announcer was sampled — but for the SNES home port (1995) one specific sound effect was famously omitted. What was it?
answer: The 'Ultra Combo' announcer's drawn-out 'Uuuuuultra!' yell
choices: The 'Ultra Combo' announcer's drawn-out 'Uuuuuultra!' yell
The 'No Mercy' final-blow announcer call shortened from the arcade version
The 'C-c-c-combo breaker!' line, which actually was preserved in the SNES port
The 'You don't even exist' announcer call kept in the SNES port intact
context: Rare's arcade collaboration with Nintendo and Midway was unusual in 1994. The game's character roster — Jago, Sabrewulf, Glacius, Cinder, Combo, Riptor, Spinal — was developed in part to attempt a North-Americanized *Street Fighter*-style fighting franchise.

question: *Virtua Fighter* (1993), Sega's first 3D polygonal fighting game, predated *Tekken* by a year. It introduced eight fighters in a square ring, with no health bars at first — only round-based knockout victories. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Yu Suzuki, who had previously designed 'Out Run' (1986) at Sega
choices: Yu Suzuki, who had previously designed 'Out Run' (1986) at Sega
Tomonobu Itagaki, who would later design 'Dead or Alive' (1996) at Tecmo
Toshihiro Nagoshi, who would later design 'Daytona USA' (1994) at Sega
Tetsuya Mizuguchi, who would later design 'Sega Rally' (1995) at Sega
context: *Virtua Fighter* used the Sega Model 1 arcade board. The character designs were deliberately less stylized than *Street Fighter II* — closer to live-action martial arts demonstrations. The original eight fighters: Akira, Pai, Jacky, Sarah, Wolf, Jeffry, Lau, and Kage.

question: *Tekken* (1994), Namco's response to Sega's *Virtua Fighter* (1993), used three-dimensional polygonal graphics and a unique limb-by-limb four-button control scheme: one button for each limb. What unique hardware did it use?
answer: Sony PlayStation arcade hardware (the System 11 board, ported soon to PS1)
choices: Sony PlayStation arcade hardware (the System 11 board, ported soon to PS1)
Sega Model 2 arcade hardware (which was actually used by 'Daytona USA')
SNK Neo Geo arcade hardware (which used 2D sprites, not polygons)
Capcom CPS-2 arcade hardware (which used 2D sprites for fighting games)
context: Namco's System 11 board was derived from PlayStation 1 hardware — designed to ease arcade-to-console porting. *Tekken*'s home PS1 port came in early 1995, only a few months after the arcade release, and helped sell the PlayStation in its first year.

question: *Super Mario Bros.* (1985), Shigeru Miyamoto's seminal NES platformer, established the Mario, Luigi, Bowser, and Princess Peach franchise. The first level (World 1-1) is one of the most studied in video-game design. Who composed its iconic main theme?
answer: Koji Kondo, who had joined Nintendo in 1984 as a sound designer
choices: Koji Kondo, who had joined Nintendo in 1984 as a sound designer
Nobuo Uematsu, who would compose the 'Final Fantasy' theme in 1987
Yasunori Mitsuda, who would compose 'Chrono Trigger' (1995)
Yoko Shimomura, who would compose 'Kingdom Hearts' (2002)
context: Kondo composed the *Super Mario Bros.* theme on a Yamaha DX7 — its 5-note opening hook is one of the most recognized musical phrases of the late 20th century. He also composed the *Zelda* overworld theme the next year.

question: *Super Mario Bros. 2* (1988 USA) is famously a different game from *Super Mario Bros. 2* in Japan. The Japanese SMB2 (the actual sequel to SMB1) was deemed too difficult by Nintendo of America. Instead, a 1987 Famicom Disk System game was reskinned as the US SMB2. What was the original Japanese game called?
answer: *Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic* (1987), with characters from a Fuji TV festival
choices: *Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic* (1987), with characters from a Fuji TV festival
*Super Mario USA* (1992), which was actually a re-release of US SMB2 in Japan
*Mario Bros. Special* (1984), a Hudson Soft licensed PC sequel to the arcade
*Wrecking Crew* (1985), the NES game that pre-dated Super Mario Bros.
context: Japanese 'real' SMB2 was eventually released in the West as 'The Lost Levels' (in *Super Mario All-Stars*, 1993). The US SMB2's Shy Guys, Birdo, and gameplay (lift things, throw things, pluck vegetables) are all *Doki Doki Panic* mechanics imported wholesale.

question: *Super Mario Bros. 3* (1988 Japan, 1990 US) was the third NES Mario platformer. Its world map was divided into eight uniquely-themed worlds — Grass Land, Desert Land, Water Land, etc. — each with its own end-of-world airship boss. How many worlds were there?
answer: Eight worlds, ending with Bowser's castle as the final level
choices: Eight worlds, ending with Bowser's castle as the final level
Twelve worlds, an extended map only available in the 1993 SNES re-release
Six worlds, the standard layout of the earlier 1985 'Super Mario Bros.'
Sixteen worlds, the count of the 1995 'Super Mario World' sequel on SNES
context: World 7 was 'Pipe Land' (or 'Piranha Plant Land'). The 'Tanooki Suit' transformation in Worlds 5 and 6 (turning Mario into a flying raccoon-tail Mario) became one of the most iconic NES power-ups. The game sold over 17 million copies on NES.

question: *Super Mario World* (1990 Japan, 1991 US), the launch title for the Super Famicom and SNES, introduced one of Mario's most beloved companions — a green dinosaur that could carry, eat, and spit out enemies. What was his name?
answer: Yoshi, who would star in his own series beginning with 'Yoshi's Island' (1995)
choices: Yoshi, who would star in his own series beginning with 'Yoshi's Island' (1995)
Bowser Jr., who would not be introduced until 'Super Mario Sunshine' (2002)
Toad, who had appeared in 'Super Mario Bros. 2' (1988) as a playable character
Diddy Kong, who would appear in 'Donkey Kong Country' (1994)
context: Yoshi's design — egg, dinosaur, friend, tongue, can swallow things — was reportedly something Miyamoto had wanted to put into the original *Super Mario Bros.* but couldn't fit on the NES hardware. *Super Mario World*'s SNES hardware allowed it for the first time.

question: *The Legend of Zelda* (1986 Japan, 1987 US), Shigeru Miyamoto's first Zelda game, was a top-down adventure on the Famicom Disk System (Japan) and NES cartridge (US). It featured a memorable golden-colored cartridge in North America. Who composed its overworld theme?
answer: Koji Kondo, the same composer behind 'Super Mario Bros.' the year before
choices: Koji Kondo, the same composer behind 'Super Mario Bros.' the year before
Nobuo Uematsu, who would compose 'Final Fantasy' the next year
Yoshiaki Iwata, the lead composer of 'Castlevania' (1986) at Konami
Tomohiro Nishikado, who designed but did not compose 'Space Invaders'
context: Kondo's *Zelda* overworld theme is one of the most recognized melodies in gaming. It was reportedly composed in a single all-night session. The golden NES cartridge was unique for the time — most NES carts were gray plastic.

question: *The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past* (1991 Japan, 1992 US) was the third Zelda title and the SNES debut for the franchise. It returned to the top-down view and introduced the parallel Light World/Dark World mechanic. Who directed it?
answer: Takashi Tezuka, with Miyamoto as producer at Nintendo
choices: Takashi Tezuka, with Miyamoto as producer at Nintendo
Hiroyuki Imaishi, who would later direct 'Promare' (2019) at Trigger
Shigeru Miyamoto alone, as creator-director on the first three Zelda titles
Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who would direct 'Breath of the Wild' (2017)
context: Tezuka had directed *Super Mario World* (1990). *A Link to the Past* is widely cited as the model template for the top-down Zelda formula, and its 16-megabit cartridge was one of the largest NES/SNES carts at release (1991 Japan).

question: *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* (1998), the franchise's first 3D entry on the Nintendo 64, was directed by a different team member than the SNES era. The game's combat introduced 'Z-targeting' — locking onto enemies via a cursor — which became a standard adventure-game mechanic. Who directed?
answer: Eiji Aonuma, alongside Toru Osawa and Yoshiaki Koizumi at Nintendo
choices: Eiji Aonuma, alongside Toru Osawa and Yoshiaki Koizumi at Nintendo
Shigeru Miyamoto alone, who was producer not director for Ocarina
Takashi Tezuka, who had directed 'A Link to the Past' (1991)
Hiroyuki Imaishi, who would later direct 'Promare' for Studio Trigger
context: Aonuma became the lead Zelda director from *Ocarina* onward. The game took over 2.5 years to develop and shipped on a 256-megabit (32 MB) cartridge with the game-specific 4 MB RAM expansion pack required for the 'Master Quest' debug build.

question: *Metroid* (1986 Japan, 1987 US), the original NES Metroid game, ended with the reveal that bounty hunter Samus Aran — wearing the Power Suit throughout the game — was a woman. Without spoiling later game variants, the game gave faster completion times in-game an unusual reward. What was it?
answer: Different ending images depending on how fast Samus completed the game
choices: Different ending images depending on how fast Samus completed the game
Unlockable mini-games separate from the main adventure structure
A 'New Game Plus' mode with more enemies and higher difficulty levels
A secret final boss accessible only after several complete playthroughs
context: The 'under 5 hours' ending showed Samus without her helmet. The 'under 3 hours' showed her in different clothing. The 'under 1 hour' ending — exceedingly rare for original players in 1986 — showed Samus in her now-famous bikini-suit ending image.

question: *Super Metroid* (1994), the third Metroid game and the SNES debut, is widely cited as a masterpiece of game-world design. Its central world Zebes was a single interconnected map — no level-select. Who composed its score?
answer: Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, the Nintendo R&D1 sound team
choices: Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, the Nintendo R&D1 sound team
Koji Kondo, the composer of 'Super Mario Bros.' (1985)
Nobuo Uematsu, the composer of 'Final Fantasy' (1987)
Yasunori Mitsuda, the composer of 'Chrono Trigger' (1995)
context: Yamamoto and Hamano composed *Super Metroid* with a deliberately moody, atmospheric tone — closer to John Carpenter horror than to Nintendo's usual catchy themes. The game's speed-run scene has been active for thirty years, with new techniques discovered as recently as the 2020s.

question: *Final Fantasy* (1987 Japan, 1990 US), Squaresoft's debut RPG on the Famicom, was reportedly given its name because the company was on the verge of bankruptcy and the game was thought to be the final effort the company would manage. Who designed it?
answer: Hironobu Sakaguchi, who would direct most of the series through FF X
choices: Hironobu Sakaguchi, who would direct most of the series through FF X
Yoshitaka Amano, who designed the characters but did not direct
Nobuo Uematsu, who composed the music but did not direct
Yuji Horii, who actually designed the rival 'Dragon Quest' for Enix
context: Squaresoft was rescued by *Final Fantasy*'s commercial success. Sakaguchi had nearly left the company; the game's hit status saved the studio. The first three entries did not come to North America in their original eras — *FF I* US release was 1990, on the NES.

question: *Final Fantasy VII* (1997), the franchise's PlayStation 1 debut, was the global breakthrough for Japanese RPGs in the West. It used 3D character models on pre-rendered 2D backgrounds. Who directed it?
answer: Hironobu Sakaguchi (producer) and Yoshinori Kitase (director)
choices: Hironobu Sakaguchi (producer) and Yoshinori Kitase (director)
Yuji Naka and Naoto Ohshima, the Sonic Team duo (unrelated to FF)
Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, the SNES Mario duo at Nintendo
Toshiyuki Takezaki and Konami staff, who actually worked on 'Castlevania'
context: *FF VII* had a $40 million marketing budget — unprecedented for an RPG. Squaresoft moved from Nintendo to Sony specifically because of cartridge limits — *FF VII* required three CD-ROMs. The Nintendo-Square break was a defining moment of the late-90s console wars.

question: *Chrono Trigger* (1995), Squaresoft's time-travel RPG on the Super Famicom and SNES, was the product of a 'dream team' collaboration between three legendary Japanese developers. Two of the three came from Square's *Final Fantasy* team. Who was the third?
answer: Yuji Horii, the designer of Enix's 'Dragon Quest' series
choices: Yuji Horii, the designer of Enix's 'Dragon Quest' series
Shigeru Miyamoto, the Nintendo designer of 'Super Mario' (unrelated to this game)
Hironobu Sakaguchi, who was actually already on the Square FF team
Akira Toriyama, who designed the characters but did not direct
context: Horii (Dragon Quest), Sakaguchi (Final Fantasy), and Toriyama (Dragon Ball / character art) joined forces. The 1995 game was directed by Takashi Tokita and Yoshinori Kitase. The Japanese press called the team a 'super-collaboration' that has never quite been repeated.

question: *GoldenEye 007* (1997), Rare's first-person shooter for the Nintendo 64 based on the 1995 James Bond film, was a console-shooter touchstone. Its multiplayer mode (deathmatch, capture the flag, license-to-kill) reportedly drove a generation of dorm-room rivalries. Who directed it?
answer: Martin Hollis, who had been at Rare since 1994 working on Killer Instinct
choices: Martin Hollis, who had been at Rare since 1994 working on Killer Instinct
Tim Stamper and Chris Stamper, the Rare founders (Ultimate Play the Game)
Sid Meier, then at MicroProse working on 'Civilization II' (1996)
John Carmack, at id Software working on 'Quake' (1996)
context: *GoldenEye* sold over 8 million copies on N64. The multiplayer Oddjob — extremely short and hard to hit — became infamous enough that 'no Oddjob' is a standard dorm-room house rule. Rare went on to make *Perfect Dark* (2000) using the *GoldenEye* engine.

question: *Super Smash Bros.* (1999 Japan, 1999 US) was Nintendo's first cross-IP fighter, pitting Mario, Link, Pikachu, Samus, Kirby, and others against each other in platform-fighter brawls. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Masahiro Sakurai, who would continue to direct every Smash Bros. through Ultimate
choices: Masahiro Sakurai, who would continue to direct every Smash Bros. through Ultimate
Shigeru Miyamoto, the 'Mario' and 'Zelda' creator at Nintendo
Satoshi Tajiri, the 'Pokemon' creator at Game Freak
Hideki Kamiya, the 'Resident Evil 2' and 'Devil May Cry' designer at Capcom
context: Sakurai had previously worked at HAL Laboratory on *Kirby's Adventure* (1993) and *Kirby Super Star* (1996). *Smash Bros. Melee* (2001) on GameCube became the breakout competitive title — its frame-perfect mechanics have sustained a competitive scene for over two decades.

question: *Metal Gear Solid* (1998), Hideo Kojima's PlayStation 1 stealth-action sequel to the earlier MSX/NES *Metal Gear* games, became one of the most cinematic console games of its era. Who directed it?
answer: Hideo Kojima, who had also directed the 1987 MSX2 'Metal Gear' original
choices: Hideo Kojima, who had also directed the 1987 MSX2 'Metal Gear' original
Yu Suzuki, who was directing 'Shenmue' (1999) at Sega at the same time
Akira Yamaoka, who was actually composer for 'Silent Hill' (1999) at Konami
Toshihiro Nagoshi, who was working on 'Daytona USA' at Sega in 1998
context: Kojima reportedly directed cutscenes shot-by-shot like a film director. The game's 30+ hours of voice acting were a defining feature for 1998 — most contemporaneous console games had little to no voiced dialogue. David Hayter became Snake's voice in English for nearly 20 years afterward.

question: *Silent Hill* (1999), Konami's PlayStation 1 psychological horror game set in a fog-covered American town, was developed by an internal Konami team that gave themselves a self-deprecating name. What were they called?
answer: Team Silent, the in-house Konami development team for the early Silent Hill series
choices: Team Silent, the in-house Konami development team for the early Silent Hill series
Team Ico, which was actually at Sony Japan working on 'Ico' (2001)
Team Ninja, which was actually at Tecmo working on 'Dead or Alive' (1996)
Team Reptile, an unrelated indie studio active a generation later
context: Team Silent included Keiichiro Toyama (director), Akihiro Imamura (producer), Akira Yamaoka (composer), and Masahiro Ito (monster designer). The team disbanded after *Silent Hill 4* (2004); later Silent Hill games were made by outside Western and Japanese studios.

question: *Resident Evil* (1996), Capcom's survival-horror debut for the PlayStation 1, introduced fixed camera angles, low ammo, and a tank-control scheme to mainstream gaming. Who directed it?
answer: Shinji Mikami, who would later direct 'Resident Evil 4' (2005)
choices: Shinji Mikami, who would later direct 'Resident Evil 4' (2005)
Hideo Kojima, who was instead directing 'Metal Gear Solid' (1998) at Konami
Hideki Kamiya, who would direct 'Resident Evil 2' (1998) before leaving Capcom
Tomonobu Itagaki, who was instead directing 'Dead or Alive' (1996) at Tecmo
context: Mikami originally conceived the game as a remake of Capcom's *Sweet Home* (1989) for the Famicom. The Spencer Mansion setting, document-collecting, and limited ink ribbon save system became the survival-horror template for over a decade.

question: *Resident Evil 4* (2005), released first on Nintendo GameCube before later ports, radically redesigned the franchise: over-the-shoulder third-person camera, no fixed angles, dramatic shift toward action. Who directed?
answer: Shinji Mikami, returning to direct after producing the earlier sequels
choices: Shinji Mikami, returning to direct after producing the earlier sequels
Hideki Kamiya, who had moved to Clover Studio and was making 'Okami' (2006)
Shu Takumi, the 'Ace Attorney' director at Capcom
Yoshiki Okamoto, the 'Street Fighter II' producer at Capcom
context: Mikami's first cut of RE4 was a more traditional fixed-camera entry, then scrapped and rebuilt over two years. The 'over-the-shoulder' camera became an industry-defining choice — *Gears of War* (2006), *Dead Space* (2008), and many more all borrowed from RE4's design.

question: *Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike* (1999), Capcom's third entry in the parry-and-counter-heavy *Street Fighter III* series, became famous for a single piece of footage from the 2004 Evolution Championship Series. Daigo Umehara performed a 15-hit parry on Justin Wong's super combo, then countered for the win. What is the moment universally called?
answer: EVO Moment #37, also known as 'Daigo Parry' or 'The Beast'
choices: EVO Moment #37, also known as 'Daigo Parry' or 'The Beast'
EVO Moment #1, the founding parry sequence — actually not the same moment
The Chun-Li Parry, which actually was Justin Wong's character not Daigo's
Mortal Kombat 9 Final, an entirely different tournament from a later year
context: Daigo was playing Ken; Justin was playing Chun-Li. The match was a Loser's Final at EVO 2004. The crowd's eruption — fully captured on video by SRK forum members — has been viewed tens of millions of times online and is widely cited as the founding moment of competitive fighting-game video culture.

question: *Crash Bandicoot* (1996), Naughty Dog's PlayStation 1 platformer, became Sony's unofficial mascot for the late 1990s. Who designed it?
answer: Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin, Naughty Dog's co-founders at the time
choices: Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin, Naughty Dog's co-founders at the time
Tomonobu Itagaki and Itagaki's team at Tecmo (unrelated to Crash)
Mark Cerny, the PS1 architect who later designed the PS4 and PS5 architecture
Yuji Naka and Naoto Ohshima, the Sega Sonic Team duo (unrelated to Crash)
context: Mark Cerny was a producer and design consultant on *Crash*. Naughty Dog had been making smaller console games since 1986; *Crash* was their first major hit. The studio later sold to Sony in 2001 and went on to make the *Jak and Daxter*, *Uncharted*, and *The Last of Us* series.

question: *Spyro the Dragon* (1998), Insomniac Games's PlayStation 1 platformer about a small purple dragon collecting treasure and rescuing imprisoned dragons, debuted in September 1998. Who founded Insomniac, the studio behind it?
answer: Ted Price, Brian Hastings, and Al Hicks, Insomniac's three co-founders
choices: Ted Price, Brian Hastings, and Al Hicks, Insomniac's three co-founders
Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin, who actually co-founded Naughty Dog
Mark Cerny, who was actually a Crystal Dynamics and later Sony consultant
Ron Gilbert and Tim Schafer, who actually co-founded Double Fine in 2000
context: Insomniac was founded in 1994; their first PS1 title was *Disruptor* (1996). The *Spyro* trilogy (1998-2000) made the studio's name. Later they made *Ratchet & Clank* (2002), the *Resistance* series, and *Marvel's Spider-Man* (2018) for Sony.

question: *Tomb Raider* (1996), Core Design's PlayStation 1 (and later PC, Saturn) adventure game starring British archaeologist Lara Croft, made its protagonist one of the most iconic video-game characters of the 1990s. Where was the studio based?
answer: Derby, England, with the publisher Eidos Interactive in London
choices: Derby, England, with the publisher Eidos Interactive in London
Tokyo, Japan, at Capcom (where Resident Evil was actually made)
Vancouver, Canada, at Electronic Arts Sports (unrelated to Tomb Raider)
San Diego, USA, at Sony Computer Entertainment America's studio
context: Toby Gard designed the original Lara Croft character. Core Design's *Tomb Raider* sequels appeared annually through 2000 (the third sequel, *The Last Revelation*, was the last by the original studio); Crystal Dynamics took over in 2002 with *Tomb Raider: The Angel of Darkness*.
