Discord, who actually is from 'My Little Pony' not 'The Sandman'
Doom, who actually is the seven dwarves in 'Snow White' not 'The Sandman'
Disarray, who actually is not a name used in any Sandman issue or arc
context: Delirium was once Delight; the change is treated as ancient in the series. She is the youngest sibling and central to the *Brief Lives* arc (#41-49, 1992-93). All seven Endless have purple eyes (or two-colored eyes in Desire's case).

question: *Hellboy* (1993, Dark Horse Comics), Mike Mignola's pulp-horror series, introduced a red-skinned demon adopted by the United States military and raised to fight occult threats. Without spoiling later arcs, who founded the in-universe organization Hellboy works for?
answer: Trevor Bruttenholm, the British paranormal-investigator who adopted Hellboy as a child
choices: Trevor Bruttenholm, the British paranormal-investigator who adopted Hellboy as a child
Stan Lee, who actually had no involvement with 'Hellboy' (Marvel competitor)
Will Eisner, who actually created 'The Spirit' (1940) not Hellboy
Sergei Eisenstein, who actually was a Soviet filmmaker not a comics character
context: The B.P.R.D. (Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense) became its own spin-off comic series. Mignola has cited H.P. Lovecraft, M.R. James, Manly Wade Wellman, and Bram Stoker as primary influences. The Mignola line of Dark Horse comics has become one of the most-praised independent comics universes.

question: *Preacher* (1995-2000) at DC's Vertigo imprint followed a Texas preacher, his hitman girlfriend, and an Irish vampire on a road trip across America. Who wrote and drew it?
answer: Garth Ennis (writer) and Steve Dillon (artist), with Glenn Fabry on covers
choices: Garth Ennis (writer) and Steve Dillon (artist), with Glenn Fabry on covers
Alan Moore (writer) and Bill Sienkiewicz (artist), Vertigo veterans of the era
Grant Morrison (writer) and Steve Yeowell (artist), Vertigo veterans of the era
Warren Ellis (writer) and Darick Robertson (artist), Vertigo veterans of the era
context: Ennis and Dillon were both British. Their *Preacher* ran 66 issues plus specials, then was adapted to a 2016-19 AMC TV series by Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. The series is widely cited as one of Vertigo's defining works alongside *Sandman* and *Y: The Last Man*.

question: *Sin City* (1991-92), Frank Miller's stark black-and-white noir comics series, debuted in Dark Horse's *Dark Horse Presents* anthology before becoming a standalone series. The series's visual style — extreme contrast, almost no halftones — became its signature. Who lettered and inked it?
answer: Frank Miller himself, doing nearly all art duties as a single-author project
choices: Frank Miller himself, doing nearly all art duties as a single-author project
Klaus Janson, who actually had worked with Miller on 'Dark Knight Returns' (1986)
Lynn Varley, who actually was Miller's wife and colorist on 'Dark Knight Returns'
David Mazzucchelli, who actually had worked with Miller on 'Batman: Year One' (1987)
context: Miller wrote, drew, inked, and lettered most *Sin City* stories himself. The 2005 *Sin City* film by Robert Rodriguez recreated panels from the comic frame-by-frame; Miller co-directed. The 2014 sequel *Sin City: A Dame to Kill For* underperformed and ended the planned trilogy.

question: Frank Miller's *300* (1998), his five-issue Dark Horse Comics graphic novel about the Spartan stand at Thermopylae, was followed in 2006 by Zack Snyder's film adaptation. The film's stylized digital-grading approach borrowed heavily from Miller's color art. Who colored the *300* original comic?
answer: Lynn Varley, Miller's wife and longtime collaborator on his color work
choices: Lynn Varley, Miller's wife and longtime collaborator on his color work
John Higgins, who actually colored 'Watchmen' (1986-87) for Alan Moore
Steve Oliff, who actually colored 'Tetsuo: The Iron Man' anime adaptations
Tom McCraw, who actually colored DC's 'Legion of Super-Heroes' in the era
context: Varley's painted-on-glass coloring technique gave *300* its distinctive look. The Snyder film recreated her exact color palette in its grading. Miller and Varley divorced in 2005; she had also colored *The Dark Knight Returns* (1986) and *Elektra Lives Again* (1990).

question: *Calvin and Hobbes* — Bill Watterson's daily comic strip about a six-year-old boy and his stuffed-tiger best friend — ran for exactly ten years. Watterson famously fought his syndicate over merchandising and refused virtually all licensing. What years did the strip run?
answer: 1985 to 1995, debuting November 18 and ending December 31
choices: 1985 to 1995, debuting November 18 and ending December 31
1980 to 1990, contemporaneous with 'Bloom County' and 'The Far Side'
1990 to 2000, much shorter run than its cultural footprint suggests
1975 to 1985, ending before 'Bloom County' really took off
context: Watterson refused to license Calvin onto merchandise — no plush Hobbes toys, no Calvin pajamas, no advertising. His decision is widely cited as one of the most disciplined creative stands in modern comics. The strip's 30+ year footprint on culture is enormous despite the short run.

question: *The Far Side*, Gary Larson's single-panel daily cartoon about cows, scientists, and absurd anthropomorphic scenarios, ran in syndicated newspapers from 1980 to 1995 — almost exactly the same fifteen-year window as Bill Watterson's *Calvin and Hobbes*. What did Larson do after retiring the strip?
answer: Largely withdrew from cartooning; he began a website in 2019 with new work
choices: Largely withdrew from cartooning; he began a website in 2019 with new work
Continued with a new daily strip 'Mr. Boffo' under another pseudonym
Began writing animated screenplays for Hollywood, including 'Tarzan' (1999)
Took over 'Bloom County' from Berkeley Breathed when Breathed retired
context: Larson's daily strip ended January 1, 1995. He returned briefly with *The Far Side Gallery 5* (1995) and a 2002 special *There's a Hair in My Dirt!*. His 2019 website TheFarSide.com was his first new public cartooning in over twenty years — a small but devoted celebration.

question: Berkeley Breathed's *Bloom County* — a political satire daily strip featuring Opus the Penguin, Bill the Cat, and a Texas farm — ran in syndicated newspapers from 1980 to 1989. Its successor strips continued the same characters in *Outland* (1989-95) and an irregular online revival. Who won Pulitzers off this strip?
answer: Breathed himself, who won the Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Cartooning in 1987
choices: Breathed himself, who won the Pulitzer Prize for Editorial Cartooning in 1987
Gary Larson, who actually never won a Pulitzer for 'The Far Side'
Bill Watterson, who actually never won a Pulitzer for 'Calvin and Hobbes'
Charles Schulz, who actually was never awarded a Pulitzer for 'Peanuts'
context: Breathed remains one of only three cartoonists to win the editorial Pulitzer for a syndicated comic strip (rather than a single editorial panel). His revival on Facebook beginning in 2015 has continued *Bloom County*'s satire intermittently in the social-media era.

question: *Kingdom Come* (1996), DC Comics's four-issue prestige series imagining an older Justice League facing a generation of darker successors, was painted (not penciled) by an artist whose photorealistic comics style became his trademark. Who?
answer: Alex Ross, who used painted gouache art for the entire 200-page series
choices: Alex Ross, who used painted gouache art for the entire 200-page series
Bill Sienkiewicz, who actually painted 'Stray Toasters' (1988-89)
Dave McKean, who actually painted 'Arkham Asylum' (1989) with Morrison
Brian Bolland, who actually painted 'The Killing Joke' (1988) with Moore
context: Ross painted *Kingdom Come* from photo-reference using friends and family as Justice League stand-ins. He had previously painted Marvel's *Marvels* (1994) with writer Kurt Busiek. The Ross painted style became a defining DC look across the late 1990s; he painted hundreds of covers for both companies.

question: *Marvels* (1994), Marvel Comics's four-issue prestige series retelling the Marvel Universe's history from the perspective of a Daily Bugle photographer, was painted by Alex Ross. Who wrote it?
answer: Kurt Busiek, who would later create 'Astro City' (1995) with Ross
choices: Kurt Busiek, who would later create 'Astro City' (1995) with Ross
Alan Moore, who actually was at DC's Vertigo at the time (no Marvels)
Neil Gaiman, who actually was at Vertigo with 'Sandman' (no Marvels)
Grant Morrison, who actually was at Vertigo with 'Doom Patrol' (no Marvels)
context: Busiek and Ross's collaboration on *Marvels* led directly to *Astro City* (1995), an original superhero universe at Image and later Vertigo. Ross's photo-reference style relied heavily on real models; the *Marvels* protagonist Phil Sheldon was modeled on Ross's own father.

question: *The Adventures of Tintin*, the Belgian comic-strip serial about a young reporter traveling the world with his white terrier Snowy, began in January 1929 in a Catholic-newspaper supplement called *Le Petit Vingtieme*. Who created it?
answer: Herge (pen name of Georges Remi), a 21-year-old Belgian cartoonist
choices: Herge (pen name of Georges Remi), a 21-year-old Belgian cartoonist
Albert Uderzo, the artist who would actually create 'Asterix' (1959)
Rene Goscinny, the writer who would actually create 'Asterix' (1959)
Maurice de Bevere (Morris), who actually created 'Lucky Luke' (1946)
context: *Tintin* ran in twenty-four albums between 1929 and 1976; the final album *Tintin and Alph-Art* (1986) was published posthumously and unfinished. Herge died in 1983. The character's distinctive style — clear-line drawing (ligne claire) — became a foundational European comics aesthetic.

question: *Asterix the Gaul*, the French-language comic-strip series about a village of indomitable Gauls resisting Roman occupation in 50 BC, began in October 1959 in *Pilote* magazine. Who created it?
answer: Rene Goscinny (writer) and Albert Uderzo (artist), a long collaboration
choices: Rene Goscinny (writer) and Albert Uderzo (artist), a long collaboration
Herge (Georges Remi), who actually created Belgian 'Tintin' alone
Maurice de Bevere (Morris), who actually created 'Lucky Luke' alone
Andre Franquin, who actually created 'Spirou' and 'Gaston'
context: Goscinny died in 1977; Uderzo continued writing and drawing *Asterix* through 2009. The series has sold over 380 million copies worldwide — translated into more than 100 languages. The Roman names (Caligulaminix, Crismus Bonus) are puns; the puns were a translator's nightmare.

question: Charles Schulz's *Peanuts* — the comic strip about Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus, Lucy, and the rest — ran in syndicated newspapers for fifty years. The strip's first appearance was a small comic called 'Li'l Folks' starting in 1947 at a Minneapolis newspaper. What was the *Peanuts* run, formally?
answer: 1950 to 2000, with the final strip running February 13, 2000
choices: 1950 to 2000, with the final strip running February 13, 2000
1955 to 2005, with continuation strips through 2010
1965 to 2015, contemporaneous with 'Calvin and Hobbes' (1985-95)
1945 to 1995, before 'Calvin and Hobbes' debuted in 1985
context: Schulz drew nearly every strip himself for fifty years — over 17,500 strips. He died on February 12, 2000, the night before his final original Sunday strip was published. The strip has run in reprints continuously since 2000; United Feature Syndicate distributes the reruns daily.

question: *Bone*, Jeff Smith's indie black-and-white fantasy graphic novel series, ran for 55 issues from 1991 to 2004. It featured three Bone cousins — Fone Bone, Phoney Bone, and Smiley Bone — accidentally separated and lost in a fantasy valley with dragons and rat creatures. What was Smith's publishing approach?
answer: Self-publishing through his Cartoon Books imprint with Image distribution
choices: Self-publishing through his Cartoon Books imprint with Image distribution
Marvel Comics publication under their black-and-white anthology imprint
DC Vertigo publication alongside 'Sandman' and 'Preacher' in the 1990s
Image Comics direct publication, separately from Cartoon Books distribution
context: *Bone* is widely cited as one of the most-praised self-published comics ever. Smith reportedly invested years of his own savings into Cartoon Books. The full-color reissue by Scholastic (2005-onward) brought the series to a generation of younger readers in school libraries.

question: *Usagi Yojimbo*, Stan Sakai's long-running funny-animal samurai comic following a rabbit ronin in 17th-century Japan, debuted in *Albedo Anthropomorphics* in 1984. Sakai has continued the series with various publishers for over four decades. Who is Usagi modeled after?
answer: Miyamoto Musashi, the real 17th-century swordsman (Usagi is 'Miyamoto Usagi')
choices: Miyamoto Musashi, the real 17th-century swordsman (Usagi is 'Miyamoto Usagi')
Yagyu Munenori, the Tokugawa shogunate's official sword instructor
Tokugawa Ieyasu, the Edo-period shogun who founded the Tokugawa rule
Akira Kurosawa, the 20th-century film director (an anachronism)
context: Sakai used the historical Musashi as a starting point — Usagi's wandering ronin life, his two swords (daisho), and his philosophical reflections mirror Musashi's *Book of Five Rings*. Sakai has spoken publicly about how much research he does to make *Usagi* historically convincing despite the talking-animal cast.

question: *Cerebus the Aardvark*, Dave Sim's self-published comic about a sword-and-sorcery aardvark in a Conan-parody world, ran for exactly the issue count Sim publicly committed to from the start. How many issues, and over what span?
answer: 300 issues, from December 1977 to March 2004 — a 27-year run
choices: 300 issues, from December 1977 to March 2004 — a 27-year run
200 issues, from 1980 to 1995, ending early due to commercial pressures
150 issues, from 1985 to 2000, alongside Calvin and Hobbes's run
500 issues, the most-issued single-author comic in indie comics history
context: Sim self-published *Cerebus* through Aardvark-Vanaheim, his own imprint. The early Conan-parody phase shifted into politically and philosophically charged territory in later issues, dividing readers. Sim's later writings have remained polarizing.

question: Richie Rich, 'the poor little rich boy', was a Harvey Comics character whose long run is one of the longest in American comics. He first appeared in *Little Dot* #1 in September 1953 and got his own *Richie Rich* title in 1960. Who created the character?
answer: Alfred Harvey (publisher) with Warren Kremer (artist) credited as primary creators
choices: Alfred Harvey (publisher) with Warren Kremer (artist) credited as primary creators
Stan Lee, who actually was at Timely Comics, the future Marvel
Bob Kane, who actually was at Detective Comics, the future DC
Will Eisner, who actually had his own studio outside of Harvey Comics
context: Harvey Comics's other long-running characters (Casper the Friendly Ghost, Hot Stuff, Wendy the Witch, Audrey, Sad Sack) made up a self-contained universe of kid-friendly characters published continuously from the 1940s through the 1990s. Richie Rich was the wealthiest fictional character in comics for decades.

question: Archie Comics — Pep Comics, Riverdale, Betty and Veronica, Jughead — first introduced its title character in *Pep Comics* #22 (December 1941). The publisher was originally called MLJ Magazines. What did MLJ stand for?
answer: Maurice Coyne, Louis Silberkleit, and John Goldwater (the three publishers' first letters)
choices: Maurice Coyne, Louis Silberkleit, and John Goldwater (the three publishers' first letters)
Mickey Loves Judy, a slogan from an early proposed series of names
Magic Land Journey, an unrelated abandoned series concept of 1940
Marvelous Lights of Junkers, a German wartime publication MLJ adapted
context: MLJ was renamed 'Archie Comic Publications' after Archie's character became dominant. The Riverdale High School ensemble was created by Bob Montana and John L. Goldwater. The character was televised in *Archie's Place* (1976), *Archie's Weird Mysteries* (1999), and the very different *Riverdale* (2017-23).

question: *MAD Magazine* — the satirical magazine started by EC Comics in 1952 as a comic book — adopted its now-iconic gap-toothed redhead cover boy in 1956. He was named after a long-running American character of unknown origin who had appeared on various humorous postcards since around 1900. What is his name?
answer: Alfred E. Neuman, with the catchphrase 'What, Me Worry?'
choices: Alfred E. Neuman, with the catchphrase 'What, Me Worry?'
Charlie Brown, who actually appeared in 'Peanuts' (1950 onward) at United Features
Henry Penny, who actually was a Hanna-Barbera character not a MAD figure
Pogo Possum, who actually was Walt Kelly's main character at Walt Kelly Comics
context: Alfred E. Neuman's face had been a public-domain mascot used by toothpaste companies, dentists, and even political campaigns since 1894. Harvey Kurtzman, *MAD*'s original editor, adopted the image; cover artist Norman Mingo developed the standardized portrait. Neuman has graced almost every *MAD* cover since.

question: *Crisis on Infinite Earths* (1985-86), DC Comics's 12-issue maxi-series, collapsed the multiverse and rebooted dozens of DC characters. The series was meant to clean up decades of continuity for new readers. Who wrote and drew it?
answer: Marv Wolfman (writer) and George Perez (artist), the 'New Teen Titans' duo
choices: Marv Wolfman (writer) and George Perez (artist), the 'New Teen Titans' duo
Frank Miller (writer-artist) and Klaus Janson (inks), the 'Dark Knight' duo
Alan Moore (writer) and Dave Gibbons (artist), the 'Watchmen' duo
Neil Gaiman (writer) and Sam Kieth (artist), the 'Sandman' duo
context: Wolfman and Perez had been collaborating on *New Teen Titans* since 1980. *Crisis on Infinite Earths* killed Supergirl, the Flash (Barry Allen), and many others — landmark deaths that have remained largely permanent. The 1985 series's reboot was undone, restored, and rewoven multiple times in later decades.

question: *Marvel Super Heroes Secret Wars* (1984), Marvel Comics's first crossover maxi-series, was the result of a marketing collaboration with Mattel's toy division. Toys came first; the comics followed. Who wrote the 12-issue series?
answer: Jim Shooter, who at the time was Marvel's editor-in-chief
choices: Jim Shooter, who at the time was Marvel's editor-in-chief
Chris Claremont, who at the time was writing 'Uncanny X-Men' for Marvel
Roger Stern, who at the time was writing 'Avengers' for Marvel
John Byrne, who at the time was writing 'Fantastic Four' for Marvel
context: Shooter's role as both EIC and *Secret Wars* writer was unusual. The series was actually plotted backward from the toy line. The black symbiote costume that Spider-Man came home with — leading to Venom (1988) — is the series's most enduring legacy.

question: *Civil War* (2006-07), Marvel Comics's seven-issue maxi-series about superhero registration tearing the Marvel Universe in two, was written by a Scottish writer who had previously written 'The Authority' and 'Ultimate X-Men'. Who?
answer: Mark Millar, with Steve McNiven as the regular series artist
choices: Mark Millar, with Steve McNiven as the regular series artist
Brian Michael Bendis, who at the time was writing 'New Avengers'
Joe Quesada, who at the time was Marvel's editor-in-chief
Ed Brubaker, who at the time was writing 'Captain America' with Winter Soldier
context: Millar pitched *Civil War* with Iron Man's pro-registration side and Captain America's anti-registration side. Brubaker's *Captain America* run had been positioning Cap as a Cold War-era figure suspicious of government overreach — making Brubaker's character work feed directly into Millar's event.

question: *The Infinity Gauntlet* (1991), Marvel Comics's 6-issue maxi-series about Thanos collecting the six Infinity Gems and reshaping the universe, was the apotheosis of the cosmic-Marvel storytelling of the era. Who wrote and drew it?
answer: Jim Starlin (writer) with George Perez (issues 1-4) and Ron Lim (issues 5-6) on art
choices: Jim Starlin (writer) with George Perez (issues 1-4) and Ron Lim (issues 5-6) on art
Chris Claremont (writer) with John Byrne (artist), the X-Men duo of the late 70s
Marv Wolfman (writer) with George Perez (artist), the Teen Titans/Crisis duo
Steve Englehart (writer) with Marshall Rogers (artist), the early Detective duo
context: Starlin had created Thanos in *Iron Man* #55 (1973) and shepherded the character across decades. The 1991 *Infinity Gauntlet* series became the basis for the *Avengers: Infinity War* (2018) and *Endgame* (2019) MCU films — the closest comics-to-screen adaptation of any maxi-series ever made.

question: *The Death of Superman* (1992) — DC Comics's massive crossover event killing the Man of Steel at the hands of the alien Doomsday — was the bestselling comic of the year. The actual death issue was *Superman* #75 (January 1993). Who wrote that issue?
answer: Dan Jurgens, who also pencilled the issue and devised the Doomsday character
choices: Dan Jurgens, who also pencilled the issue and devised the Doomsday character
Marv Wolfman, who actually had not been on Superman by that time
John Byrne, who actually had left Superman titles years earlier in 1988
Roger Stern, who actually was working on related Superman titles but not #75
context: *Superman* #75 used full-page panels for nearly the entire issue — a deliberate slowing to give the moment weight. The 'World Without a Superman' aftermath arc and 'Reign of the Supermen' (introducing replacements like the Eradicator, Steel, and Cyborg-Superman) ran through 1993.

question: *Batman: Knightfall* (1993-94), DC Comics's lengthy crossover storyline in which Bane breaks Batman's back, ran across *Batman* and *Detective Comics* for over a year. Without spoiling later restoration arcs, who created Bane?
answer: Chuck Dixon, Doug Moench, and Graham Nolan, in 'Batman: Vengeance of Bane' #1
choices: Chuck Dixon, Doug Moench, and Graham Nolan, in 'Batman: Vengeance of Bane' #1
Frank Miller, who actually wrote 'Dark Knight Returns' (1986) not Knightfall
Denny O'Neil, who actually was the Batman group editor not a Bane creator
Alan Grant, who actually wrote Detective in the era but didn't create Bane
context: Bane debuted in *Vengeance of Bane* #1 (January 1993), a few months before *Knightfall* began. The Venom drug system that powers Bane was a reference to the earlier 1991 Batman arc by O'Neil. Bane's masked design and prison-bred backstory were Nolan's contributions.

question: *Secret Invasion* (2008), Marvel Comics's 8-issue maxi-series in which alien Skrulls had been replacing key Marvel Universe characters for years, was written by Brian Michael Bendis. Who provided art?
answer: Leinil Francis Yu, with Mark Morales on inks for the full eight issues
choices: Leinil Francis Yu, with Mark Morales on inks for the full eight issues
Steve McNiven, who actually drew 'Civil War' (2006-07) for Mark Millar
Frank Quitely, who actually drew 'All-Star Superman' (2005-08) for Morrison
John Cassaday, who actually drew 'Astonishing X-Men' (2004-08) for Whedon
context: *Secret Invasion* paid off a multi-year setup Bendis had threaded through his various Avengers titles. The 2023 *Secret Invasion* Disney+ MCU series adapted some elements but pivoted heavily. Bendis stayed at Marvel until 2018, when he moved to DC for a five-year exclusive contract.

question: Robert E. Howard, the Texas writer who created Conan the Cimmerian, was born in Peaster, Texas, in January 1906. He died by suicide on June 11, 1936 — the day his mother went into a coma from which she was not expected to wake. At what age?
answer: 30 years old, having published more than 100 stories across his short career
choices: 30 years old, having published more than 100 stories across his short career
33 years old, having just finished his final unpublished Conan story
27 years old, just after the 1932 sale of 'The Phoenix on the Sword'
42 years old, after a long correspondence with H.P. Lovecraft
context: Howard wrote 21 Conan stories, plus the Solomon Kane, Bran Mak Morn, Kull of Atlantis, El Borak, and Breckinridge Elkins series, plus innumerable other fiction. His correspondence with H.P. Lovecraft, August Derleth, and Clark Ashton Smith fills several published volumes today.

question: Robert E. Howard's first published Conan story was 'The Phoenix on the Sword' in *Weird Tales* magazine, December 1932. The story had originally been written as a story about a different one of Howard's heroes — and then rewritten with Conan. Who was the original protagonist?
answer: Kull of Atlantis (later Kull the Conqueror), whose throne-story was reworked
choices: Kull of Atlantis (later Kull the Conqueror), whose throne-story was reworked
Solomon Kane, the Puritan swordsman from Howard's earlier 1928 stories
Bran Mak Morn, the Pictish king from Howard's mid-1920s stories
El Borak (Francis X. Gordon), Howard's Texas-Afghanistan adventurer
context: Howard had drafted the story as a Kull tale, then realized after rejection that a new character — a barbarian instead of an exiled king — could carry the story better. Conan became Howard's most lucrative creation; Kull only got a handful of stories.

question: Robert E. Howard's puritanical, dark-clad swordsman Solomon Kane was the writer's first major adventure-hero character — debuting before Conan, before Kull, before Bran Mak Morn. He appeared in Howard's first published story for *Weird Tales*. What year was Solomon Kane's debut?
answer: 1928, in 'Red Shadows' for Weird Tales (Howard's first major fiction sale)
choices: 1928, in 'Red Shadows' for Weird Tales (Howard's first major fiction sale)
1932, the same year as the Conan debut in 'The Phoenix on the Sword'
1925, two years earlier than the actual first Solomon Kane story
1935, only a year before Howard's 1936 death (much later than actual debut)
context: Howard wrote about a dozen Solomon Kane stories over his career. Kane was an English Puritan from Devon, wandering the world hunting evil. The character was adapted into a 2009 film starring James Purefoy that received modest reception. Howard's other early hero was Sailor Steve Costigan.

question: Robert E. Howard's Bran Mak Morn was the last king of the Picts, a doomed Celtic warrior fighting Rome's encroachment on Britain. The character appeared in only four published stories during Howard's lifetime. What is the most famous of these?
answer: 'Worms of the Earth' (1932), in which Bran summons ancient subterranean beings
choices: 'Worms of the Earth' (1932), in which Bran summons ancient subterranean beings
'The Phoenix on the Sword' (1932), which is actually a Conan story not Bran's
'The Tower of the Elephant' (1933), which is actually a Conan story not Bran's
'A Witch Shall Be Born' (1934), which is actually a Conan story not Bran's
context: 'Worms of the Earth' is widely cited as one of Howard's most accomplished single stories. The four published Bran tales are short by Howard's standards but dense; he wrote them in the early 1930s alongside his Conan output. The Picts also appear as a recurring background tribe in Conan's Hyborian Age stories.

question: Howard Phillips Lovecraft, the Providence-based weird-fiction writer who created the Cthulhu mythos, was born and died in Providence, Rhode Island. He published almost all his work in *Weird Tales* magazine and through correspondence networks. What were his dates?
answer: 1890 to 1937, with his death from intestinal cancer at age 46
choices: 1890 to 1937, with his death from intestinal cancer at age 46
1880 to 1925, with his death just before Howard's debut in 'Weird Tales'
1900 to 1947, much later than his actual life ended in 1937
1885 to 1930, with his death before his most famous tales were written
context: Lovecraft was poorly known and unsuccessful during his lifetime. His circle — August Derleth, Donald Wandrei, Robert Bloch — kept his work in print posthumously through Arkham House (founded 1939 by Derleth). The Cthulhu mythos has now spread far beyond Lovecraft's original stories.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's most-cited single story 'The Call of Cthulhu' was published in *Weird Tales* in February 1928. It introduced the iconic Great Old One Cthulhu, the sunken city of R'lyeh, and the mythos framework. What is the famous couplet from the story?
answer: 'That is not dead which can eternal lie, and with strange aeons even death may die.'
choices: 'That is not dead which can eternal lie, and with strange aeons even death may die.'
'In his house at R'lyeh, dead Cthulhu waits dreaming.' (which is a separate sentence)
'Cthulhu fhtagn!' (the chant of the cultists, but not the couplet itself)
'The most merciful thing in the world is the inability of the human mind...' (story opening)
context: Lovecraft attributed the couplet to the fictional *Necronomicon* of the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred. The opening line — 'The most merciful thing in the world...' — is also widely quoted as one of the finest opening sentences in 20th-century weird fiction.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's mythos features a fictional ancient grimoire of forbidden knowledge written by the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred — the *Necronomicon*. Many fans over the years have asked Lovecraft and his correspondents whether the book is real. What was Lovecraft's stock answer?
answer: He told correspondents the book was entirely his invention, with no real source
choices: He told correspondents the book was entirely his invention, with no real source
He claimed to have inherited a 19th-century English translation from a Providence cousin
He attributed it to a real ancient manuscript at Yale's Beinecke Library
He cited a non-existent 1928 doctoral dissertation from Miskatonic University
context: Lovecraft fabricated a detailed publication history (in 730 AD by Alhazred, translated by John Dee in 1586, etc.) but always confirmed in personal letters that the book was fiction. Several 'real' *Necronomicons* have been published as pranks or fan-fiction over the decades; none predate Lovecraft.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's novella *At the Mountains of Madness* — a Antarctic-expedition horror story about explorers finding the ruins of a pre-human civilization — was written in 1931 but did not sell to *Weird Tales* (the editor rejected it). Where was it eventually published?
answer: *Astounding Stories* in February-April 1936, serialized in three parts
choices: *Astounding Stories* in February-April 1936, serialized in three parts
*Weird Tales* in 1932, after Lovecraft revised the novella once
Arkham House posthumously in 1939, never serialized in any magazine
*Black Mask* magazine in 1934, alongside hardboiled detective stories
context: F. Orlin Tremaine of *Astounding* paid Lovecraft for the serialization. Editor Farnsworth Wright of *Weird Tales* had rejected the novella partly because of its length, partly because Wright felt the science-fiction element pushed it outside his magazine's brief.

question: Clark Ashton Smith (1893-1961), the third pillar of *Weird Tales* alongside Lovecraft and Howard, was a California recluse who wrote highly stylized prose fantasies. His most famous setting was a future-Earth far in the dying-sun age. What is the setting called?
answer: Zothique, the last continent of a far-future dying Earth
choices: Zothique, the last continent of a far-future dying Earth
Hyperborea, an arctic continent in a pre-human ice age (one of CAS's other settings)
Xiccarph, a far-future Mars setting in some of CAS's other stories
Averoigne, a medieval France setting in some of CAS's other stories
context: Smith wrote 16 Zothique stories between 1932 and 1948. Jack Vance and Gene Wolfe have both cited Smith's Zothique as a primary influence on their own dying-Earth fiction. Smith was a sculptor and painter as well as a writer; his California home is now a Smith heritage site.

question: Fritz Leiber's *Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser* stories — two wandering swordsmen-thieves in a fantasy world centered on the city of Lankhmar — began in 1939 and ran for nearly fifty years. Leiber himself coined the term 'sword and sorcery' for the genre. What is the duo's home city?
answer: Lankhmar, the great city of Nehwon (Leiber's pun on 'Nowhen')
choices: Lankhmar, the great city of Nehwon (Leiber's pun on 'Nowhen')
Sanctuary, the city of Robert Asprin's 'Thieves' World' shared-world setting
Greyhawk, the city in Gary Gygax's D&D campaign setting (later)
Waterdeep, the city in the Forgotten Realms D&D setting (much later)
context: Lankhmar was deeply influential on Dungeons & Dragons; Gary Gygax acknowledged Leiber's debt. Leiber and Harry Otto Fischer co-created Fafhrd and the Mouser in 1934 college letters; the first story 'Two Sought Adventure' was published 1939 in *Unknown* magazine.

question: Fritz Leiber coined the term 'sword and sorcery' to describe his Fafhrd and Gray Mouser stories — and Howard's Conan, and similar fantasy fiction — in 1961, in response to a magazine reader's letter asking what to call the genre. In what letter-page exchange was the term first used?
answer: In *Amra* fanzine, a Conan-related fan publication of the 1960s
choices: In *Amra* fanzine, a Conan-related fan publication of the 1960s
In a letter column of the original 'Weird Tales' magazine in the 1930s
In the foreword to the first 'Conan the Barbarian' Lancer paperbacks of 1966
In a Worldcon panel discussion at the 1965 LonCon convention proceedings
context: Michael Moorcock had proposed 'epic fantasy' in a competing letter; Leiber's 'sword and sorcery' won the genre-name vote. Leiber was a Hugo and Nebula-winning writer in many subgenres — *The Big Time* (1958), *Conjure Wife* (1943), and the Lankhmar stories are his best-known.

question: Michael Moorcock's Elric of Melnibone — an albino sorcerer-king of a dying empire, wielding the soul-eating black sword Stormbringer — debuted in *Science Fantasy* magazine in 1961 and ran across many novels through the 2000s. What is Elric's relationship to Moorcock's broader cosmology?
answer: Elric is one incarnation of the 'Eternal Champion', Moorcock's recurring concept
choices: Elric is one incarnation of the 'Eternal Champion', Moorcock's recurring concept
Elric is a one-off character not connected to any other Moorcock series
Elric is the older brother of Corum, who actually is a separate Eternal Champion
Elric is descended from Howard's Conan in Moorcock's literary lineage
context: Moorcock has written 'Eternal Champion' across many series and centuries: Elric, Corum, Hawkmoon, Erekose, Von Bek. The cosmology argues these are all 'the same person' in different aspects across the multiverse — a foundational concept in fantasy and influence on much later multiverse-fiction.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Tarzan first appeared in *All-Story Magazine* (October 1912) as 'Tarzan of the Apes', a serialized novel about a British infant raised by Mangani great apes in the African jungle. The character's English name is what?
answer: John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, with the ape-name 'Tarzan' (meaning 'white skin')
choices: John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, with the ape-name 'Tarzan' (meaning 'white skin')
John Carter, who actually is Burroughs's Mars hero from 'Princess of Mars'
Lord John Roxton, who actually is Conan Doyle's 'Lost World' character
Lord Henry Wotton, who actually is Wilde's 'Picture of Dorian Gray' character
context: Burroughs wrote 24 Tarzan novels between 1912 and 1948. The character has been adapted in over 80 films, TV series, comics, and theme parks. The 1932 Johnny Weissmuller MGM *Tarzan the Ape Man* established many of the screen tropes (loincloth, vine-swinging, 'Me Tarzan, you Jane') not present in Burroughs's books.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's John Carter of Mars debuted in *All-Story Magazine* in 1912 (the same year as Tarzan), as a Confederate veteran transported to a dying Mars (Barsoom). Carter's beloved is a four-armed princess of Helium named Dejah Thoris. What was the novel's serial title before book publication?
answer: *Under the Moons of Mars*, later book-published as 'A Princess of Mars' (1917)
choices: *Under the Moons of Mars*, later book-published as 'A Princess of Mars' (1917)
*The Gods of Mars*, which actually was the second Mars book (1913)
*Warlord of Mars*, which actually was the third Mars book (1914)
*Thuvia, Maid of Mars*, which actually was the fourth Mars book (1916)
context: Burroughs wrote 11 John Carter novels. The 2012 Disney film *John Carter* underperformed at the box office, partly attributed to the title's lack of mention of Mars (despite the films' source title 'A Princess of Mars'). Carter influenced Frank Herbert's *Dune* and many science-fantasy works.

question: *Doc Savage* — the Man of Bronze, an Arctic-trained superhero with five expert associates and a base on the 86th floor of a New York skyscraper — debuted in *Doc Savage Magazine* in March 1933. The hero's first author wrote the entire pulp run under house pen-name Kenneth Robeson. Who really wrote it?
answer: Lester Dent, who wrote 159 of the 181 monthly Doc Savage novels (1933-49)
choices: Lester Dent, who wrote 159 of the 181 monthly Doc Savage novels (1933-49)
Walter B. Gibson, who actually wrote 'The Shadow' under another house name
Norvell W. Page, who actually wrote 'The Spider' for Popular Publications
Frank Gruber, who wrote pulp Westerns and detective stories, not Doc Savage
context: Dent wrote roughly two Doc Savage novels per month for sixteen years. The 1975 *Doc Savage: The Man of Bronze* film (with Ron Ely) was disappointing; James Bama's painted 1960s Bantam paperback covers became iconic to a generation of pulp readers. Dent's other pulp work fills several volumes.

question: *The Shadow* — the pulp hero who 'knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men' — debuted on radio in 1930 and in *The Shadow Magazine* (April 1931). The character's iconic catchphrase opening was used at the start of every radio episode. What was it?
answer: 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men? The Shadow knows!'
choices: 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men? The Shadow knows!'
'Up, up, and away!' (which actually was Superman's tagline from the 1940s)
'Out of the night, when the full moon is bright...' (which is Zorro's, not Shadow's)
'I am the night!' (which actually is associated with Batman, not the Shadow)
context: Walter B. Gibson wrote 282 of the 325 Shadow pulp novels under the house pseudonym Maxwell Grant. Orson Welles voiced the Shadow on radio from 1937 to 1938. The 1994 *Shadow* film (Alec Baldwin) is the character's most recent major adaptation; it underperformed at the box office.

question: *The Phantom* — the 'Ghost Who Walks' — was created by Lee Falk for King Features Syndicate as a daily newspaper comic strip in 1936, predating Superman by two years. The Phantom is widely considered the first costumed superhero. Where does he live?
answer: The Skull Cave in the fictional country of Bangalla in Africa
choices: The Skull Cave in the fictional country of Bangalla in Africa
The Batcave in Gotham City, which is actually Batman's lair not the Phantom's
The Fortress of Solitude in the Arctic, which is actually Superman's not the Phantom's
The Hall of Justice in Washington DC, which is actually Justice League not Phantom
context: Falk created *Mandrake the Magician* (1934) and *The Phantom* (1936) — both still running daily comic strips today. The Phantom passes the mask down generation to generation; the current 'Phantom' is the 21st of his line. The 1996 *Phantom* film with Billy Zane was a modest performer.

question: *Flash Gordon* — the King Features science-fiction comic strip about Earth athletes traveling to the planet Mongo to oppose Ming the Merciless — debuted in January 1934. Who created it?
answer: Alex Raymond, with Don Moore as writer (Raymond did the art)
choices: Alex Raymond, with Don Moore as writer (Raymond did the art)
Hal Foster, who actually created 'Prince Valiant' for King Features in 1937
Burne Hogarth, who actually drew the Tarzan comic strip in the 1930s
Roy Crane, who actually drew 'Wash Tubbs' and 'Captain Easy' in the same era
context: *Flash Gordon* was King Features's response to the licensed *Buck Rogers* strip. Raymond's art style became one of the most-imitated in newspaper comic strips. The 1936 *Flash Gordon* Universal serial (with Buster Crabbe) inspired George Lucas's *Star Wars* opening crawl decades later.

question: *Buck Rogers in the 25th Century* — the pulp space-opera character whose name became synonymous with rocket-ship adventure — first appeared in *Amazing Stories* in August 1928. The novella was 'Armageddon 2419 AD' by what author?
answer: Philip Francis Nowlan, who would later script the Buck Rogers comic strip from 1929
choices: Philip Francis Nowlan, who would later script the Buck Rogers comic strip from 1929
Edgar Rice Burroughs, who actually wrote 'John Carter of Mars' (1912) not Buck Rogers
Hugo Gernsback, who actually founded 'Amazing Stories' but didn't write Buck Rogers
John W. Campbell, who actually edited 'Astounding' but didn't create Buck Rogers
context: Nowlan and artist Dick Calkins began the *Buck Rogers* daily strip in January 1929 — the first widely successful science-fiction newspaper comic. The 1939 Universal *Buck Rogers* serial (Buster Crabbe again) ran parallel to *Flash Gordon*; both were Saturday matinee staples for decades.

question: *Prince Valiant in the Days of King Arthur* — the King Features Sunday newspaper comic about an exiled Viking prince at Camelot — has run continuously since February 1937. Who created and originally drew it?
answer: Hal Foster, who had previously drawn the 'Tarzan' Sunday strip from 1931 to 1937
choices: Hal Foster, who had previously drawn the 'Tarzan' Sunday strip from 1931 to 1937
Alex Raymond, who actually was drawing 'Flash Gordon' for the same era
Burne Hogarth, who actually was drawing the 'Tarzan' Sunday strip after Foster
Roy Crane, who actually was drawing 'Wash Tubbs' for the same syndicate
context: Foster drew *Prince Valiant* for 34 years; John Cullen Murphy took over in 1971; Gary Gianni since 2004 and Thomas Yeates as artist since 2012. The strip is notable for using captions rather than speech bubbles — a deliberate aesthetic choice maintained for 87+ years.

question: *Black Mask* magazine (1920-51) was one of the most important American pulp magazines, particularly for hardboiled crime fiction. Two of the most influential American crime writers had their first major work appear in its pages. Who were they?
answer: Dashiell Hammett (creator of Sam Spade) and Raymond Chandler (creator of Philip Marlowe)
choices: Dashiell Hammett (creator of Sam Spade) and Raymond Chandler (creator of Philip Marlowe)
Edgar Allan Poe (creator of Auguste Dupin) and Arthur Conan Doyle (Sherlock Holmes)
Robert E. Howard (creator of Conan) and H.P. Lovecraft (creator of Cthulhu)
Mickey Spillane (creator of Mike Hammer) and James Cain (no Black Mask connection)
context: Hammett serialized *Red Harvest*, *The Maltese Falcon*, and other novels in *Black Mask* during the 1920s. Chandler's 1933 debut 'Blackmailers Don't Shoot' appeared there; the magazine's editor Joseph T. Shaw was Chandler's mentor. *Black Mask* defined the hardboiled style of American crime fiction.

question: Isaac Asimov's *Foundation* trilogy — the future-galaxy political-history sequence about psychohistorian Hari Seldon's plan to shorten a galactic dark age — was serialized in *Astounding Science-Fiction* magazine in eight short stories. When did the original series run?
answer: 1942 to 1950, with the book-collected trilogy appearing 1951-53
choices: 1942 to 1950, with the book-collected trilogy appearing 1951-53
1952 to 1960, contemporaneous with Asimov's robot novels
1937 to 1942, alongside Heinlein's Future History stories
1960 to 1968, much later than the actual serialization dates
context: Asimov added *Foundation's Edge* (1982) and *Foundation and Earth* (1986) later, plus the prequels *Prelude to Foundation* (1988) and *Forward the Foundation* (1993). The 2021- Apple TV adaptation departs heavily from the books. John W. Campbell at *Astounding* shaped the original stories' direction.

question: Robert Heinlein's *Starship Troopers* — the science-fiction novel about a future Mobile Infantry's war against alien Arachnids, framed as a 'juvenile' Heinlein but rejected by his usual youth publisher Scribner — was published in 1959. What was the original novel's controversial element?
answer: Its political ideology, which restricted citizenship to those who completed Federal Service
choices: Its political ideology, which restricted citizenship to those who completed Federal Service
Its depiction of human-alien war as morally complex, not the actual main controversy
Its full-page violence sequences, which actually were not heavy in the novel
Its non-traditional narrative structure, which actually was very conventional
context: Heinlein wrote *Starship Troopers* as a juvenile but Scribner's editor declined; Putnam's published it as adult fiction. Paul Verhoeven's 1997 film adaptation famously inverted Heinlein's politics into satirical fascism — a reading Heinlein's estate has disputed. The novel won the 1960 Hugo Award.

question: Ray Bradbury's *Fahrenheit 451* — a dystopian novel about a future fire department that burns books — was first published as a 1953 novel. Its title refers to the temperature at which paper auto-ignites. What was the novel's original short-story precursor?
answer: 'The Fireman' (1951), published in 'Galaxy Science Fiction' magazine
choices: 'The Fireman' (1951), published in 'Galaxy Science Fiction' magazine
'The Pedestrian' (1951), a related but distinct Bradbury short story
'The Veldt' (1950), an unrelated Bradbury short story in 'The Saturday Evening Post'
'A Sound of Thunder' (1952), an unrelated Bradbury time-travel story in 'Collier's'
context: Bradbury wrote the novel-length expansion in nine days on a dime-rented typewriter at UCLA's basement library. *The Martian Chronicles* (1950) had been a similarly assembled work — short stories woven into a longer narrative. *Something Wicked This Way Comes* (1962) is Bradbury's other novel-length 'major work'.

question: Frank Herbert's *Dune* — the science-fiction epic of Paul Atreides on the desert planet Arrakis, the spice melange, and the ecology of the sandworms — was first serialized in two parts in *Analog* magazine (1963-64 and 1965) before its 1965 novel publication. What other Herbert work did *Analog* serialize?
answer: Most of Herbert's pre-Dune short fiction, but no other novels of this magnitude
choices: Most of Herbert's pre-Dune short fiction, but no other novels of this magnitude
*Children of Dune* (1976), which actually was direct novel publication
*God Emperor of Dune* (1981), which actually was direct novel publication
*Heretics of Dune* (1984), which actually was direct novel publication
context: *Dune* was rejected by twenty-three publishers before Chilton Book Company (a print-shop publisher better known for auto-repair manuals) bought it. The novel won the 1965 Nebula Award and the 1966 Hugo Award. Herbert wrote five sequels through 1985; his son Brian Herbert has continued the franchise since.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's *The Hobbit* — the children's fantasy novel about Bilbo Baggins and Thorin Oakenshield's company — was published by George Allen & Unwin in London in 1937. Tolkien wrote it for his own children and submitted it to the publisher only on a friend's suggestion. What did the publisher do to test it?
answer: Gave it to the publisher's 10-year-old son Rayner Unwin to review for a fee
choices: Gave it to the publisher's 10-year-old son Rayner Unwin to review for a fee
Sent it to a panel of professional children's reviewers in London
Tested it via prose-reading at Oxford's Eagle and Child pub gatherings
Published it directly without external review of the typescript
context: Rayner Unwin read *The Hobbit* and recommended publication; his shilling review fee may be the most cost-effective publishing decision in English-language history. Rayner Unwin later became Tolkien's primary contact at the firm and was the editor for *The Lord of the Rings* (1954-55).

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's *The Lord of the Rings* was published in three volumes by Allen & Unwin in 1954-55, the publisher having split the long single novel into three books due to paper-rationing economics. What were the original three-volume titles?
answer: *The Fellowship of the Ring* (1954), *The Two Towers* (1954), *The Return of the King* (1955)
choices: *The Fellowship of the Ring* (1954), *The Two Towers* (1954), *The Return of the King* (1955)
*The Lord of the Rings: Book One*, *Book Two*, *Book Three* (a simpler scheme)
*The Ring* (1954), *The Wars* (1954), *The Crown* (1955) (a much-altered title scheme)
*Frodo's Journey* (1954), *Saruman's War* (1954), *Aragorn's Crown* (1955)
context: Tolkien himself preferred a six-book structure, with two books per volume; the publisher overrode him. Tolkien wrote *Lord of the Rings* slowly over 16 years (1937-1953). The 2001-03 Peter Jackson films adapted the trilogy; the 2012-14 *Hobbit* trilogy adapted the shorter source novel.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's *The Silmarillion* — the long-promised 'mythology' that underpins Middle-earth — was published posthumously in 1977. Tolkien had worked on it for over fifty years; he died in 1973. Who edited it to publishable form?
answer: Christopher Tolkien, the author's youngest son and literary executor
choices: Christopher Tolkien, the author's youngest son and literary executor
Guy Gavriel Kay, who actually worked with Christopher Tolkien on the editing
Rayner Unwin, who actually was the publisher contact not the editor
Humphrey Carpenter, who actually edited Tolkien's 'Letters' (1981) instead
context: Christopher Tolkien spent four years editing *The Silmarillion* with the help of Guy Gavriel Kay (a young Canadian assistant who would later become a notable fantasy novelist himself). Christopher edited Tolkien's posthumous publications for over four decades until his own death in 2020.

question: T.H. White's *The Once and Future King* — the four-volume Arthurian sequence ('The Sword in the Stone', 'The Queen of Air and Darkness', 'The Ill-Made Knight', 'The Candle in the Wind') — was published in collected form in 1958. When did the first volume appear?
answer: 1938, with 'The Sword in the Stone' as a standalone novel for children
choices: 1938, with 'The Sword in the Stone' as a standalone novel for children
1948, contemporaneous with C.S. Lewis's first 'Narnia' book in 1950
1952, the same year as the Disney 'Sword in the Stone' film's source
1958, the year the collected omnibus was published in single volume
context: Disney's *The Sword in the Stone* (1963) adapted only White's first volume. The 1960 Lerner-and-Loewe Broadway musical *Camelot* adapted parts of White's third volume. White's 1977 posthumous fifth volume *The Book of Merlyn* completes the cycle.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley's *The Mists of Avalon* (1983) retold the Arthurian legend from the perspective of the women of the court — Morgaine, Igraine, Gwenhwyfar, Viviane. The novel became an unexpected commercial breakthrough for its publisher. What was Bradley's main earlier work?
answer: The *Darkover* science-fantasy series (from 1958) of telepathic feudal sci-fi
choices: The *Darkover* science-fantasy series (from 1958) of telepathic feudal sci-fi
*A Wrinkle in Time* (1962), which actually was by Madeleine L'Engle
*Earthsea* (from 1968), which actually was by Ursula K. Le Guin
*The Mists of Avalon* sequels, which were her main 1980s work
context: Bradley had been an SFWA grand master in 1999. Sequels and prequels to *Mists* by Bradley and Diana L. Paxson continued into the 2000s. Bradley's later years were complicated by serious posthumous allegations from her daughter; the books remain widely read but their author's reputation is now contested.

question: Robin Hood — the legendary outlaw of Sherwood Forest — first appears in the historical record as a literary character in *The Vision of Piers Plowman* (1377) by William Langland, where a sloth-figure says 'I know Robin Hood'. What is the earliest surviving full Robin Hood text?
answer: *A Gest of Robyn Hode* — a 15th-century ballad-collection printed around 1500
choices: *A Gest of Robyn Hode* — a 15th-century ballad-collection printed around 1500
*The True Tale of Robin Hood* (1632) by Martin Parker, the earliest text
*The Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode* (1577), the first printed ballad collection
*The Ballads of Robin Hood* (1660), a Restoration-era compilation
context: The historicity of Robin Hood remains disputed; most scholars now treat him as a literary figure with possible mixed sources. The 'Robin and Marian' love story is a later addition; the original ballads featured Robin alone or with Little John, Will Scarlet, and Friar Tuck.

question: Chretien de Troyes, the 12th-century French poet, is the originator of much of what we now think of as 'Arthurian romance' — the Grail quest, Lancelot's affair with Guinevere, the introduction of Perceval. He worked at which French court?
answer: The court of Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, in Troyes
choices: The court of Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, in Troyes
The court of King Louis VII of France, in Paris around 1170
The court of Eleanor of Aquitaine, in Poitiers around 1160
The court of King Henry II of England, in Westminster around 1175
context: Chretien wrote *Erec and Enide*, *Cliges*, *Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart*, *Yvain, the Knight of the Lion*, and the unfinished *Perceval, the Story of the Grail*. The latter introduced the Holy Grail to literature. Chretien's work was translated and rewritten across medieval Europe for three centuries.

question: *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* — the 14th-century Middle English Arthurian romance about a New Year's Eve challenge — survives in only a single manuscript (British Library Cotton Nero A.x). The poet is anonymous. What other works are in the same manuscript?
answer: *Pearl*, *Patience*, and *Cleanness* — all by the same anonymous 'Pearl Poet'
choices: *Pearl*, *Patience*, and *Cleanness* — all by the same anonymous 'Pearl Poet'
*Piers Plowman* and *Canterbury Tales* by Langland and Chaucer respectively
*Confessio Amantis* by John Gower and *Sir Orfeo* by anonymous
*Le Morte d'Arthur* by Malory and *Sir Eglamour of Artois*
context: The 'Pearl Poet' (or 'Gawain Poet') wrote in a Northwest Midlands dialect of Middle English, distinct from Chaucer's London English. *Pearl* is a Christian elegy; *Patience* a Jonah retelling; *Cleanness* a moral poem. J.R.R. Tolkien edited and translated all four poems during his Oxford career.

question: Frank Miller's *Batman: Year One* (1987), the four-issue arc in *Batman* #404-407 retelling Batman's origin, was illustrated by an artist Miller would later collaborate with on *Daredevil: Born Again* (1986) and *Born Again* sequels. Who?
answer: David Mazzucchelli, who would later create his own 'Asterios Polyp' (2009)
choices: David Mazzucchelli, who would later create his own 'Asterios Polyp' (2009)
Klaus Janson, who had inked Miller's 'Dark Knight Returns' (1986)
Bill Sienkiewicz, who had drawn 'New Mutants' and 'Stray Toasters'
Brian Bolland, who actually drew 'The Killing Joke' (1988) with Moore
context: Mazzucchelli's *Year One* art used heavy black-spotting and minimalist lines — a deliberate counterpoint to Miller's busier *Dark Knight Returns* style. *Year One* has been adapted to animation (2011) and is a key source for Christopher Nolan's *Batman Begins* (2005). Mazzucchelli's *Asterios Polyp* won the 2010 LA Times Book Prize.

question: Brian Michael Bendis's *Powers* (2000-onward) — the long-running indie crime-comic about police detectives in a superhero universe investigating super-powered crimes — has run at Image, Marvel's Icon imprint, and Jinxworld over its long history. Who provided the original art?
answer: Michael Avon Oeming, with a deliberately stylized cartoon-noir art approach
choices: Michael Avon Oeming, with a deliberately stylized cartoon-noir art approach
David Mack, who actually was the co-creator of 'Daredevil' Bullseye stories
Alex Maleev, who actually drew Bendis's 'Daredevil' run (2001-06)
Mike Allred, who actually drew 'Madman' for Dark Horse and Image
context: Oeming and Bendis have continued *Powers* for over twenty years across many publishers. Their stylized approach — black-spotted figures, minimalist backgrounds, intense facial work — became one of the defining looks of early-2000s indie crime comics. The 2015 PlayStation Network *Powers* TV series adapted the comic.

question: Mark Millar's *Kick-Ass* (2008) — the comic about a teenager who tries to be a real-life superhero with no powers and gets violently destroyed in the process — was published through Marvel's creator-owned Icon imprint. Who drew it?
answer: John Romita Jr., the Marvel third-generation artist (son of John Romita Sr.)
choices: John Romita Jr., the Marvel third-generation artist (son of John Romita Sr.)
Steve McNiven, who actually drew 'Civil War' (2006-07) for Mark Millar
Tony Harris, who actually drew 'Ex Machina' (2004-10) for Brian K. Vaughan
Bryan Hitch, who actually drew 'The Ultimates' (2002-03) for Mark Millar
context: *Kick-Ass* was adapted to a 2010 film by Matthew Vaughn — released before the comic itself had fully concluded its first arc. The film's depictions of Hit-Girl (an 11-year-old in violent action) drew widespread media commentary. Romita Jr. and Millar's collaboration continued with *Kick-Ass 2* (2010-12) and *Hit-Girl* (2012-13).

question: Frank Miller's 1998 graphic novel *300* was adapted into a 2006 film that grossed over $450 million on a $65 million budget. The film's stylized look — digital sand-and-sepia, slow-motion action, painted skies — was directed by whom?
answer: Zack Snyder, in only his second feature after 2004's 'Dawn of the Dead' remake
choices: Zack Snyder, in only his second feature after 2004's 'Dawn of the Dead' remake
Robert Rodriguez, who actually directed 'Sin City' (2005), the Miller adaptation
Christopher Nolan, who actually directed 'Batman Begins' (2005) the year before
Bryan Singer, who actually directed 'X-Men' (2000) and 'Superman Returns' (2006)
context: Snyder went on to direct *Watchmen* (2009), the *Sucker Punch* (2011), and DC films from *Man of Steel* (2013) onward. *300*'s success in 2007 — released over a Super Bowl weekend — was the first major hit for the digital green-screen filmmaking technique that would later define late-2000s action cinema.

question: Mary Stewart's Merlin Trilogy — *The Crystal Cave* (1970), *The Hollow Hills* (1973), *The Last Enchantment* (1979) — retold the Arthurian legend from the perspective of Merlin as a Welsh-born young magician. What is the trilogy's setting?
answer: 5th and 6th century Britain, with historically realistic post-Roman geography
choices: 5th and 6th century Britain, with historically realistic post-Roman geography
11th century Wales, set after the Norman conquest period
8th century Anglo-Saxon Britain, set during Beowulf's era
12th century Provence, set during the Crusades and troubadour tradition
context: Stewart wrote a fourth book *The Wicked Day* (1983) from Mordred's perspective. Stewart was also known for romantic suspense novels (*Nine Coaches Waiting*, 1958) before turning to Arthurian historical fantasy. Her Merlin Trilogy is widely cited as the most-researched 20th-century Arthurian retelling.

question: Frank Miller's *The Dark Knight Returns* (1986) reimagined a 55-year-old Batman returning from retirement to face the gangs of Gotham. The four-issue prestige series used a unique color approach that pushed beyond what most superhero comics of the era attempted. Who handled colors?
answer: Lynn Varley, Miller's wife and longtime color collaborator on prestige projects
choices: Lynn Varley, Miller's wife and longtime color collaborator on prestige projects
Tatjana Wood, who actually colored the contemporaneous 'Crisis on Infinite Earths'
John Higgins, who actually colored 'Watchmen' (1986-87) for Alan Moore
Steve Oliff, who actually colored Marvel comics like 'X-Men' through this era
context: Varley's hand-painted color separations gave *Dark Knight Returns* a watercolor-textured look entirely different from the era's flat four-color comic printing. She also colored *300* (1998), *Elektra Lives Again* (1990), and other Miller works. Miller and Varley divorced in 2005.

question: Alan Moore's *Saga of the Swamp Thing* run (1984-87) revolutionized the title by revealing in his first issue that the Swamp Thing was not, as previously believed, the transformed Alec Holland — but a plant creature that had absorbed Holland's consciousness. What issue did this reveal occur?
answer: *Saga of the Swamp Thing* #21 'The Anatomy Lesson' (February 1984)
choices: *Saga of the Swamp Thing* #21 'The Anatomy Lesson' (February 1984)
*Saga of the Swamp Thing* #1, which actually was a Marty Pasko issue
*The Saga of the Swamp Thing* #36, which actually was a separate Moore arc
*Swamp Thing Annual* #2, which actually was Moore's John Constantine debut
context: Moore's *Swamp Thing* run introduced John Constantine in *Swamp Thing* #37 (1985), who later got his own *Hellblazer* series (1988) and his own DC universe presence for decades. Steve Bissette and John Totleben provided art for most of Moore's run; later artists included Rick Veitch and Stan Woch.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin film — the most-debated 59 seconds of Bigfoot footage ever recorded — was shot on a single Bolex 16mm camera by Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin in northern California. The figure walking through frame became known by a nickname based on the film name. What year was the film shot?
answer: October 20, 1967, at Bluff Creek in Six Rivers National Forest
choices: October 20, 1967, at Bluff Creek in Six Rivers National Forest
August 15, 1958, the same year Jerry Crew coined 'Bigfoot' in Humboldt
October 31, 1972, on the same Bluff Creek where the 1958 prints appeared
July 4, 1976, during the American Bicentennial summer's wilderness boom
context: The film figure is widely called 'Patty' by Bigfoot researchers. Patterson died of cancer in 1972, never publicly recanting. Gimlin was still alive into the 2020s. Frame-by-frame analyses, gait studies, and costume claims have failed to produce consensus; the film remains the most contested 59 seconds in cryptozoology.

question: The word 'Bigfoot' was coined by a small Northern California newspaper, the *Humboldt Times*, after a road-construction crew foreman named Jerry Crew brought in a plaster cast of footprints he found near his bulldozer. The footprints were 16 inches long. What year?
answer: 1958, with the casts photographed and the term coined that October
choices: 1958, with the casts photographed and the term coined that October
1967, the same year as the Patterson-Gimlin film at Bluff Creek
1924, during the famous Mount St. Helens 'Ape Canyon' incident
1976, the Bicentennial wilderness-craze year that boosted cryptozoology
context: The 1958 'Bluff Creek' tracks were later revealed (in 2002, after Ray Wallace's death) to have been fabricated by Wallace using carved wooden feet as a prank on his construction crew. The wooden feet survived; the family released them. The 1958 founding incident of modern Bigfoot lore is now generally considered a hoax.

question: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit of Mount Everest on May 29, 1953 — the first confirmed ascent. During the expedition they reported seeing strange tracks high on the mountain, attributed to the local Yeti or 'Abominable Snowman'. What is the Sherpa name?
answer: Yeti, from the Tibetan 'meh-teh' or 'yeh-teh' meaning 'rock-thing' or 'bear-man'
choices: Yeti, from the Tibetan 'meh-teh' or 'yeh-teh' meaning 'rock-thing' or 'bear-man'
Skunk Ape, which actually is Florida regional folklore and not Tibetan
Mapinguari, which actually is Amazon Basin folklore from Brazil
Almas, which actually is Caucasus Mountain folklore, not Tibetan
context: Hillary led a 1960 Himalayan Scientific and Mountaineering Expedition specifically to investigate Yeti evidence. A purported scalp brought back from the Khumjung monastery was later identified as serow goat hide. Hillary concluded the Yeti was likely folklore, though local Sherpa communities continued to treat sightings as serious.

question: The first modern Loch Ness Monster sighting that made international news happened in 1933. Aldie and John Mackay reported a creature in the loch that summer. A few months later a famous photograph was taken that gave the world its long-running image of 'Nessie'. What year and who took the photo?
answer: April 21, 1934, by Robert Kenneth Wilson, with a Marmaduke Wetherell hoax behind it
choices: April 21, 1934, by Robert Kenneth Wilson, with a Marmaduke Wetherell hoax behind it
August 22, 1933, by Aldie Mackay, who actually reported the first sighting
December 2, 1933, by Hugh Gray, who took an actually earlier (and blurrier) photo
July 30, 1955, by Peter MacNab, with a much later double-humped sighting photo
context: Christian Spurling confessed in 1994 that the 1934 photo was a hoax: his stepfather Marmaduke Wetherell had arranged a small plastic model on a toy submarine. Wilson, a gynecologist, fronted the photo to give it credibility. The hoax confession was published one year before Spurling's death.

question: The 1934 'Surgeon's Photograph' of the Loch Ness Monster — showing a slender curved neck rising from the loch's surface — was the iconic Nessie image for sixty years. In April 1994 a member of the original 1934 conspirator's stepfamily confessed the photo was a hoax. Who was the stepson confessor?
answer: Christian Spurling, who confessed before his own 1995 death at age 90
choices: Christian Spurling, who confessed before his own 1995 death at age 90
Robert Kenneth Wilson, who actually fronted the photo but didn't confess
Marmaduke Wetherell, who actually was the original hoaxer but had died in 1939
Aldie Mackay, who actually had the 1933 sighting predating the photo
context: Spurling's confession explained that Wetherell — a big-game hunter humiliated by the *Daily Mail* over earlier Nessie claims — built a 12-inch wooden model on a toy submarine fin. Wilson, a respected London surgeon, was recruited to lend credibility. The photo stood as Nessie's main 'evidence' for 60 years.

question: The Mothman of Point Pleasant, West Virginia, was reported by witnesses between November 1966 and December 1967 — large, winged, glowing red eyes, often near the abandoned TNT bunkers. The reports ended on December 15, 1967, with a tragic event in the town. What happened?
answer: The Silver Bridge over the Ohio River collapsed during evening rush hour, killing 46
choices: The Silver Bridge over the Ohio River collapsed during evening rush hour, killing 46
The TNT Area Bunker Complex was demolished by federal contractors in 1967
The Mothman was captured and killed by local police on Christmas Eve 1967
The town's mayor publicly denounced the sightings and ordered investigations halted
context: John Keel's 1975 book *The Mothman Prophecies* connected the sightings to the bridge collapse via reported premonitions. The 2002 Richard Gere film *The Mothman Prophecies* adapted Keel's book. The Silver Bridge collapse killed 46 people; an eye-bar failure was the engineering cause, unrelated to Mothman in any provable sense.

question: The Jersey Devil — a winged, hooved, kangaroo-like creature reported in the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey since at least the 18th century — has a specific traditional origin story involving the cursed thirteenth child of a colonial mother. Who is traditionally identified as the mother?
answer: Mother Leeds, who in 1735 reportedly cursed her thirteenth child to be a devil
choices: Mother Leeds, who in 1735 reportedly cursed her thirteenth child to be a devil
Mother Goose, who actually is a fictional nursery-rhyme figure not Pine Barrens
Mother Shipton, who actually is a 16th-century English seer figure
Mother Carey, who actually is a maritime folklore figure not Pine Barrens
context: The Mother Leeds story may have evolved from political tensions with the real Leeds family of colonial New Jersey, whose Almanac competed with Benjamin Franklin's. The 'Jersey Devil' name was adopted by the New Jersey Devils NHL team in 1982; the team's logo is a stylized devil shape.

question: The chupacabra ('goat-sucker') first appeared in modern folklore in Puerto Rico in 1995, after a series of livestock deaths in the town of Canovanas were attributed to a strange creature. The original eyewitness gave a description that was later linked to a specific Hollywood film. What was the film?
answer: The 1995 horror film *Species*, which witness Madelyne Tolentino had recently seen
choices: The 1995 horror film *Species*, which witness Madelyne Tolentino had recently seen
*Independence Day* (1996), which actually came out the year after the sightings
*Alien* (1979), which Tolentino reportedly had seen as a child
*Predator* (1987), which Tolentino reportedly had seen in college
context: Folklorist Benjamin Radford traced the original chupacabra description back to Madelyne Tolentino's account, which closely matched the film *Species*'s creature. Later 'chupacabra' photos in Texas and the Southwest from the 2000s typically turned out to be coyotes with mange — a different and more dog-like creature than Tolentino's reported alien.

question: The wendigo — a cannibalistic spirit-creature from northern Algonquian-speaking peoples' tradition — has been described in different ways across communities (Anishinaabe, Cree, Ojibwe, Innu). The English-language understanding mostly comes from one 19th-century anthropologist. What unifying feature appears in most accounts?
answer: It is associated with extreme hunger, winter starvation, and the taboo of cannibalism
choices: It is associated with extreme hunger, winter starvation, and the taboo of cannibalism
It is associated with the summer hunting season and surplus harvest plenty
It is associated with fishing and ocean travel, not winter forest dangers
It is associated with agricultural pests like deer and rabbit overpopulation
context: Some Algonquian communities have developed the concept of 'windigo psychosis' as a culturally-specific clinical syndrome — though anthropologists debate whether it should be treated as a real culture-bound illness or as a cultural-narrative framework for treating real psychiatric conditions.

question: The skinwalker — in Dine (Navajo) tradition, a witch capable of transforming into animal form by donning the skin of that animal — is one of the most taboo subjects in traditional Navajo culture. Practitioners and victims are often unwilling to discuss them. What name is the practice called in Navajo?
answer: *Yee naaldlooshii*, meaning roughly 'one who walks on all fours'
choices: *Yee naaldlooshii*, meaning roughly 'one who walks on all fours'
*Dineh*, which actually is the broader term for 'Navajo people' themselves
*Hozho*, which actually is the concept of 'beauty/balance' in Navajo thought
*Hataali*, which actually is the term for traditional ceremonial singers
context: The Skinwalker Ranch in Uintah County, Utah, purchased by Terry Sherman in 1994 and later by Robert Bigelow in 1996, became a focus of UFO and skinwalker reports. A History Channel series *The Secret of Skinwalker Ranch* began airing in 2020. Many Navajo communities have asked outsiders not to romanticize the tradition.

question: Amelia Earhart — the most famous female aviator of the early 20th century — disappeared on July 2, 1937, attempting to fly her Lockheed Electra 10E from Lae, New Guinea, to Howland Island. She was attempting the first round-the-world flight along the equatorial route. Who was her navigator?
answer: Fred Noonan, a former Pan Am navigator with extensive Pacific experience
choices: Fred Noonan, a former Pan Am navigator with extensive Pacific experience
Charles Lindbergh, who was actually still alive but was not Earhart's navigator
Wiley Post, who actually had died in his own 1935 Alaska plane crash
George Putnam, who actually was Earhart's husband and publicist, not navigator
context: Earhart's last radio transmission was received by the Coast Guard cutter Itasca at 8:43 AM local time on July 2, 1937. She and Noonan were never seen again. The U.S. Navy and Coast Guard searched 250,000 square miles of Pacific Ocean and found nothing. Theories range from crash-and-sink to Nikumaroro castaway.

question: One major theory about Amelia Earhart's 1937 disappearance — investigated extensively by The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR) — argues Earhart and Fred Noonan landed on a remote uninhabited Pacific atoll and survived for some weeks as castaways. Which atoll?
answer: Nikumaroro (formerly Gardner Island), in the Phoenix Islands group of Kiribati
choices: Nikumaroro (formerly Gardner Island), in the Phoenix Islands group of Kiribati
Howland Island, which was Earhart's intended destination on July 2, 1937
Tarawa, which actually was the site of a famous 1943 World War II battle
Wake Island, which actually was a different US Pacific possession in 1937
context: TIGHAR's evidence includes a 1940 partial skeleton found on Nikumaroro (lost before modern DNA testing), a sextant-box, and a sole-of-shoe matching Earhart's published size. The theory remains unproven. Nikumaroro was inhabited briefly in the 1940s-60s and is now uninhabited again, part of Kiribati.

question: The Russian government reopened the Dyatlov Pass case in 2019. A 2020 conclusion attributed the deaths to an avalanche, despite the lack of typical avalanche debris around the tent. A 2021 academic paper provided physical modeling for the official conclusion. Where was the paper published?
answer: *Communications Earth & Environment*, a Nature-Springer open-access journal
choices: *Communications Earth & Environment*, a Nature-Springer open-access journal
*Nature* itself, the flagship 1869 British scientific journal
*Science*, the AAAS journal published in Washington, DC
*The Lancet*, the British medical journal at the Royal Society
context: Authors Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin modeled a slow-moving slab avalanche that fit the bizarre features (lack of large debris, delayed effects). The model is not universally accepted; many Dyatlov researchers continue to investigate alternative explanations. The hikers' tongue removal is generally attributed to scavenging postmortem.

question: Flight 19 — the most famous disappearance attributed to the Bermuda Triangle — was a 1945 training flight of five US Navy TBM Avenger torpedo bombers that vanished off the Florida coast on a routine navigation exercise. What date?
answer: December 5, 1945, three months after the end of World War II in Asia
choices: December 5, 1945, three months after the end of World War II in Asia
September 15, 1945, the same month as the V-J Day Allied surrender
January 10, 1946, four months after the end of World War II
August 6, 1945, the day of the Hiroshima atomic bombing (much earlier)
context: Flight 19 left NAS Fort Lauderdale at 2:10 PM. By 4 PM, navigation problems were severe; the flight became lost. By 7:04 PM all radio contact ended. A PBM Mariner search aircraft launched to find them also disappeared — likely a separate accident (the Mariner was prone to fuel-tank explosions). Twenty-seven men died.

question: The term 'Bermuda Triangle' was coined by writer Vincent Gaddis in a 1964 magazine article titled 'The Deadly Bermuda Triangle'. The article was published in a pulp adventure magazine. Which magazine first published the term?
answer: *Argosy* magazine, a long-running American pulp adventure title (1964)
choices: *Argosy* magazine, a long-running American pulp adventure title (1964)
*Astounding Science Fiction*, a different pulp aimed at science-fiction readers
*Weird Tales*, the horror pulp better known for Lovecraft and Howard
*Black Mask*, the hardboiled crime pulp Hammett and Chandler wrote for
context: Gaddis's *Argosy* article was expanded into his 1965 book *Invisible Horizons*, which popularized the Bermuda Triangle concept. Charles Berlitz's 1974 *The Bermuda Triangle* became a #1 bestseller. The Lloyds of London insurance market does not charge higher premiums for ships passing through the area — actuarial data shows no unusual loss rate.

question: The *Mary Celeste* — the American merchant brigantine found drifting in the Atlantic, fully provisioned but abandoned, with her crew vanished — was discovered by the British ship *Dei Gratia* in December 1872. What was she carrying?
answer: Industrial alcohol bound for Genoa from New York (1,701 barrels of denatured spirit)
choices: Industrial alcohol bound for Genoa from New York (1,701 barrels of denatured spirit)
Cotton bound for Liverpool from New Orleans (a Civil War-era manifest)
Cocoa beans bound for Liverpool from the Caribbean (a sugar-trade cargo)
Gunpowder bound for Constantinople from New York (a wartime cargo manifest)
context: Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, his two-year-old daughter, and seven crew were never found. Modern theories include alcohol-vapor explosion fear (no actual explosion), waterspout, or seaquake. The ship's name became a household word for nautical mystery; the term 'Mary Celeste' is still used metaphorically.

question: Three lighthouse keepers at the Flannan Isles Eilean Mor lighthouse vanished in December 1900. When the relief boat arrived, the lighthouse was undisturbed but the men were gone. What is the date most often cited for their disappearance?
answer: Around December 15-17, 1900, with the last logbook entry dated December 15
choices: Around December 15-17, 1900, with the last logbook entry dated December 15
August 21, 1899, the year before the actual disappearance
January 5, 1901, the year after the actual disappearance
October 1, 1900, two months before the actual disappearance date
context: James Ducat, Thomas Marshall, and Donald MacArthur were the three keepers. The last log entry recorded a severe storm. The most-cited modern theory is that a single freak wave (such as a tsunami or 'rogue wave') swept across the rocks while two of the men were tending to lashed-down ropes. Their bodies were never found.

question: The Lost Colony of Roanoke — the failed English settlement on the Outer Banks of present-day North Carolina — was last attended in 1587 when Governor John White returned to England for supplies. By the time he returned three years later, the colony was empty. What single word was carved on a post?
answer: CROATOAN — the name of a nearby Native American tribe (modern Croatan)
choices: CROATOAN — the name of a nearby Native American tribe (modern Croatan)
DARE — a reference to White's daughter Eleanor Dare or grandbaby Virginia Dare
ROANOKE — simply the colony's own name carved as a marker
ELIZABETH — a reference to the colony's namesake Queen Elizabeth I
context: White was unable to investigate the Croatoan island further due to weather and ship-master refusal. The colony's 115 settlers, including Virginia Dare (the first English child born in North America), have never been definitively traced. Modern theories favor integration with one or more Native American communities.
