question: DB Cooper — the hijacker who jumped from a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 with $200,000 in $20 bills over the Cascade Mountains in November 1971 — has never been identified. On what holiday was the hijack carried out?
answer: Thanksgiving Eve, November 24, 1971 — the day before Thanksgiving
choices: Thanksgiving Eve, November 24, 1971 — the day before Thanksgiving
Christmas Eve, December 24, 1971 — actually a separate date
New Year's Eve, December 31, 1971 — actually a separate date
Halloween, October 31, 1971 — actually a separate date a month earlier
context: The man bought a one-way ticket from Portland to Seattle under the name Dan Cooper (the press misreported it as 'DB Cooper'); his real identity was never established. The FBI officially suspended the active investigation in 2016 after 45 years. Some $5,800 of the ransom money turned up along the Columbia River in 1980.

question: The Tamam Shud case — the unexplained 1948 death of an unidentified man on Somerton Beach near Adelaide, Australia — became famous when investigators found a rolled-up scrap of paper in his fob pocket bearing the Persian words 'Tamam Shud' ('It is ended'). The scrap was traced to which book?
answer: A copy of Edward FitzGerald's English translation of 'The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam'
choices: A copy of Edward FitzGerald's English translation of 'The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam'
A copy of Sir Richard Burton's 'Arabian Nights' translation from the 1885 era
A copy of the King James Bible's Book of Ecclesiastes in a Persian translation
A copy of the Persian original 'Shahnameh' by Ferdowsi in an English-language version
context: The book was found in a passing motorist's car, dropped through an open window during the relevant period. The book contained a phone number for a nurse who denied knowing the man. A code (or set of letters that looks like a code) was also in the book. In 2022, DNA from the man's exhumed body identified him as Carl 'Charles' Webb.

question: The Black Dahlia case — the 1947 mutilation and murder of 22-year-old aspiring actress Elizabeth Short in Los Angeles — remains officially unsolved. Short's nickname 'Black Dahlia' was given posthumously by reporters as a play on the 1946 film *The Blue Dahlia*. What date was her body discovered?
answer: January 15, 1947, in Leimert Park, Los Angeles — found by a mother walking her child
choices: January 15, 1947, in Leimert Park, Los Angeles — found by a mother walking her child
December 24, 1946, on Christmas Eve in Hollywood near Sunset Boulevard
February 14, 1947, on Valentine's Day at Griffith Park
October 31, 1948, on Halloween night near downtown Los Angeles
context: Short's body was found severed at the waist and drained of blood — the surgical precision led to speculation about a medical-trained killer. The case received over 60 confessions over the years, all eventually discredited. Multiple suspects (including Walter Bayley and George Hodel) have been named in various decades; none has been proved.

question: The Zodiac Killer — the unidentified Northern California serial killer who killed at least five (and claimed 37 across letters) between 1968 and 1969 — became famous in part for the cryptographic puzzles he sent to newspapers. The most-cited published cipher is the '340' (after its number of characters). When was it solved?
answer: December 2020 by a private team of independent codebreakers, fifty-one years after sending
choices: December 2020 by a private team of independent codebreakers, fifty-one years after sending
1969, by the FBI within months of the letter's October publication
1985, by amateur sleuths analyzing the cipher with mainframe computers
Still unsolved as of 2024, despite extensive professional code-breaking efforts
context: The 340 cipher was solved by David Oranchak, Sam Blake, and Jarl Van Eycke. The decoded text did not name the killer, only continued his earlier themes. The earlier 408 cipher (1969) was solved within a week of publication by schoolteacher Donald Harden and his wife Bettye. The Zodiac case is officially still open in California.

question: Lizzie Borden — tried and acquitted in 1893 for the August 1892 axe-murders of her father and stepmother in their Fall River, Massachusetts home — became one of the most famous American true-crime figures. The 'forty whacks' rhyme exaggerates. How many axe-blows did the actual victims sustain?
answer: Father Andrew was hit 11 times; stepmother Abby was hit 19 times
choices: Father Andrew was hit 11 times; stepmother Abby was hit 19 times
Each victim sustained 40 axe-blows, exactly as the famous rhyme alleges
Father Andrew was untouched; stepmother Abby alone took some 35 blows
The exact number was never determined because of incomplete autopsy records
context: Lizzie Borden was acquitted by a jury in June 1893. She inherited her father's substantial estate. The 'forty whacks' rhyme is folkloric exaggeration. The Borden house at 230 Second Street in Fall River is now a popular bed-and-breakfast where overnight guests can sleep in the room where Abby Borden was killed.

question: The Voynich Manuscript — a 240-page 15th-century codex written in an unknown script with botanical, astrological, and bathing-women illustrations — has resisted decipherment for over a century. Where is it now held?
answer: The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University
choices: The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University
The Bodleian Library at Oxford University in England
The British Library in London (which actually has the Magna Carta instead)
The Bibliotheque nationale de France in Paris (which actually has many medieval manuscripts but not Voynich)
context: The manuscript is named for Wilfrid Voynich, the Polish-American bookseller who acquired it in 1912. Carbon-dating in 2009 placed the vellum at the early 15th century (roughly 1404-1438). Many decipherment claims have appeared over decades; none has gained acceptance from the academic cryptography community.

question: The Antikythera Mechanism — a corroded bronze 'computer' device recovered from a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901 — has now been identified as an ancient Greek astronomical calculator. What does it actually compute?
answer: Positions of the sun, moon, and planets, plus phases of the moon and eclipse timing
choices: Positions of the sun, moon, and planets, plus phases of the moon and eclipse timing
Tide-table calculations specific to the eastern Aegean Sea
Astrological compatibility between Greek and Roman zodiac signs
Naval gunnery solutions for ancient Greek warship combat
context: X-ray scans (notably 1971 and 2005) revealed the mechanism's 30+ bronze gears. It dates to roughly 100 BC. The most-cited reconstruction is by Tony Freeth and his team, published in *Nature* (2006 and 2008). The Antikythera Shipwreck Site has produced other artifacts; the mechanism remains the most famous.

question: Gobekli Tepe — the megalithic temple complex in southeastern Turkey, near Sanliurfa — was excavated beginning in the mid-1990s by German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt. Its T-shaped limestone pillars have been carved with relief animals. What is its approximate age?
answer: Approximately 11,500 years old, predating agricultural settlements by 1,000+ years
choices: Approximately 11,500 years old, predating agricultural settlements by 1,000+ years
Approximately 6,000 years old, contemporaneous with the Sumerian Ubaid period
Approximately 4,500 years old, contemporaneous with the Egyptian pyramids
Approximately 2,500 years old, contemporaneous with classical Greek architecture
context: Gobekli Tepe predates Stonehenge by some 6,000 years. Its age was a major surprise to scholars when announced: it was constructed by hunter-gatherers, not agriculturalists, suggesting that monumental architecture may have preceded settled agriculture. Excavation continues; estimates suggest only 5% of the site has been excavated.

question: The Nazca Lines — the enormous geoglyphs in the Nazca Desert of southern Peru, depicting animals (hummingbird, monkey, spider) and abstract patterns — were rediscovered in modern times only after the advent of commercial aviation. They are essentially invisible from ground level. What culture made them?
answer: The Nazca culture, between 200 BC and 600 AD, predating the Inca by centuries
choices: The Nazca culture, between 200 BC and 600 AD, predating the Inca by centuries
The Inca, between 1438 and 1533, in the era of their main empire
The Moche, between 100 and 700 AD, on the north coast of Peru
The Wari, between 600 and 1000 AD, also in central Andes Peru
context: The lines were created by removing a thin top layer of iron-oxide-coated stones, exposing the lighter sand below. They have survived 2,000+ years because Nazca's desert receives almost no rain. The geoglyphs were popularized to the West by Maria Reiche, a German mathematician who spent fifty years studying them.

question: The Tunguska Event — the largest documented asteroid or comet impact in recorded human history — flattened approximately 2,000 square kilometers of Siberian taiga forest in June 1908. The atmospheric explosion left no impact crater. What is the most-accepted date?
answer: June 30, 1908, just after 7:00 AM local time, near the Stony Tunguska River
choices: June 30, 1908, just after 7:00 AM local time, near the Stony Tunguska River
June 30, 1918, ten years later than the actual date
March 15, 1908, three months earlier than the actual date
December 25, 1908, in the same year but at year's end (much later than actual)
context: The most-accepted explanation is an air-bursting stony meteoroid of roughly 50-60 meters diameter, exploding at 5-10 km altitude. Eyewitness accounts described a column of fire visible at hundreds of kilometers. The Russian Tunguska Expedition (Leonid Kulik's 1927) was the first major scientific investigation, twenty years after the event.

question: Betty and Barney Hill — a New Hampshire couple who reported a UFO abduction in September 1961 — gave one of the first widely-documented modern abduction accounts. Their case introduced now-iconic abduction tropes (small grey beings, medical examinations, missing time). What helped publicize the case in 1966?
answer: The book *The Interrupted Journey* by John G. Fuller, recounting Betty and Barney's hypnosis sessions
choices: The book *The Interrupted Journey* by John G. Fuller, recounting Betty and Barney's hypnosis sessions
Project Blue Book's official acknowledgment, which actually never occurred
A National Geographic feature article, which actually wasn't published in 1966
A 1966 *Star Trek* episode directly based on the Hills' account, which never happened
context: The Hills' case was a foundational moment for modern UFO narrative-formation. Betty Hill's now-famous 'star map' (reportedly recalled under hypnosis and later interpreted as the Zeta Reticuli system) became a touchstone for later abduction accounts. The 1975 TV movie *The UFO Incident* dramatized the case.

question: The Phoenix Lights — a series of unexplained lights seen by thousands over a large stretch of Arizona airspace on the same night — became one of the most-witnessed UFO events of the late 20th century. What was the date?
answer: March 13, 1997, with two main sighting waves at 8 PM and 10 PM
choices: March 13, 1997, with two main sighting waves at 8 PM and 10 PM
August 11, 1996, the year before the actual sighting date
January 23, 1999, two years after the actual sighting date
October 14, 1998, more than a year after the actual sighting date
context: Air Force later attributed the 10 PM waves to flares dropped during a training exercise at Barry Goldwater Range. The 8 PM event — a V-shaped pattern reported by thousands across Arizona — has not been definitively explained. Then-governor Fife Symington dismissed the event publicly at the time but in 2007 said he had also witnessed it.

question: The Roswell Incident — a debris field of unknown materials found by rancher Mac Brazel on the Foster ranch near Corona, New Mexico in early July 1947 — became famous after the Roswell Army Air Field briefly announced the recovery of a 'flying disc' before retracting. What did the Army Air Force later identify the debris as?
answer: Initially a 'weather balloon', later (1990s) identified as 'Project Mogul' surveillance
choices: Initially a 'weather balloon', later (1990s) identified as 'Project Mogul' surveillance
An experimental long-range bomber prototype, declassified in 1985
A Soviet U-2 spy plane, which actually didn't exist until 1955
A meteorite, which actually was discounted by all involved investigators
context: Project Mogul was a Cold War-era classified program of high-altitude balloon arrays to detect Soviet nuclear tests. The 1947 'flying disc' announcement and quick retraction was a major contributor to UFO lore. The 1995 'Roswell autopsy' film was eventually confirmed as a hoax by its producer.

question: Travis Walton — an Arizona logger who reported being abducted by a UFO on November 5, 1975, while logging in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest, then reappearing five days later — gave one of the most-detailed early abduction accounts. His case formed the basis for a 1993 film. What was the film called?
answer: *Fire in the Sky*, with D.B. Sweeney as Travis Walton
choices: *Fire in the Sky*, with D.B. Sweeney as Travis Walton
*Communion*, which actually was based on Whitley Strieber's 1987 book
*The Forgotten*, which actually was a 2004 sci-fi film unrelated to Walton
*Phoenix Forgotten*, which actually was a 2017 film not about Walton
context: The other logging crew members' polygraph tests have been variously cited as supporting Walton's account. Skeptics have pointed to financial motives and crew-stress factors. Walton has remained publicly committed to his account for forty-plus years; he has continued speaking at UFO conferences and writing about the case.

question: The English crop-circle phenomenon — patterns flattened in grain fields — peaked in the 1980s and 1990s. In 1991 two men confessed to having created many of the major patterns themselves with planks and ropes since 1978. Who were they?
answer: Doug Bower and Dave Chorley, retired British circle-makers from Southampton
choices: Doug Bower and Dave Chorley, retired British circle-makers from Southampton
Doug Bower and Tim Carson, an unrelated American pair from Texas
John Lundberg and Rod Dickinson, who actually were later 'Circlemakers' team
Colin Andrews and Pat Delgado, who actually were crop-circle researchers, not creators
context: Bower and Chorley demonstrated their planks-and-rope technique to journalists in 1991, then continued occasionally creating circles into the 2000s. Many later circles (especially elaborate fractal patterns of the 1990s) were the work of other artists; the Circlemakers and other groups continued the tradition openly as land art.

question: The SCP Foundation — the collaborative-fiction wiki documenting fictional 'anomalous objects' contained by a fictional Foundation — began as a single post on the 4chan paranormal board /x/. What was the original post that became 'SCP-173'?
answer: A photograph of a sculpture by Japanese artist Izumi Kato in 2007
choices: A photograph of a sculpture by Japanese artist Izumi Kato in 2007
An audio recording of a deep echoing voice from a 2008 internet AMA
An article from a fake Russian newspaper translated by an 2007 Reddit user
A series of dated photographs from a fake archaeological dig in 2009
context: Izumi Kato's untitled 2004 sculpture was photographed without permission and posted to 4chan in 2007. The original post described it as an anomalous statue. The community built around the concept moved to its own wiki (scp-wiki.net) in 2008 and has since grown to thousands of contributors. SCP-173 has since been retired from official images.

question: The Backrooms — the now-iconic internet horror concept of an infinite labyrinth of yellow office spaces and fluorescent buzzing humming through endless empty hallways — began with a single image and short caption posted to 4chan's /x/ board in 2019. What was the original caption format?
answer: A 'noclip' instruction describing falling out of reality into an infinite empty office
choices: A 'noclip' instruction describing falling out of reality into an infinite empty office
A documented anomaly entry in the style of SCP Foundation articles
A poem in the style of a creepypasta about lost workspace souls
A leaked corporate-training video transcript with redacted segments
context: The original image (yellow-wallpaper office hallway) is from a 4chan post May 12, 2019. The 'noclip' framing — a video-game term for accidentally moving outside intended game space — gave the Backrooms its central conceit. Kane Pixels's 2022 YouTube short-film series gave the Backrooms its most-developed visual canon.

question: Slender Man — the tall, thin, faceless, tentacled internet horror figure — was created in June 2009 for a Photoshop horror-image contest on the Something Awful forums. The character became a cultural phenomenon and was implicated in a 2014 real-world attempted murder. Who created the character?
answer: Eric Knudsen (Victor Surge), who posted two images to the contest thread
choices: Eric Knudsen (Victor Surge), who posted two images to the contest thread
Marble Hornets's Troy Wagner, who actually was the first major Slender Man story creator
Tim Sutton, who actually directed the 2018 film 'Slender Man'
Sylvia Likens, who actually was a real 1965 murder victim, not a Slender Man creator
context: Knudsen's June 10, 2009 entries posted to the 'Create Paranormal Images' Something Awful thread included two photoshopped images of black-and-white photos with a tall figure inserted. The character spread rapidly through ARG-style content. The 2014 Waukesha attack (two 12-year-old girls stabbing a third in 'tribute' to Slender Man) brought the character to widespread media attention.

question: Black-eyed kids — the modern American urban legend of pale children with completely black eyes who approach strangers and ask to be let into homes or vehicles — first appeared in the cultural record in 1996. A Texas journalist's online column became the founding text. Who was he?
answer: Brian Bethel, a reporter for the Abilene Reporter-News whose 1996 post went viral
choices: Brian Bethel, a reporter for the Abilene Reporter-News whose 1996 post went viral
Stephen King, who actually has written extensively about children but not BEK
Brian Lumley, who actually wrote 'Necroscope' but not the BEK origin
Whitley Strieber, who actually wrote 'Communion' but not the BEK origin
context: Bethel's 1996 account described two black-eyed boys approaching his car in a movie-theater parking lot at night. The post spread on early-internet 'creepypasta' message boards. Black-eyed kids remain one of the most-cited modern American urban legends, distinct from older 'cursed child' folklore.

question: Jeff the Killer — the now-iconic creepypasta character with the white-painted face, carved smile, and 'GO TO SLEEP' tagline — became famous in 2008. The character is associated with a specific Photoshop-modified image that became one of the most-shared horror images on the early internet. What is the most-cited identification of the original image?
answer: A modified version of a Japanese imageboard photo of an anonymous woman or girl
choices: A modified version of a Japanese imageboard photo of an anonymous woman or girl
A modified version of a 1990s movie still from a horror film
A modified version of an early-internet meme image from 2003-04
A modified version of a single original sketch posted to deviantArt in 2008
context: The original source of the Jeff the Killer image has been the subject of extensive internet investigation. Multiple proposed identifications have circulated; none has been definitively confirmed. The character itself was developed in early creepypasta forums; the most-cited original 'Jeff the Killer' story is from 2008 on a Newgrounds user account.

question: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 — a Boeing 777-200ER bound from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing carrying 239 people — disappeared over the South China Sea about 38 minutes into its flight on March 8, 2014. Where is the wreckage most likely located, based on the recovered debris analysis?
answer: Southern Indian Ocean, west of Australia in the broader 'seventh arc' search zone
choices: Southern Indian Ocean, west of Australia in the broader 'seventh arc' search zone
Northern Pacific Ocean, in waters between Japan and Russia
Mediterranean Sea, off the Egyptian coast near the Sinai Peninsula
Bay of Bengal, in waters between India and the Andaman Islands
context: Debris confirmed as MH370 has washed up on Reunion Island (a 2015 flaperon), Mozambique, Madagascar, and South Africa — consistent with Indian Ocean drift modeling. The Australian-led search of 120,000 sq km of seafloor (2014-17) and Ocean Infinity's private 112,000 sq km search (2018) found no wreckage.

question: Oak Island, off Nova Scotia, has been the subject of treasure-hunting digs since 1795, when local teenagers reportedly discovered an artificial depression and dug down to find layers of timber every ten feet. The 'Money Pit' has resisted extraction for over two centuries. What was found at roughly 90 feet down in the original 1804 dig?
answer: A flat stone with carved unidentified symbols, since lost to history
choices: A flat stone with carved unidentified symbols, since lost to history
A wooden chest containing Spanish gold coins from the late 1500s
A skeleton clutching a rotted scroll that turned to dust on contact
A perfectly preserved Knights Templar shield in a cedar-lined recess
context: The 1804 Onslow Company dig reportedly reached 90 feet before flooding. The 'Money Pit' is widely believed to be flooded through engineered underground channels from the sea. The History Channel series *The Curse of Oak Island* (2014-onward) has continued digs without finding the alleged treasure.

question: The Princes in the Tower — twelve-year-old Edward V of England and his nine-year-old brother Richard, Duke of York — disappeared from the Tower of London in summer 1483 after being placed there by their uncle, the future Richard III. What was the political context?
answer: Edward IV had died in April 1483; the brothers were declared illegitimate by Parliament
choices: Edward IV had died in April 1483; the brothers were declared illegitimate by Parliament
The Wars of the Roses had ended decisively at Tewkesbury, then resumed in 1483
Henry VII had begun his rebellion from France with Welsh and French support
Henry VIII had broken with the Catholic Church (this was 50 years earlier)
context: Bones found in the Tower in 1674 (and reinterred at Westminster Abbey) have not been definitively identified. Modern DNA testing has been requested by historians and refused by the Church of England. The case remains one of the most-debated historical mysteries of medieval England.

question: The Isdal Woman — an unidentified woman found burned to death in the Isdalen Valley near Bergen, Norway, in November 1970 — was one of Europe's longest-running unidentified-person mysteries. She had clearly been actively concealing her identity. What was unusual about her clothing?
answer: All clothing labels and identifying marks had been deliberately removed
choices: All clothing labels and identifying marks had been deliberately removed
She was found wearing only an evening gown and high heels (no other clothing)
Her clothing was made entirely of newspaper folded into a makeshift outfit
She wore a Soviet-issue military uniform with the rank insignia removed
context: Investigators found multiple wigs, falsified identity papers, and a coded notebook in her hotel luggage. Her teeth had been fitted with gold work in a style associated with Latin American dentistry of the era. The case has been investigated by Norwegian police and Reuters journalist Marit Higraff in modern times. Her identity remains unknown.

question: The yowie — Australia's large hominid cryptid, similar in concept to Bigfoot or the yeti — has been reported in Aboriginal oral tradition and (later) by European settlers since at least the early 19th century. Most yowie reports come from a specific region of Australia. Which?
answer: The east coast of Australia, particularly the Blue Mountains of New South Wales
choices: The east coast of Australia, particularly the Blue Mountains of New South Wales
The Western Australian outback, particularly the Nullarbor Plain
Tasmania, on the southern island state separated from the mainland
Cape York, the far northern tropical peninsula of Queensland
context: Reports from Aboriginal communities use various names — 'yahoo', 'doolagahl', 'gugaa' — depending on region. The contemporary 'yowie' name appears to have been popularized in the 1970s. Cadbury Australia made a 'Yowies' chocolate-and-toy line in 1995, with figures of Aboriginal-mythology-themed creatures — controversial for use of Indigenous tradition.

question: Champ — the lake monster of Lake Champlain on the New York-Vermont border — has been reported by Indigenous Abenaki and European settlers since the 1600s. The most-cited modern sighting was a 1977 photograph by Sandra Mansi showing a long-necked creature breaking the lake's surface. What state legislature has formally protected Champ?
answer: Both Vermont (1982) and New York (1983), with formal sanctuary legislation
choices: Both Vermont (1982) and New York (1983), with formal sanctuary legislation
Only Vermont (1982), with New York refusing to follow
Only New York (1983), with Vermont refusing to follow
Federal protection alone under the Lacey Act — neither state-level protection
context: Vermont state law (Title 10, Chapter 124) and New York Assembly Bill 5957A (1983) created formal sanctuary protections. The Mansi photograph has been disputed but never definitively debunked. The Vermont towns of Port Henry and Burlington both have Champ-themed tourism and statues.

question: Ogopogo — the lake monster of Lake Okanagan in British Columbia, Canada — has been reported by both the Syilx (Okanagan) Indigenous people (who called it 'N'ha-a-itk') and by European settlers since the late 1800s. The name 'Ogopogo' was coined when?
answer: 1924, in a song parody by Toronto singer Bill Brimblecombe
choices: 1924, in a song parody by Toronto singer Bill Brimblecombe
1872, when Susan Allison wrote of seeing the creature crossing the lake
1933, the same year as the first modern Loch Ness Monster sighting
1947, in the same era as the Roswell Incident and Kenneth Arnold's UFOs
context: Bill Brimblecombe's 1924 song parody borrowed an English music-hall novelty song ('The Ogo-Pogo'). The Syilx had reportedly considered the original lake creature dangerous — many traditional accounts described offerings made to the creature. Modern Ogopogo is depicted as a friendly tourist mascot for Kelowna.

question: The skunk ape — Florida's regional Bigfoot-equivalent, particularly associated with the Everglades — is named for the strong unpleasant odor often reported by witnesses. What is the most-cited Florida town for skunk-ape sightings?
answer: Ochopee, Florida, near the Big Cypress Swamp on the Tamiami Trail
choices: Ochopee, Florida, near the Big Cypress Swamp on the Tamiami Trail
Miami, Florida, on the southeastern Atlantic coast (urban not swamp)
Orlando, Florida, in central Florida (urban not swamp)
Tampa, Florida, on the Gulf coast (urban not swamp)
context: Dave Shealy runs the Skunk Ape Headquarters at Ochopee, a private museum and tourist site on the Tamiami Trail. The most-cited skunk ape photos (2000) were taken by an anonymous Sarasota woman; their authenticity remains debated. Anti-cryptid skeptics have proposed Florida black bears as the most likely source of regional reports.

question: The Mogollon Monster — a 7-foot-tall hairy hominid reported in the Mogollon Rim region of Arizona since the early 1900s — is one of the American Southwest's primary Bigfoot-equivalent cryptids. Where does its name come from?
answer: The Mogollon Rim escarpment crossing central Arizona at high elevation
choices: The Mogollon Rim escarpment crossing central Arizona at high elevation
Pancho Mogollon, an Apache tribesman who first reported it in 1903
The Spanish governor Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollon (16th century viceregal)
The Mogollon culture, a Native American pre-Columbian agricultural society
context: The Mogollon Rim is named for Spanish colonial governor Juan Ignacio Flores Mogollon. Reports of large hairy hominids in the region date to at least 1903 (Don Davis's account near Payson). The dense ponderosa pine forests of the Rim provide ideal terrain for the cryptid's supposed habitat.

question: The Dover Demon — a small hairless 4-foot creature with a 'watermelon-shaped' head and glowing orange eyes, reported by teenagers in Dover, Massachusetts on April 21-22, 1977 — is one of New England's most-cited unique cryptids. How many separate witnesses reported the sighting?
answer: Four teenage witnesses across three separate sightings in 24 hours
choices: Four teenage witnesses across three separate sightings in 24 hours
A single witness reported all four sightings in the original account
Two witnesses, both from the same family, in a single overnight sighting
Twelve witnesses including the family of one of the original teenagers
context: Bill Bartlett, John Baxter, and Abby Brabham each described similar creatures from different locations on the same night. Their separate sketches showed similar features. Cryptid researcher Loren Coleman investigated the case extensively. The 'Dover Demon' name is Coleman's coinage; the locals usually called it 'the creature'.

question: The Beast of Bray Road — a werewolf-like creature reported in Elkhorn, Wisconsin since the 1930s — became famous after Linda S. Godfrey's 1991 newspaper investigation for the *Walworth County Week*. What is unusual about the cryptid's reported behavior?
answer: Witnesses report it sometimes stands upright on two legs like a man
choices: Witnesses report it sometimes stands upright on two legs like a man
It is always reported as walking on four legs in a wolf-typical posture
It is reported as having red eyes that glow during daytime sightings
It is reported as having mind-control or hypnotic abilities over witnesses
context: Godfrey's 1991 investigation was assigned as a routine humorous-folklore piece; her serious treatment of witnesses pushed it into broader media. The Beast has been classified by cryptozoologists as either a 'Bigfoot variant' (Sasquatch with canid features) or a 'Manwolf' (werewolf-style upright canid). Godfrey wrote multiple books on the phenomenon.

question: The Loveland Frog — a 4-foot tall bipedal frog-like creature reported in Loveland, Ohio, since 1955 — got fresh media attention in August 2016 when two teenage gamers playing Pokemon Go on a Loveland walking trail reported seeing it. What is the original 1955 report's source?
answer: A businessman named Robert Hunnicutt who said he saw three frog-like beings on a bridge
choices: A businessman named Robert Hunnicutt who said he saw three frog-like beings on a bridge
A Cincinnati police officer who reported it directly to the FBI in 1955
A high-school biology teacher who allegedly captured one and dissected it
An anonymous postcard sent to the Loveland Herald newspaper in 1955
context: Hunnicutt's account described three creatures with froglike faces and human-like bodies, holding a wand-like device. A 1972 'sighting' by a Loveland police officer revived the legend. The 2016 Pokemon Go sighting helped re-popularize the Loveland Frog as a regional cryptid for the social-media age.

question: The Popobawa — a 'bat-wing' demon in Zanzibar tradition, said to attack sleeping men at night with sexual assault — has triggered several waves of mass-hysteria in modern Zanzibar (1965, 1970, 1995). The name itself describes a defining physical feature. What does 'Popobawa' literally mean?
answer: 'Bat-wing' in Swahili (popo = bat, bawa = wing)
choices: 'Bat-wing' in Swahili (popo = bat, bawa = wing)
'Night-walker' in Swahili (popo = night, bawa = walker)
'Shadow-monster' in Swahili (popo = shadow, bawa = monster)
'Sea-spirit' in Swahili (popo = sea, bawa = spirit)
context: The most-recent major Popobawa panic was in 1995, with multiple Zanzibar villagers reporting attacks and sleeping outside in groups to avoid being alone. Anthropologists have studied the Popobawa phenomenon as a culturally-specific framework for processing real sexual assault and political anxiety; the literal supernatural existence remains a separate question.

question: The Tikbalang — a Filipino folklore creature with a horse's head, a human body, and impossibly long limbs — is said to lead travelers astray in forest paths. According to tradition, what is the way to stop a Tikbalang's pranks?
answer: Wear your shirt inside-out, which the Tikbalang interprets as confusion
choices: Wear your shirt inside-out, which the Tikbalang interprets as confusion
Carry an iron bell, since the Tikbalang is afraid of metallic ringing
Cross a river, since the Tikbalang cannot cross flowing fresh water
Speak the Tikbalang's true name three times, which dispels its glamour
context: The 'inside-out shirt' is a real folkloric Filipino remedy. Other traditional protections include holding a religious icon or whistling a specific tune. Tikbalang appear in many recent Filipino films and TV shows, often as more benevolent forest-spirits than the malicious figures of traditional tales.

question: The Thunderbird — a giant bird of Native American mythology, said to bring thunder by flapping its wings and lightning from its eyes — appears in the traditions of many North American peoples (Anishinaabe, Algonquin, Haudenosaunee, Pacific Northwest peoples). The Thunderbird is particularly central to which Northwest Coast peoples' tradition?
answer: The Pacific Northwest Coast peoples (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth)
choices: The Pacific Northwest Coast peoples (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth)
The Plains peoples (Cheyenne, Lakota, Crow) more than the Northwest peoples
The Pueblo peoples (Hopi, Zuni) of the Southwest United States
The Inuit peoples of Alaska and northern Canada (Greenland and Nunavut)
context: Thunderbird carvings appear on Northwest Coast totem poles. Many Native American traditions describe the Thunderbird as a giant chief of all birds. The 1948-50 'thunderbird photograph' (a frequently-cited cryptid case) was probably an apocryphal Mandela-effect memory; no such photo has ever been definitively identified.

question: Lake Iliamna — Alaska's largest lake, in southwest Alaska — has been the subject of monster reports for decades, with Dena'ina Athabaskan traditions describing large fish-like creatures in its depths. The most-cited modern scientific explanation involves a real large fish species sometimes seen in the lake. Which species?
answer: Sleeper sharks (Pacific sleeper shark, Somniosus pacificus), a deep-cold-water species
choices: Sleeper sharks (Pacific sleeper shark, Somniosus pacificus), a deep-cold-water species
Beluga whales, which actually do enter the lake from Bristol Bay seasonally
Giant Pacific octopuses, which do live in the broader region
Saltwater crocodiles, which do not actually exist in Alaska at all
context: Pacific sleeper sharks can reach lengths of 14+ feet and have been documented to enter Lake Iliamna via the Kvichak River (an unusual habit for sharks). Some Iliamna 'monster' sightings have been correlated with confirmed sleeper-shark encounters. Other reports remain unexplained.

question: The Lead Masks Case — the unexplained 1966 deaths of two Brazilian electronic technicians, Manoel Pereira da Cruz and Miguel Jose Viana, found dead on the Vintem Hill in Niteroi, Rio de Janeiro — got its name from a specific item they were wearing. What was unusual about their condition?
answer: Both were wearing identical homemade lead masks shaped to fit their faces
choices: Both were wearing identical homemade lead masks shaped to fit their faces
Both wore aluminum-foil hats (a different motif from later 'tinfoil hat' lore)
Both were wearing copper armbands engraved with mathematical formulas
Both had silver tooth-caps installed shortly before their deaths
context: The two men reportedly told their families they were leaving to buy materials for an experiment, taking notes that described 'capsules' to consume. They were found on August 20, 1966, with a notebook describing instructions: 'at 4:30 PM swallow the capsules. Effects observed by 6:30 PM cover with masks. Then wait...'. Causes of death never definitively determined.

question: The Lost Cosmonauts conspiracy theory — that the Soviet Union covered up early cosmonaut deaths before Yuri Gagarin's official 1961 first flight — got its primary documentation from two Italian brothers who ran an amateur radio listening station from their family home. Who were they?
answer: Achille and Giovanni Battista Judica-Cordiglia, ham-radio enthusiasts in Italy
choices: Achille and Giovanni Battista Judica-Cordiglia, ham-radio enthusiasts in Italy
Marconi brothers, who actually were the children of radio inventor Guglielmo Marconi
Castelli brothers, who actually had no involvement in the lost cosmonauts story
Fermi brothers, who actually had no connection to amateur radio investigations
context: The Judica-Cordiglia brothers' recordings include several distressed Russian voices and 'heartbeat' transmissions that have been used to argue for failed Soviet missions before Gagarin. The recordings are real; their interpretation has been heavily disputed. The most-cited 'Lost Cosmonaut' is the 'Komov' Russian-speaking woman heard on May 17, 1961.

question: Numbers stations — shortwave radio broadcasts of monotone recitations of numbers, letters, or phonetic alphabets, often in multiple languages — have been on the air since at least the 1940s and were studied during the Cold War. What is their most-accepted purpose?
answer: Encrypted one-way communications to intelligence-agency operatives in foreign countries
choices: Encrypted one-way communications to intelligence-agency operatives in foreign countries
Weather forecasts for commercial aviation in the days before satellite uplinks
Amateur-radio operator-identification confirming long-distance contacts
Mathematical lottery numbers broadcast by ham-radio enthusiasts for hobby use
context: The British 'Lincolnshire Poacher' (1972-2008) and the Cuban 'HM01' (still active) are well-known examples. The Conet Project (1997) released a 4-CD compilation of numbers-station recordings. Several stations have been traced to specific government broadcast sites; their content remains officially unconfirmed by the agencies operating them.

question: The Mandela Effect — the phenomenon in which a large group of people independently recall events or facts in the same way that is inconsistent with the historical record — was named for one specific incorrect memory shared by many people. What is the Mandela memory?
answer: That Nelson Mandela had died in prison in the 1980s before his 1990 release
choices: That Nelson Mandela had died in prison in the 1980s before his 1990 release
That Nelson Mandela had won the Nobel Peace Prize alone, not jointly
That Nelson Mandela had served as US Secretary General of the UN in the 1990s
That Nelson Mandela had been a left-handed boxer before his political career
context: Fiona Broome coined the term 'Mandela Effect' in 2009 after meeting other people who recalled Mandela dying in prison. Mandela actually died in December 2013, having served as President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. Other common Mandela Effects include the spelling of 'Berenstein/Berenstain Bears' (it has always been Berenstain) and 'Sex and the City' vs 'Sex in the City'.

question: Gary Gygax — co-creator of Dungeons & Dragons, founder of TSR, and the spiritual father of the role-playing game industry — was born and lived most of his life in a single small town in Wisconsin. He died at his home in March 2008. Where?
answer: Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, where TSR was also headquartered for most of its life
choices: Lake Geneva, Wisconsin, where TSR was also headquartered for most of its life
Madison, Wisconsin, the state capital where TSR briefly had offices
Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where Origins Games Fair was held in early years
Green Bay, Wisconsin, which had no Gygax-era connection to the company
context: Gygax (1938-2008) grew up in Lake Geneva and lived there nearly all his life. Lake Geneva became a kind of pilgrimage site for D&D fans; Gen Con was held there for many years before moving to Milwaukee (1985) and Indianapolis (2003). Gygax was 69 when he died, of complications from an abdominal aneurysm.

question: Before Dungeons & Dragons, Gary Gygax co-authored a medieval miniatures wargame called *Chainmail* (1971) with a coauthor named Jeff Perren. *Chainmail* included a 'Fantasy Supplement' that introduced wizards, elves, and dragons to wargaming. Who published *Chainmail*?
answer: Guidon Games of Evansville, Indiana (a small wargames publisher)

TSR, which Gygax actually wouldn't found until 1973 (two years after Chainmail)

context: Guidon Games's print run was small; *Chainmail* sold roughly 5,000 copies. The fantasy supplement caught the attention of Minneapolis wargamer Dave Arneson, who developed his own 'Blackmoor' campaign extending *Chainmail*'s fantasy rules — leading directly to D&D.

question: *Dungeons & Dragons* — the original three-booklet 'white box' (also called the 'Original D&D' or 'OD&D' or 'Little Brown Books') — was published by TSR in January 1974. What were the three booklets in the white box?
answer: *Men & Magic*, *Monsters & Treasure*, *The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures*

context: The first 1,000 copies of OD&D were assembled by hand by the Gygax family on their dining table in Lake Geneva, with photocopied pages and woodgrain-paper covers. The original price was $10. Print runs continued through 1979; many supplements (Greyhawk, Blackmoor, Eldritch Wizardry) were added over the years.

question: Dave Arneson — co-creator of Dungeons & Dragons with Gary Gygax — developed the 'Blackmoor' campaign in Minnesota in 1971-72, which provided the dungeon-crawl and character-improvement mechanics that became D&D. He died in April 2009. What were his dates?

1950 to 2015, much later than the actual death year
1942 to 2003, with death predating the OD&D 30th anniversary
context: Arneson was a Minneapolis-based wargamer when he developed the Blackmoor campaign. He sued TSR in 1979 over royalties; the settlement gave him compensation but the legal split has long colored D&D historiography. Arneson and Gygax shared D&D's creator credit on every published version of the game.

question: TSR Hobbies, Inc. — the company that published Dungeons & Dragons — was founded by Gary Gygax and a co-founder in October 1973. The original company name 'Tactical Studies Rules' was abbreviated to TSR. Who was Gygax's co-founder?
answer: Don Kaye, a childhood friend who put up the initial $1,000 startup capital

context: Don Kaye died of a heart attack in 1975 at 36; Brian Blume bought out Kaye's share. Blume's brother Kevin and sister Loraine Williams joined the firm in subsequent years; Williams's 1985 maneuvering led to Gygax's ouster from TSR. Gygax sold his Tactical Studies Rules shares to the Blumes that year.

question: *Supplement I: Greyhawk* (1975) was the first supplement to original D&D. It added the thief class, the variable hit-die system (different dice for different classes), and the critical-hit rule. It was authored by Gygax and Robert Kuntz. What world setting was it named for?
answer: The City of Greyhawk and the World of Oerth, Gygax's home campaign setting

Greyhawk Castle, an entirely different setting from the published World of Greyhawk

Lankhmar, which actually was Fritz Leiber's literary city (later licensed by TSR)
context: Gygax had been running a campaign set in his fictional World of Oerth since 1972. The City of Greyhawk and its surrounding Castle were the focal points. The *World of Greyhawk Fantasy Setting* (1980) was the first published D&D campaign setting; the later Forgotten Realms (1987) eclipsed it commercially.

question: The Advanced Dungeons & Dragons *Monster Manual* (1977) was the first hardcover Dungeons & Dragons publication — a major industry move at the time. Gary Gygax wrote it. What was its cover price at release?
answer: $9.95, with cover art by David C. Sutherland III featuring a beholder
choices: $9.95, with cover art by David C. Sutherland III featuring a beholder
$4.95, much lower than the actual published cover price
$14.95, much higher than the actual published cover price
$24.95, far higher than the actual published cover price at the time
context: The *Monster Manual* introduced D&D's now-iconic creature lineup: the beholder, mind flayer, owlbear, displacer beast, intellect devourer, bulette, rust monster, and many more. Its $9.95 price was significant for a hobby book in 1977; the format set the template for the *Player's Handbook* (1978) and *Dungeon Master's Guide* (1979).

question: The Advanced Dungeons & Dragons *Player's Handbook* (1978) was the second AD&D hardcover. It collected character classes (fighter, magic-user, cleric, thief, ranger, paladin, druid, illusionist, monk, assassin, bard), races, spells, and equipment. Who designed its iconic cover?
answer: David Trampier (DAT) painted the cover with the iconic 'lizard-men sacking' scene
choices: David Trampier (DAT) painted the cover with the iconic 'lizard-men sacking' scene
Erol Otus painted the cover, though he actually only painted the Monster Manual
Larry Elmore painted the cover, though he didn't join TSR until later
Jeff Easley painted the cover, though he didn't join TSR until later
context: Trampier's cover (lizard-men sacking a temple while adventurers loot a giant idol) became iconic. Trampier dropped out of the industry abruptly in 1988 and was unreachable for decades; he was rediscovered driving a cab in Bloomington, Illinois, before his 2014 death. He had refused to license his work or accept royalties for the AD&D cover.

question: The Advanced Dungeons & Dragons *Dungeon Master's Guide* (1979) was the third AD&D hardcover and is widely cited as one of the densest game manuals ever published. Roughly how many pages was the original 1979 printing?
answer: 240 pages of dense rules, tables, and DM-only secret information
choices: 240 pages of dense rules, tables, and DM-only secret information
120 pages, much shorter than the actual length
500 pages, much longer than the actual length
60 pages, far shorter than the actual length
context: The DMG's combat-procedure, encounter-table, treasure-generation, and random-dungeon-stocking systems were enormously detailed. The book's wandering monster tables, the appendices for fungi and lycanthropy, the random harlot table, and Gygax's tone — half-formal, half-conversational — gave it an unmistakable voice.

question: Gary Gygax was ousted from TSR in October 1985, after a struggle for control of the company involving the Blume family, his attempted alliance with Lorraine Williams, and (some say) Williams's later double-cross. Who emerged as TSR's CEO after Gygax left?
answer: Lorraine Williams, sister of Brian Blume's wife, who ran TSR until 1997
choices: Lorraine Williams, sister of Brian Blume's wife, who ran TSR until 1997
Brian Blume himself, who tried but failed to retain control of TSR after 1985
Kevin Blume, Brian's brother, who actually was bought out of TSR before 1985
Tim Kask, who actually was D&D's first employee but had left TSR in 1979
context: Lorraine Williams's CEO tenure (1985-1997) was controversial within TSR's creative culture. She reportedly refused to play D&D and held the gaming hobby in low regard. TSR was sold to Wizards of the Coast in 1997 after a near-collapse caused by inventory mismanagement and the diversion to novelistic publishing.

question: Wizards of the Coast — the company that purchased TSR in June 1997 and revived Dungeons & Dragons — had been a Magic: the Gathering publisher founded in Renton, Washington in 1990. Who founded Wizards of the Coast?
answer: Peter Adkison, who founded Wizards in 1990 with money from his earlier game work
choices: Peter Adkison, who founded Wizards in 1990 with money from his earlier game work
Richard Garfield, who actually was Magic's designer but not Wizards's founder
Lorraine Williams, who actually was TSR's CEO until selling to Wizards
Gary Gygax, who actually had been ousted from TSR and was not at Wizards
context: Adkison published Garfield's *Magic: the Gathering* through Wizards in August 1993; Magic's commercial success funded the TSR purchase. Adkison led Wizards from 1990 to 2001, when Hasbro (which had acquired Wizards in 1999 for $325 million) replaced him. Adkison ran Gen Con from 2002 to 2006.

question: The 'Satanic Panic' of the 1980s targeted Dungeons & Dragons among other youth pursuits, alleging the game was a path to occultism or suicide. A specific evangelical Christian comic tract published in 1984 became one of the most widely-distributed anti-D&D documents. Who published it?
answer: Jack T. Chick of Chick Publications, in the tract 'Dark Dungeons' (1984)
choices: Jack T. Chick of Chick Publications, in the tract 'Dark Dungeons' (1984)
Pat Robertson, who actually was a televangelist not a tract publisher
James Dobson, who actually founded Focus on the Family but not anti-D&D tracts
Jerry Falwell, who actually was an anti-D&D preacher but not a tract publisher
context: Chick's *Dark Dungeons* (still in print) describes a young D&D player (Marcie) committing suicide after her character dies, and another (Debbie) being inducted into 'real magic' by a Dungeon Master named Ms. Frost. The tract has been parodied and remade many times; a live-action film adaptation (2014) is a faithful low-budget recreation.

question: The 1979 disappearance of James Dallas Egbert III — a 16-year-old Michigan State University student who vanished in the steam tunnels under campus — drew national attention to college D&D culture. The case was investigated by a private detective who later wrote a book about it. Who?
answer: William Dear, the Texas-based PI who wrote 'The Dungeon Master' (1984)
choices: William Dear, the Texas-based PI who wrote 'The Dungeon Master' (1984)
Patricia Pulling, who founded BADD (Bothered About D&D) after her son's suicide
Sam Spade, who actually was a fictional Dashiell Hammett character not real
Jessica Fletcher, who actually was the fictional 'Murder, She Wrote' character
context: Egbert was found alive a month later in Louisiana, where he had fled after a suicide attempt. He died by suicide later in 1980. The 1981 novel *Mazes and Monsters* by Rona Jaffe (and the 1982 Tom Hanks TV-film adaptation) was loosely based on the case, presenting D&D as a dangerous influence — and helped fuel the Satanic Panic.

question: Module B1: *In Search of the Unknown* (1979) was TSR's first Basic D&D module, written for the Holmes 'Blue Box' edition. The module included an introduction explaining how to design dungeons. Who wrote it?
answer: Mike Carr, a TSR employee who also wrote 'Fight in the Skies' (1968) for SPI
choices: Mike Carr, a TSR employee who also wrote 'Fight in the Skies' (1968) for SPI
Gary Gygax, who actually wrote many modules but not B1 specifically
Tom Moldvay, who actually wrote B4 'The Lost City' (1982) for Basic D&D
Tracy Hickman, who actually wrote 'Ravenloft' (1983) for AD&D not Basic
context: Carr's B1 deliberately omitted monsters and treasure from many rooms, leaving the DM to populate the dungeon as a learning exercise. The module's iconic 'Caverns of Quasqueton' have been published in multiple D&D editions over the years. Carr left TSR in the early 1980s.

question: Module B2: *The Keep on the Borderlands* (1980) was TSR's second Basic D&D module and one of the most-played adventures in D&D history. It featured a frontier keep and a nearby 'Caves of Chaos' housing various humanoid tribes. Who wrote it?
answer: Gary Gygax, who designed the keep and the caves complex personally
choices: Gary Gygax, who designed the keep and the caves complex personally
Mike Carr, who actually wrote B1 'In Search of the Unknown' (1979) not B2
Tom Moldvay, who actually edited Basic D&D (1981) but didn't write B2
David Cook, who actually wrote X1 'Isle of Dread' (1981) but not B2
context: The Caves of Chaos contained orcs, goblins, hobgoblins, gnolls, bugbears, ogres, and a chaotic temple. The Keep was a structured human settlement giving players a base. Gygax wrote B2 as the bundled module for the original 1977 Holmes Basic Set; it was reprinted with virtually every Basic D&D set through 1983.

question: Module X1: *The Isle of Dread* (1981) was TSR's first Expert D&D module and the bundled adventure for the Moldvay-Cook 1981 Basic/Expert revision. It was a wilderness-exploration adventure set on a tropical island modeled on Skull Island from *King Kong*. Who wrote it?
answer: Tom Moldvay and David Cook, who also co-edited the Expert Set itself
choices: Tom Moldvay and David Cook, who also co-edited the Expert Set itself
Gary Gygax, who actually wrote 'Temple of Elemental Evil' (1985) but not X1
Frank Mentzer, who actually wrote the 1983 Mentzer Basic Set but not X1
Larry Elmore, who actually was a TSR artist but did not write modules
context: X1 mapped a colonial-era island with multiple village cultures, dinosaurs, sentient kopru, and various wilderness threats. The module is widely cited as one of the most-played D&D adventures of all time. The 'Isle of Dread' became a recurring location in subsequent campaign settings (Mystara, Greyhawk).

question: Module T1: *The Village of Hommlet* (1979) was Gary Gygax's first published Advanced D&D module. It introduced an entire village (NPCs, building plans, local politics) and a small dungeon (the moathouse of evil cultists) to give DMs a complete starter setting. What was its expanded sequel?
answer: Module T1-4: *The Temple of Elemental Evil* (1985) by Gygax and Frank Mentzer
choices: Module T1-4: *The Temple of Elemental Evil* (1985) by Gygax and Frank Mentzer
Module T2: *Greater Hommlet*, which actually was never released by TSR
Module T3: *Veluna's Edge*, which actually was never published by TSR
Module T1: *Hommlet Revisited*, which actually was a fan-made retroclone
context: *Temple of Elemental Evil* was promised since 1979 but only published in 1985 after Gygax brought in Frank Mentzer to help complete it. The Temple's nine levels — chaotic evil, neutral evil, lawful evil, etc., reflecting the alignment grid — represent one of the most-detailed published D&D dungeons of the era.

question: Module G1: *Steading of the Hill Giant Chief* (1978) was Gary Gygax's first 'big' module — part of his Giants series followed by the Drow series. The 'G1-2-3' modules together formed a giant-themed campaign. Who is the named chief of the hill giants in G1?
answer: Chief Nosnra, a hill giant who controls the steading and its bugbear allies
choices: Chief Nosnra, a hill giant who controls the steading and its bugbear allies
Chief Grugnur, a hill giant who actually appears in G3 not G1
King Snurre, a fire giant who actually appears in G3 not G1
Jarl Grugnur, a frost giant who actually appears in G2 not G1
context: G1 was published from Gygax's Origins '78 tournament. The Giants modules led directly into the Drow modules (D1-3) and the Demonweb Pits (Q1), all together forming one of the most-cited series in D&D adventure history. The series is called the 'GDQ' campaign in fan parlance.

question: Module D3: *Vault of the Drow* (1978) by Gary Gygax was the most extensive published depiction of D&D's dark elves up to that point. The module introduced many drow conventions (Underdark, Lolth as their demon-queen, drow noble houses) that became permanent fixtures. Who is the demon queen the drow worship?
answer: Lolth (later Lloth in some Forgotten Realms texts), the Demon Queen of Spiders
choices: Lolth (later Lloth in some Forgotten Realms texts), the Demon Queen of Spiders
Tiamat, who actually is the dragon-goddess not a drow goddess
Vecna, who actually is the lich-god from the Vecna Eye and Hand artifacts
Asmodeus, who actually is the king of the Nine Hells not a drow patron
context: Lolth's introduction in D3 shaped four decades of drow lore. R.A. Salvatore's Drizzt Do'Urden character (from *The Crystal Shard*, 1988) is a drow ranger who has rejected Lolth and her culture. Drow houses, the Demonweb, and the drow social hierarchy all developed from Gygax's original D3 framework.

question: Module S1: *Tomb of Horrors* (1978) by Gary Gygax has the long-standing reputation as the deadliest published D&D module. It was used by Gygax at Origins '75 as a tournament dungeon specifically to challenge confident players. What is the boss creature?
answer: Acererak the lich-king (later 'demilich'), whose magical tomb traps the unwary
choices: Acererak the lich-king (later 'demilich'), whose magical tomb traps the unwary
Vecna the god-lich, who actually has his own modules not Tomb of Horrors
Strahd von Zarovich, who actually is from 'Ravenloft' (I6) not Tomb of Horrors
Iggwilv the demonologist, who actually is from S4 not Tomb of Horrors
context: Acererak's demilich form (a floating skull) became iconic. The module's many one-shot-death traps — the green devil's mouth, the sphere of annihilation, the misty arch — are infamous among veteran D&D players. The Tomb has been re-released in nearly every D&D edition and remains a benchmark.

question: Module S3: *Expedition to the Barrier Peaks* (1980) by Gary Gygax is one of the most genre-bending D&D modules ever published. Why is it unusual?
answer: It is a science-fiction crashed-spaceship adventure with lasers and androids
choices: It is a science-fiction crashed-spaceship adventure with lasers and androids
It is a horror-themed module set in a haunted Edwardian mansion in 1900s England
It is a comedy module with cartoon-style villains and 1930s-pastiche slapstick
It is an entirely solo-play adventure designed for a single player without a DM
context: Players exploring a crashed spaceship of unknown origin find laser pistols, force fields, robots, mutant plants. Erol Otus's illustrations of the alien horrors are particularly memorable. The module was originally designed for the AD&D tournament at Origins '76; it was held back until 1980 for publication.

question: Module I6: *Ravenloft* (1983) by Tracy and Laura Hickman introduced one of the most important characters in D&D history: the vampire-count Strahd von Zarovich, ruler of the demiplane of Barovia. The module's design pioneered which game-design technique?
answer: Randomly determined boss motivation: Strahd's goals shift based on tarokka card draw
choices: Randomly determined boss motivation: Strahd's goals shift based on tarokka card draw
Mandatory player character backstories: all PCs must have lost a loved one before play
All-darkness combat rules: encounters happen entirely without light at all
Random player-character respawning: dead characters reappear at a fountain
context: The 'fortunes' card draw at the start of the adventure determines Strahd's specific motivations for that playthrough. Ravenloft was so successful it became a full campaign setting (1990) with its own line of products. The Hickmans went on to write the *Dragonlance* trilogy (1984-85) with Margaret Weis.

question: *Dragonlance Chronicles* — the three-novel sequence by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman that launched the *Dragonlance* setting — was published by TSR Books in 1984-85. What is the trilogy's combined title?
answer: *Dragons of Autumn Twilight*, *Dragons of Winter Night*, *Dragons of Spring Dawning*
choices: *Dragons of Autumn Twilight*, *Dragons of Winter Night*, *Dragons of Spring Dawning*
*Dragons of Krynn*, *Dragons of Solamnia*, *Dragons of Istar*
*Krynn Chronicles*: *War of the Lance*, *Legends of the Twins*, *Last Heroes*
*The Lance Saga*: *Tanis's Dawn*, *Raistlin's Twilight*, *Caramon's Night*
context: The Chronicles introduced Tanis Half-Elven, Sturm Brightblade, the twins Raistlin and Caramon Majere, Tasslehoff Burrfoot, Flint Fireforge, and others. The companion Legends trilogy (1986) — *Time of the Twins*, *War of the Twins*, *Test of the Twins* — focused on Raistlin. Both trilogies became foundational fantasy reading for a generation.

question: The City of Greyhawk and the surrounding World of Oerth — Gary Gygax's home campaign and the first published D&D campaign setting (1980) — featured a roster of iconic player-character archmagi whose names were also assigned to many spell names. Who is the most famous?
answer: Mordenkainen, a neutral archmage and Gygax's own personal player character
choices: Mordenkainen, a neutral archmage and Gygax's own personal player character
Elminster, who actually is a Forgotten Realms (not Greyhawk) character
Drizzt Do'Urden, who actually is a Forgotten Realms (not Greyhawk) character
Raistlin Majere, who actually is a Dragonlance (not Greyhawk) character
context: Gygax's Greyhawk archmagi — Mordenkainen, Bigby, Otiluke, Evard, Tenser, Drawmij ('Jim Ward' backwards) — gave their names to dozens of spells (Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound, Bigby's Crushing Hand, etc.). Many of these spell names migrated to later D&D editions and even the Forgotten Realms.

question: The Forgotten Realms — eventually TSR's bestselling D&D campaign setting and home of Drizzt, Elminster, and the Sword Coast — was created by an Ontario librarian as a personal home campaign. He had been writing about it in *Dragon* magazine articles since 1979. Who?
answer: Ed Greenwood, who developed the Realms over a decade before TSR licensed it
choices: Ed Greenwood, who developed the Realms over a decade before TSR licensed it
Tracy Hickman, who actually created Ravenloft and co-wrote Dragonlance
R.A. Salvatore, who actually wrote 'Crystal Shard' but didn't create the Realms
Bob Salvatore, who is not a separate person — same as 'R.A. Salvatore' above
context: Greenwood had been writing Realms material as his own home campaign since the early 1970s. TSR licensed the world in 1987 with the *Forgotten Realms Campaign Set* (gray box). Elminster — Greenwood's archmage character — became a kind of in-universe author for many later Realms supplements.

question: R.A. Salvatore's drow ranger Drizzt Do'Urden — who has rejected his evil drow heritage and lives as a hero in the surface lands — debuted in *The Crystal Shard* (1988), a Forgotten Realms novel. Drizzt was an accidental addition to the manuscript. What happened?
answer: Salvatore wrote Drizzt as an emergency replacement for a character TSR rejected
choices: Salvatore wrote Drizzt as an emergency replacement for a character TSR rejected

Salvatore wrote Drizzt as a one-scene villain who readers liked too much
Salvatore wrote Drizzt as a tribute to a real friend who had passed away
context: Salvatore's first sidekick (a barbarian named Wulfgar) had been the planned protagonist but TSR's editor wanted an additional party member. Drizzt was conceived overnight; he became the breakout star. The *Icewind Dale Trilogy* (1988-90) and the *Dark Elf Trilogy* prequel (1990-91) established Drizzt as one of fantasy literature's most successful franchise characters.

question: *Dark Sun* (1991) was TSR's most-original 1990s D&D campaign setting — a post-apocalyptic desert world (Athas) where metal is scarce, psionics are everywhere, defiling magic destroys the environment, and the sun is too close. The setting was designed by which TSR team?
answer: Timothy Brown and Troy Denning, with art by Brom (Gerald Brom)
choices: Timothy Brown and Troy Denning, with art by Brom (Gerald Brom)
Tracy Hickman and Margaret Weis, who actually were the Dragonlance team
Ed Greenwood and Jeff Grubb, who actually were the Forgotten Realms team
Gary Gygax and Frank Mentzer, who actually were the Temple of Elemental Evil team
context: Brom's painted art — barbed-wire bondage aesthetic, dark muscular figures, broken weapons — gave Dark Sun its distinctive look. The setting featured 'half-giants' as a playable race, mantis-warrior 'thri-kreen' as a player race, and metal weapons that broke after extended use. It was a deliberate departure from the standard D&D 'kitchen-sink fantasy' approach.

question: *Planescape* (1994) was TSR's most-conceptual D&D campaign setting. It treated D&D's cosmology of outer planes as the actual setting, with the City of Doors at the center of the multiverse. Who designed the setting?
answer: Zeb Cook, with art by Tony DiTerlizzi (the painted aesthetic of the boxed set)
choices: Zeb Cook, with art by Tony DiTerlizzi (the painted aesthetic of the boxed set)
Gary Gygax, who actually had been ousted from TSR ten years earlier
Tracy Hickman, who actually had moved on to write novels by 1994
Ed Greenwood, who actually was working on Forgotten Realms not Planescape
context: DiTerlizzi's painted aesthetic — Victorian patchwork, multicultural fantasy — gave Planescape its signature look. The City of Sigil (the 'City of Doors') sits on top of an infinite spire at the center of the cosmos. The setting's 15 'factions' (the Believers of the Source, the Bleak Cabal, etc.) gave it a philosophical-debate structure unique in D&D.

question: *Spelljammer* (1989) was TSR's most-bizarre 1980s D&D campaign setting: a space-fantasy world where wizards and adventurers travel between worlds in 'spelljamming' magical sailing ships. Who designed the setting?
answer: Jeff Grubb, with art by Jim Holloway among the original designers
choices: Jeff Grubb, with art by Jim Holloway among the original designers
Tracy Hickman, who actually was working on Dragonlance and Ravenloft
Ed Greenwood, who actually was working on Forgotten Realms
Gary Gygax, who actually had been ousted from TSR four years earlier
context: Spelljammer introduced the 'phlogiston' (the cosmic ether between crystal spheres), the 'giff' (hippopotamus-headed mercenary soldiers), and the 'neogi' (spider-and-eel slavers). The setting's most-cited products are the giant ship-deck floor maps. The 2022 5e revival was met with mixed fan reception.

question: Fritz Leiber's literary city of Lankhmar — home of Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser — became an officially licensed D&D campaign setting in 1985. Who designed the original *Lankhmar: City of Adventure* box set?
answer: Bruce Nesmith and Doug Niles, working under TSR's official license from Leiber
choices: Bruce Nesmith and Doug Niles, working under TSR's official license from Leiber
Fritz Leiber himself, who actually consulted but did not design the campaign set
Gary Gygax, who had been ousted from TSR in October 1985 (the same year)
Ken St. Andre, who actually designed 'Tunnels and Trolls' not Lankhmar D&D
context: Leiber consulted on the TSR set. The 1985 *Lankhmar: City of Adventure* was followed by several adventure modules and a 1993 revised set. Leiber's Lankhmar is considered one of the foundational literary sources for D&D itself — Gygax has cited Leiber repeatedly in interviews about his D&D inspirations.

question: The beholder — D&D's iconic floating eyeball monster from the original 1977 *Monster Manual* — has a famously dangerous central eye plus ten smaller eye-stalks emanating various magical rays. What does the central eye do?
answer: Projects an anti-magic cone in which no spells (the beholder's own included) can function
choices: Projects an anti-magic cone in which no spells (the beholder's own included) can function
Petrifies victims, turning them to stone with a single direct gaze
Fires a ray of disintegration that destroys matter instantly
Drains levels from a victim, draining their character experience permanently
context: The anti-magic cone is the beholder's most-cited tactical feature: it forces the beholder to choose targets carefully, since any spell from the beholder targeting an enemy inside the cone fails. Various beholder variants — the death tyrant, the elder orb, the spectator — were developed in 2nd Edition and later. Wizards have legally protected 'beholder' as IP since the 1990s.

question: The mind flayer (illithid) — the squid-faced psionic monster that eats brains — first appeared in *The Strategic Review* #1, a TSR newsletter, in spring 1975, before being included in the 1977 *Monster Manual*. Who designed it?
answer: Gary Gygax, inspired by the cover of a 1973 paperback novel by Brian Lumley

Dave Arneson, who actually was the OD&D co-creator but didn't create mind flayers
Bob Bledsaw, who actually designed Judges Guild material not TSR monsters
M.A.R. Barker, who actually designed 'Empire of the Petal Throne' not D&D monsters
context: The cover of Brian Lumley's 1973 novel *The Burrowers Beneath* features a tentacle-faced humanoid that Gygax later cited as visual inspiration. The mind flayer's social hierarchy (ulitharids, elder brains, brain-collectors) was developed across editions. The 1981 *Fiend Folio* added more illithid variants.

question: The displacer beast — D&D's six-legged-panther with backwards-facing magical displacement — was inspired by a creature from a 1939 science-fiction short story. The original story by A.E. van Vogt featured a 'coeurl' attacking spacefarers. What was the story called?
answer: 'Black Destroyer' — published in *Astounding Science-Fiction* in July 1939
choices: 'Black Destroyer' — published in *Astounding Science-Fiction* in July 1939
'The Sentinel' by Arthur C. Clarke (which actually inspired 2001: A Space Odyssey)
'Microcosmic God' by Theodore Sturgeon (which actually is a different SF story)
'The Cold Equations' by Tom Godwin (which actually is a different SF story)
context: Van Vogt's 'Black Destroyer' was later folded into his *Voyage of the Space Beagle* (1950). The story's coeurl became the displacer beast in D&D. TSR's legal team has fought to protect 'displacer beast' as IP for decades because of the van Vogt-derived design (van Vogt's estate disputed this in the 1990s before settling).

question: The owlbear — D&D's iconic 'two-things-combined' monster (owl head + bear body) from the 1977 *Monster Manual* — has an odd real-world origin. Gary Gygax purchased a bag of small plastic Hong Kong dime-store toys in the early 1970s and used them as proxies in his D&D miniatures. What is the owlbear's source?
answer: An unbranded plastic toy in a 'Chinasaur' lineup of bizarre molded creatures
choices: An unbranded plastic toy in a 'Chinasaur' lineup of bizarre molded creatures
A handmade figure by Gygax's daughter Cindy, with no commercial origin
A licensed creature from a Saturday morning cartoon Gygax watched as a child
A medieval European bestiary's depiction of a 'griff-owl' from the 12th century
context: The Hong Kong plastic-toy 'Chinasaurs' included the owlbear, rust monster, bulette ('landshark'), and several other early D&D monsters. Mike Carr saw the toys in Gygax's office and reportedly suggested adding them to the monster lineup. The original molds have been documented by D&D historians; the plastic toys themselves predate D&D.

question: The tarrasque — D&D's effectively immortal kaiju-tier monster, requiring an exotic resurrection method to kill it permanently — has a real folkloric origin. The creature is named after a beast from the medieval Provencal town of Tarascon. What is the original story?
answer: A dragon-like creature tamed by Saint Martha in Tarascon, France (medieval legend)

A whale that swallowed Jonah in the biblical book of the prophet Jonah
A Greek hydra slain by Hercules at the spring of Lerna in Argolis
A Norse serpent named Jormungandr coiled around Midgard in the world
context: The Tarascon tarrasque is celebrated annually in the city's June 'Tarasque Festival' (a UNESCO-listed intangible cultural heritage). The D&D tarrasque (Monster Manual, 1977; ridiculously high HP and saves in AD&D 1e) is a deliberate homage to the medieval folk-monster. The 'destruction-followed-by-magical-defeat' plot of Saint Martha's legend echoes through the D&D version.

question: The drow — D&D's dark elves, evil and matriarchal, dwelling in the Underdark, worshipping Lolth the Spider Demon Queen — were established by Gary Gygax across his Giants/Drow modules in 1978. Lolth's domain is named for her demonic-arachnid nature. What is the layer of the Abyss she rules?
answer: The Demonweb, layered with strands of webbing in an infinite spiral
choices: The Demonweb, layered with strands of webbing in an infinite spiral
The Pit of Spiders, a different demon-layer not associated with Lolth
The Burning Sand, which actually is Imix's elemental plane domain
The Eternal Twilight, which actually is no specific demon-layer in D&D canon
context: Module Q1: *Queen of the Demonweb Pits* (1980), by David C. Sutherland and Gary Gygax, took the GDQ series's final adventure into Lolth's home plane. The Demonweb has remained Lolth's lair across all D&D editions. The Lolth-worship and drow matriarchy framework is more deeply developed in Forgotten Realms than in Greyhawk.

question: The kuo-toa — D&D's underdark-dwelling fish-men, with bulging eyes and lobster-like claws — first appeared in module D2: *Shrine of the Kuo-Toa* (1978) by Gary Gygax. What is unusual about the kuo-toa religion?
answer: Their goddess Blibdoolpoolp is depicted as a giant lobster-headed woman
choices: Their goddess Blibdoolpoolp is depicted as a giant lobster-headed woman
They actually worship the same Lolth that the drow worship, with theological tension
They worship the elemental prince of Water, Olhydra, in a heretical drow temple
They have no religion at all, having renounced gods after a primal trauma
context: Blibdoolpoolp's lobster-headed female form became iconic D&D Underdark imagery. The kuo-toa's mental instability (a documented racial trait — they often slip into madness from prolonged Underdark exposure) gave them their distinctive monster-design hook. They remain a major Underdark population across all D&D editions.

question: The duergar — D&D's gray dwarves of the Underdark, slaved historically by the mind flayers — first appeared in *Fiend Folio* (1981) under TSR-UK's Don Turnbull. They became one of D&D's foundational Underdark races. What is their cultural enmity?
answer: They are bitter enemies of all surface dwarves, especially the shield dwarves
choices: They are bitter enemies of all surface dwarves, especially the shield dwarves
They are allies of the drow, with whom they share the Underdark peacefully
They are vassals of Tiamat, the chromatic dragon-goddess
They are allies of the surface elves against the surface humans of the Forgotten Realms
context: *Fiend Folio* was the first AD&D Monster Manual sequel. Don Turnbull's UK editorial team contributed many distinctive monsters (the slaad, the githyanki, the githzerai, the death knight). The duergar's history of slavery under mind flayers explains their hatred of surface dwarves; many duergar are albino from generations underground.

question: The githyanki and githzerai — D&D's two factions of an enslaved space-faring race who broke free from mind-flayer slavery long ago — first appeared in *Fiend Folio* (1981). What is the in-universe difference between the two factions?
answer: Githyanki live on the Astral Plane under Queen Vlaakith; githzerai live on Limbo
choices: Githyanki live on the Astral Plane under Queen Vlaakith; githzerai live on Limbo
Githyanki are good-aligned, while githzerai are evil-aligned
Githyanki use only psionic powers, while githzerai use only divine magic
Githyanki are still loyal to the mind flayers, while githzerai rebelled
context: Charles Stross designed the gith in *Fiend Folio*. The split between Vlaakith's Astral Plane githyanki (warrior-imperial) and Zerthimon's Limbo-dwelling githzerai (monastic-philosophical) is one of D&D's most-developed inter-faction conflicts. Their psionic abilities and silver-blade weaponry have made them recurring antagonists.

question: Bahamut — D&D's platinum dragon-god of justice and the good-aligned counterpart to Tiamat — has a name and aesthetic borrowed from Arabic mythology. In Arabic tradition, Bahamut is what?
answer: A giant sea-creature on whose back the world rests, in cosmological folklore
choices: A giant sea-creature on whose back the world rests, in cosmological folklore
A jinn (genie) ruler of the fire spirits in 1001 Nights tradition
A mountain-spirit said to rule the heights of Mecca in pre-Islamic legend
A river-monster from the Tigris and Euphrates basin of Babylonian myth
context: The Arabic Bahamut is described in Borges's *Book of Imaginary Beings* (1957). Gygax's adaptation as a platinum dragon may have been influenced by the Borges reference. Bahamut and Tiamat were both added to D&D in *Supplement IV: Gods, Demigods & Heroes* (1976). Bahamut's seven golden knights — paladins serving him — became an iconic D&D plot device.

question: The umber hulk — D&D's burrowing earth-creature, with mandibles and four eyes — has a particularly devastating gaze attack. From the original *Monster Manual* (1977), what does looking at an umber hulk do to characters?
answer: Causes confusion (a status effect making characters attack randomly or stand still)
choices: Causes confusion (a status effect making characters attack randomly or stand still)
Causes petrification (turning characters to stone like a medusa or gorgon)
Causes paralysis (preventing movement until a saving throw succeeds)
Causes blindness (preventing visual targeting of any kind)
context: The umber hulk's confusion gaze made it one of D&D's signature 'don't look at it' monsters — players were forced into elaborate combat tactics (averted gaze, mirrored surfaces, blindfolds). The creature's burrowing speed and surprise attacks made it especially deadly. Umber hulks remain a recurring Underdark threat in current D&D.

question: The rust monster — D&D's iconic 'eats armor and weapons' monster from the 1977 *Monster Manual* — has one of the worst reactions among veteran D&D players because of what they do to a party's gear. What is the rust monster's mechanic?
answer: Touching a rust monster (or being touched by its tentacles) instantly rusts magical metal
choices: Touching a rust monster (or being touched by its tentacles) instantly rusts magical metal
Rust monsters psychically rust metal without physical contact at a distance
Rust monsters spit rust-acid that takes effect on a saving throw allowed
Rust monsters drain the magical enchantment of metal items, not corrode them
context: The rust monster's tentacle-touch instantly aged metal in earlier editions — a particularly devastating effect on the gold-piece value of a party's gear. The creature's original Hong Kong plastic-toy design (same lineage as the owlbear and bulette) had a strange tail-fan shape that became its signature visual. Rust monsters remain a fan-cherished horror.

question: The gibbering mouther — D&D's amorphous mass-of-mouths-and-eyes monster — first appeared in the 1981 *Fiend Folio*. The creature's design draws heavily on a specific Lovecraftian source. What is the source?
answer: The shoggoths of H.P. Lovecraft's *At the Mountains of Madness* (1936)
choices: The shoggoths of H.P. Lovecraft's *At the Mountains of Madness* (1936)
The deep ones of H.P. Lovecraft's *The Shadow Over Innsmouth* (1936)
The Mi-Go of H.P. Lovecraft's *The Whisperer in Darkness* (1931)
