choices: Geass, a 'King's Power' that lets him give an irresistible command to anyone he locks eyes with
Quirk, which actually is the term in 'My Hero Academia' (2014) not Code Geass
Nen, which actually is the term in 'Hunter x Hunter' (1998) not Code Geass
Stand, which actually is the term in 'JoJo's Bizarre Adventure' (1987) not Code Geass
context: Lelouch's Geass works only once per person and only at eye contact range. *Code Geass*'s political and military plotting — with multiple high-stakes deceptions and strategic gambits — gave it strong appeal beyond the standard mecha genre. The series's twin protagonist structure (Lelouch and Kallen vs. Suzaku) made it widely discussed.

question: *Captain Tsubasa* (1981) — Yoichi Takahashi's manga about Tsubasa Ozora and his pursuit of soccer (football) excellence — has been credited with significantly influencing the next generation of Japanese soccer players, including Hidetoshi Nakata and Shinji Kagawa. When did it begin?
answer: 1981, in 'Weekly Shonen Jump', running until 1988 in its original arc
choices: 1981, in 'Weekly Shonen Jump', running until 1988 in its original arc
1975, in 'Weekly Shonen Sunday', much earlier than the actual debut
1992, in 'Weekly Shonen Jump', much later than the actual debut
1985, in 'Weekly Shonen Magazine', a different publication entirely
context: *Captain Tsubasa* has been credited with helping seed the late-1990s and 2000s explosion of Japanese soccer talent in European clubs. Many Japanese players have cited reading the manga as kids. The 1983-86 anime adaptation, and many subsequent anime series (1990, 1994, 2018), have continued the franchise. Takahashi continues drawing new material into the 2020s.

question: *Inuyasha* (1996-2008) — Rumiko Takahashi's long-running manga about a modern Japanese schoolgirl Kagome Higurashi who falls through a well into Sengoku-era Japan — was Takahashi's longest single manga (56 volumes). Who was Inuyasha?
answer: A half-demon (half-yokai) with silver hair, dog ears, and a powerful sword called Tessaiga
choices: A half-demon (half-yokai) with silver hair, dog ears, and a powerful sword called Tessaiga
Kagome's modern Japanese boyfriend who falls through the well with her
A fully-human Sengoku-era warrior with no demonic heritage at all
A spirit-priest from a Buddhist temple in the modern day
context: Inuyasha's complex half-demon ancestry (human mother, dog-yokai father) gave the series its central character framework. Takahashi had previously created *Urusei Yatsura* (1978), *Maison Ikkoku* (1980), and *Ranma 1/2* (1987); she remains one of the bestselling manga artists ever, with over 200 million copies sold worldwide.

question: *Ranma 1/2* (1987-96) — Rumiko Takahashi's gender-bending martial-arts gag manga — featured Ranma Saotome, a teenage martial artist who turns into a girl when splashed with cold water and back into a boy when splashed with hot. When was it serialized?
answer: 1987 to 1996 in 'Weekly Shonen Sunday', overlapping with Takahashi's 'Urusei Yatsura' early years
choices: 1987 to 1996 in 'Weekly Shonen Sunday', overlapping with Takahashi's 'Urusei Yatsura' early years
1978 to 1987 — actually the years of 'Urusei Yatsura', not 'Ranma 1/2'
1980 to 1987 — actually the years of 'Maison Ikkoku', not 'Ranma 1/2'
1996 to 2008 — actually the years of 'Inuyasha', not 'Ranma 1/2'
context: *Ranma 1/2*'s anime adaptation (1989-92) was widely popular both in Japan and on early American anime distribution (Viz Media released subtitled videos in the early 1990s). The series's gender-fluidity, comedic martial-arts combat, and large supporting cast made it a fan favorite. Takahashi continues drawing into the 2020s.

question: Studio Ghibli's *Only Yesterday* (1991), directed by Isao Takahata, was a slice-of-life film about a 27-year-old Tokyo office worker named Taeko who visits her sister's family in the countryside, and reflects on her childhood self in flashbacks. The film deliberately took an adult drama approach. What was its commercial reception?
answer: Strong in Japan as the year's #1 grossing domestic film, modest in international release
choices: Strong in Japan as the year's #1 grossing domestic film, modest in international release
Universally panned in Japan and pulled from theaters within two weeks
Restricted to art-house theaters in Japan with no major distribution
Banned in Japan due to controversial content about menstruation cycles
context: *Only Yesterday* was originally not released in the United States for over twenty years due to a Disney distribution dispute about a brief scene discussing menstruation. The film was finally released in North America by GKIDS in 2016 — 25 years after its 1991 Japanese release. Takahata's slow, contemplative style is on full display in this film.

question: *Naruto*'s first major tournament-style arc was the Chunin Exams in the original manga (chapters 35-138, 2000-02). The arc introduced multiple foreign-village ninja teams, the Sound Village's Orochimaru, and the curse mark on Sasuke. What three-stage structure did the Chunin Exams use?
answer: Written exam, Forest of Death (survival test), and one-on-one tournament finals
choices: Written exam, Forest of Death (survival test), and one-on-one tournament finals
Three rounds of one-on-one tournament finals with no written or survival components
Written exam, oral exam, and a final dissertation on shinobi history and lore
Survival test, written exam, and team-vs-team three-versus-three combat round only
context: The three-stage Chunin Exam framework became one of *Naruto*'s most-celebrated arcs. The Forest of Death (Stage 2) and the one-on-one tournament finals (Stage 3, with Naruto vs. Neji and Naruto vs. Gaara) were animated in the original *Naruto* TV anime from 2002-04. The arc's impact has been compared to the Hunter Exam of *Hunter x Hunter*.

question: *Kid Icarus* (1986 Japan, 1987 US) — Nintendo's NES Greek-mythology platformer — was developed by the same Nintendo R&D1 team that made *Metroid* (1986). The character of Pit (the angel-archer protagonist) became dormant for decades before returning. When did Pit appear in *Super Smash Bros.*?
answer: Brawl (2008), Pit's first major appearance since 'Kid Icarus' (1986)
choices: Brawl (2008), Pit's first major appearance since 'Kid Icarus' (1986)
Original Smash 64 (1999), Pit was actually not in the original 1999 game
Melee (2001), Pit was actually not in the GameCube 2001 game
Ultimate (2018), Pit was actually added a decade earlier than this
context: Pit's Brawl appearance was widely cheered by long-time Nintendo fans. *Kid Icarus: Uprising* (2012) on Nintendo 3DS — directed by Masahiro Sakurai — was the franchise's revival; the game's flight-and-rail-shooter mechanics were unusual for the franchise but well-received. The 3DS title sold strongly in Japan and the West.

question: *Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!* (1987) — the NES home version of Nintendo's earlier arcade boxing game — used real Mike Tyson as the final boxing opponent named after him. The licensing agreement was finite. When did the Tyson likeness leave the game?
answer: 1990, when Tyson's image was replaced by 'Mr. Dream' in 'Punch-Out!!' re-releases
choices: 1990, when Tyson's image was replaced by 'Mr. Dream' in 'Punch-Out!!' re-releases
1988, just a year after the game's release
1996, after Tyson's much-later return to boxing championships
2002, when Tyson's career was effectively over for the new boxing era
context: Tyson lost his 1987 license with Nintendo by losing the WBA Heavyweight Championship to Buster Douglas in February 1990. Nintendo's contract had been performance-tied; after Tyson's loss, Nintendo replaced his sprite with 'Mr. Dream' (an unrelated tan-skinned generic boxer). The Tyson-included original cartridges are now collectibles.

question: *Earthbound* (1995 US) — Nintendo's quirky RPG localization of *Mother 2* (1994 Japan, by APE/HAL Laboratory) — was developed by a small Nintendo Treehouse team and led by which Japanese designer?
answer: Shigesato Itoi, a famous Japanese copywriter and Nintendo collaborator
choices: Shigesato Itoi, a famous Japanese copywriter and Nintendo collaborator
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually was producer not director of Earthbound
Satoru Iwata, who actually was at HAL Laboratory but didn't design Earthbound
Hironobu Sakaguchi, who actually was at Squaresoft (Final Fantasy)
context: Itoi's *Mother* series was a deliberately offbeat reimagining of JRPG conventions — set in a small-town American setting (Onett, Twoson, Threed), with deliberately quirky enemies (cult members, alien-possessed objects, sentient piles of vomit). *Earthbound* sold poorly at retail in 1995; it became a cult classic on internet forums in the late 1990s and 2000s.

question: *Super Mario 64* (1996), Nintendo's revolutionary 3D platformer for the Nintendo 64, was the first major mainstream 3D platformer and helped define many subsequent 3D platforming conventions (analog camera control, full 3D movement). Who directed it?
answer: Shigeru Miyamoto and Yoshiaki Koizumi (latter as lead designer of camera)
choices: Shigeru Miyamoto and Yoshiaki Koizumi (latter as lead designer of camera)
Takashi Tezuka alone, who actually was more known for SNES Mario games
Yoshio Sakamoto, who actually was the Metroid franchise lead at Nintendo
Hideki Konno, who actually was the Mario Kart franchise lead at Nintendo
context: Koizumi's design of *Super Mario 64*'s analog camera control was a foundational 3D-platforming innovation. He would later direct *Super Mario Galaxy* (2007) and produce *Super Mario Odyssey* (2017). Miyamoto's *Super Mario 64* prototype was the most-anticipated game at E3 1995 and shipped with the Nintendo 64 launch in 1996.

question: *The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask* (2000) — the Nintendo 64 sequel to *Ocarina of Time* (1998) — used the same engine and assets to deliver a much darker game in only 18 months. It used a unique 3-day cycle mechanic. Who directed it?
answer: Eiji Aonuma, with Yoshiaki Koizumi as lead designer at Nintendo
choices: Eiji Aonuma, with Yoshiaki Koizumi as lead designer at Nintendo
Shigeru Miyamoto alone, who actually was producer not director
Takashi Tezuka, who actually directed earlier 2D Zelda titles only
Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who actually directed 'Breath of the Wild' (2017) much later
context: *Majora's Mask*'s parallel-Termina setting (the dark mirror of Hyrule) and 3-day apocalypse cycle gave it a unique tonal identity within the Zelda franchise. Koizumi's mask system — Link wearing masks to transform into a Deku Scrub, Goron, Zora — became one of the most-cited Zelda mechanics. The Expansion Pak was required for the N64 version.

question: *The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker* (2002), Nintendo's GameCube Zelda, was famous for its cel-shaded cartoon-style visual approach, which provoked widespread fan backlash when first announced. The fan disappointment fueled the so-called 'Zelda cycle' (initial fan rejection of changes, later embrace). Who directed it?
answer: Eiji Aonuma, with input from Yoshiaki Koizumi at Nintendo
choices: Eiji Aonuma, with input from Yoshiaki Koizumi at Nintendo
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually was producer not director
Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who actually directed later Zelda titles
Takashi Tezuka, who actually directed earlier Zelda titles only
context: *The Wind Waker*'s cel-shading was unprecedented in 2002 for a major Nintendo franchise. The visual approach is now widely cited as one of the most successful art-direction decisions in gaming. The 2013 *The Wind Waker HD* on Wii U was a remaster with smoothing of the original's mid-game pacing complaints.

question: *The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess* (2006) — released simultaneously for Nintendo Wii (with Wii Remote sword controls) and GameCube — was the Wii's launch-day pack-in Zelda for North America. Who directed it?
answer: Eiji Aonuma at Nintendo's EAD division, with development beginning in 2004
choices: Eiji Aonuma at Nintendo's EAD division, with development beginning in 2004
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually was producer not director
Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who actually directed 'Breath of the Wild' (2017)
Takashi Tezuka, who actually directed earlier Zelda titles only
context: *Twilight Princess* was originally a GameCube title; Nintendo announced the Wii version (with motion-control sword swinging) at E3 2005 to surprise. The game's darker tone — Link transforming into a wolf in the Twilight Realm — gave it a more adult feel than recent entries. It sold strongly on both Wii and GameCube.

question: *Metroid: Zero Mission* (2004) — Nintendo's Game Boy Advance remake of the 1986 NES *Metroid* — was an extended reimagining with new content (a long final section showing Samus escaping the planet without her Power Suit). Who directed it?
answer: Yoshio Sakamoto, the long-time Metroid director at Nintendo R&D1
choices: Yoshio Sakamoto, the long-time Metroid director at Nintendo R&D1
Yoshiaki Koizumi, who actually directed Mario games not Metroid
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually was a producer not director on most Metroid
Eiji Aonuma, who actually directed Zelda games not Metroid
context: Sakamoto's *Zero Mission* gave Samus's space-pirate-escape sequence a level of detail not present in the original 1986 *Metroid*. The Power Suit-less segment became a fan-favorite design moment. The game's compressed cartridge size on the GBA made significant graphical enhancements over the original NES game.

question: *Metroid Dread* (2021) — Nintendo Switch's first major Metroid game in many years — was developed by Spanish studio MercurySteam in collaboration with Nintendo. It had been in development hell for over a decade before its 2021 release. What was its original development title?
answer: *Metroid Dread* — the title was used during DS-era development (2005-09) before cancellation
choices: *Metroid Dread* — the title was used during DS-era development (2005-09) before cancellation
*Metroid Prime 4* — actually a separate Nintendo project announced years later
*Metroid: Federation Force* — actually a different 3DS multiplayer title in 2016
*Metroid: Samus Returns* — actually a 2017 3DS remake of 'Metroid II'
context: *Metroid Dread* had been planned for Nintendo DS as early as 2005-06 before being cancelled. The 2021 game retained the title and the 'EMMI' enemy-stalker concept from the early DS-era pitches. MercurySteam had previously developed *Metroid: Samus Returns* (2017) for Nintendo, building studio expertise on the franchise.

question: *Halo: Combat Evolved* (2001) — Bungie's flagship Xbox launch title — became the foundational console FPS of the 2000s. The game's lead level designer became one of the most-influential video-game directors of the era. Who?
answer: Jaime Griesemer, lead designer of single-player at Bungie
choices: Jaime Griesemer, lead designer of single-player at Bungie
John Romero, who actually was at id Software working on Doom 3
Cliff Bleszinski, who actually was at Epic Games working on Gears of War
Sid Meier, who actually was at MicroProse working on Civilization
context: Jaime Griesemer's *Halo* level design pioneered the 'thirty seconds of fun' concept — repeat-the-same-encounter-loop-with-variation gameplay. The Master Chief vs. Covenant story arc, the Halo ring concept, and the music (composed by Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori) all combined to make *Halo: CE* the killer app for the original Xbox.

question: *Gears of War* (2006), Epic Games's launch title for Xbox 360, used a then-new game engine that Epic licensed widely. The engine became one of the most-used game engines of the late 2000s and 2010s. What is it called?
answer: Unreal Engine 3, with Mark Rein as Epic's licensing executive
choices: Unreal Engine 3, with Mark Rein as Epic's licensing executive
Source Engine 2, which actually is Valve's engine (Half-Life series)
CryEngine 3, which actually is Crytek's engine (Crysis series)
id Tech 4, which actually is id Software's engine (Doom 3, Quake 4)
context: Unreal Engine 3 powered hundreds of games across the late 2000s and 2010s, from *Gears of War* itself to *BioShock* (2007), *Mass Effect* (2007), *Borderlands* (2009), and many more. Epic's licensing model (a small per-unit fee for indies, larger flat fees for big studios) made it the most-popular Western game engine for that era.

question: *Super Smash Bros.* (1999), Nintendo's first cross-IP fighter on the N64, had a much smaller roster than later entries. How many playable characters did the original 1999 N64 game have?
answer: 12 characters — with 8 starters and 4 unlockables in the original 1999 game
choices: 12 characters — with 8 starters and 4 unlockables in the original 1999 game
26 characters — actually the number in 'Smash Bros. Melee' (2001)
39 characters — actually the number in 'Smash Bros. Brawl' (2008)
89 characters — actually the number in 'Smash Bros. Ultimate' (2018)
context: The 12 original characters: Mario, Donkey Kong, Link, Samus, Yoshi, Kirby, Fox, Pikachu (starters) + Captain Falcon, Luigi, Ness, Jigglypuff (unlockables). The cast has grown to 89 characters in *Smash Bros. Ultimate* (2018), including DLC additions. Sakurai has directed every Smash Bros. game since the 1999 original.

question: Bigfoot — the most-famous American cryptid — is associated primarily with the Pacific Northwest's old-growth forests of Oregon, Washington, and northern California. Bigfoot sightings are reported throughout North America but are most numerous in this region. What is the most-cited regional name for the cryptid?
answer: Sasquatch, an Anglicization of the Halkomelem 'sasq'ets'
choices: Sasquatch, an Anglicization of the Halkomelem 'sasq'ets'
Skookum, which actually is a Chinookan word for 'powerful spirit' (related but distinct)
Wendigo, which actually is the Algonquian cannibal-spirit (a different cryptid)
Skinwalker, which actually is the Navajo shapeshifter (a different cryptid)
context: 'Sasquatch' was popularized by journalist J.W. Burns in the 1920s, drawn from Halkomelem (Coast Salish) tradition. 'Bigfoot' came from 1958 Northern California construction crew accounts (later attributed to a hoaxer). Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples have many distinct traditional names for similar beings; outsider-collected names are often inaccurate.

question: The Patterson-Gimlin film's subject — the female-appearing figure walking through frame at Bluff Creek, October 1967 — has been nicknamed by Bigfoot researchers for the diminutive of one of the film-makers' names. What is the nickname?
answer: Patty, the diminutive of 'Patterson' (Roger Patterson, the film-maker)
choices: Patty, the diminutive of 'Patterson' (Roger Patterson, the film-maker)
Bobbie, the diminutive of 'Bob Gimlin' (the other film-maker)
Bluffy, named for Bluff Creek where the film was shot
Sasquatchy, a generic nickname applied to the female-Bigfoot footage subject
context: 'Patty' is the most-cited nickname among Bigfoot researchers. The subject's apparent female anatomical features (breasts in the gait analysis) suggested a female of the species in the cryptozoological framework. Skeptics have alleged the film shows a man in a costume; multiple costume-experts have come to opposite conclusions in different analyses over the decades.

question: The Loch Ness Monster has been most-cited as a plesiosaur — a Mesozoic-era long-necked aquatic reptile — by enthusiasts since at least the 1930s. What is the standard scientific objection to the plesiosaur hypothesis?
answer: Loch Ness is only ~10,000 years old (post-glacial), too young for relict plesiosaurs
choices: Loch Ness is only ~10,000 years old (post-glacial), too young for relict plesiosaurs
Plesiosaurs were actually shorter than reported sightings suggest
Plesiosaurs could not survive in cold freshwater lakes anywhere in the world
Plesiosaurs are clearly visible in fossil record; Nessie is not
context: Loch Ness was carved by glaciers ~10,000 years ago after the last Ice Age. Plesiosaurs became extinct ~66 million years ago at the K-Pg boundary. A surviving plesiosaur population would require either pre-glacial-loch survival (geologically impossible) or relatively recent introduction (also implausible). The plesiosaur hypothesis remains popular among believers despite the timing problem.

question: *The Mothman Prophecies* (1975), John Keel's book about the Point Pleasant, West Virginia, sightings of 1966-67, became the founding text of Mothman lore. Keel's framework treated the sightings as part of a broader 'paranormal' phenomenon. What 2002 film adapted the book?
answer: *The Mothman Prophecies* (2002), starring Richard Gere as a reporter investigating
choices: *The Mothman Prophecies* (2002), starring Richard Gere as a reporter investigating
*Mothman* (1996), an unrelated TV-movie that came before Keel's adaptation
*The Mothman Curse* (2014), an unrelated documentary not directly based on Keel
*Behold the Mothman* (2010), an unrelated low-budget independent horror film
context: *The Mothman Prophecies* (2002) directed by Mark Pellington starred Richard Gere, Laura Linney, and Debra Messing. The film was a loose adaptation — Gere's reporter character investigates the Silver Bridge collapse and Mothman sightings together. Keel's actual book has more paranormal-research framework than the film's psychological-horror approach.

question: Skinwalker Ranch — the 512-acre property in Uintah County, Utah, that has become associated with UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and Navajo skinwalker reports — was purchased in 1994 by a family who would later sell to billionaire Robert Bigelow in 1996. Who was the first family?
answer: The Sherman family, who experienced unexplained events and sold to Bigelow for relief
choices: The Sherman family, who experienced unexplained events and sold to Bigelow for relief
The Bigelow family, who owned the ranch from inception (which is false)
The Brigham Young family, who owned much Utah ranchland historically
The Navajo Nation tribal council, who owned the ranch before Sherman
context: Terry and Gwen Sherman lived on the ranch from 1994 to 1996. They reported strange lights, cattle mutilations, and other phenomena. Bigelow's National Institute for Discovery Science (NIDS) studied the ranch from 1996. The History Channel's *The Secret of Skinwalker Ranch* (2020-onward) has continued the public investigation.

question: The Sherman family — the original 1994-96 owners of what later became Skinwalker Ranch — experienced a particular kind of livestock loss that has become central to ranch lore. What kind?
answer: Cattle mutilations, with strange surgical-style removals of specific organs
choices: Cattle mutilations, with strange surgical-style removals of specific organs
Sheep poisonings, with no other animals affected on the ranch property
Chicken disappearances, with feathers but no bodies remaining behind
Horse stampedes that destroyed fencing without obvious cause or external pressure
context: Cattle mutilations have been reported on multiple American ranches since the 1960s, with debates over coyote attacks, natural decay artifacts, scavenger surgical-style work, and other proposed causes. The Sherman family's specific accounts described the disappearances as nearly instantaneous and impossible — explanations that researchers have continued to investigate without consensus.

question: The Dyatlov Pass victims' bodies were found in unusual condition, with details that have fueled speculation for decades. Three of the bodies had severe internal injuries (broken ribs, fractured skulls) without significant external trauma. What additional detail has been most-cited?
answer: Lyudmila Dubinina's tongue was missing (likely scavenger-related per modern medical analysis)
choices: Lyudmila Dubinina's tongue was missing (likely scavenger-related per modern medical analysis)
All nine bodies had no fingerprints (which was actually not reported in any autopsies)
Their eyes were missing (which actually was reported only of two of the nine)
Their tongues were all missing (which actually was reported only of one of the nine)
context: Lyudmila Dubinina's missing tongue, lips, and eye tissue have been cited in many sensationalist accounts as evidence of foul play. Modern forensic analysis suggests scavenger animal activity on the partially-submerged bodies during the weeks between deaths and discovery. Other injuries (broken ribs, etc.) are consistent with the 2021 avalanche-slab model.

question: Atlantis — the legendary submerged civilization first described in writing by Plato in two of his dialogues — has become one of the most-cited 'lost civilization' archetypes. Which two Platonic dialogues introduce Atlantis?
answer: *Timaeus* and *Critias*, both written around 360 BC
choices: *Timaeus* and *Critias*, both written around 360 BC
*Republic* (the Cave allegory) and *Phaedo* (Socrates's death)
*Symposium* and *Phaedrus* (the Eros dialogues)
*Meno* and *Theaetetus* (the knowledge dialogues)
context: Plato's *Timaeus* mentions Atlantis briefly; *Critias* (unfinished) gives the most detail. The text describes Atlantis as a powerful empire from 9,000 years before Plato's time (i.e., ~9,400 BC). Modern scholars treat Atlantis as a Platonic literary device rather than a real history. The myth has been variously attached to the Minoan civilization, the Azores, the Bahamas, and other actual places by enthusiasts.

question: The Hollow Earth theory — the long-running pseudoscientific claim that the Earth contains a habitable interior — has been associated with Admiral Richard E. Byrd via a widely-circulated but disputed 'diary' allegedly found after his 1957 death. What did the supposed diary claim?
answer: That Byrd had flown into the Earth's interior via an opening at the North Pole
choices: That Byrd had flown into the Earth's interior via an opening at the North Pole
That Byrd had encountered Nazis at the South Pole during Operation Highjump
That Byrd had found ancient temples beneath the Antarctic ice cap
That Byrd had been abducted by aliens during his Antarctic missions
context: Byrd's 'secret diary' first appeared in print in the 1970s, well after his 1957 death. No academic historian has authenticated the document; Byrd's actual diaries (in the Ohio State Archive) contain nothing of the kind. The Hollow Earth theory predates Byrd; John Cleves Symmes Jr. proposed it in 1818 and lobbied Congress for an expedition through the supposed polar opening.

question: The skookum — a Pacific Northwest cryptid distinct from Bigfoot/Sasquatch and sometimes paired with it in regional folklore — comes from a Chinookan term. In Chinook trade-jargon, 'skookum' means what?
answer: 'Strong' or 'powerful' (used as both an adjective and a noun for a powerful spirit)
choices: 'Strong' or 'powerful' (used as both an adjective and a noun for a powerful spirit)
'Tall' or 'high' (used specifically for tall figures or hills)
'Hidden' or 'invisible' (used for things that cannot normally be seen)
'Forest' or 'tree-dwelling' (used specifically for forest spirits)
context: Chinook Jargon was a trade language used throughout the Pacific Northwest from the 18th to 20th centuries. 'Skookum' came from Chinook tradition meaning roughly 'powerful' or 'strong'. The skookum is sometimes distinct from Sasquatch in regional folklore; sometimes they are treated as related. The Skookum cast (2000) of a Bigfoot-like body imprint became briefly famous in cryptozoology circles.

question: Chris Claremont's *Uncanny X-Men* (1975-91) had multiple long-term artist collaborators. The most-celebrated of these came onto the title with issue #108 (December 1977) and stayed until issue #143 (March 1981). Who?
answer: John Byrne, who also did the Dark Phoenix Saga (#129-137) with Claremont
choices: John Byrne, who also did the Dark Phoenix Saga (#129-137) with Claremont
Frank Miller, who actually did Daredevil (1979-83) not X-Men
Marc Silvestri, who actually came onto X-Men years later (mid-1980s)
Jim Lee, who actually came onto X-Men years later (1990 onwards)
context: Byrne's pencils on the Dark Phoenix Saga (1980) became the definitive 'late-70s X-Men' look. Byrne and Claremont fell out over creative differences in the early 1980s; Byrne left to write and draw *Fantastic Four* (1981-86) at Marvel and *Superman* (1986 post-Crisis) at DC. The Claremont-Byrne partnership remains one of comics' most-celebrated.

question: *Preacher* (1995-2000, Vertigo), Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon's 66-issue maxi-series, followed a Texas preacher named Jesse Custer on a road trip with two companions. Who were the companions?
answer: Tulip O'Hare (Jesse's girlfriend, a hitwoman) and Cassidy (an Irish vampire)
choices: Tulip O'Hare (Jesse's girlfriend, a hitwoman) and Cassidy (an Irish vampire)
Sookie Stackhouse and Bill Compton (characters from a different series)
Buffy Summers and Spike (characters from a different series)
Selene and Kraven (characters from a different vampire series)
context: Tulip's hitwoman backstory and Cassidy's Irish-vampire identity gave *Preacher* its core trio. The series's road-trip-across-America framework let Ennis and Dillon explore American culture from an outsider Anglo-Irish perspective. The 2016-19 AMC TV adaptation by Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg adapted the series with significant changes.

question: *The Sandman* (Vertigo, 1989-96) had multiple artists across its 75-issue run. The 'Kindly Ones' arc (#57-69, 1995-96) — Sandman's penultimate major story — featured the work of a single artist whose distinctive woodcut-style aesthetic became central to the arc. Who?
answer: Marc Hempel, with a heavily stylized post-Cubist woodcut-style approach
choices: Marc Hempel, with a heavily stylized post-Cubist woodcut-style approach
Sam Kieth, who actually drew only the first five issues of Sandman (1989)
P. Craig Russell, who actually drew the 'Wake' final arc (#70-75) instead
Mike Dringenberg, who actually drew the early issues (#1-15) of Sandman
context: Hempel's *Kindly Ones* art was a deliberate departure from the more naturalistic art of earlier Sandman arcs. Many readers found Hempel's style off-putting; others have come to consider his work the perfect choice for the arc's mythic-fairy-tale tone. The arc's plot draws heavily on Greek tragedy and the Furies.

question: John Constantine — the magician-occult-detective of Vertigo Comics — was created by Alan Moore in *Saga of the Swamp Thing* #37 (June 1985). The character was reportedly inspired by which musician's appearance?
answer: Sting (Gordon Sumner) of The Police, whose haircut/look provided the visual model
choices: Sting (Gordon Sumner) of The Police, whose haircut/look provided the visual model
David Bowie, who actually was the visual model for many comic-book characters but not Constantine
Mick Jagger, who actually was the visual model for some Marvel comic characters but not Constantine
John Lennon, who actually was not a visual model for Constantine specifically
context: Moore has confirmed in multiple interviews that Sting's late-1970s/early-1980s Police-era look (sandy blonde hair, sharp features, trenchcoat) was Constantine's visual template. Constantine got his own ongoing series *Hellblazer* (1988-2013, Vertigo), the longest-running Vertigo title — 300 issues plus annuals over a 25-year run.

question: Fritz Leiber's *Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser* stories ran for fifty years (1939-1988). The two characters were created in college letters between Leiber and a friend in the early 1930s. Who was Leiber's co-creator friend?
answer: Harry Otto Fischer, with whom Leiber co-created the duo in 1934 correspondence
choices: Harry Otto Fischer, with whom Leiber co-created the duo in 1934 correspondence
Robert E. Howard, who actually was the Conan creator and a contemporary
H.P. Lovecraft, who actually was a Leiber correspondent but not Fafhrd's co-creator
Clark Ashton Smith, who actually was another Weird Tales contemporary
context: Fischer wrote the original outlines of Fafhrd (Leiber's character) and the Gray Mouser (Fischer's character) in 1934 college letters. Leiber published the first stories from 1939 onward; Fischer did not pursue a writing career. Leiber dedicated *The Swords of Lankhmar* (1968) to Fischer, who lived until 1986.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Pellucidar series — set in a hollow-earth-like 'inner world' where time-keeping is irrelevant because of an eternal sun and where prehistoric creatures (mammoths, sabertooth tigers, dinosaurs) coexist — was published starting in 1914. What was the first novel?
answer: *At the Earth's Core* (1914), in which David Innes drills through the crust
choices: *At the Earth's Core* (1914), in which David Innes drills through the crust
*Pellucidar* (1923), which actually is the second Pellucidar novel
*Tarzan at the Earth's Core* (1929), which actually is a Tarzan crossover into Pellucidar
*Land of Terror* (1944), which actually is a much-later Pellucidar novel
context: Burroughs wrote seven Pellucidar novels (1914-44), including the Tarzan crossover *Tarzan at the Earth's Core* (1929). The inner-world setting allowed Burroughs to combine prehistoric-creature adventure with science-fantasy framework. The 1976 film *At the Earth's Core* (Doug McClure) was a minor adaptation.

question: Mike Mignola's *Hellboy* (Dark Horse, 1993-onward) spawned an entire 'Mignolaverse' of related comics and characters. The first major spinoff series was launched in 2002 and focused on Hellboy's American supernatural-investigation organization. What is the spinoff called?
answer: *B.P.R.D.* (Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense)
choices: *B.P.R.D.* (Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense)
*Lobster Johnson*, which actually came later as a separate Mignolaverse spinoff
*Sledgehammer 44*, which actually came later as a separate Mignolaverse spinoff
*Witchfinder*, which actually came later as a separate Mignolaverse spinoff
context: *B.P.R.D.* (2002-onward) became one of Dark Horse's longest-running titles, with John Arcudi and Mignola as primary writers. The Mignolaverse has grown to include *Lobster Johnson*, *Witchfinder*, *Abe Sapien*, *Sledgehammer 44*, *Frankenstein Underground*, and many more series — all sharing characters and overall continuity.

question: *The Strategic Review* — the TSR newsletter that preceded *Dragon Magazine* — ran for seven issues from spring 1975 to spring 1976. Its successor *The Dragon* (later *Dragon Magazine*) began publication in June 1976 with issue #1 sharing a notable feature. What was on the cover of *Dragon* #1?
answer: A barbarian and a dragon by William Hannan, with the title 'The Dragon'
choices: A barbarian and a dragon by William Hannan, with the title 'The Dragon'
A wizard and a tower by Tom Wham, who actually did later Dragon covers
A unicorn and a maiden by Larry Elmore, who actually did much-later Dragon covers
An adventurer-party in a dungeon by Erol Otus, who actually did later Dragon covers
context: *The Dragon* #1 was 32 pages, edited by Tim Kask. The magazine became one of the longest-running gaming magazines in history (35 years, ending 2007). Many TSR designers and writers contributed throughout the years: Gygax, Mentzer, Cook, Mohan, Greenwood, Hickman, Salvatore, and dozens more.

question: The Mystara setting (the 'Known World' of the 1981 Basic and Expert D&D Boxed Sets) was officially detailed by TSR throughout the 1980s. Its core continent featured a recurring set of nations frequently used in Basic D&D modules. Which is the most-prominent nation?
answer: Karameikos (a Slavic-themed grand duchy ruled by Stefan Karameikos III)
choices: Karameikos (a Slavic-themed grand duchy ruled by Stefan Karameikos III)
Cormyr, which actually is a Forgotten Realms nation not Mystara
Damara, which actually is a Forgotten Realms nation not Mystara
Krynn, which actually is a Dragonlance setting nation not Mystara
context: Karameikos was the 'starter' nation in Basic D&D — Mike Carr's B1, Gygax's B2, etc. were typically set in the Grand Duchy. Other Mystara/Known World nations: the Republic of Darokin (mercantile democracy), the Empire of Thyatis (Roman-influenced), the Empire of Alphatia (magic-state), the Five Shires (halfling refuge), and many more.

question: *Oriental Adventures* (1985) — TSR's first major non-European-fantasy D&D supplement — added new character classes (samurai, ninja, kensai, sohei) and a Japanese-influenced campaign setting called Kara-Tur. Who designed it?
answer: David 'Zeb' Cook, with extensive research consulting from Gary Gygax
choices: David 'Zeb' Cook, with extensive research consulting from Gary Gygax
Gary Gygax alone, who actually had been ousted from TSR in October 1985
Tracy Hickman, who actually was working on Dragonlance through 1985
Ed Greenwood, who actually was just licensing Forgotten Realms by 1985
context: Cook's *Oriental Adventures* was set on the Kara-Tur subcontinent of Toril (the Forgotten Realms world). The book's blending of Japanese, Chinese, and Southeast Asian fantasy archetypes — while popular at release — has been criticized in modern retrospectives for its conflation of Asian cultures into a single fantasy framework. The Kara-Tur Campaign Set followed in 1988.

question: *Al-Qadim* (1992) — TSR's 'Arabian Adventures' campaign setting for AD&D 2e — was set on Zakhara, a continent of the world of Toril (the Forgotten Realms world). The setting drew on 'One Thousand and One Nights' / 'Arabian Nights' framing. Who designed it?
answer: Jeff Grubb (designer) and Andria Hayday (lead writer)
choices: Jeff Grubb (designer) and Andria Hayday (lead writer)
Tracy Hickman, who actually had moved on to novel-writing by 1992
David Cook, who actually was working on Planescape (1994) by 1992
Ed Greenwood, who actually was producing more Forgotten Realms material
context: Grubb's *Al-Qadim* introduced new classes (the corsair, the matrud, the holy slayer) and a magic system based on enchanted lamps and djinn-binding. The setting was popular through three years of supplements (1992-95) but did not enjoy the same enduring fame as Forgotten Realms or Greyhawk. The 2014 D&D 5e *Sword Coast Adventurer's Guide* nodded back to Al-Qadim in some passages.

question: *Maztica* (1991) — TSR's Aztec-and-Maya-influenced campaign setting for AD&D 2e — was set on a continent of Toril (the Forgotten Realms world) reached from Faerun by sea. The setting drew heavily on pre-Columbian Mesoamerican history and mythology. Who designed it?
answer: Douglas Niles, with extensive consultation on Mesoamerican history
choices: Douglas Niles, with extensive consultation on Mesoamerican history
Tracy Hickman, who actually was writing Dragonlance novels by 1991
David Cook, who actually was working on Planescape (1994) by 1991
Ed Greenwood, who actually was producing more Forgotten Realms material
context: Niles's *Maztica* (1991) included three novels (the *Maztica Trilogy*: *Ironhelm*, *Viperhand*, *Feathered Dragon*) and an 'Empires of the Sands' boxed set. The setting was popular but did not see major D&D supplement continuation; in 2017's D&D 5e *Tomb of Annihilation* hardcover, references to Maztica continued the lore.

question: *Birthright* (1995) — TSR's most-political AD&D 2e campaign setting — gave each player character access to 'bloodline' powers inherited from divine ancestors, and made domain rulership a central player activity. Players ran kingdoms, not just dungeon-delving parties. Who designed it?
answer: Rich Baker and Colin McComb, with editorial input from various TSR staff
choices: Rich Baker and Colin McComb, with editorial input from various TSR staff
Gary Gygax, who actually had been ousted from TSR ten years earlier
Tracy Hickman, who actually was writing Dragonlance novels by 1995
Ed Greenwood, who actually was producing more Forgotten Realms material
context: Baker's *Birthright* was an explicitly different play-mode from dungeon-delving — players engaged in domain politics, diplomatic intrigue, and inheritance disputes. The setting was popular in design conversations but did not sell well at retail. *Birthright* has not had a 5e revival, though many of its mechanical ideas have appeared elsewhere.

question: BECMI's *Immortals Set* (1986) — the fifth and most rules-revolutionary box of the Mentzer-era D&D — let characters ascend beyond level 36 to become divine 'Immortals'. Who designed it?
answer: Frank Mentzer, who also edited the earlier BECMI boxes (Basic through Master)
choices: Frank Mentzer, who also edited the earlier BECMI boxes (Basic through Master)
Gary Gygax, who actually had been ousted from TSR by 1986
Tracy Hickman, who actually was writing Dragonlance novels by 1986
David Cook, who actually was working on AD&D 2e (1989) by 1986
context: The Immortals Set's rules for divine play were unusual: players could create their own demigod-level characters. The Immortals-tier campaign setting was set 'above' the standard Mystara world; the Set introduced 'Hierarches' (the gods of the gods). The Set was difficult to play in practice and remains the most-niche of the BECMI boxes.

question: Fritz Leiber's literary city of Lankhmar — the home of his Fafhrd and Gray Mouser characters — became an officially-licensed D&D setting in 1985. TSR's *Lankhmar: City of Adventure* boxed set included full city maps, NPC stats, and adventure hooks. What unique licensing arrangement applied?
answer: Leiber consulted and the agreement included royalty splits, but Leiber wrote no game material
choices: Leiber consulted and the agreement included royalty splits, but Leiber wrote no game material
Leiber wrote all the modules himself with TSR providing only editorial support
TSR designed the Lankhmar material independently without any Leiber consultation
Leiber sold the Lankhmar IP outright to TSR for a one-time payment with no royalties
context: Bruce Nesmith and Doug Niles designed the original Lankhmar set. Leiber's consultations gave the supplements his blessing. Leiber (1910-1992) was already in his 70s during the TSR collaboration. The 1985 set was followed by Lankhmar adventure modules (CM3, CM4) and a 1990s Fafhrd-and-Mouser game from Pinnacle.

question: *Eberron* (2004) — D&D 3.5e's most-original 2000s campaign setting — was the winning entry in a Wizards of the Coast 'Fantasy Setting Search' contest (2002-03). The setting introduced the concept of magical-industrial 'magic-as-technology' in a quasi-1920s-pulp fantasy aesthetic. Who created it?
answer: Keith Baker, then a freelance game designer in Seattle
choices: Keith Baker, then a freelance game designer in Seattle
Gary Gygax, who actually had no involvement with Eberron at any time
Ed Greenwood, who actually created the rival Forgotten Realms setting
Bruce Cordell, who actually was a Wizards staff designer on different projects
context: Baker's *Eberron Campaign Setting* (2004) introduced lightning rail networks, airships powered by elemental bindings, the Last War (a continent-spanning recent war), and the artificer character class. The setting has continued through 4e, 5e, and into D&D Beyond's modern adventures.

question: Psionics — D&D's psychic-power system, distinct from arcane and divine magic — was introduced in *Supplement III: Eldritch Wizardry* (1976). The system was designed to add a 'mental discipline' framework for D&D characters. Who authored *Eldritch Wizardry*?
answer: Gary Gygax and Brian Blume, with playtesting by Tim Kask and others
choices: Gary Gygax and Brian Blume, with playtesting by Tim Kask and others
Tracy Hickman, who actually had no involvement (he joined TSR years later)
David Cook, who actually was a 1980s TSR designer not on Eldritch Wizardry
Frank Mentzer, who actually joined TSR years after Eldritch Wizardry's publication
context: Gygax and Blume's psionics system was complex and not widely embraced by early D&D players. It was simplified in AD&D 1e *Player's Handbook* (1978) Appendix. AD&D 2e (1989) initially omitted psionics, then re-added them in the *Complete Psionics Handbook* (1991). The system has remained a periodic D&D addition through 5e.

question: *Monster Manual II* (1983) — the second AD&D 1e hardcover monster book — added many monsters not in the original 1977 Monster Manual. The book contributed many classic D&D creatures (the umberlee, the death dog, the morkoth, the slaad variations). Who wrote it?
answer: Gary Gygax, the author of the original Monster Manual (1977)
choices: Gary Gygax, the author of the original Monster Manual (1977)
Tracy Hickman, who actually was working on Ravenloft (1983) instead
David Cook, who actually was working on Oriental Adventures (1985)
Frank Mentzer, who actually was editing the BECMI Basic Sets
context: Gygax's *Monster Manual II* was one of his last major TSR products before his 1985 ouster. The book featured many of the era's most-cited monster designs (the displacer beast subspecies, the umber hulk variants, the slaad varieties). The book was discontinued in 2e (most monsters moved to the AD&D 2e *Monstrous Compendium*).

question: *Fiend Folio* (1981) — the first AD&D Monster Manual sequel — was a TSR-UK publication compiled by Don Turnbull. The book introduced many monsters that became D&D staples (the githyanki, githzerai, drow variants, death knight, beholders' variants). Why was it controversial?
answer: Some of its monsters were submitted from White Dwarf magazine readers, with mixed quality
choices: Some of its monsters were submitted from White Dwarf magazine readers, with mixed quality
It was the first major D&D book published outside TSR's Wisconsin offices
Gary Gygax disapproved of UK editorial input and prevented its US distribution
It introduced the Cthulhu Mythos to D&D for the first time, controversially
context: *Fiend Folio* compiled monsters originally submitted to White Dwarf magazine's 'Fiend Factory' column (1977-79). Quality was uneven; some monsters were memorably bizarre (the apparition, the gambado, the screaming devilkin), others became classic. Gygax did approve the book but reportedly preferred his own *Monster Manual II* (1983). Charles Stross was a key designer-contributor.

question: *Spelljammer* (1989) — TSR's D&D-in-space campaign setting — introduced a particularly disturbing race of intelligent spider-eel hybrid slavers called the neogi. The neogi's social structure is unusual. What was it?
answer: Adult neogi grow as 'larval umber hulks' implanted in larger members of their species
choices: Adult neogi grow as 'larval umber hulks' implanted in larger members of their species
Adult neogi are entirely male, with females being slaughtered at birth in their culture
Adult neogi cannot speak; all neogi communication is through telepathy alone
Adult neogi are blind from hatching and use sonar to navigate their environment
context: Neogi reproduction reportedly involves implanting larval umber hulks in the bodies of larger neogi adults — a horrifying scenario that became a recurring Spelljammer-Underdark crossover. The neogi's slaver-trader caste was an antagonist in many published modules. The 2022 Spelljammer 5e revival reintroduced the neogi alongside the giff.

question: Atari's *Pong* (1972) prototype was installed at a single bar in Sunnyvale, California in August 1972 to test public reception. The cabinet jammed with coins within days. What was the bar?
answer: Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, where the prototype filled with quarters
choices: Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, where the prototype filled with quarters
Cyrano's Bar in Berkeley, where many other early Atari tests were run
The Lazy J Saloon in Mountain View, near Atari's Sunnyvale offices
The Brass Rail in San Jose, where the rejected Computer Space had failed
context: Andy Capp's prototype was Atari's first commercial Pong placement. The cabinet jammed because the coin-mechanism design used by Allan Alcorn could not handle the volume of quarters. Atari's commercial Pong launch followed in late 1972; the company shipped 8,000 cabinets within a year.

question: *Altered Beast* (1988) — Sega's Genesis launch title in North America and Japan — was a hack-and-slash arcade game ported to Genesis as the system's pack-in. The game features a Greek warrior resurrected by Zeus to rescue Athena from the underworld. What was the iconic opening phrase?
answer: 'Rise from your grave!' — Zeus's command to resurrect the protagonist
choices: 'Rise from your grave!' — Zeus's command to resurrect the protagonist
'You must defeat my master!' — Athena's plea from the underworld
'I have returned!' — the warrior's first words after resurrection
'Where is Athena?' — the warrior's first question to Zeus
context: *Altered Beast*'s digitized speech samples were rare for Genesis-era games. The 'Rise from your grave!' line became iconic. *Altered Beast* was replaced by *Sonic the Hedgehog* (1991) as the Genesis pack-in title in late 1991 — a savvy marketing move that gave Sonic an immediate mass-market presence.

question: *Streets of Rage 2* (1992), Sega's Genesis beat-'em-up, is widely cited as one of the best beat-'em-ups ever made. Yuzo Koshiro's score — particularly 'Go Straight' — became a defining Genesis-era music track. Who programmed the soundtrack engine?
answer: Yuzo Koshiro himself, using his own custom MUCOM-88 sound driver for Genesis
choices: Yuzo Koshiro himself, using his own custom MUCOM-88 sound driver for Genesis
Tomohiro Nishikado, who actually was at Taito (Space Invaders, 1978)
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually was at Nintendo at the time
Hideaki Anno, who actually was an anime director not a game programmer
context: Koshiro's MUCOM-88 sound driver (originally developed for NEC PC-88 home computers) was ported to Sega Genesis hardware for *Streets of Rage*. The driver wrung more sound out of the Yamaha YM2612 FM synthesis chip than other contemporary Genesis games. Koshiro went on to score many more Sega games and remains active into the 2020s.

question: *Joust* (1982) — Williams's medieval bird-mounted-knight arcade game — uniquely required players to repeatedly press a flap-button to keep their ostrich/stork airborne. The game's design influenced later 'flap-to-fly' games for decades. Who designed it?
answer: John Newcomer, with sound design by Sam Dicker at Williams Electronics
choices: John Newcomer, with sound design by Sam Dicker at Williams Electronics
Eugene Jarvis, who actually designed 'Defender' (1981) at the same studio
Larry DeMar, Jarvis's longtime partner who actually worked on 'Robotron' (1982)
Bill Pfutzenreuter, who actually worked on 'Sinistar' (1983) at Williams
context: Newcomer's *Joust* allowed two-player simultaneous play with friendly-fire — players could fight each other or cooperate. The game's pterodactyl boss creature was famously dangerous. Newcomer left Williams in 1983; *Joust* remained a Williams classic that spawned spinoffs and a 1986 NES port.

question: *Punch-Out!!* originated as a 1984 Nintendo arcade game with a two-monitor cabinet — one screen showing the opponent boxer, the other showing stats and the player's character (Little Mac). Who designed the original arcade version?
answer: Genyo Takeda, who would later design Nintendo's GameCube controller
choices: Genyo Takeda, who would later design Nintendo's GameCube controller
Shigeru Miyamoto, who actually designed Donkey Kong (1981) and Mario games
Hidetake Ishihara, who actually was at Sega working on different titles
Yu Suzuki, who actually was at Sega working on Out Run (1986)
context: Takeda joined Nintendo in 1972 and contributed to many of the company's foundational hardware and software designs. Beyond *Punch-Out!!*, he led the development of the Nintendo 64 controller, the GameCube controller's distinctive shape, and other major Nintendo hardware projects. He was at Nintendo for over 50 years.

question: Atari's *Asteroids* (1979) used vector graphics — drawing line-segment shapes directly with the electron beam rather than raster pixels. The game's score-display had a distinctive look. What was unique about the highest-score storage in the original arcade cabinet?
answer: Initials saved to a non-volatile RAM chip via a battery backup
choices: Initials saved to a non-volatile RAM chip via a battery backup
Initials stored only in volatile RAM, lost when the cabinet was powered off
Initials stored only in the operator's manual notebook, not in the game itself
Initials stored via punch-card mechanism on a paper roll printout
context: *Asteroids* was one of the first arcade games with battery-backed high-score saving — initials could persist across power cycles. The feature was a significant attraction for repeat-playing customers. The game's combination of vector graphics, simple controls (rotate, thrust, fire, hyperspace), and physics-based asteroid splitting made it Atari's biggest 1979 hit.

question: Nintendo's Wii Sports (2006) — bundled with the Wii at North American launch and many international launches — became the bestselling pack-in title in video game history. The collection included five distinct sports games. What were they?
answer: Tennis, Baseball, Bowling, Golf, and Boxing
choices: Tennis, Baseball, Bowling, Golf, and Boxing
Tennis, Baseball, Football, Basketball, and Boxing
Tennis, Football, Soccer, Basketball, and Hockey
Tennis, Bowling, Golf, Basketball, and Hockey
context: *Wii Sports* sold over 82 million copies, making it the bestselling video game ever (eventually surpassed by Minecraft). Its motion-control gameplay let non-gamers participate at family gatherings. Bowling — the most-cited family-favorite — became a kind of cultural shorthand for Wii's appeal. *Wii Sports Resort* (2009) added more sports to the franchise.

question: *Halo: Combat Evolved* (2001) introduced the iconic super-soldier protagonist Master Chief Petty Officer John-117. The character's helmet has remained sealed in nearly all official Halo media. Who has voiced him across the franchise?
answer: Steve Downes, with voice acting from 'Halo: Combat Evolved' (2001) onward
choices: Steve Downes, with voice acting from 'Halo: Combat Evolved' (2001) onward
Keith David, who actually voiced the Arbiter not Master Chief
Ron Perlman, who actually has had no Halo voice roles
Liam Neeson, who actually has had no Halo voice roles
context: Downes was a longtime Seattle DJ before joining the Halo cast. His voice work on Master Chief became iconic across the franchise. Bungie's 2010 *Halo: Reach* prequel and 343 Industries's 2012 *Halo 4* sequel both featured Downes. The 2022 Paramount+ *Halo* TV series controversially had Pablo Schreiber play and voice Master Chief instead.

question: *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater* (1999), Neversoft's PlayStation 1 skateboarding game, used real licensed bands for its soundtrack — including the Dead Kennedys's 'Police Truck' and Goldfinger's 'Superman'. What developer did Neversoft become after acquisition?
answer: Activision-owned, with the studio eventually absorbed into Infinity Ward (2014)
choices: Activision-owned, with the studio eventually absorbed into Infinity Ward (2014)

Ubisoft-owned (which actually never acquired Neversoft)
context: Activision acquired Neversoft in 1999, the same year *Tony Hawk's Pro Skater* launched. The studio went on to make many Tony Hawk sequels through 2005 and *Guitar Hero III* (2007). Neversoft was effectively merged into Infinity Ward in 2014 and disbanded as a separate studio. The Tony Hawk franchise has had multiple revivals since.

question: *Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!* (1987) — the home NES boxing game licensed with Mike Tyson as the final opponent — was widely beloved in the late 1980s. After Tyson's 1990 license expiration, his sprite was replaced. What was the final opponent's new name?
answer: Mr. Dream — a generic name unrelated to Tyson, with the same gameplay
choices: Mr. Dream — a generic name unrelated to Tyson, with the same gameplay

Soda Popinski — actually a different existing boxer in the same game

context: Mr. Dream was Nintendo's generic replacement for Tyson's image after the 1990 license expiration. Original cartridges featuring Tyson became collectibles. The 2009 Wii *Punch-Out!!* remake by Next Level Games re-created many of the original opponents but did not feature Tyson (Nintendo had not renewed the license).

question: Underwater investigations of Loch Ness — including the famous 1972 Rines Robert Project expeditions — have produced occasional 'flipper' photographs that have been controversially interpreted. The 1972 photo showed what?
answer: An indistinct large object photographed by sonar and underwater camera by Dr. Robert Rines
choices: An indistinct large object photographed by sonar and underwater camera by Dr. Robert Rines
A clear photograph of a long-necked plesiosaur (which actually was never produced)
A photograph of a known underwater debris field misidentified initially
A photograph of an aircraft propeller that had crashed into the loch in WWII
context: Dr. Robert Rines's Academy of Applied Science conducted multiple Loch Ness expeditions from 1972 onward. The 'flipper photographs' — heavily processed images — have been disputed for decades. Rines died in 2009. Adrian Shine has continued related research with the Loch Ness Project from the 1990s onward. No conclusive evidence of an animal has been produced.

question: The Bermuda Triangle's reputation for unusual ship and aircraft losses has been popularly contrasted with the Lloyd's of London insurance market's actual pricing of shipping in the area. What is the insurance industry's actual position?
answer: Lloyd's does NOT charge higher premiums for the Bermuda Triangle; loss rates are normal
choices: Lloyd's does NOT charge higher premiums for the Bermuda Triangle; loss rates are normal
Lloyd's DOES charge a 20% surcharge for ships transiting the area each season
Lloyd's stopped insuring Bermuda Triangle transits entirely in the 1970s
Lloyd's offers a special 'Triangle Insurance' product specifically for the area
context: Multiple Lloyd's of London statements over the decades have confirmed that the Bermuda Triangle is not treated as a higher-risk shipping area. Statistical analyses (notably by skeptic Larry Kusche in 1975) have shown ship and plane losses in the area are proportionate to traffic volume — there are simply more ships and planes there, leading to absolute (not relative) more losses.

question: Easter Island's environmental collapse — historically attributed to deforestation and unsustainable moai-construction practices — has been re-examined by modern archaeologists. The Diamond-style 'ecocide' narrative has been challenged by what alternative theory?
answer: European-introduced disease and slavery decimated the population in the 1860s, not pre-contact collapse
choices: European-introduced disease and slavery decimated the population in the 1860s, not pre-contact collapse
The moai were constructed entirely by European settlers, not the original Rapa Nui
The Rapa Nui were never on the island; the moai were carved by an unknown earlier civilization
The trees on Easter Island never fully existed in the first place — it was naturally a grassland
context: Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo's 2011 book *The Statues That Walked* argued the population peak was much smaller than Diamond's 'ecocide' theory required, and that Peruvian slave raids of the 1860s (not pre-contact collapse) caused the major population reduction. The 'walking moai' theory was developed by the same researchers. Their reinterpretation remains debated by archaeologists.

question: The 'Antarctic pyramids' — pyramid-shaped natural mountains in the Patriot Hills region of Antarctica — have circulated since 2013 as supposed evidence of an ancient lost civilization. The most-cited photographs show pyramid-shaped peaks. What is the geological consensus?
answer: They are natural nunatak peaks shaped by glacial erosion (a known geological process)
choices: They are natural nunatak peaks shaped by glacial erosion (a known geological process)
They are artificial pyramids constructed by an ancient pre-glacial civilization
They are alien-built structures preserved by the ice cap for millennia
They are Nazi-era German constructions from Operation Highjump
context: Nunataks are exposed mountain peaks rising above continental ice sheets. Glacial erosion can carve them into surprisingly geometric shapes — including pyramids. The Patriot Hills pyramidal peaks are recognized geological features, not artifacts. Antarctic 'lost civilization' theories have circulated since the early 1900s; none have been supported by physical evidence.

question: *Missing 411* — David Paulides's series of books documenting unusual missing-persons cases in U.S. national parks and wilderness areas — has been a major contemporary cryptozoology and unexplained-mysteries publication since 2011. What is Paulides's professional background?
answer: Former San Jose, California police officer turned cryptozoologist researcher
choices: Former San Jose, California police officer turned cryptozoologist researcher
Former FBI Special Agent in the Behavioral Analysis Unit (which actually isn't his background)
Former U.S. Forest Service ranger in the western states (not his actual background)
Former academic anthropologist at a major university (not his actual background)
context: Paulides retired from law enforcement before pursuing cryptozoology and missing-persons research. The Missing 411 books document unusual disappearance patterns (clothes removed at distance from body, victims found higher than starting point, etc.) but do not commit to a specific paranormal explanation. The series has continued through several volumes; rangers and law enforcement have disputed some specific case details.

question: *Magic: the Gathering* — when Wizards of the Coast first published the game in August 1993 — was designed for casual play but quickly developed a competitive scene. What is the most-cited first competitive tournament?
answer: Gen Con 1994 (the World Championship, won by Zak Dolan with a Type 1 deck)
choices: Gen Con 1994 (the World Championship, won by Zak Dolan with a Type 1 deck)
Gen Con 1993 (the Alpha launch, with no actual sanctioned tournament held)
Origins 1993 (which actually was not a sanctioned Magic tournament)
DragonCon 1994 (which actually was not a sanctioned Magic tournament)
context: The 1994 Gen Con World Championship was the first major sanctioned Magic tournament. Wizards of the Coast created the Duelist Convocation International (DCI) to handle competitive sanctioning. The first Pro Tour was held in New York City in February 1996, two years later. Many of the era's defining decks (Necropotence, Sligh, Counter-Sliver) emerged from this competitive period.

question: AD&D 1st Edition's *Player's Handbook* (1978) provided a specific count of character classes. Beyond Fighter, Magic-User, Cleric, and Thief, the book provided 'sub-classes' (Paladin under Fighter, Druid under Cleric, etc.). How many total classes/sub-classes were listed?
answer: Eleven classes: Fighter, Ranger, Paladin, Cleric, Druid, Magic-User, Illusionist, Thief, Assassin, Monk, Bard
choices: Eleven classes: Fighter, Ranger, Paladin, Cleric, Druid, Magic-User, Illusionist, Thief, Assassin, Monk, Bard
Fifteen classes, including various 'special' sub-classes not actually in PHB
Five classes, the original Holmes Basic Set lineup without sub-classes
Twenty classes, adding many later 'kits' that weren't actually in PHB
context: AD&D 1e's eleven-class system — including the prerequisite-heavy Ranger, Paladin, Bard, Monk, and Druid — gave the game its character-building complexity. The Bard's three-stage class progression (Fighter → Thief → Druid + Bard) was notorious for being nearly impossible to qualify for. AD&D 2e (1989) simplified to ten classes (or 'kits' approach).

question: BECMI Basic D&D (Mentzer, 1983-86) — the boxed-set system that ran from levels 1 to 36 — extended D&D character progression far beyond AD&D's typical 1-20 range. What did characters become after level 36?
answer: Immortals — divine-tier beings with multi-planar campaign play (Immortals box, 1986)
choices: Immortals — divine-tier beings with multi-planar campaign play (Immortals box, 1986)
Ancients — actually a term in BECMI but not the immortality framework
Heroes — actually the original Basic Set's level 1-3 designation, not post-36
Demigods — actually a Forgotten Realms (Realmspace) tier not BECMI
context: The Immortals Set (1986) introduced post-36 'Immortal' play — divine-tier characters interacting with the cosmology of the Mystara world. The system was complex and demanded heavy DM commitment; few Immortals campaigns reached final play. The system was effectively absorbed into the Forgotten Realms's divine-ascension mechanics in AD&D 2e.

question: Wizards of the Coast — the company that purchased TSR (1997) and revived D&D — was itself purchased by Hasbro in 1999 for $325 million. The Hasbro acquisition gave WotC the resources to revive D&D as a major Hasbro product line. Who led WotC at the time?
answer: Peter Adkison, who had founded WotC in 1990 and led through 2001
choices: Peter Adkison, who had founded WotC in 1990 and led through 2001
Lorraine Williams, who actually had been TSR's CEO not Wizards's
Richard Garfield, who actually was Magic's designer not Wizards's CEO
Hasbro's CEO Alan G. Hassenfeld, who actually was Hasbro's CEO not WotC's
context: Adkison's $325 million deal made WotC a Hasbro subsidiary. The acquisition gave WotC access to Hasbro's distribution and toy-industry expertise; in exchange, Hasbro got the rights to Magic, D&D, and the broader gaming portfolio. Adkison left WotC in 2001 (returning to Magic-related projects through Wizards's offices later).

question: *Berserk*'s 'Golden Age' arc — the manga's most-praised early storyline (volumes 4-14, chapters 9-95, mid-1990s) — follows the rise of a mercenary band led by a charismatic young commander. Without spoiling the specific events, what is the band's name?
answer: The Band of the Hawk, led by Griffith and joined by Guts
choices: The Band of the Hawk, led by Griffith and joined by Guts
The White Sword Knights, an actual military order that opposed the Band of the Hawk
The Iron Brotherhood, a different mercenary band Guts later joined
The Lions of Midland, a generic name not used in the manga
context: The Band of the Hawk's rise from poor mercenaries to the elite force of Midland's army defines the Golden Age arc. The arc has been adapted in multiple anime forms (1997 TV anime, 2012-13 film trilogy, 2016-17 CG-anime). The arc concludes with one of the most-cited events in manga history — known as the 'Eclipse', but generally not spoiled for new readers.

question: *Neon Genesis Evangelion*'s (1995) opening battle features Eva Unit 01 piloted by Shinji Ikari fighting the Third Angel Sachiel in Tokyo-3. The battle establishes much of the show's mecha-combat framework. What is unusual about Eva combat versus typical anime mecha combat?
answer: Eva Units are partly biological — they bleed and feel pain when damaged
choices: Eva Units are partly biological — they bleed and feel pain when damaged
Eva Units are fully robotic and only differ from earlier anime mecha in scale
Eva Units do not use any conventional weapons — only psychic projection attacks
Eva Units fly entirely under their own power, with no umbilical cable required
context: Eva Units are biomechanical — their 'flesh' beneath the armor is alive. Their umbilical cables (providing power) require return to base after a few minutes of combat. The pain Shinji feels when Eva 01 is wounded gives the series its distinctive psychological-combat tone. The Evas' true nature is a slow revelation across the series.

question: *Demon Slayer* (manga 2016, anime 2019 onward) features an elite tier of warriors called Hashira (Pillars) — the strongest demon slayers in the Demon Slayer Corps. Each Pillar is named for the breathing style they wield. How many Hashira are there at any given time?
answer: Nine Hashira, with each holding a unique breathing style (Water, Flame, Stone, etc.)

Six Hashira, the typical number in many other shonen-elite groups
Twelve Hashira, matching the number of Upper-Rank demons (which is actually different)
Twenty-one Hashira, far more than the actual canonical number in the series
context: The nine Hashira at the start of *Demon Slayer*'s main arc: Water, Flame, Stone, Wind, Insect, Snake, Mist, Love, Sound (with Sound being introduced after the first Pillar event). The breathing styles all derive from the original Sun Breathing. Each Pillar's distinctive personality and combat style has become a fan-favorite character framework.

question: *Naruto*'s protagonist is the host (jinchuriki) for the Nine-Tailed Fox demon (Kyuubi/Kurama). The fox attacked the Hidden Leaf village in *Naruto*'s backstory and was sealed inside infant Naruto. Without spoiling later arcs, who originally sealed the fox into Naruto?
answer: The Fourth Hokage Minato Namikaze, who is also Naruto's father

Jiraiya, who actually is Minato's teacher and Naruto's later mentor
Tsunade, who actually is the Fifth Hokage and a separate character
context: Minato Namikaze sealed Kurama into Naruto using the Death Reaper Seal — a forbidden technique. The reveal that Minato is Naruto's father is one of *Naruto*'s most-emotional manga moments and is the start of significant later arcs. Kishimoto's father-son thematic structure runs deep in the manga.

question: *Akira* (1988), Katsuhiro Otomo's film, features an iconic motorcycle action sequence where the protagonist's motorcycle skids dramatically with red taillights leaving glowing trails. The shot has been recreated in many subsequent films and pop culture references. What is the protagonist's name?
answer: Shotaro Kaneda, the leader of the bike gang and the film's primary protagonist
choices: Shotaro Kaneda, the leader of the bike gang and the film's primary protagonist

context: Kaneda's red motorcycle has become one of cinema's most-iconic vehicles. *Akira*'s motorcycle slide has been recreated in dozens of films (the Wachowskis's *Matrix Reloaded*, Edgar Wright's *Scott Pilgrim*, etc.). The film's depiction of biker-gang Tokyo culture was informed by Otomo's real research into 1970s-80s bosozoku (motorcycle gang) culture.

question: *Back to the Future* (1985) cast Christopher Lloyd as Doc Brown, the eccentric inventor of the DeLorean time machine. Lloyd's wild-haired, manic performance has become one of the most-imitated film characters of the 1980s. What was his catchphrase?
answer: 'Great Scott!' (used multiple times across the trilogy)

All three of the above are real Doc Brown catchphrases from the trilogy

Lloyd was 47 at the original *Back to the Future*'s 1985 release; his hair was reportedly dyed white. Lloyd returned to the role in *Back to the Future Part II* (1989) and *Back to the Future Part III* (1990).

question: *Back to the Future* (1985) was directed and co-written by a Steven Spielberg protege whose earlier credits included *Romancing the Stone* (1984). Who was the director?
answer: Robert Zemeckis, who also co-wrote with Bob Gale (his longtime writing partner)

Tim Burton, who actually directed 'Pee-wee's Big Adventure' (1985) for a different studio
context: Zemeckis and Bob Gale had been trying to sell the *Back to the Future* script since 1981. Universal Studios rejected it dozens of times before greenlighting it in 1985. Zemeckis went on to direct the entire trilogy plus *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* (1988), *Forrest Gump* (1994), *Cast Away* (2000), and many others.

question: *Neon Genesis Evangelion* (1995)'s Eva Units have distinctive color schemes. The protagonist's Unit 01 is primarily purple with green accents. Unit 02, piloted by Asuka, has what primary color?
answer: Red — Unit 02's primary armor color in the standard Tokyo-3 configuration

The 2007-2021 'Rebuild of Evangelion' film tetralogy uses different and additional Eva Units; the original 1995-96 TV series and 1997 'End of Evangelion' film use a smaller core lineup.

question: Studio Orange — the Tokyo animation studio that produced *Trigun Stampede* (2023) and the *Beastars* (2019) anime — has specialized in 3D CG animation for anime production. Who founded Studio Orange?
answer: Eiji Inomoto, in 2004 as a smaller animation production house

question: *ThunderCats* (1985-89) — the Pacific Animation Corporation-produced syndicated animated series — featured the iconic Sword of Omens wielded by Lion-O. The sword had a unique feature when held aloft and a battle-cry was uttered. What was the cry?

question: In a fog-soaked corridor of the Bradbury Building in downtown Los Angeles, a 1982 Ridley Scott film shoots its climactic rooftop confrontation. question: The score of the 1982 film Blade Runner — analog synthesizers, smoky saxophone, a haunting end-credits theme — was composed by a Greek musician who had won Best Original Score for Chariots of Fire the year before. He worked alone in his London studio, improvising long passages. Who?

question: The Dutch actor Rutger Hauer played the replicant Roy Batty in Blade Runner 1982. In the rooftop scene during a downpour, he delivered a now-iconic monologue about C-beams and Tannhauser Gate. The line about tears in rain was famously his own contribution. What did he do to the script?

question: Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride opens not in a fairy-tale kingdom but in a suburban bedroom, where a sick boy played by Fred Savage is playing a baseball video game on a Commodore personal computer. question: Andre the Giant played the gentle giant Fezzik in Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride. question: In the 1993 western Tombstone, Val Kilmer's portrayal of consumptive gambler Doc Holliday is a fan-favorite character study. question: On May 6, 2021, Kentaro Miura, the manga artist behind Berserk since 1988, died suddenly of an aortic dissection at age 54. The manga had been running for over thirty years. The series did not end with him. Who and what continued the story?

question: The opening sequence of Watanabe and Kanno's 1998 anime Cowboy Bebop features a bursting big-band jazz number with names flashing across grids of colored panels. The song is performed by the show's composer Yoko Kanno with her band The Seatbelts. What is its title?

question: James Cameron directed his breakout film The Terminator in 1984 on a tight budget. Cameron had previously worked at Roger Corman's New World Pictures as a model-maker and second-unit director. What did Cameron famously say he sold to producer Gale Anne Hurd to get the film made?

His Roger Corman royalty cuts on Battle Beyond the Stars to free him from other producing commitments.
His union card from the IATSE so he could direct as a non-union project under right-to-work rules.
His percentage of the future Aliens screenplay so he could focus on the Terminator project full-time.

question: James Cameron's 1986 Aliens, the sequel to Ridley Scott's 1979 Alien, was a major box-office and critical success. The film featured Sigourney Weaver returning as Ellen Ripley. What kind of military force accompanies her on the return mission to LV-426?

Interstellar Commercial Defense Force, the trade-union militia of the United Colonies in 22nd century.

question: Paul Verhoeven's 1990 sci-fi film Total Recall was based on a Philip K. Dick short story and starred Arnold Schwarzenegger as Doug Quaid, a construction worker who pays for an implanted Mars vacation memory that may not be a memory at all. Which PKD short story is its source?

The Minority Report, a different PKD story adapted in 2002 by Spielberg with Tom Cruise in the lead.
A Scanner Darkly, which Richard Linklater later adapted in 2006 using rotoscoped animation throughout.
context: PKD wrote nearly 50 novels and 120 short stories. Many have been adapted: Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, Scanner Darkly, The Adjustment Bureau, Man in the High Castle.

question: In 1983 an animated arcade game using LaserDisc playback startled the industry. Players guided a knight named Dirk the Daring through a dragon's castle by pressing direction-pad buttons at precisely the right times. The game's animation was led by which Disney defector?

question: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe began airing in 1983 as a Filmation animated series tied to Mattel's toy line. The series' setting was the planet Eternia, home to Castle Grayskull and the floating Snake Mountain. Who is He-Man's archvillain?

question: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero aired from 1985 onward and ended each episode with a PSA — a short Knowing is Half the Battle public service announcement. In the early 2000s, fan-made parody PSAs spread across the internet. What did they typically replace the original message with?

Real-world product placements promoting modern Hasbro toys throughout the still-airing series.

Anti-piracy warnings featuring the same Joes denouncing illegal media downloads in a parody format.

question: The 1984 animated series The Transformers premiered with a three-part pilot called More Than Meets the Eye. The series introduced two warring factions of transforming robots from the planet Cybertron. Who were the two leaders, voiced by Peter Cullen and Frank Welker?

question: Voltron: Defender of the Universe, which premiered in U.S. syndication in 1984, was edited and rewritten from a Japanese animated series. Five robotic lions piloted by a multinational space-explorer team combine to form the giant Voltron. What is the Japanese source series?

question: DiC's 1989 NBC Saturday cartoon Captain N: The Game Master featured Kevin Keene transported into Videoland to join the N Team. Members included a vain Mega Man, a buffoonish Simon Belmont, the bird-boy Kid Icarus, and one other game character. Who?

question: DuckTales premiered on the Disney Channel in September 1987 and starred Scrooge McDuck and his great-nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie. The series' theme song featured the lyric Woo-oo and an unforgettable melody. Who wrote the theme song?

question: Animaniacs premiered in 1993 on Fox Kids, produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment with Warner Bros. The show featured the Warner siblings — Yakko, Wakko, and Dot — locked in the Warner Bros. water tower. The series spun off a popular two-mice-trying-to-take-over-the-world segment. What was it?

question: Neon Genesis Evangelion (1995) features giant bio-mechanical war machines called Evangelions, piloted by 14-year-olds. The series gradually reveals that the Eva Units are not truly machines at all. What are they?

question: Katsuhiro Otomo's 1988 anime Akira features a startlingly experimental soundtrack. The music is performed by a Japanese collective that drew on Indonesian gamelan, Bulgarian polyphonic chant, and Noh-theater instrumentation. Who composed and performed it?

question: Otomo's 1988 anime Akira is set in a sprawling, dystopian futuristic megacity rebuilt on the ashes of an earlier conflict. The setting was thirty-one years in the film's future. What year is Akira set in?

question: Koyoharu Gotouge's Demon Slayer features the Demon Slayer Corps, with nine elite swordsmen called Hashira (Pillars) serving as the strongest fighters in the organization. Each Pillar represents a different Breathing style. How many Hashira are there at the start of the modern arc?

question: Wyatt Earp, born 1848, was the legendary lawman of the Old West who fought in the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral in 1881. He lived a long life after his marshal years and died in Los Angeles in 1929. Famously, who was at his bedside as he died at age 80?

His brother James Earp, the eldest of the Earp brothers who survived him into the late 1930s only.
