question: Clint Eastwood's 1992 Western Unforgiven won four Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director. Eastwood was 62 when he made it; the film also won Best Supporting Actor. Who took that prize?

Saul Rubinek, who plays the dime-novel writer accompanying English Bob through the territory.

question: Robert Zemeckis's 1985 film Back to the Future, produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment, became one of the highest-grossing films of the year. The script went through years of rewrites. What year does Marty travel back to from 1985?

1935, exactly fifty years earlier; a Great Depression setting that was rejected as too dark.

question: Back to the Future Part II opened in November 1989 and Part III in May 1990 — the two sequels were shot back-to-back over almost a year of production. The future setting in Part II is famously a specific date. What date does Marty visit?

question: The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles began not as a cartoon or a toy line but as a 1984 black-and-white indie comic book published by Mirage Studios. Two creators put up their own money to print 3,000 copies of issue one. Who were they?

question: The first Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles animated series premiered in December 1987 as a five-episode miniseries before being expanded into a full daily syndicated show. The animation studio for the long-running 1987-96 series was based where?

question: Studio Ufotable produced the 2019 anime adaptation of Demon Slayer that became a global hit. The studio is famous for its specific visual style — a fusion of hand-drawn character animation with digital effects, especially during action sequences. What studio is this?

Bones, the studio behind Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood and My Hero Academia anime adaptations.

question: Game Freak's Pokemon Red and Green released in Japan on February 27, 1996, for the Game Boy. The English-localized release adapted Red and Blue versions for North America with several Pokemon swapped. When did Red and Blue release in the United States?

March 12, 1999, the same week the first US-localized Pokemon film opened in American movie theaters.
context: The two-year gap allowed Nintendo to wait for the anime translation to be in place. The launch was a phenomenon, soon driving Pokemon to be one of the most lucrative franchises ever.

question: The original Tomb Raider video game came out in 1996 from Core Design under publisher Eidos Interactive. The protagonist Lara Croft was conceived by which designer at Core?

context: Tomb Raider became a defining 1990s game, blending platforming with adventure. Lara Croft became a pop-culture figure, with two Angelina Jolie films and an Alicia Vikander reboot following.

question: Garfield's Halloween Adventure aired on CBS on October 30, 1985. The show, based on Jim Davis's comic strip, features Garfield and Odie trying to trick-or-treat. The special won the 1986 Primetime Emmy Award for what category?

Outstanding Variety, Music or Comedy Special, an entirely unrelated Emmy slot not for animation.
Outstanding Children's Special, a recognition slot that animated Halloween shows have been entered in.
context: Garfield won the Outstanding Animated Program Emmy for the special. The first Garfield primetime special was Here Comes Garfield (1982).

question: John Badham's 1983 film WarGames features a young David Lightman (Matthew Broderick) who war-dials and accidentally accesses NORAD's nuclear-launch simulator. What specific make and model of microcomputer does David use in his bedroom?
answer: IMSAI 8080 with an external modem and Memorex 5.25-inch floppy drives in the dial-up scenes.
choices: IMSAI 8080 with an external modem and Memorex 5.25-inch floppy drives in the dial-up scenes.
Apple II Plus with the AppleSoft BASIC ROM that was standard for hobbyist users of that 1983 era.
Commodore 64 paired with an external 1541 floppy drive, common for home users in 1983-84 era.
IBM PC XT with a 360KB floppy drive and an internal Hayes-compatible 1200 baud modem of the time.
context: The IMSAI 8080 was an actual hobbyist S-100 machine of the era, deliberately retro even at the time of filming. Real users had largely moved to Apple, Commodore, and IBM by 1983.

question: The Simpsons aired an episode in season 9 (1997) titled The Cartridge Family, depicting Homer buying a handgun and the family's deteriorating safety habits. The episode famously aired in the US edited and in the UK as the BBC initially refused. What event followed in 1998-99?

question: Ichiro Suzuki arrived in Seattle in 2001 from the Orix Blue Wave in Japan, signed by Mariners GM Pat Gillick. In his rookie season, Ichiro won several major awards. What did he win in 2001?

question: Neversoft and Activision released Tony Hawk's Pro Skater for the PlayStation in 1999. The game featured a multi-trick combo system and a punk-rock soundtrack that introduced bands like Goldfinger and Anthrax to a generation of suburban teens. What song opens the soundtrack?

question: Osamu Tezuka, often called the God of Manga, founded the modern manga industry in 1952 with the Astro Boy series. Tezuka also drew the 1973 manga Black Jack, about a rogue surgeon who charges enormous fees. Tezuka had a relevant educational background. What?

question: Rumiko Takahashi's Ranma 1/2 began serialization in Weekly Shonen Sunday in 1987 and ran until 1996. The series features martial-arts schools that the protagonist's family and his betrothed's family are rival heirs to. What is the school name?

question: Rumiko Takahashi's Inuyasha began serialization in Shonen Sunday in 1996 and ran until 2008. question: Hayao Miyazaki's 1984 film Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind predates the formal founding of Studio Ghibli (in 1985 by Miyazaki, Takahata, and producer Toshio Suzuki). What studio released Nausicaa?

question: Hayao Miyazaki's 2001 film Spirited Away (Sen to Chihiro no Kamikakushi) won the 2002 Berlin Film Festival's Golden Bear and the 2003 Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. The film was unusual for its Best Animated Feature win in what way?

question: In May 1980, Namco released an arcade game designed by 24-year-old Toru Iwatani. The protagonist's shape was famously inspired by an everyday object Iwatani noticed at lunch one day. What object?

question: On July 4, 1982, a 21-year-old construction worker named Steve Sanders played Donkey Kong at Twin Galaxies in Ottumwa, Iowa, achieving a score of 1,000,000 — the first publicly verified million. question: In Donkey Kong, the arcade-mode level numbering continues until a precise point where the game becomes unplayable due to a code bug. Mario falls dead almost immediately when the level begins. What level is this kill screen?

question: In April 2018, after years of internet investigation, Twin Galaxies disqualified all of Billy Mitchell's Donkey Kong scores including the famous 1,047,200. What was the alleged evidence?

question: Super Mario Bros. (1985) contains one of gaming's most famous glitches. By entering one of the pipes in World 1-2 in a specific way (a small jump from a specific brick position), the player ends up in a strange water level called World 36-1. What is it usually called?

question: Metroid (1986) for the NES was famous for ending with an unexpected reveal — the protagonist Samus Aran removes their helmet and is revealed to be a woman. The ending varied by completion time. What was the fastest reward?

question: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998) for the N64 features a Water Temple roughly halfway through the main game. The temple gained legendary infamy among players. Why?

question: Ms. Pac-Man was released in 1982 by Bally Midway. It was originally an unauthorized modification of Pac-Man developed by a group at MIT-affiliated General Computer Corporation. What was the original mod called before Bally Midway licensed it?

question: Shigeru Miyamoto designed Donkey Kong in 1981 for Nintendo. The protagonist was a carpenter named Jumpman in the original arcade game. question: Alexey Pajitnov's Tetris was developed in 1984 at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. The Game Boy version of Tetris (1989) used a soundtrack that included an iconic theme song. The theme is an adaptation of a 19th-century Russian folk song. What is its name?

question: Metal Gear Solid (1998) for the PlayStation features a boss fight against Psycho Mantis, a telepathic enemy. question: Halo: Combat Evolved (2001), Bungie's Xbox launch title, follows the Master Chief, a Spartan supersoldier, and his AI companion. The AI's name and the Chief's are central to the franchise. What is the AI's name?

question: On August 1, 2004, at Evolution Championship Series, Daigo Umehara and Justin Wong met in Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike. With Daigo's Ken at one pixel of health, Justin's Chun-Li launched a full super attack. Daigo did something no one had seen before. What?

question: Square's Final Fantasy IV was released in Japan on July 19, 1991 for the Super Famicom. The North American release came in November 1991. The U.S. release was numbered differently and modified for content. What did the U.S. version do?

question: Secret of Mana (1993) for the Super NES, known in Japan as Seiken Densetsu 2, featured a real-time combat system and three-player simultaneous play (with a Multitap accessory). The composer was a young man whose career would soon include Final Fantasy work. Who?

question: Earthworm Jim (1994), developed by Shiny Entertainment for the Sega Genesis and Super NES, was a quirky platformer with a worm-piloting-a-robot-suit protagonist. The character was created by an artist who would later work on Neverhood. Who?

question: Bally Midway's Tron (1982) was an arcade game based on the same year's Disney film. The cabinet had striking blue and yellow neon lighting and four distinct minigames mapped to the joystick. What gameplay was unique to this cabinet?

question: Konami released Frogger to arcades in 1981. The game involves guiding a frog across a busy road and a river of moving logs and turtles. The cabinet's distinctive sound chip allowed multiple music tracks to play. Who composed the music?

question: Williams's Robotron: 2084 (1982) was designed by Eugene Jarvis, who had also designed Defender (1981). The cabinet used a then-unusual dual-joystick control scheme — one to move and one to shoot independently. What other game pioneered the twin-stick layout before Robotron?

question: Williams's Joust (1982) was designed by John Newcomer. The game features players controlling ostrich- or stork-riding knights who must joust enemy buzzard-riding warriors. The cabinet had unusual controls. What were they?

question: Atari released Centipede in 1981. The game was one of the few early-arcade games designed primarily by a woman. She had previously worked as an Atari engineer and became one of the few female game designers of her era. Who?

question: Williams Electronics released Defender to arcades in 1981. The game was famous for its complex control scheme — a five-button setup including thrust, reverse, smart-bomb, hyperspace, and fire. The cabinet was designed by Eugene Jarvis. What earlier game inspired Defender?

Cinematronics's Star Castle (1980), with the orbiting-defender concept directly carried over to Defender.
context: Asteroids had thrust mechanics and a side-firing weapon. Defender added side-scrolling and the smart bomb. Star Castle and Space Invaders are real predecessors.

question: Q*bert (1982) was an arcade game by Gottlieb featuring a quirky orange creature with a large nose, hopping on isometric cube pyramids. The character is famous for an indistinct cursing sound when enemies hit him. What does the cabinet actually output?
answer: Random synthesized phonemes (gibberish dialog speech), played through a Votrax SC-01 chip.
choices: Random synthesized phonemes (gibberish dialog speech), played through a Votrax SC-01 chip.
A pre-recorded sample of designer Warren Davis saying a censored variant of an English curse phrase.
A digitized audio sample of Q*bert's voice actor Jerry Houser, a real animation voice actor of that era.
Backwards-played English curse words masked by audio processing to obscure their original form.
context: Q*bert's curse sound came from the Votrax SC-01 speech synthesizer, programmed with nonsense input. The speech bubble shows @#!&%* characters in modern toy versions.

question: Taito's Space Invaders (1978) was so popular in Japan that the government had to react. The 100-yen coin was the standard arcade-quarter equivalent and the game's primary input. What happened to Japan's economy?
answer: Japan reportedly had a 100-yen coin shortage requiring increased production at the Mint of Japan.
choices: Japan reportedly had a 100-yen coin shortage requiring increased production at the Mint of Japan.
The Japanese government banned children under 12 from arcades due to truancy and yen exchange problems.
Taito had to limit weekly cabinet production after gambling-tax authorities raised inquiry concerns.
Japan's stock market dropped 4% in early 1979 amid concerns about productivity and arcade habits.
context: The 100-yen-coin-shortage story is famous but actually exaggerated in some retellings. Demand did spike noticeably. Space Invaders is credited with shaping the arcade economy of late 1970s Japan.

question: Capcom's Street Fighter II: The World Warrior (1991) revolutionized fighting games with its eight selectable characters from around the world. Two of the most popular were the white-gi and red-headband-wearing Ken and Ryu. Who designed the original Street Fighter II?
answer: Akira Nishitani (planner) and Akiman / Akira Yasuda (character designer); Yoshiki Okamoto produced.
choices: Akira Nishitani (planner) and Akiman / Akira Yasuda (character designer); Yoshiki Okamoto produced.
Yoshinori Ono (planner) and Daigo Ikeno (character designer); the team behind later Street Fighter IV.
Hideaki Itsuno (planner) and Bengus (character designer); both involved in Capcom's late 1990s lineup.
Shoei Okano (planner) and Naoto Ohshima (character designer); the team behind Sonic the Hedgehog.
context: Nishitani and Akiman defined SF2. Yoshiki Okamoto produced. SF2 sold over 6 million SNES units, launching the fighting-game genre into the 1990s.

question: Mortal Kombat (1992) was developed by Ed Boon and John Tobias at Midway Games. The game was notable for its digitized-actor graphics — real performers in costume motion-captured for the sprites. The game was also notable for what major rating-system consequence?
answer: It directly led to the 1994 founding of the ESRB rating system in the United States after Senate hearings.
choices: It directly led to the 1994 founding of the ESRB rating system in the United States after Senate hearings.
It was the first arcade game to be banned in Germany under the country's 1980s violent-content laws.
It led to the 1993 PG-13 expansion that affected animated and live-action films retroactively.
It was the first game to require an MPAA rating decision before its Japanese-market release was allowed.
context: The 1993 Senate hearings on violent video games (Senators Lieberman and Kohl) followed Mortal Kombat and Night Trap. ESRB was founded September 1994 in response.

question: When Mortal Kombat (1992) was ported to home consoles in 1993, the Sega Genesis version featured a famous cheat code that unlocked full-color blood and the Fatalities. The cheat made the Genesis version vastly outsell the SNES version. What was the code?
answer: ABACABB, a six-button sequence reportedly inspired by the Genesis album Abacab from 1981.
choices: ABACABB, a six-button sequence reportedly inspired by the Genesis album Abacab from 1981.
DULLARD, a six-button sequence with no specific meaning that the developers chose for memorability.
BLOOD9, a five-button sequence that opened the Test Menu where the blood option could be toggled.
ABCABC, a six-button sequence that some versions in fact required as an alternative form of the code.
context: The Genesis sold roughly 6 to 1 over the SNES version specifically because of the blood code. The SNES version replaced blood with sweat.

question: Killer Instinct (1994) was a fighting game developed by Rare (the UK studio behind GoldenEye 007 and Donkey Kong Country) and published by Midway. The game was famous for its specific combo-system mechanic. What was the trademark combo?
answer: Ultra Combos, multi-hit chain attacks that the announcer would name (Ultra, Combo Breaker, Triple Combo).
choices: Ultra Combos, multi-hit chain attacks that the announcer would name (Ultra, Combo Breaker, Triple Combo).
Fatalities, the trademark Mortal Kombat finishing moves that Killer Instinct also borrowed from MK.
Super Moves, the standard fighting-game special-meter attacks that Killer Instinct used like Street Fighter II.
Air Combos, vertical-string attacks that were Killer Instinct's primary innovation in the fighting genre.
context: Killer Instinct's announcer (Chris Sutherland) became iconic with B-R-U-T-A-L! and C-R-A-Z-Y! Combo callouts. The game ran on Nintendo's never-released Ultra 64 hardware.

question: Tekken (1994) was Namco's first 3D fighting game, developed for the arcade and the PlayStation. The game's launch on PlayStation (1995) was a major sales success. The Tekken team was led by which designer?
answer: Seiichi Ishii (Tekken 1) and Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken 2 onward); Harada has led the series ever since.
choices: Seiichi Ishii (Tekken 1) and Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken 2 onward); Harada has led the series ever since.
Yoshinori Ono, the Street Fighter IV producer; he has never worked on Tekken at Namco at all.
Yu Suzuki, the Virtua Fighter designer; Virtua Fighter was Sega's, not Namco's, fighting franchise.
Tomonobu Itagaki, the Dead or Alive (1996) designer; he worked for Tecmo, not Namco, on his fighter.
context: Yu Suzuki designed Virtua Fighter (1993, Sega). Tomonobu Itagaki designed Dead or Alive (Tecmo). Tekken is Namco's. Harada is now the public face of Tekken.

question: Sega's Virtua Fighter (1993), designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega AM2, was the first commercially released 3D fighting game. The arcade cabinet used the Model 1 board. What technical limitation was famously visible in the original game?
answer: All characters were rendered in flat-shaded polygons with no textures — like wireframe figures with color.
choices: All characters were rendered in flat-shaded polygons with no textures — like wireframe figures with color.
The game ran at only 15 frames per second on the original Model 1 board configuration in arcades.
Combat was confined to a 2D plane embedded within a 3D environment — characters could not strafe.
Only 4 of the planned 8 characters made it into the original release due to development time limits.
context: Virtua Fighter's flat-shaded polygons gave it a distinctive minimalist look. Textures arrived in Virtua Fighter 2 (1994). The game launched the 3D-fighter genre.

question: Super Mario 64 (1996) launched the Nintendo 64 in North America. The game was the first major 3D platformer with full free-camera movement. The game's camera was operated by a friendly in-game character. Who was the cameraman?
answer: Lakitu, the cloud-riding turtle holding a 1990s-style video camera; he serves as Mario's camera operator.
choices: Lakitu, the cloud-riding turtle holding a 1990s-style video camera; he serves as Mario's camera operator.
Toad, the mushroom-headed servant of Princess Peach, who guides the player through the early castle level.
Yoshi, who appears as a hidden character on the roof of the castle after collecting 120 stars.
Bowser, the antagonist, who controls the camera-perspective in-universe through his magical powers somehow.
context: Lakitu first appeared in Super Mario Bros. (1985) on a cloud. In SM64, his role is rebranded as cameraman. Toad and Yoshi appear elsewhere.

question: Metroid: Zero Mission (2004) for the Game Boy Advance was a remake of the original 1986 Metroid. The remake added a previously unmentioned sequence at the end. What was the new content?
answer: A Zero Suit Samus stealth sequence after the main game, with no Power Suit, escaping the Space Pirates.
choices: A Zero Suit Samus stealth sequence after the main game, with no Power Suit, escaping the Space Pirates.
A multiplayer-only competitive mode for two GBA cartridges linked via cable, never previously offered.
A retold Metroid 2 prologue showing Samus visiting SR388 before the events of the original mission.
A flashback to Samus's childhood on Zebes with the Chozo, providing additional emotional backstory.
context: Zero Suit Samus debuted in Zero Mission. The Zero Suit became a major recurring character look. Samus's childhood Chozo flashbacks instead appeared in Metroid: Other M (2010).

question: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link (1987 Japan, 1988 US) was an unusual sequel to The Legend of Zelda (1986). The game had a major gameplay direction change compared to the first game. What was the change?
answer: Top-down overworld but with side-scrolling action in towns, dungeons, and combat encounters.
choices: Top-down overworld but with side-scrolling action in towns, dungeons, and combat encounters.
Pure top-down perspective as the first game, with added experience points and leveling mechanics.
First-person dungeon exploration, similar to early Wizardry games, while keeping overworld top-down.
Isometric perspective throughout the game, becoming the first major Zelda title in isometric layout.
context: Zelda II's side-scrolling action is the most divisive choice in series history. A Link to the Past (1991) returned to fully top-down. Zelda II also introduced experience points, swords, magic spells.

question: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid (1998) for the PlayStation used a built-in communication device called the Codec for the player's calls with allies. The default frequency for Colonel Roy Campbell's calls was a specific number. What was it?
answer: 140.85, the default frequency the player calls to talk to Colonel Campbell throughout the entire game.
choices: 140.85, the default frequency the player calls to talk to Colonel Campbell throughout the entire game.
144.07, the default frequency the player calls Mei Ling for save-game functions during play.
141.80, the default frequency the player calls Naomi for surveillance information across the game.
143.96, the default frequency the player calls Otacon (Hal Emmerich) once they meet in the storyline.
context: All four are real Codec frequencies. Campbell at 140.85 is the default. The Codec system was a Kojima trademark across the Metal Gear series and other works.

question: Silent Hill 2 (2001) for the PlayStation 2 was developed by Konami's Team Silent. The protagonist, James Sunderland, arrives in the town of Silent Hill after receiving a letter from his dead wife. Who composed the iconic score?
answer: Akira Yamaoka, who scored all the original Team Silent Hill games until his departure from Konami in 2010.
choices: Akira Yamaoka, who scored all the original Team Silent Hill games until his departure from Konami in 2010.
Yasunori Mitsuda, who scored Chrono Trigger and Xenogears for Square instead of Konami at the time.
Yoko Shimomura, who scored Kingdom Hearts (2002) for Square but never worked for Konami at all.
Hitoshi Sakimoto, who scored Final Fantasy XII (2006) for Square but is not a Konami composer at all.
context: Yamaoka's industrial-ambient score features Promise, Theme of Laura, and the Forest theme. The score is integral to the game's tone of grief and dread.

question: Capcom's Resident Evil 2 (1998) for the PlayStation features two protagonists with intersecting storylines — A-side and B-side scenarios that alternate based on which character the player picks first. Who are the two protagonists?
answer: Leon Kennedy (rookie cop) and Claire Redfield (college student searching for her brother Chris).
choices: Leon Kennedy (rookie cop) and Claire Redfield (college student searching for her brother Chris).
Chris Redfield (S.T.A.R.S. operative) and Jill Valentine (S.T.A.R.S. operative), the RE1 protagonists.
Carlos Oliveira (UBCS mercenary) and Jill Valentine (S.T.A.R.S. operative), the RE3 protagonists.
Ada Wong (spy) and HUNK (mercenary), the secondary playable characters in unlockable bonus modes.
context: Chris, Jill, Carlos, Ada, and HUNK are all real RE characters. RE2's protagonists are Leon and Claire. Leon would return in RE4 (2005); Claire in RE Code Veronica.

question: Resident Evil 4 (2005) was released first for the Nintendo GameCube, then ported to PlayStation 2 and other consoles. The game departed sharply from earlier RE games in perspective. What was the new camera style?
answer: Over-the-shoulder third-person perspective, replacing the fixed-camera angles of all previous RE games.
choices: Over-the-shoulder third-person perspective, replacing the fixed-camera angles of all previous RE games.
First-person perspective from Leon's viewpoint, anticipating the later VR Resident Evil 7 in 2017.
Top-down isometric perspective, which would become standard in 2D-style adventure-survival games.
Side-scrolling 2D perspective, which RE Code Veronica had partially tested in some sub-scenarios only.
context: RE4 directed by Shinji Mikami became hugely influential. Gears of War (2006) used the same over-the-shoulder camera. RE4's launch on GameCube was a Nintendo exclusive originally.

question: Yu Suzuki's Shenmue (1999) for the Sega Dreamcast was the most expensive video game ever made at its release, with a reported budget of roughly $47-70 million. The game's gameplay popularized one specific mechanic that became standard in action gaming for two decades. What?
answer: Quick Time Events (QTE), where the player must press a displayed button in a tight timing window.
choices: Quick Time Events (QTE), where the player must press a displayed button in a tight timing window.
Skill trees, where players unlock new combat moves by collecting experience points across the world.
Cover-based shooting, which God of War (2005) and Gears of War (2006) would later popularize fully.
Open-world driving, where the player navigates a large 3D city in real time without loading zones.
context: QTEs would dominate gaming through the 2000s-2010s before falling out of fashion. Shenmue's open Yokosuka city setting was also ahead of its time.

question: Sony's Team Ico studio released Ico (2001) for the PlayStation 2. The game has minimal dialogue and follows a young boy with horns escorting a girl named Yorda through a castle. Who designed it?
answer: Fumito Ueda, who would direct Shadow of the Colossus (2005) and The Last Guardian (2016) for Sony.
choices: Fumito Ueda, who would direct Shadow of the Colossus (2005) and The Last Guardian (2016) for Sony.
Goichi Suda (Suda51), the No More Heroes director, who never worked for Team Ico at Sony however.
Hidetaka Miyazaki, the FromSoftware director of the Dark Souls series, who had no connection to Team Ico.
Yoshiaki Koizumi, the Nintendo designer who worked on Super Mario Galaxy and other Mario games.
context: Ueda's signature aesthetic minimalism defined Team Ico. Ico, Shadow of the Colossus, and The Last Guardian form a thematic trilogy with the famous hand-holding mechanic in Ico.

question: Fumito Ueda's Shadow of the Colossus (2005) for the PlayStation 2 features a young man named Wander riding his horse Agro across a vast forbidden land. The game's structure is unusual. What is its gameplay structure?
answer: Sixteen colossi to defeat in any order; no other enemies in the world; no shops, no towns, no level grind.
choices: Sixteen colossi to defeat in any order; no other enemies in the world; no shops, no towns, no level grind.
Twelve dungeons to clear in linear order; standard JRPG-style party progression with overworld combat.
An open hub world with 30 procedurally generated arenas containing different boss-fight variants.
Eight massive city-zones with internal mini-dungeons and shopkeepers between major story missions.
context: The 16-colossi structure is one of gaming's most distinctive designs. Each colossus is a puzzle-boss as climbable terrain. Hideo Kojima cited it as a major influence on Death Stranding.

question: Sony Santa Monica's God of War (2005) for the PlayStation 2 follows Kratos, a Spartan warrior who serves the Greek gods. The game's director went on to direct Twisted Metal and several later franchises. Who?
answer: David Jaffe, who had earlier directed Twisted Metal Black (2001) for Sony's Incognito Entertainment.
choices: David Jaffe, who had earlier directed Twisted Metal Black (2001) for Sony's Incognito Entertainment.
Cory Barlog, who actually directed God of War II (2007) but not the original 2005 first game.
Stig Asmussen, who actually directed God of War III (2010) at Sony Santa Monica years later.
David Cage, the French Heavy Rain director who has no Sony Santa Monica connection at all.
context: Jaffe directed God of War (2005). Cory Barlog directed God of War II (2007). Both later collaborated on the 2018 reboot.

question: Square's Kingdom Hearts (2002) for the PlayStation 2 was a high-profile collaboration between Square (Final Fantasy) and Disney (animation library). The game's protagonist is a young Destiny Islands boy with a giant key-shaped sword. Who is the protagonist?
answer: Sora, the spiky-haired protagonist whose voice (Haley Joel Osment) has continued across the series.
choices: Sora, the spiky-haired protagonist whose voice (Haley Joel Osment) has continued across the series.
Roxas, Sora's Nobody from Kingdom Hearts II (2005); he is a sequel character, not the original lead.
Riku, Sora's rival friend; he is a major character but not the playable protagonist of Kingdom Hearts I.
Ventus, a prequel-trilogy character from Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep (2010), released years later.
context: Sora is voiced by Osment in English and Miyu Irino in Japanese. Tetsuya Nomura directs the series. Disney characters from Aladdin, Hercules, Tarzan, Alice, etc. all appear.

question: Squaresoft's Xenogears (1998) for the PlayStation was a JRPG written by Tetsuya Takahashi and was originally pitched as a Final Fantasy VII project. The game features piloted giant robots called Gears and a deeply complex philosophical-religious story. What was unique about its second disc?
answer: The second disc was largely told through narration over still images due to production-budget constraints.
choices: The second disc was largely told through narration over still images due to production-budget constraints.
The second disc was the bonus disc; the main game was complete on disc one with no plot continuation.
The second disc included only the final dungeon and the ending cutscene with no other content at all.
The second disc was the multiplayer-only mode for split-screen gear battles with multiple controllers.
context: Xenogears's second-disc presentation is famous and somewhat infamous. Takahashi later created Xenosaga (2002) and Xenoblade Chronicles series for Monolith Soft.

question: Yu Suzuki's Shenmue (1999) for the Sega Dreamcast features a young man named Ryo Hazuki investigating his father's murder in 1980s Yokosuka, Japan. The game's price tag and Suzuki's ambitions made it famous for one specific reason. What?
answer: Production budget ~$70 million, the most expensive game ever made at the time of its release in 1999.
choices: Production budget ~$70 million, the most expensive game ever made at the time of its release in 1999.
Disc count of 8 CDs to fit the entire game world, an unprecedented amount of game content per release.
First game to use real-time weather and 24-hour clock simulation in a 3D open-world setting.
First game to use motion capture of professional actors at every step of the production process.
context: Shenmue's budget remained a notable financial gamble. Sega never recouped costs. Suzuki finally completed the saga with the Kickstarter-funded Shenmue III (2019).

question: Sega's Phantasy Star IV: The End of the Millennium (1993) for the Sega Genesis is widely considered the high point of the series. The game's storyline ties together all four games of the saga and concludes the Algol Solar System story. What franchise was it influenced by?
answer: Star Wars and other space-opera media; the series predates Final Fantasy and is a sci-fi-fantasy hybrid.
choices: Star Wars and other space-opera media; the series predates Final Fantasy and is a sci-fi-fantasy hybrid.
Dune; the Algol setting was directly inspired by Frank Herbert's 1965 novel and Lynch's 1984 film.
Lord of the Rings; the magic-system origins and elven races were drawn from Tolkien's Middle-earth.
Star Trek: The Next Generation; the optimistic Federation-like government inspired Algol's politics.
context: Phantasy Star (1987) predates Final Fantasy. The series is a science-fantasy hybrid. Phantasy Star IV's storyline is its capstone.

question: Konami's Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (1997) for the PlayStation was directed by Koji Igarashi. The game introduced an exploration-heavy structure that the gaming press would later use to define an entire subgenre. What is that subgenre named?
answer: Metroidvania, combining Metroid's exploration design with Castlevania's level-traversal structure too.
choices: Metroidvania, combining Metroid's exploration design with Castlevania's level-traversal structure too.
Soulslike, the term that postdates Symphony of the Night and refers to FromSoftware's later Dark Souls.
Roguelite, the term referring to dungeon-crawl design more applicable to Rogue and its descendants.
Action-RPG, a broader category that long predates Symphony of the Night by over a decade in development.
context: Symphony of the Night sold modestly at release but became a cult classic. The Metroidvania label has come to describe many indie games. Koji Igarashi has continued the formula independently.

question: Capcom's Mega Man 2 (1988) for the NES was the second entry in the series after Mega Man (1987). The series introduced the format of choosing one of eight Robot Masters in any order. What is the most celebrated track on Mega Man 2's soundtrack?
answer: Dr. Wily's Castle Stage 1 (Wily Stage 1), often called the best 8-bit chiptune ever composed.
choices: Dr. Wily's Castle Stage 1 (Wily Stage 1), often called the best 8-bit chiptune ever composed.
Mega Man 1's Cut Man theme, often considered superior but predating Mega Man 2 by one year.
Mega Man 3's Snake Man theme, from the third game which postdates Mega Man 2 by one year only.
Mega Man 4's Bright Man theme, from the fourth game, even further afield from Mega Man 2's roster.
context: Mega Man 2's Wily Stage 1 by Takashi Tateishi is an iconic 8-bit chiptune. Mega Man 2 sold over 1.5 million copies and is the best-selling NES Mega Man.

question: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! (1987) for the NES was developed by Nintendo and starred a fictional boxer named Little Mac (the player character). Boxers were caricatured opponents from around the world. Who was the first opponent the player faces in the game?
answer: Glass Joe, the French underdog (1 win, 99 losses) with a glass jaw, a classic underdog parody.
choices: Glass Joe, the French underdog (1 win, 99 losses) with a glass jaw, a classic underdog parody.
Von Kaiser, the German trainer character, who is actually the second opponent rather than the first.
Piston Honda, the Japanese boxer character, who appears as the third opponent in the lineup.
Bald Bull, the Turkish charging-bull boxer character, who actually appears as the fifth opponent in.
context: Glass Joe (1-99 record) is the gentle introduction. Each opponent has a unique pattern. The final opponent is Mike Tyson himself in the licensed version.

question: Nintendo's Game Boy launched in Japan in April 1989 and in North America in July 1989. The handheld came packaged with a key game that became the killer app and drove millions of units of Game Boy sales worldwide. What was bundled with the Game Boy?
answer: Tetris, the puzzle game from Alexey Pajitnov, which Nintendo licensed in a contested deal with Soviet authorities.
choices: Tetris, the puzzle game from Alexey Pajitnov, which Nintendo licensed in a contested deal with Soviet authorities.
Super Mario Land, the Mario-style platformer by Nintendo R&D1 (Gunpei Yokoi's team) was bundled instead.
Pokemon Red and Blue, which actually launched on Game Boy in 1996 (Japan) and 1998 (US), much later.
Donkey Kong Land, a Rare-developed Donkey Kong title that didn't release until much later in 1995.
context: The Tetris license drama (Nintendo, Atari, Mirrorsoft) is told in the 2023 film Tetris. The bundling of Tetris with Game Boy was crucial to the handheld's success.

question: Sony's PlayStation Portable (PSP) launched in Japan in December 2004 and worldwide in 2005. The PSP used Universal Media Disc (UMD), a proprietary disc format. What was the PSP's screen technology?
answer: A 4.3-inch widescreen TFT LCD with 480x272 resolution, then the largest screen in a major handheld.
choices: A 4.3-inch widescreen TFT LCD with 480x272 resolution, then the largest screen in a major handheld.
A 3.5-inch OLED display, similar to what later Vita and modern handhelds would use over a decade later.
A 4-inch backlit STN-LCD with monochrome capability, a budget compromise compared to flagship handhelds.
A dual-screen 3-inch LCD (one on top, one on bottom), the same configuration as Nintendo DS 2004.
context: The PSP's widescreen LCD was a key feature in its launch. Sony's PSP-2000 (2007) and PSP-3000 (2008) refined the design. The UMD format proved limiting.

question: Nintendo's Wii launched in November 2006 in North America. The console used motion-sensing controllers (the Wii Remote / Nunchuck) and targeted a non-gamer audience. What internal Nintendo strategy term described this approach?
answer: Blue Ocean Strategy, Satoru Iwata's term for targeting non-traditional customers not just core gamers.
choices: Blue Ocean Strategy, Satoru Iwata's term for targeting non-traditional customers not just core gamers.
Genchi Genbutsu, the Toyota production system term for ground-truth problem-solving in manufacturing.
Kaizen, the Japanese continuous-improvement business philosophy applied to console development.
Sente, the Go board-game term for taking initiative, which Iwata applied to console competition strategy.
context: Blue Ocean Strategy is a 2005 book by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne. Iwata applied it to Wii (and DS). The Wii outsold the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in unit sales.

question: Gears of War (2006) was developed by Epic Games and published by Microsoft for the Xbox 360. The lead designer became one of the most public faces of the era's gaming industry. Who was he?
answer: Cliff Bleszinski (CliffyB), who left Epic in 2012 and later attempted multiple indie projects of his own.
choices: Cliff Bleszinski (CliffyB), who left Epic in 2012 and later attempted multiple indie projects of his own.
Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of Epic Games; he handled business but did not design Gears.
Mark Rein, the vice president of Epic Games; he is a business executive, not a game designer like Cliffy.
Lee Perry, an Epic designer who worked on Gears but not as the public-facing lead designer in interviews.
context: Gears of War popularized the cover-based shooting genre. The game ran on Unreal Engine 3. Cliff Bleszinski was Epic's public face through the mid-2000s.

question: Sony's PlayStation launched in Japan in December 1994 and in North America in September 1995. The PlayStation project began as a joint venture with Nintendo to create a CD-ROM add-on for the Super NES. What happened to that partnership?
answer: Nintendo cancelled the partnership at CES 1991 in favor of a Philips deal; Sony continued the project alone.
choices: Nintendo cancelled the partnership at CES 1991 in favor of a Philips deal; Sony continued the project alone.
Sony walked out of the partnership in 1992 after disagreements over royalty structure on CD sales.
The partnership succeeded but produced a different product (the Super NES CD) that flopped commercially.
Both companies released their own incompatible CD-ROM add-ons; both failed in the marketplace by 1993.
context: The famous Nintendo betrayal at CES 1991 (where Nintendo announced a Philips deal without telling Sony) led Sony's Ken Kutaragi to pursue PlayStation. The console outsold everything else by 1996.

question: The Sega Saturn launched in North America on May 11, 1995 — a surprise launch announcement at E3 1995, four months earlier than the planned September date. The early launch backfired for several reasons. What were the consequences?
answer: Retailers were unprepared, many games not ready, and Sony's $299 PlayStation price destroyed Saturn's $399.
choices: Retailers were unprepared, many games not ready, and Sony's $299 PlayStation price destroyed Saturn's $399.
Sega's manufacturing could not keep up, leading to a six-month shortage of Saturns at all retailers.
Sega's launch software was too good, and the holiday-2 demand exceeded availability of Saturns.
Sega's early launch prevented Sony from launching at all, but Saturn still failed to convert mass-market buyers.
context: The Saturn was a notorious commercial failure in North America. The Genesis era ended badly for Sega. Sony's $299 reveal at E3 1995 was a famous mic-drop moment.

question: When Sony's PlayStation launched in North America in September 1995, it was priced at a famously aggressive $299. The price was revealed in a memorable moment at E3 1995 in May. What did Sony of America's Steve Race say?
answer: He took the stage and said only '299' before walking off, after Sega had announced Saturn at $399.
choices: He took the stage and said only '299' before walking off, after Sega had announced Saturn at $399.
He took the stage and explained Sony's manufacturing efficiencies in a 20-minute pricing presentation.
He announced $349 first, then dropped it to $299 after Sega's $399 was revealed in the keynote.
He partnered with Larry Probst on stage for a joint EA-Sony announcement of price and launch lineup.
context: Steve Race's two-word E3 pricing presentation is the stuff of legend. The Saturn never recovered. The PlayStation sold over 100 million units lifetime.

question: Sega's Dreamcast launched in North America on 9/9/99 (September 9, 1999). The console featured a built-in modem for online gaming and a Visual Memory Unit (VMU) controller-display gimmick. When was the console officially discontinued?
answer: March 2001, only 18 months after its North American launch, ending Sega's hardware business entirely.
choices: March 2001, only 18 months after its North American launch, ending Sega's hardware business entirely.
December 2002, after the Sega-Sammy merger restructured the hardware business across both halves of the firm.
September 2000, only one year after launch, when Sega announced the company would exit hardware.
June 2003, after years of declining sales caused by competition from Sony's PS2 and Microsoft's Xbox.
context: Sega's exit from hardware in 2001 ended decades of platform competition. The Dreamcast remains beloved for its games library (Shenmue, Crazy Taxi, Sonic Adventure, Soul Calibur).

question: Bungie's Halo 2 (2004) for the Xbox launched on November 9, 2004 with breakthrough online multiplayer through Xbox Live. The game was the first to popularize what specific feature in console online play?
answer: Online matchmaking with persistent skill ranking visible to players within their account profile.
choices: Online matchmaking with persistent skill ranking visible to players within their account profile.
Voice chat between players from anywhere worldwide via headset; the Xbox 360 would come later.
Squad-based combat in a 4-vs-4 team format, the standard for console FPS multiplayer thereafter.
Downloadable content (DLC), the new map packs sold via Xbox Live Marketplace not previously available.
context: Halo 2's matchmaking with TrueSkill scoring was a defining innovation. Online play became the standard for console shooters going forward. The map packs (Killtaculars and Headhunters DLC) followed.

question: Metroid Prime (2002) for the Nintendo GameCube was developed not by Nintendo's R&D teams in Japan but by an American studio Nintendo had recently acquired. What studio?
answer: Retro Studios in Austin, Texas; they would also develop the Metroid Prime sequels and Donkey Kong Country Returns.
choices: Retro Studios in Austin, Texas; they would also develop the Metroid Prime sequels and Donkey Kong Country Returns.
Rare in Twycross, UK; they were never Nintendo-owned but did develop Donkey Kong Country and GoldenEye.
Camelot in Tokyo; they developed the Mario Golf and Mario Tennis series but not Metroid Prime ever.
Treasure in Tokyo; they developed Gunstar Heroes and many Genesis games but never Metroid Prime at all.
context: Retro Studios is Nintendo's Texas-based studio. They reorganized after acquiring the team in 2002. Metroid Prime won game-of-the-year accolades and revived the franchise.

question: HAL Laboratory's Super Smash Bros. Melee (2001) for the Nintendo GameCube was directed by Masahiro Sakurai. The game became enormously popular as a competitive tournament title. What specific technique discovered by players became a competitive cornerstone?
answer: Wavedashing, an unintended air-dodge-cancel technique that allowed instant horizontal movement boosting.
choices: Wavedashing, an unintended air-dodge-cancel technique that allowed instant horizontal movement boosting.
L-canceling, an intentional Sakurai-designed mechanic that already existed in the original Smash Bros 64.
Powershielding, a precise-timing block that lets players reflect projectiles cleanly back at attackers.
Smashing, the standard non-glitch attack that Sakurai designed as the centerpiece of the game's combat.
context: Wavedashing was an emergent technique not intended by HAL but tolerated. Sakurai removed it in Brawl (2008). The Melee community's love of wavedashing led to ongoing scene splits.

question: Atari released E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial for the Atari 2600 in December 1982. The game was developed in roughly five weeks by Howard Scott Warshaw. Sales were disastrous. A persistent urban legend involved what?
answer: Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico in September 1983.
choices: Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico in September 1983.
Atari recalled millions of cartridges from store shelves after parents complained about the game's content.
Atari sued Spielberg for the licensing fee they had paid; the case was dismissed before going to trial.
Atari banned the game from store shelves themselves before the game ever reached widespread distribution.
context: The Alamogordo landfill was a documented event; in 2014, the buried cartridges were exhumed for a documentary. The 1983 video-game crash followed in part because of E.T.'s failure.

question: The North American video-game industry crashed in late 1983, with home-console sales dropping from $3.2 billion in 1983 to $100 million by 1985. Several factors contributed. What event is widely credited as restarting the industry?
answer: The launch of the Nintendo Entertainment System (Famicom) in North America in October 1985.
choices: The launch of the Nintendo Entertainment System (Famicom) in North America in October 1985.
The launch of the Atari 7800 ProSystem in late 1984, which had been delayed from earlier in the year.
The launch of the Sega Master System in 1986, which kept up the momentum begun by the NES launch.
The launch of the IBM PCjr in November 1983, which sustained PC gaming through the broader market crash.
context: The NES launch saved the home-console market. Nintendo's strict licensing (the 10NES chip) gave them publisher control. Console gaming would not crash again for forty years.

question: Nintendo's Super Metroid (1994) for the Super Nintendo (Super Famicom) is widely considered one of the greatest games ever made. Yoshio Sakamoto directed and the game's score was composed by which pair of composers?
answer: Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, who composed in collaboration on the iconic Super Metroid soundtrack.
choices: Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano, who composed in collaboration on the iconic Super Metroid soundtrack.
Koji Kondo alone, who scored most Nintendo flagship games of the era including Mario and Zelda.
Hirokazu Tanaka, the original Metroid composer (1986) who scored most early Metroid titles in series.
Hip Tanaka and Yumiko Kanki, who jointly worked on multiple early-90s Nintendo soundtracks for SNES.
context: Tanaka scored the original Metroid (1986). Super Metroid is the Yamamoto/Hamano collaboration. Their score includes Crateria, Brinstar, and the haunting Phendrana Drifts ambient tracks.

question: Nintendo's Game Boy Color launched in October 1998. The handheld was backward-compatible with the entire Game Boy library and added a color screen. What was the maximum color count on screen at once?
answer: 56 colors on screen at once (10 sprite palettes of 3 colors plus 8 background palettes of 3 colors plus transparency).
choices: 56 colors on screen at once (10 sprite palettes of 3 colors plus 8 background palettes of 3 colors plus transparency).
32 colors on screen at once (4 sprite palettes of 4 colors plus 4 background palettes of 4 colors fully).
256 colors on screen at once, the same as the Super Nintendo's Mode 7 graphics during that era.
32,768 colors on screen at once, the same color count as the later Game Boy Advance hardware specifications.
context: GBC's 56-color limit was a significant upgrade from monochrome but limited compared to console graphics. The Game Boy Advance (2001) raised the maximum to 32,768 simultaneous colors.

question: Konami's Dance Dance Revolution (DDR) released to Japanese arcades in 1998 and became a global phenomenon. The cabinet featured a platform with arrow pads. What was unique about DDR's gameplay mechanic?
answer: Players step on directional arrow pads matching arrows scrolling up the screen, synchronized to music tracks.
choices: Players step on directional arrow pads matching arrows scrolling up the screen, synchronized to music tracks.
Players hit drum-like buttons matching beats, like Konami's separate Drummania (1999) cabinet design.
Players hold a controller to track wrist movement, similar to a Wii Remote precursor in arcade form.
Players use a touch-sensitive table surface for input, similar to early-2000s touchscreen arcade pads.
context: DDR became a fitness phenomenon. Konami's Bemani division includes Drummania, Beatmania, Guitar Freaks. DDR's arrow-platform format is widely imitated.

question: Namco's Time Crisis (1995) was a light-gun arcade game featuring a famous mechanic that no other arcade game at the time had. What was that mechanic?
answer: A foot pedal that the player must press to expose themselves; releasing it puts them into cover.
choices: A foot pedal that the player must press to expose themselves; releasing it puts them into cover.
A two-handed light gun (handgun and a separate shotgun-style alternate weapon for special moments).
A force-feedback recoil mechanism that physically pushed back against the player's hand on each shot.
An infrared-tracked headset that adjusts the displayed crosshair based on the player's eye direction.
context: The Time Crisis foot pedal mechanic was hugely innovative. Sega's House of the Dead and Konami's Silent Scope went different directions. Time Crisis sequels carried the pedal across the series.

question: Sega's Out Run (1986) was a driving game designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega AM2. The cabinet was a sit-down with motion-actuated hydraulics. The game's red Ferrari and player-selectable music made it iconic. What three soundtrack options did the game offer?
answer: Magical Sound Shower, Passing Breeze, and Splash Wave — three songs by Hiroshi Miyauchi on cabinet.
choices: Magical Sound Shower, Passing Breeze, and Splash Wave — three songs by Hiroshi Miyauchi on cabinet.
Free Fall, Last Wave, and Cruisin' — three tracks by Tomoya Iijima on the original 1986 arcade soundtrack.
Ridge Racer, Daytona USA, and Cruisin' USA — three tracks from later games miscredited to Out Run.
Magical Sound Shower, Speed Limit, and Final Take — three songs by Yu Suzuki himself for the cabinet.
context: The three Out Run songs are iconic. Hiroshi Miyauchi (not Suzuki) composed them. Magical Sound Shower remains a signature Sega arcade track in cover albums.

question: Sega's After Burner (1987) was designed by Yu Suzuki with a similarly ambitious cabinet. The full deluxe version of the cabinet rotated freely on a roller-coaster-style hydraulic chassis. What aircraft did the player pilot?
answer: An F-14 Tomcat, the famous Navy fighter prominently featured in Top Gun (1986) released the year prior.
choices: An F-14 Tomcat, the famous Navy fighter prominently featured in Top Gun (1986) released the year prior.
An F-15 Eagle, the Air Force fighter that has been operational since the 1970s in real-world combat.
An A-10 Thunderbolt II, the close-air-support gun-platform aircraft used heavily during the 1991 Gulf War.
An F/A-18 Hornet, the newer Navy multirole fighter that replaced many F-14s in the late 1990s.
context: After Burner's F-14 Tomcat was an obvious Top Gun reference. Sega's rotating deluxe cabinets remain among the most ambitious arcade machinery ever produced commercially.

question: Sega's Daytona USA (1994) was an arcade racing game using the Sega Model 2 hardware. The game's three tracks (Beginner, Intermediate, Expert) became famous for one ridiculous soundtrack track. What was the song?
answer: Let's Go Away (Beginner course theme), with the lyric Daytona repeated as an iconic chorus refrain.
choices: Let's Go Away (Beginner course theme), with the lyric Daytona repeated as an iconic chorus refrain.
Rolling Start (Intermediate course theme), with prog-rock instrumentals and no recognizable lyrics.
The King of Speed (Expert course theme), with sung lyrics about racing victory in the final stretch.
Coupe de Ville (Bonus course theme), a track that referenced Cadillac luxury cars in its hook lyric.
context: Let's Go Away is the most famous. All four tracks listed are real Daytona USA songs by Takenobu Mitsuyoshi. The Daytona arcade cabinet remained popular into the 2000s.

question: Sega's The House of the Dead (1996) was a light-gun arcade game with on-rails motion through environments full of slow-moving zombies. The 1998 sequel introduced a 2-player simultaneous mode and was a major hit. The series spawned films and other media. Who directed the 2003 film adaptation?
answer: Uwe Boll, the German director whose film adaptation became infamous for poor critical reception.
choices: Uwe Boll, the German director whose film adaptation became infamous for poor critical reception.
Paul W.S. Anderson, the British director of Mortal Kombat (1995) and the Resident Evil films from 2002.
John Carpenter, the horror director of Halloween (1978) and Escape from New York (1981) and other classics.
George A. Romero, the Night of the Living Dead (1968) director who never made a House of the Dead film.
context: Uwe Boll's House of the Dead (2003) is one of the most reviled video-game film adaptations. Boll directed many German-funded video-game films using a tax-loophole strategy in the 2000s.

question: Sega's Crazy Taxi (1999) was an arcade game also released for the Dreamcast. The game's soundtrack was famously punk-rock — featuring two specific bands that gave the game its energy. What bands?
answer: The Offspring and Bad Religion, whose tracks (including All I Want and Inner Logic) defined the soundtrack.
choices: The Offspring and Bad Religion, whose tracks (including All I Want and Inner Logic) defined the soundtrack.
Green Day and Rancid, two California punk bands whose songs Sega briefly licensed for early arcade testing.
Blink-182 and Sum 41, two pop-punk bands whose tracks would have fit but were never used in the game.
Foo Fighters and Smash Mouth, two American rock bands whose tracks were too expensive for the game.
context: The Offspring's All I Want is one of gaming's most iconic licensed tracks. Bad Religion provided most of the rest of the original soundtrack. Later versions of Crazy Taxi lost the original licenses.

question: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade game (1989) was a four-player simultaneous beat-em-up based on the cartoon series. The game's cabinet became iconic of late-80s arcade culture. What did the cabinet allow players to do at once?
answer: Up to four players fighting cooperatively as Leonardo, Donatello, Michelangelo, and Raphael simultaneously.
choices: Up to four players fighting cooperatively as Leonardo, Donatello, Michelangelo, and Raphael simultaneously.
Up to two players, with controllers letting them switch between any of the four Turtles at any time.
Up to three players, with the fourth Turtle controlled by AI and switching between the three players.
Up to four players, but in 2-vs-2 mode rather than fully cooperative gameplay against the AI enemies.
context: Four-player cooperative arcade beat-em-ups were a Konami specialty. The TMNT game led to Sunset Riders, Bucky O'Hare, X-Men, The Simpsons, and other multi-player Konami beat-em-ups.

question: Konami's The Simpsons arcade game (1991) was another four-player beat-em-up — this one let players play as Homer, Marge, Bart, and Lisa simultaneously. The Simpsons fight Mr. Burns and Smithers across various Springfield settings. Marge fights with what weapon?
answer: A vacuum cleaner, which she uses to suck up enemies and toss them into the next screen.
choices: A vacuum cleaner, which she uses to suck up enemies and toss them into the next screen.
A frying pan, which she swings with both hands as her primary melee weapon in the game.
A baby Maggie, whom she swings with one hand while holding a frying pan in her other hand.
A baseball bat that she borrows from Bart, which she uses both for melee and to hit projectiles back.
context: Marge's vacuum cleaner is iconic. The Konami Simpsons cabinet remains beloved. Players who completed the game encountered Mr. Burns's robot suit as the final boss.

question: Sega's Altered Beast (1988) was the original Sega Genesis (Mega Drive) pack-in game in North America. The protagonist transforms into various animal forms after collecting spirit balls. What was the iconic opening voice line?
answer: Rise from your grave! — the voice of Zeus addressing the resurrected hero in the opening scene.
choices: Rise from your grave! — the voice of Zeus addressing the resurrected hero in the opening scene.
Welcome to the world of Altered Beast — a generic spoken intro before each new level.
Defeat Neff and rescue Athena — a story-summary line spoken at the start of every new game.
Power up! Become werewolf! — a specific transformation announcement after collecting first spirit ball.
context: Rise from your grave! is one of gaming's most-quoted lines. Welcome to the world of Altered Beast also features. The Mega Drive version's voice synthesis was impressive for 1988.

question: Sega's Streets of Rage 2 (1992) for the Genesis was a major step up from the 1991 original. The game added two new characters to the existing Axel and Blaze duo. Who were the two new playable characters?
answer: Max Thunder (wrestler) and Skate (Eddie Hunter, Adam's young brother), the new playable team additions.
choices: Max Thunder (wrestler) and Skate (Eddie Hunter, Adam's young brother), the new playable team additions.
Mr. X and Shiva, the antagonists of Streets of Rage 1 and 2, not playable in the standard game release.
Roo (kangaroo) and Galsia (Galsia clone), characters that appeared in Streets of Rage 3 (1994), not 2.
Adam Hunter and Cherry, characters from Streets of Rage 1 and the much later Streets of Rage 4 (2020).
context: Max and Skate joined Axel and Blaze in SoR2. Adam Hunter from SoR1 was replaced by his young brother Skate. Streets of Rage 3 added Zan the cyborg.

question: Sega's Golden Axe (1989) was an arcade beat-em-up featuring three playable warriors fighting Death Adder. Each warrior had a magic specialty. What were the three warriors?
answer: Ax Battler (barbarian, earth), Tyris Flare (amazon, fire), and Gilius Thunderhead (dwarf, lightning).
choices: Ax Battler (barbarian, earth), Tyris Flare (amazon, fire), and Gilius Thunderhead (dwarf, lightning).
Kain Grinder (warrior), Mira Belle (warrior), and Trix Goldenhammer (warrior), generic descriptors.
Conan, Sonja, and Subotai — characters borrowed from Robert E. Howard's Conan the Barbarian books.
Aragorn, Boromir, and Gimli — characters borrowed from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings novels series.
context: Golden Axe characters were original creations clearly inspired by Conan-genre fantasy. The series ran through Golden Axe II (1991) and III (1993) on Genesis.

question: Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure (1994) was a 16-bit platformer for the Sega Genesis (and Super NES) developed by Interplay's Shiny Entertainment affiliate. The game leaned into grotesque scatological humor with weaponized burps and farts. Who designed it?
answer: Mike Stragey (Boogerman was developed by Interplay's Beam Software / Wayfowrward affiliates of Interplay).
choices: Mike Stragey (Boogerman was developed by Interplay's Beam Software / Wayfowrward affiliates of Interplay).
Brian Fargo, the Interplay founder, who personally designed Boogerman as a passion project of his own.
Mike Singleton, the British strategy-game designer best known for Lords of Midnight (1984), not Boogerman.
Steve Crow, Interplay's Boogerman designer; the game's lead developer with the Interplay Glenford team.
context: Steve Crow led Boogerman. The game's flatulence-based humor was extreme for its day. Boogerman achieved minor cult fame and has been re-released on multiple compilations.

question: Nintendo's Nintendo 64 launched in Japan in June 1996 and North America in September 1996. The console was marketed heavily around its 64-bit name. The Sega Saturn was 32-bit. The PlayStation was 32-bit. What was actually 64-bit about the Nintendo 64?
answer: The CPU had 64-bit instruction set (MIPS R4300i), even if most games used 32-bit operations on it.
choices: The CPU had 64-bit instruction set (MIPS R4300i), even if most games used 32-bit operations on it.
The graphics-and-audio bus was 64 bits wide; the CPU was actually 32-bit (RCP coprocessor).
The cartridge connector was 64 pins, hence the name; the actual hardware was largely 32-bit.
Marketing fluff; nothing on the console was meaningfully 64-bit; the name was a Sega-Saturn-Plus marketing pun.
context: The MIPS R4300i CPU did support 64-bit operations. Most N64 games used 32-bit code anyway. The 64-bit marketing was real but oversold; bus widths and memory limits mattered more.

question: Nintendo's Wii Sports (2006) was bundled with the North American and European Wii. The game featured five sports — Tennis, Baseball, Bowling, Golf, and Boxing — all using the Wii Remote and Nunchuck. Which sport became the unexpected sensation, particularly in nursing homes?
answer: Wii Bowling, beloved by older players for its intuitive controls and reasonable physical demand on aging arms.
choices: Wii Bowling, beloved by older players for its intuitive controls and reasonable physical demand on aging arms.
Wii Tennis, which became a hit at retirement communities for its simple swing-the-controller mechanic.
Wii Boxing, beloved by physical-therapy patients for its arm exercise but not the most-loved sport overall.
Wii Baseball, which became the most-played sport in Wii Sports tournaments at community centers worldwide.
context: Wii Bowling at retirement homes became a meme and a real social phenomenon. Wii Tennis was the demo sport at retail. Wii Sports sold 82 million copies, largely as a pack-in.

question: Bungie's Halo 3 (2007) for the Xbox 360 launched on September 25, 2007. The marketing campaign featured the tagline Finish the Fight. The game grossed over $170 million in its first 24 hours, then the largest entertainment-product opening day ever. What did Halo 3 introduce that became a console-FPS staple?
answer: Forge mode, an in-game level editor letting players modify multiplayer maps and place objects in them.
choices: Forge mode, an in-game level editor letting players modify multiplayer maps and place objects in them.
Online matchmaking, which was actually a Halo 2 (2004) introduction rather than Halo 3 first.
LAN play, which had been part of every prior Halo on Xbox since the original Halo: Combat Evolved.
Battle Royale 100-player mode, which Halo 3 did not actually have; this is a PUBG and Fortnite mechanic.
context: Forge mode was a major Halo 3 addition. Theater mode (saving and playback of game film) was another major innovation. Halo 3 sold over 14 million copies during its console generation.

question: Microsoft launched the Xbox in North America on November 15, 2001. The console's launch title was Halo: Combat Evolved by Bungie. What two other systems-defining features did the original Xbox have?
answer: Built-in hard drive (8GB) and Ethernet port for broadband online play (Xbox Live launched 2002 retail).
choices: Built-in hard drive (8GB) and Ethernet port for broadband online play (Xbox Live launched 2002 retail).
Dual-layer DVD drive and TV-tuner card for capturing television footage directly to the hard drive.
Detachable controller faceplates and a built-in webcam at the top of the original Xbox console design.
Wireless controllers and a built-in WiFi adapter, both standard at the time of the original Xbox launch.
context: The Xbox's HDD and Ethernet were major differentiators. Online play via Xbox Live launched in November 2002. Wireless controllers came with the Xbox 360 (2005). The Xbox controller faceplates became a 360 thing.

question: Sony's PlayStation Portable (PSP) used a proprietary disc format called UMD (Universal Media Disc). The format held 1.8GB of data and was used for both games and movie playback. The PSP's movie market was an experiment Sony pushed. Did it succeed?
answer: No, UMD movies sold poorly; Sony eventually quietly discontinued the format in favor of digital downloads.
choices: No, UMD movies sold poorly; Sony eventually quietly discontinued the format in favor of digital downloads.
Yes, UMD movies became a popular niche that lasted through the PSP's full lifecycle until 2014 launch.
Yes, UMD movies sold over 100 million units lifetime and outsold many home video formats during the same era.
Mixed, UMD movies sold moderately in Japan but were never well-distributed outside of Asian markets.
context: UMD movies failed commercially. Sony's pivot to digital downloads on the PSP came too late to save the format. The PSP itself sold over 80 million units lifetime, largely on games.

question: Atari's 2600 (originally Video Computer System) launched in September 1977. The original 1977 model is known by collectors for its distinctive look. What was the model's nickname?
answer: Heavy Sixer or Woody — six switches across the top, wood-grain panel; the heavy-sixer is the earliest 1977.
choices: Heavy Sixer or Woody — six switches across the top, wood-grain panel; the heavy-sixer is the earliest 1977.
Junior or Lite — the redesigned 1986 console with no switches across the top of the front panel.
Vader or Darth — the 1980 redesigned all-black plastic version that had fewer switches than the original.
Mark or 7800 — the 1986 backward-compatible successor that played original Atari games but flopped at market.
context: Heavy Sixer (1977-78) had six switches and wood-grain. Four-switch (1980-82) followed, then the all-black Vader (1982-86), then the Junior (1986-92). Atari kept making 2600 hardware for 15 years.

question: Howard Scott Warshaw was given five weeks to develop Atari's E.T. (1982) for the Atari 2600. The game was released in time for the 1982 holiday shopping season. How many copies did Atari manufacture?
answer: Approximately 4 million copies, of which approximately 3.5 million were eventually returned unsold.
choices: Approximately 4 million copies, of which approximately 3.5 million were eventually returned unsold.
Approximately 1 million copies, all of which sold but were widely returned for refunds after release.
Approximately 500,000 copies, a relatively cautious print run that nonetheless ran into difficulties.
Approximately 10 million copies, a massive overcommit that single-handedly bankrupted Atari division.
context: The 4-million number is widely cited. The unsold copies (returns and overstock) were buried in Alamogordo in 1983. The 2014 documentary Atari: Game Over excavated the site.

question: Nintendo released two different games as Super Mario Bros. 2 in North America and Japan. The 1988 North American game was actually a re-skinned arcade-style game called Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic. What was the Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 (1986)?
answer: The Lost Levels, an extremely difficult Mario sequel that was released in the U.S. via Super Mario All-Stars.
choices: The Lost Levels, an extremely difficult Mario sequel that was released in the U.S. via Super Mario All-Stars.
Doki Doki Panic itself, with the same alternate version released in both Japan and North America original.
Super Mario USA, a different Mario sequel released only in Japan (1992) after the U.S. SMB2's success.
Super Mario Land, which actually was a Game Boy game (1989) by Gunpei Yokoi's R&D1 team instead.
context: The Lost Levels (Japan's SMB2) was deemed too hard for U.S. players. Doki Doki Panic was re-skinned to SMB2. The Lost Levels reached the U.S. via Super Mario All-Stars (1993).

question: Super Mario World (1990 Japan, 1991 US) was bundled with the Super Famicom and SNES. The game introduced a character who has remained a Mario series staple ever since. What character?
answer: Yoshi, the friendly green dinosaur from Dinosaur Land who Mario rides through 96 levels of the game.
choices: Yoshi, the friendly green dinosaur from Dinosaur Land who Mario rides through 96 levels of the game.
Wario, Mario's evil counterpart, who actually debuted in Super Mario Land 2 (1992) for the Game Boy.
Daisy, the princess from Sarasaland, who actually debuted in Super Mario Land (1989) on Game Boy.
Rosalina, the Comet Observatory princess, who debuted in Super Mario Galaxy (2007) far later.
context: Yoshi's debut in SMW was a huge moment. Yoshi got his own series (Yoshi's Island 1995, Yoshi Story, etc.). Wario, Daisy, and Rosalina are all real Mario characters from different debuts.

question: Super Mario Bros. 3 (1988 Japan, 1990 US) for the NES introduced eight themed worlds. Each had a name based on its terrain. The third world was the unique one — its title reflected a non-terrain concept. What was World 3 called?
answer: Water Land, with its tropical-themed levels, including the famous airship-pursued levels of the world.
choices: Water Land, with its tropical-themed levels, including the famous airship-pursued levels of the world.
Pipe Land, the only thematically non-terrain world; its levels are filled with pipe-themed obstacles.
Sky Land, the world set among the clouds and floating platforms in the heavens above the ground.
Giant Land, the world where everything was scaled up to twice size — enemies and platforms alike doubled.
context: All four are real SMB3 worlds. Pipe Land is World 7. Sky Land is World 5. Giant Land is World 4. Water Land is World 3.

question: Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past (1991 Japan, 1992 US) for the Super Famicom and SNES introduced the Dark World — a parallel realm to the Light World of Hyrule. Who is the main antagonist of the game?
answer: Agahnim, the wizard who serves Ganon and was sent to take over Hyrule Castle in the Light World realm.
choices: Agahnim, the wizard who serves Ganon and was sent to take over Hyrule Castle in the Light World realm.
Vaati, the wind sorcerer from Four Swords (2002) and Minish Cap (2004), much later in the series.
Demise, the demon king from Skyward Sword (2011), an entirely different antagonist set far in the past.
Zant, the antagonist of Twilight Princess (2006), serving Ganondorf in the Twilight Realm parallel world.
context: Agahnim is the immediate antagonist; Ganon is the final boss revealed during the Dark World portion of the game. All four are real Zelda series antagonists from different titles.

question: The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (2000) for the Nintendo 64 was developed in roughly one year, reusing Ocarina of Time's engine. The game's central mechanic was a three-day countdown to the moon falling on the world. What is the cycle exactly?
answer: Three in-game days (72 in-game hours, roughly 54 real minutes); Link uses the Song of Time to rewind.
choices: Three in-game days (72 in-game hours, roughly 54 real minutes); Link uses the Song of Time to rewind.
Five in-game days (120 in-game hours, roughly 60 real minutes); a more generous time-loop structure.
Two in-game days; the game's tight pacing was the result of this even more restrictive cycle structure.
Seven in-game days; the same one-week cycle that the Phantom Hourglass DS game uses for time.
context: The 3-day cycle is iconic. Link can slow time with Inverted Song of Time. The Song of Time rewinds to dawn of day one. Eiji Aonuma directed this dark sequel.

question: Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker (2002 Japan, 2003 US) for the GameCube featured a cel-shaded art style — flat colors with cartoon-like outlines. The art style sparked controversy among fans. Why?
answer: Fans expected a realistic art style like 2000's Spaceworld demo; the cartoonish look felt like a regression.
choices: Fans expected a realistic art style like 2000's Spaceworld demo; the cartoonish look felt like a regression.
The art style took longer to render, causing the game to ship with reduced final dungeons by half.
The art style was an in-game easter egg only available after beating the game once on hard mode.
The art style was Capcom's choice, not Nintendo's; many Zelda fans rejected the Capcom involvement.
context: The 2000 Spaceworld demo had shown Link fighting Ganondorf in realistic style. The 2001 Wind Waker reveal in cel-shaded style was a shock. The game was later vindicated as a cult favorite.

question: The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess (2006) was a Wii launch title (and a final GameCube title). The game was the longest Zelda game ever made at the time of release. The Wii version had a notable change. What was reversed?
answer: The world was mirrored left-to-right so right-handed players could use the Wii Remote in their right hand.
choices: The world was mirrored left-to-right so right-handed players could use the Wii Remote in their right hand.
Link became left-handed; he had always been right-handed in the GameCube version of the game.
Music tracks were re-recorded; Wii's CD audio quality replaced GameCube's compressed sound files.
The game required 480p output through component cables; standard composite cables were not supported.
context: The Wii mirroring is famous. Right-handed Wii Remote players could now use Link's sword properly. The GameCube version remained unmirrored for traditional players.

question: Final Fantasy VII (1997) for the PlayStation features a famous mid-game event that shocked players who had been told the game was about a hero rescuing a damsel. While avoiding spoilers, what disc does this event occur on?
answer: The end of Disc 1 — well before the game's actual ending, a deliberate Sakaguchi pacing choice.
choices: The end of Disc 1 — well before the game's actual ending, a deliberate Sakaguchi pacing choice.
The end of Disc 3 — at the very end of the game, the climactic event saved for the last fifteen minutes.
The end of Disc 2 — at the midpoint of the game's three-disc structure, after a Wutai sub-quest.
The middle of Disc 1 — far earlier than players expect, leading to immediate scoreplay reactions.
context: Without spoiling specifics, the end of Disc 1 event reshaped JRPG storytelling. Square's Sakaguchi included it specifically to subvert expectations and surprise players in a new way.

question: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty (2001) for the PlayStation 2 was famously deceptive in its marketing. Solid Snake appeared prominently in trailers and on the box. What did players actually discover at the start of the game?
answer: The protagonist for most of the game was a new rookie named Raiden, with Snake only in the prologue act.
choices: The protagonist for most of the game was a new rookie named Raiden, with Snake only in the prologue act.
The game switched between Snake and a second character every chapter, with no clear protagonist focus.
The game was the first Metal Gear without Solid Snake at all; Big Boss was the protagonist throughout.
The game's deception was that Solid Snake was on Metal Gear in disguise the entire time as another character.
context: Raiden's appearance as the protagonist of MGS2 was a major divisive moment. Kojima defended the choice as deliberate deconstruction. Raiden returned in MGS4 (2008) and Revengeance (2013).

question: Square Enix's Final Fantasy VII Remake (2020) for the PlayStation 4 was structured as an episodic project. The first installment covered approximately what portion of the original 1997 game's storyline?
answer: Roughly the Midgar opening, the first 4-6 hours of the original 1997 game expanded to a full game.
choices: Roughly the Midgar opening, the first 4-6 hours of the original 1997 game expanded to a full game.
Roughly the entire Disc 1, before the famous mid-game event, expanded to a full 30-hour adventure.
Roughly the entire game's storyline, but with the timeline rewoven through new alternate paths only.
Roughly just the first 1-2 hours of the original, with the rest planned for future installments only.
context: FF7 Remake's expansion of just the Midgar opening was a Square design choice. The second installment, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth (2024), expanded the world-map portion of the story too.

question: Yuji Horii's Dragon Quest (1986) for the Famicom is widely credited as the foundational Japanese RPG. The series was originally known as Dragon Warrior in the United States due to a trademark dispute. With whose game brand?
answer: DragonQuest, a pen-and-paper RPG from Simulations Publications Inc. (SPI) that held the U.S. trademark.
choices: DragonQuest, a pen-and-paper RPG from Simulations Publications Inc. (SPI) that held the U.S. trademark.
Dungeons and Dragons, with TSR holding the trademark on the Dragon word in role-playing-game contexts.
Dragonlance, the TSR campaign-setting and novel series whose trademark might have conflicted with Dragon Quest.
Drakkhen, an unrelated French RPG that held the European Dragon-name trademark in role-playing games.
context: DragonQuest by SPI was a real 1980 pen-and-paper RPG. The U.S. trademark was eventually freed up, and Dragon Quest VIII (2005) released under the original name. Yuji Horii has continued directing the series.

question: Sega's Phantasy Star (1987) for the Sega Master System was the company's response to Dragon Quest. The game was technologically ambitious for the Master System and featured first-person 3D dungeon exploration. Who designed the game?
answer: Yuji Naka (programmer) and Rieko Kodama (artist); Naka would later create Sonic the Hedgehog (1991).
choices: Yuji Naka (programmer) and Rieko Kodama (artist); Naka would later create Sonic the Hedgehog (1991).
