Yu Suzuki, the Sega AM2 arcade legend who designed Out Run, After Burner, and Virtua Fighter.
Hideki Sato, a Sega executive who handled hardware engineering but did not design game software.
Toshiyuki Miyata, a Sega designer who worked on Wonder Boy series, not Phantasy Star at the time.
context: Yuji Naka, Rieko Kodama, and Tokuhiko Uwabo all worked on Phantasy Star. Naka later created Sonic. The game was a flagship Master System exclusive against Dragon Quest on Famicom.

question: Chrono Trigger (1995) for the Super Famicom was a Squaresoft Dream Team production. The game's three lead creators came from different RPG companies: Hironobu Sakaguchi (Square), Yuji Horii (Enix), and a third name from another studio. Who?
answer: Akira Toriyama (Dragon Quest series), the manga artist who also did character designs for Chrono Trigger.
choices: Akira Toriyama (Dragon Quest series), the manga artist who also did character designs for Chrono Trigger.
Yu Suzuki (Sega AM2), who never worked at Square or Enix; this was Square's internal Dream Team only.
Tetsuya Mizuguchi (Sega), the Rez and Lumines designer who would later make Space Channel 5.
Yoshio Sakamoto (Nintendo), the Metroid director who has never worked outside Nintendo at all.
context: Toriyama's Dragon Quest history made him Enix-affiliated. Chrono Trigger Dream Team was Square's coup. The game was ported repeatedly: PS1 (1999), DS (2008), PC, mobile.

question: Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars (1996) for the Super Famicom and SNES was a Square-Nintendo collaboration. The game introduced new characters not from the Mario universe. What was the lead non-Mario character?
answer: Geno, an angelic warrior who possesses a doll body; Square retained the character and Nintendo cannot use him.
choices: Geno, an angelic warrior who possesses a doll body; Square retained the character and Nintendo cannot use him.
Mallow, the marshmallow-prince-disguised-as-frog character; Nintendo retained him for later Paper Mario games.
Bowser Jr., the Bowser-son-character who actually first appeared in Super Mario Sunshine (2002) later.
Rosalina, the Star Princess character who actually debuted in Super Mario Galaxy (2007) much later.
context: Geno and Mallow are SMRPG originals. Mallow remained accessible through Paper Mario references. Geno's IP rights became famously tangled between Square and Nintendo for decades.

question: GoldenEye 007 (1997) for the N64 featured a multiplayer mode where players could choose from several weapons including a controversial choice. Which weapon was famously banned in friend-group play due to being too powerful?
answer: Proximity mines, especially on the Complex map; players could mine doorways for instant kills upon entry.
choices: Proximity mines, especially on the Complex map; players could mine doorways for instant kills upon entry.
Rocket launcher, on Facility map; one-shot kills that were too dependent on aim luck at all stages.
Sniper rifle, on Stack map; cross-map kills were too easy because of the level's open architecture.
Cougar Magnum, on Library map; the powerful pistol that could one-shot opponents at close range.
context: Proximity mines + Complex remains an in-joke among GoldenEye players. The level's tight corridors made the mines absolutely deadly. House rules banned it routinely.

question: Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. (1999) for the N64 was directed by Masahiro Sakurai at HAL Laboratory. Sakurai pitched the game internally as a Nintendo-mascot fighter at a time when Nintendo was wary of crossing characters between franchises. How did Sakurai secure the project?
answer: He produced a prototype with placeholder characters; Nintendo approved after seeing it play well.
choices: He produced a prototype with placeholder characters; Nintendo approved after seeing it play well.
He had Hiroshi Yamauchi, Nintendo president, personally request a fighting game from HAL Laboratory.
He licensed the characters from a third-party fighting game studio that had been pitching a similar game.
He persuaded Iwata, Miyamoto, and Yamauchi simultaneously over a single dinner meeting one evening.
context: Sakurai's prototype-first approach is famous. He has reused the strategy throughout his career. Smash Bros. became a Nintendo-defining franchise across multiple generations.

question: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid (1998) was developed at Konami in Tokyo. The protagonist Solid Snake's English voice actor became known for his gravelly delivery and continued as Snake through multiple games. Who voices Solid Snake in English?
answer: David Hayter, who has played Solid Snake since 1998 and also wrote X-Men (2000) screenplay.
choices: David Hayter, who has played Solid Snake since 1998 and also wrote X-Men (2000) screenplay.
Kiefer Sutherland, who replaced David Hayter as Snake/Big Boss only in Metal Gear Solid V (2015).
Cam Clarke, the voice of Solid Snake in the original MSX-era Metal Gear 1 and 2 (1987-90 ports).
Doug Erholtz, the voice of Big Boss in Metal Gear Solid Portable Ops (2006) and other handheld titles.
context: Hayter is the iconic Snake voice. Sutherland replaced him in MGSV (2015). All four are real Metal Gear voice actors. Cam Clarke voiced the original MSX Solid Snake.

question: Konami's Silent Hill (1999) for the PlayStation was developed by Team Silent. The protagonist Harry Mason searches a fog-shrouded town for his daughter. The game's fog was famously a technical workaround. What was it?
answer: PlayStation hardware draw-distance limits; fog hid background pop-in, becoming a defining atmosphere.
choices: PlayStation hardware draw-distance limits; fog hid background pop-in, becoming a defining atmosphere.
Polygon-budget limits on character models; fog meant fewer characters needed to be rendered at once.
Soundtrack-budget limits; the fog masked the lack of orchestral music and enabled industrial ambient instead.
Voice-acting budget limits; fog enabled less detailed character animations during dialog scenes.
context: Silent Hill's fog is a famous example of constraint-driven design becoming iconic. Akira Yamaoka's industrial score adds to it. Silent Hill 2 (2001) is the genre peak.

question: Capcom's Resident Evil (1996) for the PlayStation invented the survival-horror genre. Director Shinji Mikami's team developed the game over roughly two years. The game's mansion setting was inspired by what 1989 film?
answer: Sweet Home, the Capcom-licensed Famicom game adapted from Kiyoshi Kurosawa's 1989 J-horror film.
choices: Sweet Home, the Capcom-licensed Famicom game adapted from Kiyoshi Kurosawa's 1989 J-horror film.
The Shining (1980), Stanley Kubrick's adaptation of Stephen King's 1977 novel set in a haunted hotel.
Re-Animator (1985), the H.P. Lovecraft-inspired horror film that influenced the zombie mechanics directly.
The Evil Dead (1981), Sam Raimi's cabin-in-the-woods horror film about possession and demons.
context: Sweet Home was a 1989 Capcom Famicom game; its mansion exploration directly inspired Resident Evil's design language. Mikami originally pitched RE as a sequel to Sweet Home.

question: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996) for the PlayStation was developed at the Santa Monica studio. The game was a Sony exclusive at a time when Sony lacked a mascot character to rival Mario or Sonic. Crash was developed under the working title what?
answer: Sonic's Ass Game, a Naughty Dog internal joke about Crash being a back-of-character (you see his butt running).
choices: Sonic's Ass Game, a Naughty Dog internal joke about Crash being a back-of-character (you see his butt running).
Willy the Wombat, a Sega-approved working title that Naughty Dog later switched away from for Sony.
Sonic 3D Bandicoot, a working title combining mascot inspirations from Sega's brand into a 3D form.
Bandi-Cute, a working title Naughty Dog proposed that Sony immediately rejected as too cutesy.
context: Sonic's Ass Game is well-attested in Naughty Dog founder Jason Rubin and developer Andy Gavin's accounts. The you-see-his-butt running camera was the central design joke from the start.

question: Insomniac Games developed Spyro the Dragon (1998) for the PlayStation. The game starred a purple baby dragon and was Sony's third mascot platformer (after Crash). What was Spyro's first major animal companion?
answer: Sparx the dragonfly, who acts as Spyro's health indicator (color changes by hits) throughout the entire trilogy.
choices: Sparx the dragonfly, who acts as Spyro's health indicator (color changes by hits) throughout the entire trilogy.
Hunter the cheetah, who first appeared in Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage (1999), not the original Spyro.
Bentley the yeti, who first appeared in Spyro 2 and 3, not the original Spyro 1 (1998) on PS1.
Bianca the rabbit-sorceress, who debuted in Spyro 3: Year of the Dragon (2000) as a key antagonist.
context: Sparx the dragonfly is Spyro's companion from the start. He acts as a hit-point indicator. Hunter, Bentley, and Bianca are real Spyro characters from later games in the trilogy.

question: Sony's Gran Turismo (1997) for the PlayStation was developed by Polyphony Digital under Kazunori Yamauchi. The game pioneered the real-driving-simulator genre with over 140 cars. What unusual presentational choice did the game make?
answer: The driver / cockpit was hidden — all races were shown from the bumper / hood or chase camera only.
choices: The driver / cockpit was hidden — all races were shown from the bumper / hood or chase camera only.
All races were shown from a top-down isometric perspective, similar to the Micro Machines series.
All cars were rendered as flat-shaded polygons, like Virtua Fighter's character models for that era.
All sound effects were synthesized from a soundboard rather than sampled from real cars or audio.
context: GT's lack of a driver model was a deliberate sim-focused choice. Yamauchi has continued directing the series. GT2 (1999) was even larger; GT3 launched the PS2 in 2001.

question: Konami's Castlevania (1986 Famicom Disk System, 1987 NES) starred Simon Belmont, a vampire hunter armed with a whip called the Vampire Killer. Simon's appearance was based on what film actor?
answer: Frank Langella in his role as Count Dracula in the 1979 film adaptation of the Broadway play.
choices: Frank Langella in his role as Count Dracula in the 1979 film adaptation of the Broadway play.
Christopher Lee in his role as Count Dracula across multiple Hammer Films of the 1960s and 1970s.
Klaus Kinski in his role as Count Dracula in Werner Herzog's 1979 film Nosferatu the Vampyre.
Bela Lugosi in his role as Count Dracula in the 1931 Universal film, the original cinematic Dracula.
context: Simon Belmont's design is generally compared to Frank Langella's 1979 Dracula. The Castlevania series has continued under Konami; the 2017 Netflix anime adapted Symphony of the Night arcs.

question: Capcom's Mega Man (1987 Japan, 1987 US NES) was designed by Akira Kitamura and featured character designs by Keiji Inafune. The titular hero is a robot, but in Japanese the series is named differently. What is the Japanese name?
answer: Rockman, named for the rock-paper-scissors gameplay loop of weapon-versus-Robot-Master matchups.
choices: Rockman, named for the rock-paper-scissors gameplay loop of weapon-versus-Robot-Master matchups.
Megaman, the same name as in the U.S. with no Japanese alternative branding for the franchise.
Cyber Boy, an early prototype name that Capcom changed before release in both Japan and the U.S.
Robotech, a name Capcom briefly considered but rejected due to anime trademark issues at the time.
context: Rockman in Japan, Mega Man in the U.S. The rock-paper-scissors mechanic determines weapon weaknesses between Robot Masters. Keiji Inafune later left Capcom to make Mighty No. 9 (2016).

question: Capcom's Mega Man X (1993) for the Super Famicom and SNES launched a new sub-series set 100 years after the classic Mega Man series. The protagonist is X, a Reploid robot. Who is X's allied counterpart, a red-and-white maverick hunter?
answer: Zero, the sword-wielding red robot who would become playable in Mega Man X4 (1997) and later games.
choices: Zero, the sword-wielding red robot who would become playable in Mega Man X4 (1997) and later games.
Bass, a Mega Man classic-series character who actually debuted in Mega Man 7 (1995), not the X-series.
ProtoMan, an older brother character from classic Mega Man, who never crossed over to the X-series.
Sigma, who is actually the antagonist of the X-series and not an ally of X at all under any circumstances.
context: Zero is X's iconic ally. Sigma is the main villain across the X-series. ProtoMan is Mega Man's red-shielded brother. The Zero spin-off games (2002-05) became cult favorites.

question: Nintendo's Kid Icarus (1986 Famicom Disk, 1987 NES) featured a young angel named Pit, armed with a bow, climbing through the Underworld. The game was developed by Nintendo R&D1 (Gunpei Yokoi's team). What was the game's working title in Japan?
answer: Light Mythology: The Mirror of Palutena, the Japanese title using Greek-mythology references throughout.
choices: Light Mythology: The Mirror of Palutena, the Japanese title using Greek-mythology references throughout.
Sky Warrior, an alternate working title that Nintendo briefly considered before settling on Kid Icarus.
Angel Wings, an early proposed name that referenced Pit's flight ability that he gains at Stage 4-4.
Underworld Quest, a working title that emphasized the multi-level structure of the game's design.
context: Hikari Shinwa: Palutena no Kagami is the Japanese name. Greek-mythology references run throughout (Medusa, Palutena, Centurions, Eggplant Wizard).

question: Fumito Ueda's Ico (2001) for the PlayStation 2 features a young boy named Ico escorting a translucent girl named Yorda through a vast castle. The gameplay revolves around holding her hand. What does Yorda's defining language feature?
answer: She speaks a fictional untranslated language; the player only sees Ico's responses in text.
choices: She speaks a fictional untranslated language; the player only sees Ico's responses in text.
She speaks English with subtitles in the player's chosen language throughout the game's runtime.
She is mute and communicates only through gestures and body language alone in the entire game.
She speaks an in-game translation of medieval Japanese, with English subtitles available as an option.
context: Yorda's untranslated speech (an invented language) is part of Ico's unique atmosphere. Ueda recorded the language with non-actors and processed it to be uncanny without being silly.

question: Nintendo's Mario Kart 64 (1996) for the N64 was directed by Hideki Konno. The game's Battle Mode featured four arenas. One arena had no walls but rather an open void below for kart-elimination falls. What was its name?
answer: Block Fort, a multi-tier 3D arena with limited walls and many open edges to fall into the void below.
choices: Block Fort, a multi-tier 3D arena with limited walls and many open edges to fall into the void below.
Skyscraper, a high-rise outdoor arena with open walls and a steady fall into open sky for elimination.
Big Donut, a circular doughnut-shaped arena where players could fall into the central hole gap.
Double Deck, a two-level arena with limited walls; players could fall off either deck into open void.
context: All four are real MK64 Battle Mode arenas. Block Fort and Big Donut are the most beloved. The Battle Mode soundtrack remains a fan favorite of the N64 game's whole library.

question: Mattel's Intellivision launched in 1979 as a direct competitor to the Atari 2600. The console featured a 16-bit CPU (the GI CP1610) and a distinctive 16-direction controller. What unusual controller feature did the Intellivision pioneer?
answer: Overlay cards slid over a 12-key numeric keypad on the controller for game-specific input layouts.
choices: Overlay cards slid over a 12-key numeric keypad on the controller for game-specific input layouts.
Force-feedback rumble in the controller, three years before similar features in arcade cabinets.
Built-in trackball, replacing the joystick for many of the early sports games on the system release.
Voice-recognition microphone, requiring spoken commands to activate certain game actions.
context: The keypad+overlay system was Intellivision's signature feature. Different overlays for Football, Baseball, Dungeons & Dragons. The console sold roughly 3 million units lifetime before discontinuation.

question: Coleco's ColecoVision launched in 1982 as a third-generation video game console competing with the Atari 2600 and Intellivision. The console's killer app was a port of a then-recent arcade game. What was bundled with the ColecoVision?
answer: Donkey Kong, in a high-quality home port that helped the ColecoVision launch successfully against rivals.
choices: Donkey Kong, in a high-quality home port that helped the ColecoVision launch successfully against rivals.
Pac-Man, in a notably better port than the famously poor 1982 Atari 2600 Pac-Man home version.
Frogger, in a port that mirrored the arcade Frogger gameplay more faithfully than the Atari 2600 version.
Space Invaders, in a port that included a graphic upgrade not seen on the original arcade cabinet.
context: Donkey Kong was the ColecoVision pack-in. Coleco's deal with Nintendo for Donkey Kong was a coup. ColecoVision sold roughly 2 million units before the 1983 crash.

question: Nintendo's Family Computer (Famicom) launched in Japan on July 15, 1983 at a price of 14,800 yen. The console used a custom CPU based on the MOS 6502. What was the famous design quirk of the Famicom controllers?
answer: The microphone in the second controller; Player 2 had a mic, Player 1 did not, used in Zelda and others.
choices: The microphone in the second controller; Player 2 had a mic, Player 1 did not, used in Zelda and others.
The detachable cord, allowing controllers to be unplugged and switched between controller ports easily.
The four-button layout (with two extra buttons L and R), an unusually busy controller for the era.
The built-in vibration motor, which would not be standard on home consoles for another decade and a half.
context: The Famicom mic was a hardware oddity. Players could blow into it for certain game effects (Legend of Zelda's Pol's Voice enemy famously). The mic was removed for the NES (1985 US).

question: Nintendo's Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) launched in North America in October 1985 in a limited New York test, then full national launch in 1986. The system was marketed not as a game console but as something else to avoid the 1983 crash stigma. What?
answer: An 'entertainment system' with a R.O.B. (Robotic Operating Buddy) accessory, framing it as a toy.
choices: An 'entertainment system' with a R.O.B. (Robotic Operating Buddy) accessory, framing it as a toy.
A 'home computer' with optional keyboard accessory, similar to how the Atari was being marketed too.
A 'video disk player' with optional movie cassettes, with games as a secondary feature category for it.
A 'data terminal' connected to a planned Nintendo telephone-line service that ultimately never launched.
context: The R.O.B. and Light Zapper helped Nintendo position the NES as a toy after the home-console crash. The strategy worked; the NES sold over 60 million units lifetime worldwide.

question: Sony's PlayStation launched in Japan in December 1994. The console's development was led by Ken Kutaragi, who had been Sony's lead engineer on the planned Super NES CD-ROM add-on with Nintendo. When was the original PlayStation finally discontinued?
answer: March 2006 in Japan (after a near-12-year production run), the longest-lived major home console of its era.
choices: March 2006 in Japan (after a near-12-year production run), the longest-lived major home console of its era.
December 2002 in Japan, with North America following one year later in late 2003 product cycles.
March 2008 in Japan and globally, with production extended for budget retail markets globally.
November 2000 in Japan, when the PlayStation 2 launched and superseded the original console.
context: The PSone (a redesigned smaller version, 2000-2006) extended the original PlayStation's life. The console sold over 100 million units. The PlayStation 2 launched 2000 but PS1 production continued.

question: Nintendo's Game Boy Advance launched in Japan in March 2001 and North America in June 2001. The original GBA had no backlight. The 2003 redesign added a frontlight and a clamshell design. What was the redesigned model called?
answer: Game Boy Advance SP, featuring a clamshell folding case and a frontlit screen (later backlit in 2005).
choices: Game Boy Advance SP, featuring a clamshell folding case and a frontlit screen (later backlit in 2005).
Game Boy Advance Plus, a North American-only redesign that never received the global re-release brand.
Game Boy Light, a Japan-only redesign that did not receive a global release outside of Japan retail.
Game Boy Micro, the 2005 ultra-compact redesign that postdated the SP rather than predated it instead.
context: GBA SP (2003) had the iconic clamshell. Game Boy Micro (2005) was the ultra-compact final redesign. Game Boy Light was a Game Boy Color refresh, not GBA.

question: Nintendo's Nintendo DS launched in November 2004 in North America. The console's name stood for Dual Screen (its top and bottom screens). The bottom screen was touch-sensitive. What was the marketing tagline at launch?
answer: Touching Is Good, Nintendo's launch tagline emphasizing the touchscreen as a unique selling feature.
choices: Touching Is Good, Nintendo's launch tagline emphasizing the touchscreen as a unique selling feature.
Welcome to the Future, a generic Nintendo positioning statement that was actually used for the Wii.
Bridges Generations, a tagline emphasizing the backward-compatibility with Game Boy Advance games.
Nintendo Innovates, a tagline emphasizing the company's pivot away from console-vs-console competition.
context: Touching Is Good was the launch tagline. Backward-compatibility with Game Boy Advance was a feature, but the touchscreen was the marketing focus. The DS sold over 154 million units lifetime.

question: Konami's Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (1997) for the PlayStation features a soundtrack widely considered among the greatest in video-game history. The composer's score blends orchestral, choral, and rock arrangements. Who composed it?
answer: Michiru Yamane, who scored multiple Castlevania entries; she left Konami in 2008 to go independent.
choices: Michiru Yamane, who scored multiple Castlevania entries; she left Konami in 2008 to go independent.
Akira Yamaoka, who scored the Silent Hill series instead at Konami, not Castlevania at all.
Yasunori Mitsuda, who scored Chrono Trigger and Xenogears at Square in the same general era.
Hitoshi Sakimoto, who scored Final Fantasy XII (2006) and many of the SaGa series at Square Enix.
context: Michiru Yamane is the most celebrated Castlevania composer. Her work on Symphony of the Night, Aria of Sorrow, Bloodlines, and many others defined the series. Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night (2019) reunited her with Igarashi.

question: Nobuo Uematsu is the composer of most Final Fantasy series scores from FF I (1987) through FF X (2001). His most famous single composition is the climactic boss theme of Final Fantasy VII (1997). What is the song called?
answer: One-Winged Angel, with Latin choral lyrics by Sakaguchi and Uematsu jointly drawn from the Carmina Burana.
choices: One-Winged Angel, with Latin choral lyrics by Sakaguchi and Uematsu jointly drawn from the Carmina Burana.
Liberi Fatali, the opening cinematic theme from Final Fantasy VIII (1999), with Latin choral arrangement.
Dancing Mad, the multi-part Kefka final-boss theme from Final Fantasy VI (1994), without Latin lyrics.
To Zanarkand, the piano-and-orchestra theme from Final Fantasy X (2001), without Latin lyrics or chorale.
context: One-Winged Angel uses Carmina Burana-style Latin chorus. Sephiroth's theme defined orchestral video-game scoring. Uematsu has performed it live in Distant Worlds concerts globally.

question: Yuzo Koshiro is a video-game composer renowned for his early-1990s Sega Genesis work. He scored Streets of Rage (1991) and its sequels. He also scored a different game published by Enix in 1990 for the Super Famicom — what was it?
answer: ActRaiser, the Super Famicom action-RPG-and-simulation hybrid game with an orchestral soundtrack.
choices: ActRaiser, the Super Famicom action-RPG-and-simulation hybrid game with an orchestral soundtrack.
Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap, the 1989 Sega Master System action-platformer with chiptune music.
Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, which was scored by Michiru Yamane at Konami, not Koshiro.
Y's series, mostly by Yuzo Koshiro's earlier Falcom team — but he scored Y's I and II, not their late entries.
context: Koshiro's ActRaiser score is considered among the best on the Super Famicom. He also scored Y's I-III at Falcom (1987-89) before Sega freelance work.

question: Koji Kondo is the long-time Nintendo composer responsible for the Mario and Zelda series themes. His Super Mario Bros. (1985) overworld theme is one of the most recognized melodies in the world. How long is that famous theme melody?
answer: The Ground Theme (Mario's main song) is approximately 1:31 long in its full looping arrangement.
choices: The Ground Theme (Mario's main song) is approximately 1:31 long in its full looping arrangement.
The Ground Theme is exactly 30 seconds long in a single loop that repeats forever during gameplay.
The Ground Theme is approximately 3 minutes long in a longer multi-section arrangement on the title.
The Ground Theme has only 8 measures and lasts 12 seconds before looping back to the start.
context: The Ground Theme has multiple sections (A, B, C, D) totaling around 1:31. Kondo also composed Super Mario Bros. Underground Theme, Castle Theme, and the Star Power music.

question: Namco's Katamari Damacy (2004) for the PlayStation 2 was directed by Keita Takahashi. The game's quirky premise (rolling a ball of increasing junk to recreate the cosmos) was matched by an equally quirky soundtrack. What did the soundtrack include?
answer: Japanese pop, scat singing, big-band swing, and choral chanting, by composer Yuu Miyake's team.
choices: Japanese pop, scat singing, big-band swing, and choral chanting, by composer Yuu Miyake's team.
Strictly orchestral classical pieces commissioned from the Tokyo Symphony Orchestra to make it serious.
Heavy metal arrangements written and recorded specifically by the band Anthrax for the cosmic theme.
Solo piano arrangements scored by Yann Tiersen, the Amelie composer, in a deliberate French art-film homage.
context: Yuu Miyake produced. The soundtrack's whimsical eclecticism matched the game. Many tracks have become beloved earworms. Katamari Damacy spawned a series and a Nintendo Switch port in 2018.

question: The 1999 NBC series Freaks and Geeks, created by Paul Feig, was set in suburban Michigan in 1980-81. The series featured several memorable arcade scenes in its episodes. The high-school cast played pool and arcade games at a specific establishment. What kind of game did the geeks play?
answer: Atari 2600 home gaming and Galaga / Asteroids arcade visits, period-appropriate for the 1980-81 setting.
choices: Atari 2600 home gaming and Galaga / Asteroids arcade visits, period-appropriate for the 1980-81 setting.
Sega Master System home gaming, anachronistic for the 1980-81 setting; the SMS came out in 1986.
Nintendo 64 home gaming, anachronistic by 16 years; the N64 came out in 1996, well after the setting.
Game Boy handheld gaming, anachronistic by 9 years; the Game Boy came out in 1989, after the setting.
context: Freaks and Geeks's period accuracy is legendary; the show's Atari games were correctly cataloged. The series only ran 18 episodes but is considered one of the great single-season runs in TV.

question: Universal's The Wizard (1989) was a feature film starring Fred Savage as a boy who escorts his younger brother to Los Angeles for a video-game championship. The film's climax featured the U.S. debut of a then-unreleased Nintendo game. What game?
answer: Super Mario Bros. 3, six months before its U.S. February 1990 release; the warp whistle scene became famous.
choices: Super Mario Bros. 3, six months before its U.S. February 1990 release; the warp whistle scene became famous.
Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! making its U.S. debut; the film promoted the boxing-game craze of that era.
Bionic Commando, demonstrating Capcom's hook-shot mechanics for the upcoming U.S. holiday release.
Mega Man 2, demonstrating Capcom's eight-Robot-Master gameplay for the U.S. fall release.
context: The Wizard is widely viewed as a 100-minute Nintendo commercial for SMB3 and the Power Glove. The warp whistle scene is iconic to early video-game cinema history.

question: Cloak and Dagger (1984) was a spy thriller film starring Henry Thomas (then 12, from E.T.) and based on a kid's interaction with a fictional video game. The film tied in with a real arcade game of the same name. What was the gameplay?
answer: Top-down maze chase, with twin-stick controls; players directed an agent through enemy-filled stations.
choices: Top-down maze chase, with twin-stick controls; players directed an agent through enemy-filled stations.
Side-scrolling action platformer, similar to Donkey Kong; players climbed ladders and dodged barrels.
First-person 3D maze, similar to Wizardry; players explored corridors and fought enemies in 3D space.
Space-shooter game like Galaga; players dispatched enemy ships in formation from the bottom of screen.
context: Cloak and Dagger by Atari was a real 1984 arcade game tied into the film. The gameplay was twin-stick top-down. The film starred Dabney Coleman as well. The whole concept was unusual cross-promotion.

answer: Real animals are nearly extinct; owning a live animal is a status symbol; Deckard wants a real sheep.

All humans must take a daily psychiatric drug to function; the test for androids measures dosage compliance.
Androids are physically indistinguishable from humans only by genetic test; the Voigt-Kampff is a fraud.
Earth has been abandoned; only the elderly remain; android Hunters maintain the empty city as caretakers.
context: The real-vs-fake animal theme is central to the novel and largely absent from Blade Runner the film. Dick's central question was the nature of empathy as the human-android dividing line.

question: Arthur C. Clarke's 1968 novel 2001: A Space Odyssey was written in collaboration with Stanley Kubrick's film of the same year. The novel was originally based on Clarke's earlier short story, written in 1948. What was the source short story called?
answer: The Sentinel, written in 1948 as an entry for a BBC competition that it did not win.
choices: The Sentinel, written in 1948 as an entry for a BBC competition that it did not win.
Childhood's End, Clarke's 1953 novel about alien Overlords arriving and ushering humans into next stage.
Rendezvous with Rama, Clarke's 1973 novel about an alien spaceship transiting through the solar system.
The Fountains of Paradise, Clarke's 1979 novel about constructing a space elevator on the equator.
context: The Sentinel describes an alien pyramid on the Moon. The expansion into 2001 happened during Kubrick's collaboration. Childhood's End, Rendezvous with Rama, and Fountains of Paradise are all real Clarke novels.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings was published in three volumes — The Fellowship of the Ring (July 1954), The Two Towers (November 1954), and The Return of the King (October 1955). The book had been written across how many years?
answer: About 12 years (1937-49) of drafting; another 5 years of revisions before the published 1954-55 release.
choices: About 12 years (1937-49) of drafting; another 5 years of revisions before the published 1954-55 release.
About 3 years (1949-51) of frantic writing after Tolkien had retired from Oxford and could focus.
About 20 years (1929-49) — basically all of Tolkien's middle adulthood spent on the book.
About 30 years (1919-49) — Tolkien had begun working on Middle-earth right after WWI service.
context: Tolkien started LOTR in December 1937, immediately after The Hobbit. The first draft was finished by 1949. Revisions and the Council of Elrond's geneology shaping took until 1954.

question: Frank Herbert's Dune was published in 1965 after the manuscript was rejected by 20 publishers. It was finally accepted by Chilton Books — a publisher otherwise known for auto-repair manuals. What was Herbert's research basis for Dune?
answer: A 1957 magazine article assignment about the controlled-dune-restoration project at Florence, Oregon.
choices: A 1957 magazine article assignment about the controlled-dune-restoration project at Florence, Oregon.
A 1950 expedition Herbert took to the Sahara Desert in Morocco to study Berber tribes there.
A 1962 sabbatical Herbert spent at the University of Khartoum studying Sudanese desert ecology.
A 1958 government grant Herbert received to study U.S. Forest Service grazing policy in Nevada.
context: The Florence, Oregon dune project gave Herbert his ecology focus. The 6-year project of researching, writing, and revising Dune produced a 25-page essay called They Stopped the Moving Sands as a magazine pitch.

question: On April 18, 1938, Action Comics #1 hit newsstands. Cover-priced at 10 cents, it featured a strange visitor from another planet on the cover, lifting a green sedan. The character was Superman. The comic recently sold at auction. What did a high-grade copy bring in 2022?
answer: Six million dollars (CGC 8.0 copy), the highest sale for any comic book in publication history.
choices: Six million dollars (CGC 8.0 copy), the highest sale for any comic book in publication history.
One million dollars, the highest comic-book sale until much later in 2021 with a copy of Captain America.
Half a million dollars, a milestone sale that surpassed previous high marks for Golden Age comics records.
Two-hundred thousand dollars, the original mid-2000s estimate for a high-grade copy of Action 1.
context: Action Comics #1 (CGC 8.0) sold for $6 million in April 2022. Estimated print run was ~200,000. About 100 high-grade copies are known to survive today.

question: Detective Comics #27 (May 1939) introduced Batman, the Bat-Man, in a six-page story by Bob Kane and Bill Finger. The story was called The Case of the Chemical Syndicate. The first published Batman story used a simple plot. Where was Bruce Wayne shown to live?
answer: An apartment in 'Manhattan'; only later was Wayne Manor established as Batman's residence in Gotham.
choices: An apartment in 'Manhattan'; only later was Wayne Manor established as Batman's residence in Gotham.
Wayne Manor in Gotham City, exactly as he has always been depicted in later comics and films.
A penthouse in Gotham City, on the top floor of the Wayne Industries headquarters building skyscraper.
An estate in Connecticut, which was changed to a New England estate in later 1940s Batman stories.
context: The first Batman story has Bruce Wayne in an apartment, not the iconic Wayne Manor. The manor was retroactively added in subsequent stories. Bob Kane drew the original; Bill Finger plotted and dialogued.

question: Wonder Woman debuted in All Star Comics #8 (December 1941, on stands October 1941) created by William Moulton Marston with art by Harry G. Peter. Marston had a remarkable real-life background. What was he professionally?
answer: A Harvard-trained psychologist who had invented the systolic blood pressure test (a key polygraph component).
choices: A Harvard-trained psychologist who had invented the systolic blood pressure test (a key polygraph component).
A naval intelligence officer who had served in WWI and developed comic-book ideas during peacetime work.
A British classics professor who had emigrated to America after the start of WWI and taught at NYU.
A medical doctor who had been a U.S. Army surgeon before turning to writing in his early 50s.
context: Marston (Charles Moulton was his pen name) was a psychologist who developed parts of the lie-detector technology. Wonder Woman has a Lasso of Truth, an obvious nod to his polygraph work.

question: Fantastic Four #1 (November 1961) marked the beginning of the Marvel Silver Age. Stan Lee wrote and Jack Kirby drew. The team's origin was four astronauts caught in cosmic rays during a space test flight. Who are the four FF members and their powers?
answer: Reed Richards (stretch), Sue Storm (invisibility), Johnny Storm (fire), Ben Grimm (rock-strength).
choices: Reed Richards (stretch), Sue Storm (invisibility), Johnny Storm (fire), Ben Grimm (rock-strength).
Reed Richards (genius), Sue Storm (force-field), Johnny Storm (sky), Ben Grimm (juggernaut).
Reed Richards (telepathy), Sue Storm (psychic), Johnny Storm (energy), Ben Grimm (super-strength).
Reed Richards (mind), Sue Storm (water), Johnny Storm (lightning), Ben Grimm (size-changing).
context: Mr. Fantastic, Invisible Woman, Human Torch, The Thing. Doctor Doom debuted in FF #5. Galactus and Silver Surfer in FF #48-50. Black Panther in FF #52.

question: Spider-Man debuted in Amazing Fantasy #15 (August 1962) by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko. The 15th issue was originally planned as the final issue of Amazing Fantasy (formerly Amazing Adult Fantasy). Spider-Man got his own series with Amazing Spider-Man #1 (March 1963). Who was the publisher pushing back against Spider-Man's debut?
answer: Martin Goodman, Marvel publisher, who initially didn't think readers wanted teenage protagonists with bug powers.
choices: Martin Goodman, Marvel publisher, who initially didn't think readers wanted teenage protagonists with bug powers.
Vincent Sullivan, DC Comics editor, who tried to license the character away from Marvel briefly in 1962.
Mort Weisinger, Superman editor at DC, who pushed back against Marvel's increasing market share.
Joe Simon, comics legend, who was negotiating with Goodman about other Marvel projects at the time.
context: Goodman, the Marvel publisher (also Stan Lee's cousin's husband), was famously skeptical. Spider-Man's success vindicated Lee's instincts and changed Marvel's editorial direction.

question: Wolverine first appeared in The Incredible Hulk #180 (October 1974) but had only a one-panel cameo. His first full appearance was in Incredible Hulk #181 (November 1974) by Len Wein and Herb Trimpe. He was created with Canadian-government super-soldier programs in mind. Who was Wolverine's working name in the original sketches?
answer: Wolverine from the start, but he was originally going to be an actual wolverine (the animal) before redesign.
choices: Wolverine from the start, but he was originally going to be an actual wolverine (the animal) before redesign.
Badger, briefly, before settling on Wolverine for the character's more savage and predatory nature.
The Lynx, briefly, before redesigning to settle on Wolverine for international Canadian identification.
Mongoose, briefly, before reverting to Wolverine because the mongoose is not a Canadian native animal.
context: Wolverine's original concept had him be a teenage mutant who was actually a wolverine, but the design was redirected. Wolverine debuted with the Hulk fight in 181.

question: Chris Claremont's run on X-Men began in 1975 with Giant-Size X-Men #1. His most celebrated arc, the Dark Phoenix Saga, ran in X-Men #129-137 (January-September 1980). The saga involved Jean Grey transforming into the Phoenix and then into Dark Phoenix. Without spoiling specifics, what was the major editorial constraint?
answer: Jim Shooter (Marvel EIC) demanded Jean Grey face severe consequences; Claremont and Byrne reworked the ending.
choices: Jim Shooter (Marvel EIC) demanded Jean Grey face severe consequences; Claremont and Byrne reworked the ending.
Marvel's licensing department demanded reduced Phoenix-related merchandising to prevent excessive costs.
The Comics Code Authority threatened to pull approval if Jean's actions weren't more clearly punished.
Stan Lee himself demanded the ending be changed to a happier note, against Claremont's preferences.
context: Shooter's editorial intervention on Phoenix is a famous comics-history moment. Claremont and Byrne reworked the original planned ending. The 1990s X-Men: The Animated Series and the 2006 X-Men: The Last Stand both adapted it.

question: Chris Claremont wrote the X-Men comic from Giant-Size X-Men #1 (1975) to Uncanny X-Men #279 (1991), a 16-year stretch that defined modern superhero comics. After Claremont's 1991 departure, several X-Men writers took over. Who was the artist whose dispute with Claremont caused his 1991 exit?
answer: Jim Lee, whose successful X-Men #1 (1991) by Lee became the best-selling comic of all time.
choices: Jim Lee, whose successful X-Men #1 (1991) by Lee became the best-selling comic of all time.
Marc Silvestri, who later co-founded Image Comics with Lee and other Marvel star artists in 1992.
Whilce Portacio, an X-Men artist whose contributions briefly preceded Jim Lee on the title in 1990.
Rob Liefeld, whose work on New Mutants and X-Force ran parallel to the main X-Men title but didn't conflict.
context: Jim Lee's clash with Claremont over creative control led to Claremont's departure. Lee's X-Men #1 (1991) sold 8.1 million copies, a record. All five named artists (Lee, Silvestri, Portacio, Liefeld) co-founded Image in 1992.

question: Frank Miller's Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (February-June 1986) was a four-issue miniseries that reimagined Batman as a 55-year-old vigilante coming out of retirement. The miniseries shaped Batman storytelling for decades. The series was published shortly before Alan Moore's Watchmen. What year was Watchmen?
answer: Watchmen ran September 1986 to October 1987, beginning a few months after Dark Knight Returns concluded.
choices: Watchmen ran September 1986 to October 1987, beginning a few months after Dark Knight Returns concluded.
Watchmen ran 1988-89, two years after the Dark Knight Returns miniseries, with no overlap in publication.
Watchmen ran 1985, predating Dark Knight Returns; Miller's series was a response to Moore's themes.
Watchmen ran 1990-91, four years later, after both Moore and Miller had moved to other projects.
context: Watchmen, by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons, ran September 1986 to October 1987. Dark Knight Returns ran early 1986. Both books are considered Year One of mature comics for adult readers.

question: Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's Watchmen ran from September 1986 to October 1987 in 12 monthly issues from DC Comics. The series featured an alternate-history America where superheroes had existed since the 1940s. Without spoiling specifics, what real-world historical event was changed by superhero intervention in this alt-history?
answer: The Vietnam War, which the U.S. won quickly with the help of the godlike Dr. Manhattan's intervention.
choices: The Vietnam War, which the U.S. won quickly with the help of the godlike Dr. Manhattan's intervention.
World War II, which ended in 1944 with superheroes leading the Allied invasion of Normandy early.
The Cold War never happened; superheroes intervened in 1948 and prevented the Berlin Blockade entirely.
The Korean War, which the U.S. won with superhero assistance and prevented Chinese intervention there.
context: The Vietnam War's alternate ending (US victory due to Dr. Manhattan) is a key piece of Watchmen worldbuilding. Nixon is in his 5th term as President in the comic's 1985 setting.

question: Watchmen's cover for issue 1 (September 1986) featured a yellow smiley-face button with a single drop of blood. The pin became Watchmen's most iconic visual symbol. Who designed the iconic image?
answer: Dave Gibbons, the artist of Watchmen, in collaboration with Moore on the symbolic-design choices.
choices: Dave Gibbons, the artist of Watchmen, in collaboration with Moore on the symbolic-design choices.
Bill Sienkiewicz, the experimental Marvel artist who instead provided covers for the New Mutants in same era.
Bob Schreck, DC's editor at the time, who provided concept approval but not the actual design itself.
Brian Bolland, the British artist who would later draw The Killing Joke (1988) with Alan Moore.
context: Gibbons designed both the smiley face and most of Watchmen's visual symbology. The blood-spattered smiley became one of comics' most reproduced single images.

question: Alan Moore and Brian Bolland's Batman: The Killing Joke (March 1988) was a one-shot graphic novel featuring the Joker. The book gave the Joker a backstory as a failed comedian and unfolded over a single horrific night. Bolland's art was widely praised but the book had a particular technical innovation. What?
answer: First mainstream comic to use computer-aided coloring, by John Higgins, with a controversial fluorescent palette.
choices: First mainstream comic to use computer-aided coloring, by John Higgins, with a controversial fluorescent palette.
First mainstream Batman comic printed on glossy paper rather than newsprint, with high-quality color reproduction.
First mainstream comic to use motion-blur scanning techniques for fight scenes, courtesy of computer effects.
First mainstream comic to be published in a wide-screen format, doubling the standard page width.
context: John Higgins's computer-assisted coloring was new for 1988. Bolland later re-colored the book himself for the Deluxe Edition (2008), preferring more muted tones.

question: Neil Gaiman's The Sandman ran from issue 1 (January 1989) to issue 75 (March 1996) at DC Comics's mature-readers Vertigo imprint. The series followed Dream, also called Morpheus or the Sandman, lord of the Dreaming. Dream is one of seven anthropomorphic siblings. What are the Endless?
answer: Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair, and Delirium (formerly Delight) — seven Endless.
choices: Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair, and Delirium (formerly Delight) — seven Endless.
Death, Dream, Destruction, Discord, Doubt, Destruction, and Damnation — different conceptual names.
Eternal, Mortal, Dream, Hope, Despair, Joy, and Sorrow — alternative names from earlier Sandman drafts.
Time, Space, Dream, Death, Hope, Sorrow, and Fate — names from a working-title list Gaiman had used.
context: All seven Endless names start with D: Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair, Delirium. Each has their own iconography and role across the series.

question: Alan Moore's Swamp Thing run began with Saga of the Swamp Thing #21 (February 1984). Moore reimagined the character and the series became the foundation of the DC Vertigo line. His run lasted until 1987 (issue 64). What was Moore's primary revisionist move with the character's origin?
answer: Swamp Thing was a plant elemental who absorbed Alec Holland's consciousness, not Holland transformed.
choices: Swamp Thing was a plant elemental who absorbed Alec Holland's consciousness, not Holland transformed.
Swamp Thing was Alec Holland's son, not Holland himself, after the original explosion in the swamp.
Swamp Thing was a Native American shaman, not Alec Holland at all, in Moore's full retcon of canon.
Swamp Thing was a Holland clone, neither Holland nor the original swamp; a third option entirely.
context: Moore's plant-elemental retcon is the Anatomy Lesson revelation from Saga of Swamp Thing #21. The story is considered one of the great single comic issues. Bissette, Totleben, and Rick Veitch were the art team.

question: Mike Mignola's Hellboy debuted in Dark Horse Comics's San Diego Comic-Con Comics #2 (August 1993) before getting his own miniseries. The character is a half-demon paranormal investigator who works for the Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense (BPRD). What is Hellboy's filed-down distinguishing feature?
answer: His right hand, the Right Hand of Doom — a massive stone fist that he files down to prevent overgrowth.
choices: His right hand, the Right Hand of Doom — a massive stone fist that he files down to prevent overgrowth.
His horns, which he files down to nubs to maintain a more approachable appearance for fellow humans.
His tail, which he files down at the tip to prevent it from being too long for human-formal clothing.
His fangs, which he files down to mostly-human teeth to be inconspicuous when interacting with people.
context: Hellboy files down his horns. The Right Hand of Doom is solid stone and not filed. The 2004 film by Guillermo del Toro and the 2008 sequel adapted the character beautifully.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon's Preacher ran from 1995 to 2000 at DC's Vertigo imprint. The series followed Jesse Custer, a Texas preacher who gains the Word of God after a being called Genesis bonds with him. Jesse's two main companions are who?
answer: Tulip O'Hare (girlfriend) and Cassidy (Irish vampire), who join Jesse on the search for a missing God.
choices: Tulip O'Hare (girlfriend) and Cassidy (Irish vampire), who join Jesse on the search for a missing God.
Tammy Vance (girlfriend) and Frank Cassidy (Texas Ranger), a different supporting cast from late issues.
Tulip O'Hare (girlfriend) and the Saint of Killers (rival), who pursues rather than allies with Jesse.
Tulip O'Hare (girlfriend) and Arseface (former classmate), Arseface plays a minor recurring role only.
context: Jesse, Tulip, and Cassidy form the central trio. The Saint of Killers is a primary antagonist. Arseface is a recurring side character. AMC's Preacher TV adaptation ran 2016-19.

question: Frank Miller began Sin City in April 1991 in Dark Horse Presents anthology, with his first solo Sin City book (The Hard Goodbye) published in 1992. The setting is the fictional Basin City. Miller's art is famously high-contrast. What was Miller's visual style?
answer: Stark black-and-white with occasional spot color, modeled on noir film and woodcut printmaking.
choices: Stark black-and-white with occasional spot color, modeled on noir film and woodcut printmaking.
Full color with desaturated tones, similar to mid-1990s Vertigo painted comics in the European bandes desinees.
Photo-realistic photography traced as black-and-white reference art for the comics finished pages.
Watercolor washes with light pencil outlines, more like the European bande dessinée traditions.
context: Sin City's stark black-and-white is its signature. The Robert Rodriguez film (2005) faithfully adapted the look. Spot color (yellow, red, green) is used sparingly in original comics.

question: Frank Miller's 300 was a five-issue miniseries published by Dark Horse from May to September 1998. The series, with Lynn Varley on color, dramatized the Battle of Thermopylae (480 BCE) between Spartans under King Leonidas and the Persian Empire under Xerxes. What battle of Thermopylae was Miller inspired by?
answer: The 1962 film The 300 Spartans, which Miller saw as a child and which inspired his interest in Sparta.
choices: The 1962 film The 300 Spartans, which Miller saw as a child and which inspired his interest in Sparta.
Herodotus's actual account in The Histories, which Miller researched in original Greek for the project.
Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus, which Miller cited as his primary source on Spartan culture in interviews.
Steven Pressfield's 1998 novel Gates of Fire, which Miller adapted from with significant changes.
context: Miller cited the 1962 film as childhood inspiration. The 2006 Zack Snyder film adapted Miller's comic. Historical accuracy was deliberately stylized for visual impact.

question: Mark Waid and Alex Ross's Kingdom Come ran from May to August 1996 in four issues from DC Comics. The Elseworlds miniseries was painted by Ross in a photorealistic style and depicted an alternate future DC universe. Without spoilers, the central conflict was between which two camps?
answer: Old-guard heroes (Superman generation, returning from retirement) versus new violent metahuman youth.
choices: Old-guard heroes (Superman generation, returning from retirement) versus new violent metahuman youth.
DC heroes versus Marvel heroes in a crossover event, painted by Ross in his signature realistic style.
Living heroes versus dead heroes brought back from afterlives in a metaphysical struggle through time.
Earth heroes versus aliens led by Despero, in an extended cosmic conflict drawn out across the miniseries.
context: Kingdom Come's old-vs-new-heroes theme is its core. Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman lead the old guard. Magog leads the new. The painted art by Ross became iconic.

question: Alex Ross and Kurt Busiek's Marvels (January-April 1994) was a four-issue Marvel Comics miniseries narrated from the perspective of news photographer Phil Sheldon, witnessing the Marvel superhero age from the 1939 launch of Captain America forward. The series was painted by Ross in his signature photo-realistic style. What was Sheldon's profession?
answer: A newspaper photographer for the Daily Bugle, witnessing the rise of Marvel heroes through his lens.
choices: A newspaper photographer for the Daily Bugle, witnessing the rise of Marvel heroes through his lens.
A magazine reporter for Newsweek, with a journalist's quote-and-investigation approach to coverage.
A television cameraman for WCBS, with a film-and-broadcast perspective on the unfolding hero events.
A New York Times political cartoonist, with an editorial perspective on the rise of metahuman impact.
context: Phil Sheldon's Daily Bugle photography frames each issue. Marvels was a foundational Vertigo-era painted Marvel comic. Ross would later do Kingdom Come at DC.

question: Garth Ennis's run on The Punisher MAX began in 2004 with Punisher #1 (Marvel MAX imprint, mature readers). The 60-issue run ended in 2009. Ennis's take on Frank Castle was particularly violent and morally challenging. What was the imprint's purpose?
answer: Marvel's mature-readers line (no Comics Code Authority), allowing adult content not in standard Marvel comics.
choices: Marvel's mature-readers line (no Comics Code Authority), allowing adult content not in standard Marvel comics.
Marvel's anthology-format imprint, designed to mix different writers and characters in single issues.
Marvel's licensing imprint for movie- and TV-related comics that would not interact with the main universe.
Marvel's reprint imprint, designed to package classic Marvel comics for adult readers in collected editions.
context: The Marvel MAX imprint was launched in 2001 specifically for mature-readers content. Punisher MAX was its flagship title. Brian Michael Bendis's Alias on MAX introduced Jessica Jones.

question: Brian Michael Bendis and Michael Avon Oeming's Powers debuted in April 2000 at Image Comics. The series, a noir police procedural set in a world with superheroes, followed Detectives Christian Walker and Deena Pilgrim solving capes-related murders. The series later moved imprints. Where did it go?
answer: Icon, Marvel's creator-owned imprint, where Bendis and Oeming continued Powers for many years.
choices: Icon, Marvel's creator-owned imprint, where Bendis and Oeming continued Powers for many years.
Vertigo, DC's mature-readers imprint, where Powers ran from 2003 onward in an extended run.
Dark Horse Comics, where Bendis had earlier published Sam and Twitch and other crime work.
Top Shelf Productions, the indie literary-graphic-novel publisher that Bendis collaborated with also.
context: Powers moved to Marvel's Icon imprint (creator-owned) in 2004 and ran there for many years before returning to Image. Bendis is famous for both creator-owned and mainstream Marvel/DC work.

question: Ed Brubaker's run on Captain America began with Captain America #1 (Volume 5) in November 2004. Brubaker's first major arc, Winter Soldier, told a story about a long-presumed-dead WWII figure brought back as a Soviet brainwashed assassin. Without spoilers about identity, what is the catch?
answer: The Winter Soldier is a real, named WWII figure long thought dead; Brubaker reintroduced him after decades.
choices: The Winter Soldier is a real, named WWII figure long thought dead; Brubaker reintroduced him after decades.
The Winter Soldier is a new character created by Brubaker entirely, with no prior Marvel history at all.
The Winter Soldier is a Cold War-era Russian original who never had a prior Marvel comics appearance.
The Winter Soldier is a future-version of an existing character, sent back in time to assassinate Steve.
context: The Winter Soldier brings back a long-dormant Captain America-adjacent character. Brubaker's arc reshaped Marvel continuity and was adapted into the 2014 film Captain America: The Winter Soldier.

question: DC Comics published The Death of Superman in late 1992, culminating in Superman #75 (January 1993, cover-dated). The seven-issue arc featured a brutal new villain who tore through the entire Justice League before reaching Superman. Who was the villain?
answer: Doomsday, a Kryptonian-engineered killing machine created by an ancient scientist for evolutionary survival.
choices: Doomsday, a Kryptonian-engineered killing machine created by an ancient scientist for evolutionary survival.
Mongul, the alien tyrant who would also star in the Justice League animated series episodes.
Brainiac, Superman's classic AI antagonist, with a new redesign for the early-1990s storyline arc.
Lex Luthor, in his bald-businessman 90s incarnation, with a new technology that could kill Superman.
context: Doomsday is the iconic Superman-killing villain. Created by Dan Jurgens, the Funeral for a Friend storyline followed. Reign of the Supermen (1993) brought four candidate replacements before resurrection.

question: Jim Starlin and George Perez's Infinity Gauntlet (July-December 1991) was a six-issue Marvel limited series. The story featured the cosmic villain Thanos collecting the Infinity Gems and using them to eliminate half of all life in the universe to please Death (the personification). The story was adapted into what film?
answer: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Avengers: Endgame (2019), with the snap of Thanos and time-travel reversal.
choices: Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Avengers: Endgame (2019), with the snap of Thanos and time-travel reversal.
Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), which adapted only the gauntlet-acquisition arc rather than the snap event.
Captain Marvel (2019), which featured the Tesseract and other Infinity-related elements before Infinity War.
Avengers (2012), which featured Loki's scepter and the Tesseract but not the full Infinity Gauntlet story.
context: Infinity War and Endgame adapt Infinity Gauntlet (with significant changes — Death's role, Adam Warlock's role, etc.). The MCU's Infinity Saga adapted from many comic sources.

question: Mark Millar's Civil War (May 2006 to January 2007) was a seven-issue Marvel limited series with art by Steve McNiven. The series pitted Iron Man (pro-Superhuman Registration Act) against Captain America (anti-registration). What real-world event was the comic clearly responding to?
answer: Post-9/11 debates over the Patriot Act and government surveillance versus civil liberties in 2001-06.
choices: Post-9/11 debates over the Patriot Act and government surveillance versus civil liberties in 2001-06.
The Iraq War (2003 onwards) and George W. Bush's foreign-policy doctrine of preemptive military action.
The 2005 Hurricane Katrina disaster, with debates over government response and federal-local jurisdiction.
The 2004 election cycle, with the partisan tone of the polarized American political landscape.
context: The Patriot Act parallel was widely noted at the time. Civil War's Superhuman Registration Act mirrored debates over civil liberties versus security. The 2016 film Captain America: Civil War was a loose adaptation.

question: Brian Michael Bendis's Secret Invasion (April-December 2008) was an eight-issue Marvel limited series. The plot revealed that Skrulls had been impersonating Marvel heroes for years (retroactively explaining some odd behaviors). Without spoiling specifics, what was the tagline?
answer: Embrace Change — the slogan of the Skrull infiltration, suggesting their invasion as evolutionary progress.
choices: Embrace Change — the slogan of the Skrull infiltration, suggesting their invasion as evolutionary progress.
Trust No One — the slogan of the paranoid heroes trying to identify which of them are Skrulls.
All Is Lost — the slogan of the heroes recognizing that the Skrull infiltration is more advanced than feared.
Hidden Among Us — the slogan emphasizing the secret nature of the long-term Skrull infiltration plot.
context: Embrace Change was the Skrulls's slogan in promotional material. The 2023 Disney+ series Secret Invasion adapted (loosely) from the comic.

question: DC Comics published the Batman Knightfall storyline beginning in late 1992 (Batman #492, April 1993) and culminating in May 1993 (Batman #497). The arc featured a new villain breaking Batman physically. Who was the villain?
answer: Bane, a Venom-enhanced mercenary who broke Batman's back over his knee, putting Wayne out of action.
choices: Bane, a Venom-enhanced mercenary who broke Batman's back over his knee, putting Wayne out of action.
Killer Croc, the reptile-mutated villain whose physical strength was Batman's greatest physical threat.
Solomon Grundy, the undead Golden Age villain whose Knightfall appearance was a minor sub-plot.
Mr. Freeze, the cryogenic villain whose 1990s appearance helped propel the entire Knightfall storyline.
context: Bane is the iconic Knightfall villain. Azrael (Jean-Paul Valley) became the substitute Batman during Bruce Wayne's recovery. The 2012 film The Dark Knight Rises adapted the arc loosely.

question: Marvel Super Heroes Secret Wars (May 1984 to April 1985) was Marvel's first major company-wide crossover event, in 12 issues. The story was a Marvel/toy-company tie-in with Mattel. Jim Shooter wrote, with Mike Zeck and Bob Layton on art. Where did the plot transport the heroes?
answer: Battleworld, a patchwork planet created by the cosmic Beyonder, where heroes and villains fight.
choices: Battleworld, a patchwork planet created by the cosmic Beyonder, where heroes and villains fight.
The Microverse, the subatomic world that had been introduced in Micronauts comics in the 1970s.
The Negative Zone, the alternate dimension that the Fantastic Four had explored in earlier comics.
Limbo, the dimension that Belasco controlled, which Magik (Illyana Rasputin) frequently visited.
context: Battleworld was Secret Wars's signature setting. Beyonder created it. Spider-Man's black suit (later Venom) debuted there. Mattel produced the Secret Wars action figures.

question: Garth Ennis's Preacher (1995-2000) gave protagonist Jesse Custer a unique magical ability — the Word of God, the result of being merged with a divine-demonic entity called Genesis. Without spoiling specifics, what's the limit on Jesse's Word power?
answer: Anyone hearing him speak in English must do exactly what he commands; he can only command, not request.
choices: Anyone hearing him speak in English must do exactly what he commands; he can only command, not request.
Anyone in his physical line of sight will obey, regardless of language; his commands work by gaze.
Anyone within 100 feet will hear and obey; the radius is fixed regardless of vocal volume.
Anyone he names specifically will obey; he must specify the target by name for the Word to work.
context: The verbal-English command structure is fundamental to Preacher's gimmick. AMC's 2016-19 series adapted the Word power. Jesse's hat and Texas-preacher visual style are iconic.

question: Mark Millar's Kick-Ass (2008) ran at the Icon imprint. The comic was illustrated by John Romita Jr. and tells the story of teenage Dave Lizewski deciding to become a real-world costumed vigilante. The character of Hit-Girl and her father Big Daddy steal the story. Who is Big Daddy?
answer: A disgraced ex-cop seeking revenge on the mob for framing him and killing his wife.
choices: A disgraced ex-cop seeking revenge on the mob for framing him and killing his wife.
A current FBI agent who infiltrates the Genovese mob while training his daughter for revenge.
A Korean-War veteran who never reentered civilian life and raised his daughter in a cabin upstate.
A former mob hitman gone rogue who teaches his daughter the trade for high-end criminal contracts.
context: Big Daddy's framed-cop backstory is central. The 2010 film starred Nicolas Cage as Big Daddy and Chloe Grace Moretz as Hit-Girl. The comic was harsher than the film in tone.

question: Jeff Smith's Bone began self-publication in July 1991 (Bone #1 from Cartoon Books). The comic ran 55 issues over 13 years, ending in 2004. The series features the Bone cousins (Fone Bone, Phoney Bone, Smiley Bone). What was the comic's stylistic comparison?
answer: Pogo by Walt Kelly, Looney Tunes-style cartoony characters, with epic Tolkien-influenced fantasy plot.
choices: Pogo by Walt Kelly, Looney Tunes-style cartoony characters, with epic Tolkien-influenced fantasy plot.
The Far Side by Gary Larson, single-panel humor with no continuing storyline at all.
Calvin and Hobbes by Bill Watterson, daily-strip framing with extended fantasy interludes only.
Peanuts by Charles Schulz, single-strip humor with seasonal-specials extended into longer-form holiday stories.
context: Bone's Pogo and Tolkien comparison is widely cited. Jeff Smith won multiple Eisner Awards for the work. The full 1,300-page graphic novel is collected as a single volume now.

question: Stan Sakai's Usagi Yojimbo debuted in 1984 in Albedo Anthropomorphics #2 and got his own series in 1987. The series follows a wandering rabbit ronin named Miyamoto Usagi in 17th-century Japan. The series's historical setting is famously well-researched. The character's name is a riff on a real historical figure. Who?
answer: Miyamoto Musashi, the 17th-century samurai swordsman; Usagi is Japanese for rabbit and Yojimbo for bodyguard.
choices: Miyamoto Musashi, the 17th-century samurai swordsman; Usagi is Japanese for rabbit and Yojimbo for bodyguard.
Tokugawa Ieyasu, the 17th-century shogun; Sakai based Usagi's social-class-mobility plot on him.
Honda Tadakatsu, the famous samurai general; Usagi's character design was based on Honda's helmet.
Sasaki Kojiro, Musashi's famous duel-opponent; Usagi's blade-style is partly based on his style.
context: Miyamoto Musashi (1584-1645) is the real-world figure. His name in Sakai's transliteration becomes Miyamoto Usagi. Sakai also drew from Lone Wolf and Cub and other samurai cinema.

question: Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes began syndication on November 18, 1985. The strip ran exactly 10 years and 7 weeks, ending December 31, 1995. Watterson famously refused merchandising. Why?
answer: He believed the characters' integrity required protecting them from commercial-product crassness.
choices: He believed the characters' integrity required protecting them from commercial-product crassness.
Universal Press Syndicate prevented him from licensing under his original publishing contract terms.
His publisher Andrews McMeel had separate exclusive rights and prevented his licensing decisions.
Newspaper-syndicate contracts of the 1980s standardly forbade strip-character merchandising deals.
context: Watterson's anti-merchandising stance is famous. Common Calvin peeing/praying stickers on cars are bootlegs, not licensed. Watterson has remained reclusive since the 1995 retirement.

question: Gary Larson's The Far Side ran in newspapers from January 1, 1980 to January 1, 1995 — exactly 15 years. The single-panel cartoon was famous for surreal animal-and-human jokes. Larson's distinctive cartoon style and dark humor became iconic. What was a recurring Larson trope?
answer: Cows with names and personalities, who reverse-engineered situations on humans, like cars and traffic.
choices: Cows with names and personalities, who reverse-engineered situations on humans, like cars and traffic.
Cats with detailed knowledge of human household appliances and brand names, often selling them.
Squirrels with full-court-bench scenes, attorney parodies, and detailed legal-process scenarios.
Penguins as recurring corporate executives, often shown in 3-piece suits at boardroom meetings.
context: Larson's cows are iconic. The Cow Tools strip became one of the most-discussed gags. Other recurring tropes: dinosaurs, scientists, vultures, and dogs.

question: Alan Moore and David Lloyd's V for Vendetta began publication in 1982 in Warrior magazine (UK) before being completed at DC's Vertigo in 1988-89. The dystopian fascist-Britain setting features a masked anarchist freedom fighter known only as V. What mask does V wear?
answer: A Guy Fawkes mask, modeled on the 1605 Gunpowder Plot conspirator; the mask later became Anonymous's symbol.
choices: A Guy Fawkes mask, modeled on the 1605 Gunpowder Plot conspirator; the mask later became Anonymous's symbol.
A skull mask, the standard horror aesthetic that V uses to terrify the totalitarian regime he opposes.
A jester mask, modeled on medieval mask-of-folly imagery to mock the regime's serious authoritarian tone.
A bird-flu doctor's plague mask, with the long beak, a reference to medieval European plague doctors.
context: Guy Fawkes (1570-1606) tried to blow up Parliament in 1605. The mask became Anonymous's symbol in the 2000s. The 2005 film by James McTeigue adapted Moore's comic.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's prodigious correspondence (estimated at 100,000 letters lifetime) was directed to many friends and contemporaries. He had a particularly intense correspondence with one young writer in his teens who later became a leading horror writer. Who?
answer: Robert Bloch (the Psycho author), with whom Lovecraft corresponded from age 16 until Lovecraft's 1937 death.
choices: Robert Bloch (the Psycho author), with whom Lovecraft corresponded from age 16 until Lovecraft's 1937 death.
Ray Bradbury, with whom Lovecraft never corresponded; Bradbury came too late to the weird-fiction scene.
Stephen King, born 1947, ten years after Lovecraft's death; the two never corresponded at all.
Clive Barker, born 1952, fifteen years after Lovecraft's death; the two never corresponded at all.
context: Robert Bloch's letters to Lovecraft began in 1933 when Bloch was 16. Lovecraft mentored him in writing. Bloch later wrote Psycho (1959, adapted by Hitchcock).

question: Clark Ashton Smith, the third member of the Weird Tales Big Three with Lovecraft and Howard, wrote across multiple weird-fiction sub-genres. His most famous work cycle was set in a far-future, dying-Earth setting where the sun is red and exhausted. What was the setting called?
answer: Zothique, Smith's last-continent setting where dark sorcery and decadent civilizations are the norm.
choices: Zothique, Smith's last-continent setting where dark sorcery and decadent civilizations are the norm.
Hyperborea, Smith's prehistoric setting that predates Howard's Hyborian Age by hundreds of millions of years.
Averoigne, Smith's medieval-France setting that featured witches, werewolves, and decadent priests.
Xiccarph, a separate planetary setting Smith created where Maal Dweb the sorcerer-king rules.
context: All four are real Smith cycles: Zothique (future), Hyperborea (past), Averoigne (medieval), Xiccarph (alien planet). His prose style was rich and decadent, with vocabulary often exceeding even Lovecraft.

question: Lord Dunsany (Edward Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany, 1878-1957) was an Irish aristocrat who wrote influential early fantasy beginning with The Gods of Pegana (1905). Dunsany invented an entire mythology of his own gods. Two later writers cited him as a major influence. Who?
answer: Both H.P. Lovecraft (Dream Cycle stories) and J.R.R. Tolkien (Middle-earth mythology) cited Dunsany.
choices: Both H.P. Lovecraft (Dream Cycle stories) and J.R.R. Tolkien (Middle-earth mythology) cited Dunsany.
C.S. Lewis (Narnia) and Mervyn Peake (Gormenghast); both fellow British fantasy writers influenced.
Edgar Allan Poe (1809-49, predates Dunsany) and Robert E. Howard, who never cited him at all.
Algernon Blackwood and Arthur Machen, who were both elder contemporaries of Dunsany not influenced.
context: Dunsany's invented pantheon at Pegana inspired Lovecraft's Dream Cycle (Dreamlands, Kadath) and Tolkien's Silmarillion. Both wrote letters acknowledging the influence.

question: Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser stories are set primarily in the city-state of Lankhmar, in the world of Nehwon. The city was inspired by a real-world city Leiber had visited. What was the inspiration?
answer: A blend of medieval London, Constantinople, and Cairo, with elements of Leiber's home city Chicago.
choices: A blend of medieval London, Constantinople, and Cairo, with elements of Leiber's home city Chicago.
Specifically London during the Great Plague of 1665, which Leiber researched intensively.
A blend of Renaissance Florence and Venice, focusing on the canals and palazzo culture of both.
Specifically New York City of the 1930s, with the skyscrapers translated to Nehwon's vertical streets.
context: Lankhmar's tavern-and-thieves-guild urban texture was a defining setting. Leiber set later games in Lankhmar, including TSR's official Lankhmar D&D setting (1985).

question: Robert E. Howard's first published Conan story, The Phoenix on the Sword, appeared in Weird Tales in December 1932. The story featured King Conan, not the young thief, which was Howard's distinct narrative choice. What story was published first?
answer: The Phoenix on the Sword (King Conan, December 1932), set late in Conan's life as a brooding king.
choices: The Phoenix on the Sword (King Conan, December 1932), set late in Conan's life as a brooding king.
Queen of the Black Coast (June 1934), introducing Belit the pirate as a major Conan supporting character.
Tower of the Elephant (March 1933), a Young Conan adventure that came after The Phoenix on the Sword.
The Hour of the Dragon (December 1935), Conan's only full-length novel as serialized in Weird Tales.
context: Phoenix on the Sword was Howard's first published Conan tale. Tower of the Elephant came months later. Queen of the Black Coast and Hour of the Dragon are later, beloved entries.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's 1927 story The Colour Out of Space tells of a meteorite that falls on a farm near Arkham, Massachusetts, and slowly poisons the surrounding land with an indescribable color. Lovecraft considered it among his best stories. Where was it first published?
answer: Amazing Stories, edited by Hugo Gernsback; one of Lovecraft's rare appearances outside Weird Tales.
choices: Amazing Stories, edited by Hugo Gernsback; one of Lovecraft's rare appearances outside Weird Tales.
Weird Tales, like nearly all of Lovecraft's stories from 1923 onward published in that magazine.
Astounding Stories, edited by John W. Campbell; the 1936 sale to Campbell was a later move for Lovecraft.
The Vagrant, an amateur-press publication that Lovecraft and other writers contributed to in early years.
context: Amazing Stories (September 1927) was unusual for Lovecraft. The story was a Lovecraft favorite of his own work, often cited by him as among his best.

question: August Derleth (1909-1971) was a Wisconsin writer who became Lovecraft's literary executor and the leading promoter of Lovecraft's work. After Lovecraft's 1937 death, Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded a publishing house to keep Lovecraft's works in print. What is the publisher called?
answer: Arkham House, founded in 1939, named after Lovecraft's fictional Massachusetts city of Arkham.
choices: Arkham House, founded in 1939, named after Lovecraft's fictional Massachusetts city of Arkham.
Innsmouth Press, founded in 1947, named after another Lovecraft town with its grim shadowed history.
Miskatonic Books, founded in 1945, named after the fictional university in Lovecraft's stories.
Pickman Editions, founded in 1942, named after a Lovecraft story Pickman's Model from earlier era.
context: Arkham House remains active today. Derleth also wrote his own Cthulhu Mythos stories, controversially expanding Lovecraft's mythology with his own theological additions.

question: Harold Lamb (1892-1962) was an American historical novelist whose Genghis Khan and Crusades stories appeared in Adventure magazine from 1917 onward. Lamb's vivid Asian-history adventure-fiction was a major influence on which Conan author?
answer: Robert E. Howard, who cited Lamb's Cossack stories as a major influence on his pulp historical adventure.
choices: Robert E. Howard, who cited Lamb's Cossack stories as a major influence on his pulp historical adventure.
L. Sprague de Camp, who collaborated with Lamb on a 1956 anthology of historical adventure.
Edgar Rice Burroughs, who never cited Lamb and whose work predates Lamb's prime work.
Talbot Mundy, an English writer who wrote Indian-subcontinent adventure in the same era.
context: Lamb's Cossacks of the Don Cossacks and his Genghis Khan biography were favorites of Howard's. Howard's own Crusader-and-Asian-warrior stories (El Borak, Cormac Fitzgeoffrey) show Lamb's influence.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's The Silmarillion was published in 1977, four years after his 1973 death. The book represents the mythological framework underlying Middle-earth. It was edited and assembled posthumously by Tolkien's son. Who?
answer: Christopher Tolkien, J.R.R.'s third son, with Guy Gavriel Kay assisting on the editorial work.
choices: Christopher Tolkien, J.R.R.'s third son, with Guy Gavriel Kay assisting on the editorial work.
Michael Tolkien, J.R.R.'s second son, who actually had nothing to do with the editorial work.
John Tolkien, J.R.R.'s eldest son, a Catholic priest who later helped on later supplementary volumes.
Priscilla Tolkien, J.R.R.'s daughter, who edited some materials but not The Silmarillion itself.
context: Christopher Tolkien (1924-2020) was the editor of the posthumous works. Guy Gavriel Kay helped on Silmarillion. Christopher later assembled The History of Middle-earth in 12 volumes.

question: Ray Bradbury's The Martian Chronicles was published in 1950, a fix-up of short stories Bradbury had written through the late 1940s for various pulp magazines. The book is a melancholic chronicle of human colonization of Mars. Bradbury would later sell more than which other classic novel?
answer: Fahrenheit 451 (1953), Bradbury's dystopian novel of book-burning that has sold more copies lifetime.
choices: Fahrenheit 451 (1953), Bradbury's dystopian novel of book-burning that has sold more copies lifetime.
Something Wicked This Way Comes (1962), Bradbury's Halloween novel of a sinister traveling carnival.
Dandelion Wine (1957), Bradbury's nostalgic novel of Green Town, Illinois in summer 1928.
The Illustrated Man (1951), Bradbury's fix-up of stories told by the tattoos on a man's body.
context: Fahrenheit 451 (1953) is Bradbury's most-sold novel. The fire-truck book-burning premise is iconic. Bradbury said the title is the temperature at which paper auto-ignites.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs created the Pellucidar series of hollow-earth novels beginning with At the Earth's Core (1914). The series features a hollow Earth with its own inner sun and prehistoric creatures, accessed via a mechanical drilling machine. What is the drilling vehicle called?
answer: The Iron Mole, the steam-powered drilling machine that David Innes and Abner Perry use to penetrate the crust.
choices: The Iron Mole, the steam-powered drilling machine that David Innes and Abner Perry use to penetrate the crust.
