The Earth Borer, the tunneling vessel that takes the protagonists through 500 miles of solid earth.
The Crust-Cracker, a mechanical drill that David Innes pilots to reach the inner world.
The Vril Engine, named after Bulwer-Lytton's Vril, the energy source for Burroughs's drilling apparatus.
context: The Iron Mole is the drilling machine. Pellucidar has its own sun (perpetually noon) and prehistoric ecosystems. David Innes becomes Pellucidar's emperor.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Caspak trilogy (1918) takes place on an Antarctic island where evolution proceeds at high speed within a single life-cycle. The trilogy begins with The Land That Time Forgot. What is unusual about Caspak's life-cycle?
answer: All life forms in Caspak start as eggs in a swamp and metamorphose through evolutionary stages within months.
choices: All life forms in Caspak start as eggs in a swamp and metamorphose through evolutionary stages within months.
All life forms in Caspak age in reverse, starting old and growing younger over time on the island.
All life forms in Caspak shrink over time, starting at full size and reducing to insect-scale generations.
All life forms in Caspak are immortal, with no births or deaths in the entire ecosystem over millennia.
context: Caspak's reproductive cycle (each organism passes through evolutionary stages) is Burroughs's invention. The 1975 film The Land That Time Forgot starred Doug McClure.

question: Manly Wade Wellman (1903-1986) was an American writer who specialized in Appalachian folklore-based fantasy. His most famous character is a wandering musician with a silver-strung guitar who battles dark folk magic in the Appalachian mountains. Who is the character?
answer: Silver John (John the Balladeer), who wanders the Smoky and Blue Ridge Mountains with his silver guitar.
choices: Silver John (John the Balladeer), who wanders the Smoky and Blue Ridge Mountains with his silver guitar.
Long John Silver, the pirate from Stevenson's Treasure Island (1883), not Wellman's character.
Doc Watson, the bluegrass musician (1923-2012), a real person not a Wellman character.
Silver Sam, an Appalachian fiddler character that Wellman wrote in his early career but later abandoned.
context: Wellman's Silver John appeared in Who Fears the Devil? (1963) and other collections. Wellman is sometimes confused with brother (also a writer) but Manly Wade is the Silver John author.

question: Karl Edward Wagner (1945-1994) was an American horror and dark-fantasy writer. He created an immortal red-haired swordsman whose origin lies in biblical mythology. The character is hinted to be the biblical Cain, condemned to wander after killing his brother. What is the character's name?
answer: Kane, Wagner's red-haired immortal warrior who appears in Bloodstone (1975) and other dark-fantasy tales.
choices: Kane, Wagner's red-haired immortal warrior who appears in Bloodstone (1975) and other dark-fantasy tales.
Conan, of Robert E. Howard's creation, who is unrelated to Wagner's character at all in canon.
Elric of Melnibone, Michael Moorcock's albino swordsman, who is unrelated to Wagner's character.
Solomon Kane, Robert E. Howard's Puritan swordsman, who is unrelated to Wagner's character in plot.
context: Wagner's Kane is the dark mirror to Howard's Solomon Kane (and biblical Cain). Wagner edited many of the definitive Conan reprints in the 1970s-80s. Wagner died at 49 of alcohol-related causes.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's cosmic-horror philosophy is most fully articulated in his 1927 essay Supernatural Horror in Literature. What is the central principle of cosmic horror?
answer: Humanity is utterly insignificant before vast indifferent cosmic forces, and confronting this drives madness.
choices: Humanity is utterly insignificant before vast indifferent cosmic forces, and confronting this drives madness.
Humanity faces ancient gods whose power matches it; horror lies in moral combat between them and us.
Humanity is doomed by inevitable evolutionary decay; horror lies in watching civilizations collapse over time.
Humanity is haunted by ghostly remnants of past lives; horror lies in unresolved injustices from past sins.
context: Lovecraft's cosmic-indifference theme distinguishes his work from earlier ghost-story tradition. The horror is not malice but indifference; humans are bacteria to elder beings.

question: The Spider was a pulp magazine antihero created in 1933, partly as Popular Publications' competing response to The Shadow. The Spider, alias Richard Wentworth, was more violent than The Shadow — using twin .45 automatics and leaving spider-symbol seals on his victims' foreheads. Who wrote most Spider novels?
answer: Norvell W. Page, under the house name Grant Stockbridge, wrote most of the 118 Spider novels.
choices: Norvell W. Page, under the house name Grant Stockbridge, wrote most of the 118 Spider novels.
Walter B. Gibson, who instead wrote most of the The Shadow novels under the house name Maxwell Grant.
Lester Dent, who instead wrote most of the Doc Savage novels under the house name Kenneth Robeson.
L. Ron Hubbard, who wrote various pulp adventures but did not write the Spider series itself at all.
context: Page wrote 92 of the 118 Spider novels. Walter Gibson did The Shadow. Lester Dent did Doc Savage. Pulp house names disguised single-author output.

question: After Robert E. Howard's first Conan story Phoenix on the Sword (December 1932), the second Conan story to be published in Weird Tales was a Young Conan tale that became one of the most beloved in the saga. What was the second Conan story?
answer: The Tower of the Elephant (March 1933), in which the young thief Conan steals an ancient gem.
choices: The Tower of the Elephant (March 1933), in which the young thief Conan steals an ancient gem.
Queen of the Black Coast (May 1934), which introduces the pirate captain Belit; came later than #2.
Beyond the Black River (May 1935), the Picts-vs-Aquilonians story; came much later in publication order.
Red Nails (July-October 1936), the final Conan story published in Howard's lifetime; came at the end.
context: Tower of the Elephant came second (March 1933) after Phoenix on the Sword. The Yag-Kosha sequence remains among the most haunting in the Conan canon.

question: Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum introduced an international new X-Men team to revive the dormant franchise. The new team replaced the original 1960s lineup. Which characters debuted in the issue?
answer: Storm, Colossus, Nightcrawler, Thunderbird, plus already-existing Wolverine, Sunfire, Banshee, and Cyclops.
choices: Storm, Colossus, Nightcrawler, Thunderbird, plus already-existing Wolverine, Sunfire, Banshee, and Cyclops.
Storm, Phoenix, Rogue, Gambit, plus the existing Wolverine; Phoenix and Rogue joined much later.
Storm, Beast, Iceman, Angel, plus the existing Wolverine; these were the original 1963 X-Men team.
Cyclops, Marvel Girl, Beast, Iceman, Angel — the original five 1963 X-Men returning to the team in 1975.
context: Wolverine had debuted earlier (Hulk #180-181, 1974). Sunfire and Banshee were also pre-existing. The big four new debuts were Storm, Colossus, Nightcrawler, Thunderbird (the last killed almost immediately).

question: The Incredible Hulk #1 (May 1962) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby introduced Dr. Bruce Banner, who is transformed by a gamma-ray explosion into the Hulk. In the original issue, the Hulk was not the iconic green color. What color was he?
answer: Gray — Kirby originally drew the Hulk gray, but printing limitations led to the iconic green in issue 2.
choices: Gray — Kirby originally drew the Hulk gray, but printing limitations led to the iconic green in issue 2.
Red — the early Hulk was crimson red, the same color used later for the Red Hulk character of the 2000s.
Blue — Kirby's earliest sketches had the Hulk in blue, suggesting his Kryptonite-like distinct power source.
Brown — a more naturalistic muddy-color approach Kirby tried in earliest issue 1 then quickly abandoned.
context: Gray Hulk was an inconsistent printing issue. Kirby and Lee changed to green in #2 onward. Gray Hulk later returned as a separate identity in Peter David's run as Mr. Fixit.

question: Marvel's Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83 (August 1962) by Stan Lee, Larry Lieber (Lee's brother), and Jack Kirby. The character's secret identity in the original was a Don Blake — a doctor with a cane. What was the cane?
answer: The hammer Mjolnir in disguise; Don Blake transformed into Thor by tapping the cane on the ground.
choices: The hammer Mjolnir in disguise; Don Blake transformed into Thor by tapping the cane on the ground.
A signal-emitting cane to call Mjolnir from Asgard; Blake had no power without the actual hammer present.
A glowing artifact that turned Don Blake into Thor's spirit but kept Mjolnir separate from him entirely.
A staff from an ancient Egyptian mummy's tomb that Blake had handled during an expedition years earlier.
context: The cane-becomes-Mjolnir transformation is iconic to early Thor. Walter Simonson's 1980s run eventually retconned the relationship between Blake and Thor.

question: Iron Man debuted in Tales of Suspense #39 (March 1963) by Stan Lee, Larry Lieber, Don Heck, and Jack Kirby. Tony Stark, a wealthy industrialist, was captured in what war?
answer: The Vietnam War in the original 1963 origin; later retconned to the Gulf War and then Afghanistan.
choices: The Vietnam War in the original 1963 origin; later retconned to the Gulf War and then Afghanistan.
The Korean War in the original 1963 origin; later retconned to the Vietnam War in the 1970s.
The Falklands War in the original 1963 origin; later retconned several times to fit current conflicts.
World War II in the original 1963 origin; never retconned to keep Stark's age frozen in the comics.
context: Vietnam was the original 1963 setting. Stark was held by Wong-Chu (later Mandarin's lieutenant). Iron Man Volume 5 retconned to Afghanistan to match the 2008 film.

question: X-Men #1 (September 1963) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby introduced the original five teenagers — Cyclops, Marvel Girl, Beast, Iceman, Angel — under Professor Charles Xavier. Who was their first villain?
answer: Magneto, the master of magnetism, who would become their most enduring antagonist for decades.
choices: Magneto, the master of magnetism, who would become their most enduring antagonist for decades.
Apocalypse, the ancient mutant, who actually appeared first in X-Factor #5 (1986), not X-Men #1.
Sebastian Shaw, the Black King of the Hellfire Club, who first appeared in X-Men #129 (1980).
Mister Sinister, the cloned-mutant manipulator, who first appeared in Uncanny X-Men #221 (1987).
context: Magneto debuts in X-Men #1. Brotherhood of Evil Mutants forms in #4. Apocalypse, Shaw, and Sinister are all later iconic villains, but Magneto came first.

question: Avengers #1 (September 1963) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby assembled Marvel heroes into a team. The first issue introduced Loki, who tricks the heroes into thinking the Hulk has gone berserk. Who were the founding Avengers?
answer: Iron Man, Thor, Hulk, Ant-Man (Hank Pym), and Wasp (Janet Van Dyne) — five founding members in Avengers #1.
choices: Iron Man, Thor, Hulk, Ant-Man (Hank Pym), and Wasp (Janet Van Dyne) — five founding members in Avengers #1.
Iron Man, Thor, Captain America, Hawkeye, and Black Widow — but Cap joined in #4, not #1, and others later.
Iron Man, Thor, Hulk, Captain America, and Wasp — but Cap joined in Avengers #4, not the first issue.
Iron Man, Thor, Spider-Man, Hulk, and Doctor Strange — Spider-Man and Strange never joined original Avengers.
context: Cap returned in Avengers #4 (March 1964). Hawkeye joined in #16. Wanda and Pietro in #16. The original five were Iron Man, Thor, Hulk, Ant-Man, Wasp.

question: Daredevil #1 (April 1964) by Stan Lee and Bill Everett introduced Matt Murdock, a blind lawyer who develops enhanced senses after being blinded by radioactive waste. Daredevil's distinctive original costume was a different color from his later iconic red. What was it?
answer: Yellow and red (red shirt, yellow leggings, yellow gloves) — replaced by all-red in Daredevil #7.
choices: Yellow and red (red shirt, yellow leggings, yellow gloves) — replaced by all-red in Daredevil #7.
Blue and white (blue cape, white tights) — replaced by red in #7 after a brief run.
Green and black (green ninja-style hood, black tights) — Daredevil never had this color scheme.
Black and gold (Frank Miller-era inspired) — Daredevil never had this color scheme historically.
context: Yellow-and-red was Bill Everett's original. The red appeared starting Daredevil #7 (April 1965), designed by Wally Wood. Frank Miller's run from 1979 made the red costume iconic.

question: Fantastic Four #48-50 (March-May 1966) introduced the Silver Surfer and his master Galactus. Galactus is a planet-devouring cosmic entity, and the Silver Surfer is his herald. The artist who designed both characters was?
answer: Jack Kirby, who designed the Surfer for FF #48 as a herald without consulting Stan Lee on the addition.
choices: Jack Kirby, who designed the Surfer for FF #48 as a herald without consulting Stan Lee on the addition.
Steve Ditko, who designed Doctor Strange and Spider-Man but did not design Silver Surfer himself at all.
John Buscema, who later drew the Surfer's solo title but didn't design the original character himself.
Wally Wood, who drew the early Daredevil but never worked on FF or designed Silver Surfer himself either.
context: Kirby added the Silver Surfer without consulting Lee. The character became a cosmic icon. Kirby later said the Surfer was the most spiritually significant character he ever designed.

question: Black Panther made his comics debut in Fantastic Four #52 (July 1966) by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. T'Challa is the king of Wakanda, a fictional African nation. Wakanda is hidden from outside observation because of what feature?
answer: Cloaking technology powered by vibranium, the fictional metal native to Wakanda's vibranium mound.
choices: Cloaking technology powered by vibranium, the fictional metal native to Wakanda's vibranium mound.
A magical force field placed by ancient Wakandan kings using a kept-secret ritual every generation.
Heavy jungle terrain making aerial surveillance impossible; Wakanda is technologically advanced but undiscovered.
An alliance with the Egyptian sun god Ra, who places a divine seal of obscurity around the country.
context: Wakanda's vibranium-shielded cloaking is canon. The mound of vibranium is a key plot element. Christopher Priest's 1998-2003 run defined modern Black Panther.

question: Frank Miller began his work on Daredevil with #158 (May 1979). His full writer-and-artist run started with #168 (January 1981), introducing the character of Elektra Natchios, a Greek-American assassin and Murdock's college girlfriend. Elektra's most distinctive weapons are which?
answer: Sai (twin pronged daggers, Japanese origin), which she throws and wields in martial-arts combat scenes.
choices: Sai (twin pronged daggers, Japanese origin), which she throws and wields in martial-arts combat scenes.
Twin nunchaku, the Bruce Lee-popularized weapon that Miller might have considered but didn't use.
A single katana, the iconic Japanese sword that other Marvel characters like Wolverine occasionally wield.
A bo staff, the long wooden weapon that Miller used briefly for other Marvel characters but not Elektra.
context: Elektra's sai are iconic. The 2003 Daredevil film with Jennifer Garner adapted her. Miller's run rebuilt Daredevil for a generation.

question: Brian Michael Bendis and Mark Bagley's Ultimate Spider-Man (2000-2009) was a 133-issue run of the Marvel Ultimate Universe's reimagining of Spider-Man. The series re-introduced Peter Parker as a high schooler in modern-day setting. What was the Ultimate Universe?
answer: A parallel Marvel continuity (Earth-1610) created in 2000 to give new readers entry points to the franchise.
choices: A parallel Marvel continuity (Earth-1610) created in 2000 to give new readers entry points to the franchise.
A re-branded main Marvel universe (Earth-616) with no continuity changes, just a new editorial direction.
A short-lived Marvel imprint of 2010-12 that focused only on Asian-market story adaptations.
An anthology format of stand-alone stories with no shared continuity at all in any other Marvel title.
context: Ultimate Marvel (Earth-1610) was created by Jemas, Quesada, and Bendis. Ultimate Spider-Man ran the longest. The 2015 Secret Wars eventually merged Ultimate into the main 616.

question: Mark Millar and John Romita Jr.'s Kick-Ass debuted in 2008 at Marvel's Icon imprint. The book follows teenage Dave Lizewski who decides to dress in costume and fight crime. The breakout character of the book is a young girl trained as a vigilante by her father. What is her name?
answer: Hit-Girl (Mindy Macready), trained from infancy by her father Big Daddy for vigilante violence and revenge.
choices: Hit-Girl (Mindy Macready), trained from infancy by her father Big Daddy for vigilante violence and revenge.
Kick-Girl, an alternate female version of Kick-Ass who appeared in early-issue cameos but not as a lead.
Red Mist (Chris Genovese), who is actually a male antagonist, not the breakout young-girl vigilante.
Big Sister, an early Millar draft character whose role was rewritten into Hit-Girl in the final published version.
context: Hit-Girl is the breakout character. Red Mist (later Motherfucker) is a male antagonist. Chloe Grace Moretz played Hit-Girl in the 2010 film at age 13.

question: Frank Miller and Lynn Varley's 300 (May-September 1998) at Dark Horse Comics adapted the 480 BCE Battle of Thermopylae. The five-issue miniseries was painted by Varley. The story is famous for the dramatized Spartan dialogue. What is the most-quoted line, spoken to a Persian messenger?
answer: Tonight we dine in Hell! — King Leonidas's defiant pre-battle line as he addresses his hopeless few.
choices: Tonight we dine in Hell! — King Leonidas's defiant pre-battle line as he addresses his hopeless few.
This is Sparta! — Leonidas's response (via kick down a pit) to a Persian envoy demanding surrender.
We are with you to the end! — the Spartan oath shouted before the battle and the noble last stand.
Come back with your shields or upon them! — the historical Spartan mother's command to her son.
context: All four lines are from 300. THIS IS SPARTA! is the most-quoted, with the kicking the messenger scene. Lynn Varley's painted color was extraordinary.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon's Preacher (1995-2000) featured the Saint of Killers as one of its most iconic antagonists. The Saint is a 19th-century gunslinger killed and resurrected as an avenging-angel figure. What is his signature weapon?
answer: A pair of Walker Colt revolvers reforged from the sword of the Angel of Death; bullets never miss.
choices: A pair of Walker Colt revolvers reforged from the sword of the Angel of Death; bullets never miss.
A bolt-action rifle that can fire through any solid material it can be aimed at without exception.
A magical sword that grew from his bones during his resurrection in a Texas-canyon's old battlefield.
A pair of Henry repeating rifles that the Devil himself blessed with the curse of unending warfare.
context: The Saint's reforged Colts are iconic. AMC's 2016-19 Preacher series adapted Graham McTavish as the Saint. The Saint's vengeance arc is among Preacher's most quoted moments.

question: Brian Michael Bendis and Michael Avon Oeming's Powers (April 2000 onward) is a noir police procedural about cops who investigate crimes involving people with powers. The two leads are Detectives Christian Walker and Deena Pilgrim. What was Walker's secret history?
answer: Walker was a superhero himself in the 20th century who lost his powers years before the series begins.
choices: Walker was a superhero himself in the 20th century who lost his powers years before the series begins.
Walker is a powered-up alien from a hidden Earth species who walks among ordinary humans as a cop.
Walker is a time-traveler from the future where humans and powers have negotiated a working peace.
Walker is a clone of a famous deceased superhero, kept ignorant of his origin until the late issues.
context: Walker's superhero past is a major plot revelation across the series. Bendis is famous for his crime-comics fluency. Powers later moved to Marvel's Icon imprint.

question: Dave Sim's Cerebus the Aardvark began self-publication in December 1977 (issue #1) and continued for exactly 300 issues, ending in March 2004. The 27-year project is one of the most ambitious self-published comics ever. What was the title character?
answer: An anthropomorphic aardvark adventurer in a Conan-parody fantasy world that evolves to political drama.
choices: An anthropomorphic aardvark adventurer in a Conan-parody fantasy world that evolves to political drama.
A mole-creature wizard's apprentice in a fantasy realm later revealed as a parallel-universe Earth setting.
A pig-merchant from a renaissance-era kingdom undergoing reformation and revolution storyline arcs.
A bear-warrior on a quest for vengeance against a tyrant king who killed his entire family at the start.
context: Cerebus was uniquely an aardvark in Sim's series. The early issues are Conan parody; later arcs become political, religious, and increasingly idiosyncratic. Sim is a complex and controversial figure.

question: Herge (Georges Remi, 1907-1983) was a Belgian comics author whose Tintin character debuted in January 1929 in Le Petit Vingtieme, a children's supplement of a Brussels newspaper. The series ran 24 books. What were Tintin's main companions?
answer: His dog Snowy (Milou), Captain Haddock (an alcoholic sea captain), and the bumbling detectives Thompson and Thomson.
choices: His dog Snowy (Milou), Captain Haddock (an alcoholic sea captain), and the bumbling detectives Thompson and Thomson.
His parrot Polynesia, Professor Lidenbrock, and the geologist Axel Lidenbrock from Jules Verne's novel.
His mule Modestine, Bilbo Baggins, and the detective Sherlock Holmes from later adventures.
His cat Felix, the Phantom of the Opera, and a detective from a Paris police-prefecture department.
context: Snowy is Tintin's dog. Captain Haddock joined in 1941. Thompson and Thomson are detectives. Tintin remains popular globally; the 2011 Spielberg film adapted multiple stories.

question: Charles Schulz's Peanuts strip ran from October 2, 1950 to February 13, 2000, exactly 17,897 strips. Schulz drew every single one himself. The strip featured Charlie Brown and his dog Snoopy. What was the original title that Schulz wanted to use?
answer: Li'l Folks — Schulz's preferred title, but United Feature Syndicate gave him Peanuts against his wishes.
choices: Li'l Folks — Schulz's preferred title, but United Feature Syndicate gave him Peanuts against his wishes.
Good Ol' Charlie Brown — Schulz's preferred title; the syndicate shortened it to Peanuts for marketing.
Charlie Brown — Schulz wanted the protagonist's name as the title; the syndicate added Peanuts instead.
Schulz Funnies — Schulz proposed the simple eponymous title; the syndicate rejected it as too plain.
context: Schulz hated Peanuts as a title (he thought it was undignified) but accepted it. The syndicate had used Li'l Folks before. He preserved Peanuts only as the strip's title, never as a phrase within.

question: Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes (1985-1995) was named after two real-world historical figures. Calvin is John Calvin (1509-1564), the Protestant theologian. Who is Hobbes named after?
answer: Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679), the English philosopher who wrote Leviathan and described life as nasty, brutish, short.
choices: Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679), the English philosopher who wrote Leviathan and described life as nasty, brutish, short.
Calvin Coolidge, the 30th U.S. President (1923-1929), who was famously taciturn; not the strip's namesake.
John Hobbes, an early Watterson cartooning teacher whom Watterson chose to honor with the character.
James Hobbes, an obscure 19th-century American newspaper-illustrator and influence on Watterson.
context: Thomas Hobbes was indeed the namesake. Calvin's deterministic theology contrasts with Hobbes's view of human nature. The pairing is a longstanding philosophical joke in the strip.

question: Berkeley Breathed's Bloom County ran December 8, 1980 to August 6, 1989 — exactly 8 years and 8 months. Breathed retired the daily strip and returned with the Sunday-only Outland (1989-95). What animal became Bloom County's mascot?
answer: Opus, the penguin with the giant nose and existentialist disposition; he survived multiple Breathed strips.
choices: Opus, the penguin with the giant nose and existentialist disposition; he survived multiple Breathed strips.
Bill the Cat, the post-cocaine-addiction yellow striped cat; an iconic Breathed character but not the mascot.
Milo Bloom, the cyniclittle boy at the center of Bloom County; named after his cyclical-cynic personality.
Steve Dallas, the sleazy attorney who became a 1980s Reagan-era political-satire centerpiece in the strip.
context: Opus was Breathed's iconic creation. Bill the Cat (Ack! Phht!) was equally famous. The strip returned briefly in 2015 as a Facebook-exclusive after a 20-year hiatus.

question: DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths (April 1985 to March 1986) was a 12-issue maxi-series written by Marv Wolfman and drawn by George Perez. The series was a deliberate consolidation of DC's multiverse — collapsing many parallel Earths into one main reality. Why was it published?
answer: DC's multiverse had become confusing; the Crisis collapsed Earth-1, Earth-2, and others into a single continuity.
choices: DC's multiverse had become confusing; the Crisis collapsed Earth-1, Earth-2, and others into a single continuity.
A licensing dispute with TSR over Earth-Crisis (parallel-earths) required DC to rebrand the multiverse.
Stan Lee, then at Marvel, had publicly mocked DC's continuity; the Crisis was a competitive response.
DC's writers' guild had threatened a strike unless the multiverse was simplified to ease story-bible work.
context: DC's pre-Crisis multiverse was indeed confusing. Crisis killed Supergirl and the Barry Allen Flash (later returned). Post-Crisis DC was a simplified single Earth continuity for decades.

question: DC's Death of Superman storyline began in Superman #74 (December 1992) and culminated in Superman #75 (January 1993, cover-dated, on stands November 18, 1992). The issue used black borders on every panel for a specific reason. What was the design choice?
answer: Every panel was a single full-page splash with a dripping-blood border indicating Superman's struggle.
choices: Every panel was a single full-page splash with a dripping-blood border indicating Superman's struggle.
Every story page used standard panel layouts; the iconic page was the tabbed double-truncated spread.
Every panel was hidden behind a perforated black bag for the polybagged collector's edition.
Every page was printed in black-and-white to dramatize the somber funeral atmosphere of the issue.
context: Superman #75 used full-page splash panels with no traditional panels. The polybagged Collector's Edition included a Daily Planet memorial-page insert. Doomsday and Superman die in mutual destruction.

question: DC's Batman: No Man's Land (1999) was a year-long Batman crossover event spanning multiple titles. The story posited Gotham City being declared off-limits to the U.S. government after a massive earthquake. The arc ran in what real-world year?
answer: 1999 — the year-long arc ran from March 1999 through December 1999 in monthly Batman titles.
choices: 1999 — the year-long arc ran from March 1999 through December 1999 in monthly Batman titles.
1997 — the prior Cataclysm earthquake arc was 1998; No Man's Land followed in 1999, not 1997.
2001 — the arc was at the end of the 1990s, not the start of the 2000s decade in DC continuity.
1995 — the arc was almost half a decade later, in the late-1990s build-up to Crisis-style story events.
context: No Man's Land ran 1999, after Cataclysm (1998) and Aftershock (1998-99). The arc's apocalyptic Gotham informed The Dark Knight Rises (2012) and other later adaptations.

question: Alan Moore began his Swamp Thing run with Saga of Swamp Thing #21 (February 1984). The story is widely called the Anatomy Lesson. What is revealed about Swamp Thing's nature in the story?
answer: Swamp Thing is not Alec Holland transformed; he is a plant elemental who absorbed Holland's consciousness only.
choices: Swamp Thing is not Alec Holland transformed; he is a plant elemental who absorbed Holland's consciousness only.
Swamp Thing has always been Alec Holland alive; the prior Wein-Wrightson run had been a feverish hallucination.
Swamp Thing is a future-evolved descendant of vegetation that the cell-research lab had been studying.
Swamp Thing's true name is Alec Holland's identical twin brother Linton, who never existed in canon prior.
context: Moore's plant-elemental revelation reframed the character. The 1984 issue is studied as a master class in revisionist comics writing. Stephen Bissette and John Totleben were the art team.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon's Preacher (1995-2000) takes place primarily in Texas and the American West. Without spoiling specifics, Jesse Custer's mission across the series is what?
answer: To find God (who has abandoned heaven) and hold him accountable for the world's suffering and injustice.
choices: To find God (who has abandoned heaven) and hold him accountable for the world's suffering and injustice.
To destroy the angel Genesis (the creature bonded with him) by returning it to the heavenly host.
To rebuild his rural Texas town, which had been destroyed by the entity's catastrophic arrival on Earth.
To reunite with his college girlfriend Tulip after years of separation and amnesia from a Texas accident.
context: Jesse's search for God to hold accountable is the through-line. Cassidy and Tulip join the mission. Saint of Killers pursues. The 2016-19 AMC adaptation kept the core premise.

question: Garth Ennis's Punisher MAX run (2004-2009) at Marvel was a 60-issue series featuring Frank Castle in stand-alone story arcs. The series leaned more realistic than mainstream Marvel — no superpowered villains, just Castle hunting mafia, sex traffickers, and arms dealers. Who succeeded Ennis on Punisher MAX?
answer: Jason Aaron, in a 2010-12 run focused on Castle's daughter and Punisher's origin in deeper detail.
choices: Jason Aaron, in a 2010-12 run focused on Castle's daughter and Punisher's origin in deeper detail.
Brian Michael Bendis, who wrote the next Punisher series instead in mainstream Marvel continuity only.
Mark Millar, whose own Punisher MAX run had preceded Ennis from 2001 instead of following him.
Greg Rucka, whose Marvel work has not specifically included a Punisher MAX run after Ennis ended.
context: Aaron's PunisherMAX (2010-12) was the direct successor. The MAX line ended in 2012. Ennis returned for occasional Punisher MAX one-shots in subsequent years.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon's Preacher introduced a recurring antagonist named Herr Starr — a bald, scar-faced agent of an ancient organization called The Grail. What is The Grail's plot in the series?
answer: Replace God with their own messianic figure they have been breeding for centuries from Christ's bloodline.
choices: Replace God with their own messianic figure they have been breeding for centuries from Christ's bloodline.
Capture and contain the entity Genesis (bonded with Jesse) to wield its power for worldly conquest plans.
Eliminate Jesse Custer specifically because his Word of God power threatens their secret religious plot.
Reform the United States government into a theocratic Christian kingdom under their handpicked king.
context: The Grail's apocalyptic Messiah plot is central to Preacher's plot. Herr Starr becomes one of the series's most beloved antagonists, with a streak of grotesque slapstick injury comedy.

question: Alan Moore and Brian Bolland's Batman: The Killing Joke (March 1988) became the most-referenced single Joker story. The book is famous for one of the most controversial moments in Batman comics — an event involving Barbara Gordon (Batgirl). What did the Joker do?
answer: Shot her in the spine, paralyzing her; she later became the wheelchair-using Oracle in subsequent comics.
choices: Shot her in the spine, paralyzing her; she later became the wheelchair-using Oracle in subsequent comics.
Beat her unconscious and made her watch as he killed her mother; this drove her vengeance arc.
Hypnotized her into believing he was her father; this led to a multi-year identity-crisis storyline.
Kidnapped her and threatened her with his Joker Toxin; she escaped relatively unharmed in the end.
context: Killing Joke's shooting of Barbara is famous and divisive. She became Oracle, leader of Birds of Prey. The 2003 Bat-stories rebuilt her arc significantly. Moore has expressed regret over the scene.

question: Alan Moore's V for Vendetta is set in a near-future totalitarian England, post-nuclear-war. The protagonist V quotes literature constantly. Which Shakespeare play does V reference most heavily?
answer: Macbeth, which V quotes during pivotal moments throughout the comic with its themes of usurpation and tyranny.
choices: Macbeth, which V quotes during pivotal moments throughout the comic with its themes of usurpation and tyranny.
Hamlet, which V quotes early in the comic but not as often as the rebellion goes on across the issues.
Julius Caesar, the political-assassination play that V invokes as he kills government officials one by one.
Richard III, the tyrant-king tragedy that V seems most thematically aligned to in his goals as protagonist.
context: Macbeth is heavily quoted. The famous V identifying himself in Shakespearean cadence (Vi Veri Veniversum Vivus Vici) is alphabetical play. The 2005 film by James McTeigue and the Wachowskis adapted.

question: Neil Gaiman's The Sandman (1989-1996) at DC's Vertigo imprint introduced an extended cast across 75 issues. The series's two most popular characters were Dream and his sister Death. How is Death portrayed?
answer: A cheerful young goth woman in black, with an ankh necklace; she is friendly and welcomes the dead.
choices: A cheerful young goth woman in black, with an ankh necklace; she is friendly and welcomes the dead.
A skeletal Grim Reaper figure with a scythe; the traditional Western iconography that Gaiman subverted later.
A burning-bright angel figure with multiple wings; a divine messenger taking souls to their afterlives.
A wraithlike old woman in tattered black; an ancient crone figure that haunts the dying at their bedsides.
context: Death's perky goth-girl portrayal is one of Sandman's defining contributions. Mike Dringenberg designed her based partly on a real friend named Cinamon Hadley. Death later got her own miniseries.

question: Mike Mignola's Hellboy (1993 onward at Dark Horse) is built on extensive folklore research. Mignola draws from world mythology — particularly Slavic, Irish, and Mesopotamian. The series is set in what time?
answer: Modern day, with Hellboy investigating cases from 1944 (his arrival as a baby) onward through the present.
choices: Modern day, with Hellboy investigating cases from 1944 (his arrival as a baby) onward through the present.
Strictly the 1940s-50s, with all Hellboy stories set during World War II and immediately after.
Strictly the 19th century, with Hellboy as a Victorian-era paranormal investigator only.
Strictly the 21st century, with the WWII flashbacks shown only as historical material later.
context: Hellboy spans decades. The 2004 Guillermo del Toro film cast Ron Perlman as Hellboy. The 2008 sequel was even more beloved. The series's mythology is extensively cataloged.

question: Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's Watchmen (1986-87) consciously imitated the structure of older superhero comics with backmatter — text features that supplemented the visual narrative. The book's twelve issues each ended with what kind of backmatter?
answer: Excerpts from in-universe documents like memoirs, news articles, and academic studies on the heroes.
choices: Excerpts from in-universe documents like memoirs, news articles, and academic studies on the heroes.
Letters columns from readers, the standard 1980s practice that nearly all DC and Marvel books used.
Behind-the-scenes art-process pages showing Gibbons's pencils and color choices for the issue.
Cross-promotional ads for upcoming DC titles, with no in-universe content of any kind included.
context: Watchmen's backmatter (Hollis Mason memoir, Treasure Island Treasury, Nostalgia perfume ad, Black Freighter excerpts) deepened the world. The 2009 Zack Snyder film adapted the visuals but cut backmatter.

question: Frank Miller's Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (1986) ran four issues and depicted a 55-year-old Bruce Wayne returning from retirement. The series's signature visual is broken into 16 panels per page. Why did Miller choose that grid?
answer: He wanted a TV-screen feel; the 16-panel grid recreated the look of cable news broadcasting on TV in 1986.
choices: He wanted a TV-screen feel; the 16-panel grid recreated the look of cable news broadcasting on TV in 1986.
Klaus Janson, his inker, insisted on it; Miller had originally drawn larger panels in his initial layouts.
DC Comics required smaller panels for higher-page-count economic reasons in 1986 budget meetings.
Miller's original homework was the Dave Sim Cerebus issue with the 16-panel grid, which he had imitated.
context: Miller's TV-screen 16-panel grid is iconic. The constant cuts to news broadcasters frame the apocalyptic Gotham. Lynn Varley's color (Frank's then-wife) was equally distinctive.

question: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby's Captain America #1 (March 1941, cover-dated) was a Timely Comics (later Marvel) book. It featured a cover of Cap punching Adolf Hitler in the face — nine months before America's entry into WWII. What was the publisher's response?
answer: Timely received threatening letters and phone calls; the NYPD reportedly stationed a guard at their offices.
choices: Timely received threatening letters and phone calls; the NYPD reportedly stationed a guard at their offices.
Timely briefly canceled the book in spring 1942 after copies were stolen from the printing press in Brooklyn.
Timely's publisher Martin Goodman was sued by an American-German cultural group; the suit was dismissed.
Timely lost its newsstand distribution in pro-German areas of New York; cover was changed for those locations.
context: Cap #1 sold over one million copies. Simon and Kirby received hate mail from Bund supporters. NYPD did station a man at Timely. Cap punching Hitler became a defining war-effort image.

question: Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum included Wolverine in the all-new team. Wolverine had previously appeared in Hulk #181 (1974) by Wein, Trimpe, and Romita. Who eventually became Wolverine's most iconic writer?
answer: Chris Claremont, whose run on X-Men (1975-91) defined Wolverine's character and origins for decades.
choices: Chris Claremont, whose run on X-Men (1975-91) defined Wolverine's character and origins for decades.
Frank Miller, whose 1982 Wolverine miniseries was foundational but more limited in scope than Claremont's.
Larry Hama, whose 1990s Wolverine series defined Logan's WWII backstory and Daken connections in arcs.
Mark Millar, whose 2008-09 Old Man Logan defined a future Wolverine setting after the death of all heroes.
context: All four are real Wolverine writers. Claremont's 16-year run is foundational. Miller's miniseries (1982) defined Japan-arc Wolverine. Hama added new continuity in the 1990s.

question: Chris Claremont's X-Men run (1975-1991) was the longest single writer's run on any major superhero comic. After Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) by Wein, Claremont took over with Uncanny X-Men #94 (August 1975). What was his last X-Men issue?
answer: Uncanny X-Men #279 (August 1991), after which a creative dispute with editor Bob Harras led to his exit.
choices: Uncanny X-Men #279 (August 1991), after which a creative dispute with editor Bob Harras led to his exit.
X-Men Vol 2 #3 (December 1991), the new launch series; Jim Lee was the architect of the relaunch.
Uncanny X-Men #300 (May 1993), well past Claremont's actual departure date in 1991.
Uncanny X-Men #250 (October 1989), an earlier landmark issue but well before Claremont's actual exit.
context: Claremont left after Uncanny #279. He briefly wrote X-Men Vol 2 #1-3 in 1991 alongside Jim Lee but exited entirely. He later returned to write X-Men: The End (2004-06).

question: Chris Claremont, John Byrne, and Terry Austin's Dark Phoenix Saga in X-Men #129-137 (January-September 1980) featured Jean Grey transformed into the cosmic Phoenix entity. The Hellfire Club had manipulated her into Black Queen status earlier in the arc. Who designed the Hellfire Club?
answer: John Byrne, who based the Black Queen costume on Diana Rigg's outfit in The Avengers TV series episode A Touch of Brimstone.
choices: John Byrne, who based the Black Queen costume on Diana Rigg's outfit in The Avengers TV series episode A Touch of Brimstone.
Dave Cockrum, who had designed the original 1975 X-Men team but not the Hellfire Club specifically.
Bob McLeod, the New Mutants co-creator, who had designed minor X-villains but not the Hellfire Club.
Bob Layton, the Iron Man artist who had no Hellfire Club design work whatsoever in his career.
context: Byrne's Diana Rigg homage is well-documented. Jason Wyngarde / Mastermind used the Black Queen identity to manipulate Jean. The Avengers TV-series episode is from 1966.

question: Robert E. Howard's first Conan story Phoenix on the Sword (December 1932) was actually a rewrite of an earlier rejected story. The original protagonist had a different name. Who was the original character that Howard reworked into Conan?
answer: King Kull, the brooding Atlantean king from Howard's earlier 1929 short story By This Axe I Rule!
choices: King Kull, the brooding Atlantean king from Howard's earlier 1929 short story By This Axe I Rule!
Solomon Kane, Howard's Puritan swordsman who would never have been a kingly protagonist.
Bran Mak Morn, the Pictish king, who was a historical-warrior character Howard wrote contemporaneously.
Cormac Mac Art, the Celtic warrior, who was unrelated to Howard's character revision in 1932.
context: Howard rewrote By This Axe I Rule! (Kull) into Phoenix on the Sword (Conan). The two characters share Atlantean ancestry in Howard's loose continuity. Kull was the precursor in many ways.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's The Dunwich Horror (1929) features the Whateley family in the fictional Dunwich, Massachusetts. The novella opens with a quotation from Charles Lamb describing demons of the imagination. The story uses what kind of narrative structure?
answer: Third-person omniscient with patches of folkloric historical interludes about Dunwich and its degenerate inhabitants.
choices: Third-person omniscient with patches of folkloric historical interludes about Dunwich and its degenerate inhabitants.
First-person narrator who is the protagonist, like much of Lovecraft's other Cthulhu Mythos work.
Epistolary, told entirely through letters between the Whateley family members and their distant relations.
Stream-of-consciousness, told from Wilbur Whateley's perspective until his death halfway through.
context: Dunwich Horror's third-person omniscient style is unusual for Lovecraft, who typically wrote in first person. The omniscient narration emphasizes the rural-decay theme.

question: Philip K. Dick wrote dozens of novels and over 120 short stories. The most-adapted PKD source for film is the 1956 short story Minority Report, adapted by Steven Spielberg in 2002. What is the central premise?
answer: Three precogs receive visions of future murders, and police prevent them; one preg-vision dissents from the others.
choices: Three precogs receive visions of future murders, and police prevent them; one preg-vision dissents from the others.
A man begins to dream of his own future death and tries to prevent it through a complex time-loop system.
An office worker discovers that everyone in his office is a robotic android impersonator and he is alone.
Three judges secretly possess precognition and pass verdicts based on future actions of defendants.
context: Minority Report's premise is the precogs and their dissenting views. The 2002 Spielberg film expanded the premise. The 2015 TV series further developed it. PKD's original short is much shorter.

question: Robert A. Heinlein's Starship Troopers (1959) is a controversial military-science-fiction novel about a young soldier in the Mobile Infantry fighting alien Bugs. The novel won the Hugo Award. Heinlein had been a U.S. Naval Academy graduate. When was he tuberculosis-discharged?
answer: 1934, after only 5 years of service; the discharge let him focus on engineering and later writing.
choices: 1934, after only 5 years of service; the discharge let him focus on engineering and later writing.
1945, at the end of WWII, after combat service in the Pacific theater.
1939, after a decade in Naval intelligence; he transitioned directly to magazine fiction writing.
1929, immediately after graduation; he never served on active duty due to the tuberculosis diagnosis.
context: Heinlein graduated Annapolis in 1929, served from 1929-34, and was discharged for tuberculosis. He then studied physics and engineering, and began writing fiction in 1939. He served in civilian roles during WWII.

question: H.P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness (1936) features an Antarctic geological expedition from Miskatonic University. The story includes a famously horrifying line. What is the iconic line uttered by the narrator describing the alien monsters?
answer: Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li! — the cry of the Shoggoths, borrowed from Poe's Pym (1837) Antarctic narrative.
choices: Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li! — the cry of the Shoggoths, borrowed from Poe's Pym (1837) Antarctic narrative.
Cthulhu fhtagn! — the iconic chant from The Call of Cthulhu, used by Cthulhu cultists rather than Shoggoths.
Iä! Shub-Niggurath! — the chant for Shub-Niggurath, the Black Goat of the Woods (a different Mythos entity).
Yog-Sothoth! — the name of the Outside Cosmic God, separate from the Shoggoth-and-Antarctic entities here.
context: Tekeli-li! is the Shoggoth cry. Lovecraft borrowed it from Poe's Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym (1838). The line links Lovecraft's mythos to Poe's earlier Antarctic strangeness.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Tarzan was adapted to film 50+ times. The first Tarzan film was a 1918 silent. The most famous early Tarzan was Johnny Weissmuller starting in 1932. What was Weissmuller's pre-Tarzan career?
answer: Olympic swimmer who won 5 gold medals (1924, 1928 Olympics) and held 67 world swimming records.
choices: Olympic swimmer who won 5 gold medals (1924, 1928 Olympics) and held 67 world swimming records.
Hollywood stuntman who had appeared in many B-movies in the 1920s before being cast as Tarzan in 1932.
Vaudeville circus strongman who had performed feats of strength on the variety-show circuit since 1925.
Professional baseball player for the St. Louis Browns who left the game after a serious injury in 1930.
context: Weissmuller (1904-1984) won 5 gold medals and broke 67 swim records. He played Tarzan in 12 films 1932-48. His Tarzan yell became iconic.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's John Carter of Mars first appeared as Under the Moons of Mars (serial title) in All-Story February-July 1912. The character spawned 11 novels from 1912 to 1948. What is the Martian race that captures John Carter at the start?
answer: The Tharks, four-armed green giants of the Martian deserts; Carter befriends their chief Tars Tarkas.
choices: The Tharks, four-armed green giants of the Martian deserts; Carter befriends their chief Tars Tarkas.
The Red Martians, the human-like race that includes Princess Dejah Thoris; they are friendlier than Tharks.
The Black Pirates of Barsoom, the air-pirate race that does not appear until the second book Gods of Mars (1913).
The Therns, the white-priest race from Gods of Mars (1913) and not from the first Princess of Mars book.
context: Tharks capture Carter in book 1. He befriends Tars Tarkas. Red Martians (including Dejah Thoris) come later. All four are real Barsoom races from Burroughs's continuity.

question: Doc Savage, the Man of Bronze, was Clark Savage Jr. The Doc Savage novels (1933 onward) featured Doc traveling the world with a team of specialist assistants. What were the names of his Fabulous Five team members?
answer: Renny (engineer), Long Tom (electrician), Johnny (geologist/archeologist), Ham (lawyer), Monk (chemist).
choices: Renny (engineer), Long Tom (electrician), Johnny (geologist/archeologist), Ham (lawyer), Monk (chemist).
Hawkeye, Black Widow, Hulk, Captain America, and Iron Man — names from later Marvel Comics, not Doc Savage.

question: The Oak Island Money Pit on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, has been the subject of treasure hunts since 1795. question: The Ouroboros is an ancient symbol of a snake (or dragon) eating its own tail. The symbol appears in ancient Egyptian iconography, Norse mythology (Jormungandr the World Serpent), and medieval alchemical texts. What does the symbol traditionally represent?

question: Lemuria is a hypothetical lost continent originally proposed by 19th-century scientists to explain biological-similarities between Madagascar and India before continental drift was understood. The concept was later expanded by Theosophists and occult writers. Who coined the name Lemuria?

question: The Philadelphia Experiment is an alleged 1943 U.S. Navy invisibility test of the USS Eldridge (DE-173). The story has the Eldridge becoming invisible to radar and reappearing miles away in Norfolk, with crew members fused to the deck and going mad. Where did the story originate?

question: Area 51 is a U.S. Air Force facility at Groom Lake, Nevada, within the Nevada Test and Training Range. The base was used for U-2 and SR-71 development and stealth aircraft testing. The U.S. government did not officially acknowledge Area 51's existence until what year?

question: The three pyramids of Giza (Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure) were built around 2580-2510 BCE during the Egyptian 4th Dynasty. A controversial theory holds that their layout mirrors a specific celestial constellation. What is the constellation?

question: Madeleine McCann, age 3, disappeared from her family's holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, Portugal, on May 3, 2007. question: The Backrooms is a 2019 internet horror phenomenon that began with a single image posted to 4chan's /x/ board. The image showed an empty office-corridor with yellow walls, fluorescent lights, and patterned carpet. The caption gave the image its name. What's the origin year?

question: Slender Man is an internet horror character created on June 10, 2009 by Eric Knudsen (Victor Surge) on the Something Awful forum. question: Sleep paralysis with hallucinations (hag-syndrome) has been linked to many global cryptids — including the Popobawa, the Old Hag of Newfoundland, and the Sasanga of Liberia. What's the biological basis?

question: The Lake Van Monster (or Van Golu Canavari) is a Turkish lake monster from Lake Van in eastern Turkey — the largest lake in Turkey, at 11,500 feet elevation. The lake is alkaline (pH 9.7-9.8) and brackish. When did the modern Lake Van Monster phenomenon begin?

question: The Loch Ness Monster's most-cited photograph is the 1934 Surgeon's Photograph, attributed to Dr. R. Kenneth Wilson but actually staged by Marmaduke Wetherell and Christian Spurling. What was the photographic apparatus?

question: John Keel's 1975 book The Mothman Prophecies expanded on his 1966-67 investigation of the Point Pleasant, West Virginia Mothman sightings. The book ties Mothman to the December 15, 1967 Silver Bridge collapse and to a broader paranormal phenomenon. What is Keel's theory?

question: The Patterson-Gimlin Film of October 20, 1967 was shot in Bluff Creek, Del Norte County, California. The location was specifically chosen by Roger Patterson because of recent footprint discoveries. Who had found the original Bluff Creek footprints in 1958?

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for Pharaoh Khufu of Egypt's 4th Dynasty around 2580-2560 BCE. The pyramid contains three main chambers — the King's Chamber, the Queen's Chamber, and the Grand Gallery. A 2017 muon-detection survey revealed something new. What?

question: TSR published Module B2: Keep on the Borderlands in 1980 by Gary Gygax. The module became one of the most widely-played D&D modules ever, packaged with the Basic Set for years. The module's central adventure location is what?
answer: The Caves of Chaos, a complex of cave-lairs housing competing humanoid tribes (orcs, hobgoblins, etc.).
choices: The Caves of Chaos, a complex of cave-lairs housing competing humanoid tribes (orcs, hobgoblins, etc.).

The Steading of the Hill Giant Chief, the giant-themed module (G1) by Gygax, not B2.
The Slave Pits of the Undercity, the slave-rescue module (A1) by Gygax, not B2 itself.

question: Gary Gygax's Module S1: Tomb of Horrors (1978) is the legendary D&D killer dungeon, originally written by Gygax as a tournament module to challenge expert players. The dungeon is the lair of Acererak the lich. What is the Tomb's most famous trap?

The Mirror of Opposition, a mirror that produces a mirror-version of an adventurer to fight them.
context: The Sphere of Annihilation in the green demon's mouth is the Tomb's signature trap. Acererak appears (as a corpse / desiccated lich) in the final chamber. The module killed countless PCs.

question: TSR's Module S2: White Plume Mountain (1979) by Lawrence Schick is a funhouse dungeon for AD&D. The module features a wizard named Keraptis and three legendary weapons that players are sent to retrieve. What are the three weapons?
answer: Wave (trident), Whelm (warhammer), and Blackrazor (sword; a knockoff of Stormbringer).
choices: Wave (trident), Whelm (warhammer), and Blackrazor (sword; a knockoff of Stormbringer).
Excalibur, Stormbringer, and Anduril — three direct lifts from Tolkien, Moorcock, and Arthurian legend.
Greenmoss, Silverdawn, and Goldfire — three made-up names Schick invented for the module's setting.
Pegasus's Bite, Dragon's Tooth, and Ogre's Last Stand — three thematic names Schick used in the module.

question: TSR's Module S3: Expedition to the Barrier Peaks (1980) by Gary Gygax mixes D&D with science-fiction elements. The module describes a crashed spaceship that adventurers explore. The ship contains laser guns, robots, and force-fields. What inspired the module?
answer: Gygax's earlier 1976 Origins convention adventure 'The Lost Ship', based on Gygax's interest in pulp SF.
choices: Gygax's earlier 1976 Origins convention adventure 'The Lost Ship', based on Gygax's interest in pulp SF.
A 1980 Star Wars roleplaying-game project at TSR that was cancelled but reused for Barrier Peaks.
Gary Gygax's published wargaming columns about Stargate scenarios, which he had run since 1973.
Brian Blume's pulp-SF reading list, which Gary referenced when assembling the module's content.

question: Gygax's giant series (G1-G2-G3) and follow-up drow series (D1-D2-D3) and demon-queen module (Q1) form one of D&D's most-celebrated module chains. G1 is The Steading of the Hill Giant Chief. What is the chief's name?

question: Gygax's Module D3: Vault of the Drow (1978) was the first major D&D depiction of dark elves (drow). The module describes a vast underground cavern containing an entire drow civilization. Who is the supreme drow deity?
answer: Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders, who would also feature in Q1: Queen of the Demonweb Pits (1980).
choices: Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders, who would also feature in Q1: Queen of the Demonweb Pits (1980).

question: TSR's Module I6: Ravenloft (1983) by Tracy and Laura Hickman introduced the Castle Ravenloft setting and the iconic vampire Count Strahd von Zarovich. The module became so popular it spawned a full campaign setting line. When did the Ravenloft setting line launch?

question: Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman's Dragonlance Chronicles trilogy began with Dragons of Autumn Twilight (November 1984) at TSR. The trilogy was packaged with companion modules (DL1-DL14) for D&D play. What was the second novel?

question: R.A. Salvatore's Drizzt Do'Urden became Forgotten Realms's most popular character. Drizzt first appeared in The Crystal Shard (1988), as a supporting character. He is a renegade drow with conscience. Who were Drizzt's traveling companions in the original Icewind Dale trilogy?

question: Ed Greenwood created the Forgotten Realms as a personal setting for his fiction and home D&D campaigns starting in 1967. He had been developing the setting for nearly 20 years before TSR officially licensed it. When did TSR officially publish the Forgotten Realms?

question: Gygax's Greyhawk setting featured a roster of iconic NPC wizards, each known for a signature spell named after them. Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound, Bigby's Crushing Hand, Tenser's Floating Disc. Many of these characters had real-world inspirations. What was the in-joke?

question: Gygax's Greyhawk Supplement I for original D&D (1975) introduced several enduring features to the game. The supplement was the first to introduce one specific class. What class debuted in Greyhawk Supplement I?

question: Gary Gygax and Brian Blume's Supplement III: Eldritch Wizardry (1976) for original D&D added several new game features. The supplement is famous for adding what mechanical system?

question: The Beholder is one of D&D's most iconic original monsters — a floating spherical eyeball with eyestalks. The Beholder's central eye shoots an anti-magic cone, and each of its 10 eyestalks fires a different magical ray. Who designed the original Beholder?
answer: Terry Kuntz (Rob Kuntz's brother), in Gygax's Greyhawk home campaign; the Beholder first appeared in Greyhawk Supplement I (1975).
choices: Terry Kuntz (Rob Kuntz's brother), in Gygax's Greyhawk home campaign; the Beholder first appeared in Greyhawk Supplement I (1975).

Dave Arneson, in the original Blackmoor campaign; the Beholder was a Blackmoor creation rather than Greyhawk.

question: The Mind Flayer (Illithid) is another iconic original D&D monster. It is a humanoid creature with an octopus-like head, four tentacles, and the ability to extract victims' brains for consumption. When did the Mind Flayer first appear in D&D?
answer: The Strategic Review #1 (Spring 1975), TSR's house magazine that became Dragon Magazine in 1976.

Blackmoor Supplement II (1975), as one of Dave Arneson's contributions to the official monster bestiary.

question: The Displacer Beast is a 6-legged panther-like creature with a magical displacement ability — it appears to be a few feet away from its actual location, making it difficult to hit. The creature was inspired by an A.E. van Vogt science-fiction story. What story?
answer: Black Destroyer (1939), van Vogt's short story featuring an alien Coeurl that Gygax used as inspiration.

The Voyage of the Space Beagle (1950), the novel containing Black Destroyer; correct inspiration partly.
context: Black Destroyer (1939, later in The Voyage of the Space Beagle, 1950) features the Coeurl. Gygax explicitly cited it. The story's alien predator inspired the Displacer Beast.

question: The Owlbear is a recurring D&D monster — a creature with the body of a bear and the head of an owl. The monster's name is so generic it's become a meme. Gary Gygax claimed the Owlbear was inspired by a specific real-world object. What?
answer: A plastic toy figure (made in Hong Kong); part of a set of similar mash-up creatures Gygax bought cheaply.
choices: A plastic toy figure (made in Hong Kong); part of a set of similar mash-up creatures Gygax bought cheaply.
A medieval French heraldic figure (the gryphon-eared bear) that Gygax found in a heraldry book.
An ancient Sumerian relief sculpture (the owl-headed bear-god) that Gygax saw in a museum exhibit.
A Maurice Sendak illustration from Where the Wild Things Are (1963); Sendak's creatures inspired Gygax.
context: Gygax bought a plastic toy figure made in Hong Kong (likely an knockoff Ultraman creature) and used it as the Owlbear template. The Bulette and Rust Monster also derive from the same toy set.

question: The Bulette (Landshark) is another iconic D&D monster originally derived from a Hong Kong plastic toy figure that Gygax bought cheaply. The Bulette's distinctive shark-like fin and dinosaur-like body came from a single specific toy set. What was the toy set's origin?
answer: Marx Toys Prehistoric Playset's later 1970s plastic figures, mass-produced cheaply in Hong Kong.

Gygax's original chess-set custom pieces; one piece had been an unusual Hong Kong-import substitute.

A Marx Toys Dinosaur Playset from 1965; Gygax bought it secondhand to use for D&D miniatures.
context: The Marx Toys-set Hong Kong plastic figures gave rise to Bulette, Owlbear, and Rust Monster. These three monsters are now among D&D's most iconic original creations from the dollar-bin toys.

question: Drow are the dark elves of D&D — black-skinned, white-haired humanoid elves who dwell in the Underdark beneath the surface. The drow's primary deity is Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders. When did drow first appear in D&D?

Module D1 (Descent into the Depths of the Earth, 1978), where they first take center stage in the D-series.

Module D3 (Vault of the Drow, 1978), where drow culture is depicted in detail in their underground civilization.
context: Drow first appeared briefly in G3 (Hall of the Fire Giant King). They appeared more prominently in D1 (Descent), D2 (Shrine of the Kuo-Toa), and prominently in D3 (Vault of the Drow). G123-D123-Q1 forms the GDQ series.

question: The Tarrasque is one of D&D's most powerful monsters — a colossal reptilian creature that cannot be killed by ordinary means. The Tarrasque first appeared in the AD&D Monster Manual II (1983). What is its key irrevocable ability?

It is immortal until the next full moon; it always regenerates within 28 days of being defeated.
context: The Tarrasque's regeneration is its defining feature; only Wish can prevent it. The monster is loosely based on the French legendary tarasque (a Rhone-Provence beast).

question: Kuo-Toa are fish-folk who live in the Underdark, often serving the demon-goddess Blibdoolpoolp. They first appeared in D&D in 1978. In which module?

context: Kuo-Toa debuted in D2 (Shrine of the Kuo-Toa, 1978). The module is part of the GDQ series. Blibdoolpoolp (the Sea Mother) is their demon-deity. The Kuo-Toa's hallucinatory religious customs are darkly comedic.

question: Wizards of the Coast released Magic: The Gathering Alpha in August 1993. The game was designed by Richard Garfield, then a PhD student at the University of Pennsylvania. Where did Garfield earn his PhD?

question: Wizards of the Coast was founded in 1990 by Peter Adkison and others in Renton, Washington. Before MTG, the company published roleplaying game material. What was Wizards's first RPG product?
answer: The Primal Order (1991), a deity-and-cosmology supplement designed to work with any RPG system.

question: MTG Alpha's print run in August 1993 was modest. Wizards of the Coast had not anticipated the demand. How many Alpha cards were printed?
answer: Approximately 2.6 million cards, sold out within weeks; Beta was rushed into print to meet demand.

question: MTG Beta was released in October 1993 — just two months after Alpha — to meet the demand from Alpha selling out. Beta had several corrections from Alpha. What were the main differences?
answer: Beta included two missing cards (Volcanic Island, Circle of Protection Black) that had been omitted from Alpha.

question: MTG Unlimited Edition was released in December 1993. The set was identical in card pool to Alpha and Beta but had a distinguishing visual feature. What was the visual difference?
answer: Unlimited cards had white borders; Alpha and Beta cards had black borders.

question: MTG's first expansion set, Arabian Nights, was released in December 1993. The set drew on stories from The One Thousand and One Nights (Arabian Nights). The set introduced several iconic cards. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Richard Garfield himself, with art-direction handled by Jesper Myrfors; many cards have Arabian-themed art.

question: MTG's second expansion, Antiquities (March 1994), focused on artifact cards. The set's plot involved the Brothers' War between Urza and Mishra — a major MTG storyline that has continued to be reused. Who designed Antiquities?

question: MTG Revised Edition (3rd Edition) was released in April 1994. The set's card pool was a mix of Alpha-Beta cards (with some removed) and Arabian Nights and Antiquities cards (added). Why was Revised's card-pool selection controversial?

question: MTG's third expansion, Legends, was released in June 1994. The set introduced a new card type that has become central to MTG. What was the new card type?

question: MTG's Power Nine is the term for nine of the most powerful cards from Alpha. The cards are considered unbalanced by modern standards. What are the nine cards?
answer: Black Lotus, the five Moxes (Pearl, Sapphire, Jet, Ruby, Emerald), Ancestral Recall, Time Walk, Timetwister.

question: MTG's Black Lotus card is one of the most valuable trading cards in the world. A mint-condition Alpha Black Lotus has sold for over $500,000 at auction. What does Black Lotus do mechanically?
answer: Tap and sacrifice Black Lotus: Add three mana of any one color to your mana pool; very high cost-efficiency.
