context: Black Lotus's tap-sacrifice for 3 mana is the most efficient mana-acceleration card ever printed. The card has been on the Reserved List since 1996 and is banned in all major formats.

question: MTG's Reserved List was created in 1996 in response to player anger over reprints. The Reserved List included all of the Power Nine and many Alpha/Beta cards. What was the official Wizards commitment?
answer: Cards on the Reserved List would never be reprinted in functional form; promises a stable secondary market.
choices: Cards on the Reserved List would never be reprinted in functional form; promises a stable secondary market.
Cards on the Reserved List would be reprinted only with major modifications to their text and mechanics.
Cards on the Reserved List would be reprinted in promotional sets only (not standard expansions).
Cards on the Reserved List would be available only at major MTG tournaments through prize support.
context: Reserved List cards will not be functionally reprinted. The list has been criticized but Wizards has maintained it. Some cards have been removed (early 2000s) but Wizards stopped removing in 2010.

question: MTG's Serra Angel is one of the most iconic creatures from Alpha. The card features a striking white angel and is widely cited as the visual face of MTG. What are Serra Angel's stats?
answer: Mana cost 3WW, 4/4 with Flying and Vigilance (originally 'does not tap to attack' in Alpha terms).
choices: Mana cost 3WW, 4/4 with Flying and Vigilance (originally 'does not tap to attack' in Alpha terms).
Mana cost 2WW, 4/4 with Flying alone (without the Vigilance ability that was added in later rules).
Mana cost 4WW, 5/5 with Flying and First Strike; not Serra Angel's actual stats from Alpha.
Mana cost 3WW, 3/4 with Flying and Trample; Serra Angel has Vigilance, not Trample.
context: Serra Angel: 3WW, 4/4, Flying, Vigilance. The art (by Douglas Schuler) is iconic. The card has been reprinted in many sets.

question: MTG's Lightning Bolt is one of the most efficient damage spells ever printed. The card is a single red mana, instant speed, dealing 3 damage to any target. What's notable about Lightning Bolt's printings?
answer: It was in Alpha through 4th Edition; banned and unbanned in various formats; later returned in Magic 2010-2011.
choices: It was in Alpha through 4th Edition; banned and unbanned in various formats; later returned in Magic 2010-2011.
It was never reprinted after Alpha; it remains an Alpha-exclusive card with no other reprint history.
It was reprinted in every set from Alpha onward; the card has been in every major MTG expansion.
It was a Reserved List card; it has never been reprinted after 1994 due to its market-value protection.
context: Lightning Bolt has been in many sets: Alpha through 4th Edition, then Magic 2010, Magic 2011, then Modern Masters. It's not Reserved-Listed.

question: MTG's Counterspell is the archetypal blue instant — counter target spell for two blue mana. The card was in Alpha and has been a benchmark for blue magic ever since. What's the most ironic fact about Counterspell?
answer: It was reprinted in 4th Edition (1995) and many later sets; it's a common card despite its iconic status.
choices: It was reprinted in 4th Edition (1995) and many later sets; it's a common card despite its iconic status.
It was a Reserved List card and is therefore expensive; it has never been reprinted after Alpha.
It was banned in all standard formats since 1996; the only Alpha card to remain banned for all time.
It was redesigned after 2001 to cost three blue mana instead of two; the original UU version was retired.
context: Counterspell has been reprinted extensively (4th Ed, 5th Ed, Tempest, etc.). It's mostly common. The card remains a benchmark for blue counter spells.

question: The first MTG World Championship was held August 18-21, 1994 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin at Gen Con. Who won the inaugural championship?
answer: Zak Dolan, an American player; his Constructed deck and tournament strategy became influential in early MTG.
choices: Zak Dolan, an American player; his Constructed deck and tournament strategy became influential in early MTG.
Bertrand Lestree, a French player; he was a major player in the early 1990s but did not win the 1994 worlds.
Eric Tam, a Canadian player; he played in early worlds but did not win the inaugural championship.
Olle Rade, a Swedish player; he later became a famous MTG personality but did not win the 1994 worlds.
context: Zak Dolan won the inaugural Worlds. The championship was at Gen Con 1994. The prize was minor by modern standards. Dolan's deck and strategy were widely discussed in the early MTG community.

question: MTG's Planeswalkers (powerful spell-caster card types) were introduced as a new card type in Lorwyn (October 2007). Before 2007, Planeswalkers were lore-only entities. What was special about the original five Lorwyn Planeswalkers?
answer: Each represented one of MTG's five colors; they were Jace (blue), Liliana (black), Chandra (red), Garruk (green), Ajani (white).
choices: Each represented one of MTG's five colors; they were Jace (blue), Liliana (black), Chandra (red), Garruk (green), Ajani (white).
Each was named after a Wizards employee; the in-jokes were intentional and well-documented in the company.
Each was a deity from a different MTG plane; they were not Planeswalkers in the traditional sense.
Each was originally designed as a Legendary creature; the Planeswalker type was a retcon in later editions.
context: Lorwyn introduced Jace, Liliana, Chandra, Garruk, Ajani as the five-color Planeswalker debut. Planeswalker as a mechanic has expanded greatly since.

question: MTG's default fictional plane is Dominaria, the setting of the Alpha cards and many subsequent expansions. The plane's history is detailed and serves as the home of many iconic MTG characters. Who is the most prominent recurring Dominaria character?
answer: Urza Planeswalker, whose story spans Antiquities, Urza's Saga block, Apocalypse, and many later sets.
choices: Urza Planeswalker, whose story spans Antiquities, Urza's Saga block, Apocalypse, and many later sets.
Garruk Wildspeaker, the green Planeswalker from Lorwyn; not from Dominaria originally.
Liliana Vess, the black Planeswalker from Lorwyn; she has visited Dominaria but is not native.
Jaya Ballard, a red Planeswalker from Ice Age; she is from Dominaria but less prominent than Urza.
context: Urza is the central recurring Dominaria character. His brother Mishra, his apprentice Karn, and many others people the planes. The Brothers' War set (2022) revisited his story.

question: Wizards of the Coast launched the MTG Pro Tour in 1996. The first Pro Tour was held in New York City in February 1996. The Pro Tour was a major investment in professionalizing MTG. What was the first Pro Tour's prize pool?
answer: $50,000, with $10,000 for the winner; modest by modern standards but groundbreaking for trading-card games then.
choices: $50,000, with $10,000 for the winner; modest by modern standards but groundbreaking for trading-card games then.
$100,000, with $25,000 for the winner; a substantial prize pool that established MTG as a major sport.
$500,000, with $100,000 for the winner; this is from much later in the Pro Tour's history, not 1996.
$10,000, with $2,500 for the winner; far too small for the Pro Tour's foundational launch event.
context: The 1996 Pro Tour had a $50,000 prize pool with $10,000 for first. Michael Loconto won. The Pro Tour established competitive MTG and led to the modern Magic Pro League.

question: Hasbro acquired Wizards of the Coast in 1999. The acquisition came shortly after WotC had acquired TSR (1997). What was the acquisition price?
answer: Approximately $325 million, in a cash-and-stock deal that gave Hasbro control of both MTG and D&D.
choices: Approximately $325 million, in a cash-and-stock deal that gave Hasbro control of both MTG and D&D.
Approximately $50 million; a much smaller acquisition price than the actual 1999 deal.
Approximately $1 billion; a much larger price than the actual 1999 acquisition.
Approximately $100 million; closer to the actual price but still below the actual deal value.
context: Hasbro paid approximately $325 million for Wizards of the Coast in 1999. The deal closed the consolidation of major game publishers into a single corporate parent. WotC retained operational autonomy.

question: TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) was founded in October 1973 by Gary Gygax and Don Kaye to publish wargames. Don Kaye died of a heart attack in early 1975 at age 36. After his death, who held majority control of TSR?
answer: Brian Blume (and his brother Kevin Blume), who had bought Don Kaye's shares and combined with Gygax's percentage.
choices: Brian Blume (and his brother Kevin Blume), who had bought Don Kaye's shares and combined with Gygax's percentage.
Gary Gygax alone, who bought out Kaye's estate's share and remained the majority owner until 1985.
Rob Kuntz, Gygax's longtime friend; Kuntz had no significant ownership of TSR during Kaye's lifetime.
Dave Arneson, the D&D co-creator; Arneson had no significant ownership of TSR at any point.
context: Brian Blume bought Kaye's shares. The Blume brothers later acquired more shares. Lorraine Williams (Blume's sister) bought the Blume shares in 1985, taking control from Gygax.

question: MTG's color pie was designed to encourage card combinations within a single color and to discourage three-color combinations. Garfield called this the design principle of 'colors hating each other'. Which color combinations are intended to be most uncomfortable?
answer: Enemy colors (e.g., White-Black, Blue-Red, etc.); designed to be mechanically tension-filled.
choices: Enemy colors (e.g., White-Black, Blue-Red, etc.); designed to be mechanically tension-filled.
Allied colors (e.g., White-Blue, Black-Red, etc.); allied colors are actually designed to be easier together.
Three-color combinations within enemy color pairs; the design is symmetrical for 3-color combinations.
Two-color combinations within ally pairs only; the design is the opposite of what the question describes.
context: Enemy colors are designed to be mechanically tension-filled. Allied colors (White-Blue, Black-Red, Green-White, etc.) are designed to share mechanics more. The color pie is foundational to MTG design.

question: Richard Garfield's vision for MTG included tournaments. The first official MTG tournament was held in 1994. What was the format of the first tournaments?
answer: Limited (sealed deck), where players opened booster packs at the event and built decks on-site.
choices: Limited (sealed deck), where players opened booster packs at the event and built decks on-site.
Vintage (free deck construction), where players brought their own pre-built decks from home.
Standard (deck format restricted to recent sets), which actually only emerged later in 1995.
Draft (booster pack draft), which actually only emerged later in 1996 as a competitive format.
context: Sealed deck was the original format. Players opened a starter and three boosters at the event. Drafting emerged from sealed (with the natural innovation of trading at the table).

question: Gary Gygax's AD&D Dungeon Masters Guide (1979) is famous for its dense, comprehensive coverage of D&D mechanics. The DMG contains many tables, including a famous one about adventure-encounter probabilities. The book has a specific reputation among classic D&D players. What is the DMG known for?
answer: Encyclopedic, often digressive, sometimes contradictory; Gygax's voice shines through in long passages.
choices: Encyclopedic, often digressive, sometimes contradictory; Gygax's voice shines through in long passages.
Concise, well-organized, easy to reference at the table; a model of game-design clarity throughout.
Strictly mechanical, with little flavor text; Gygax kept his voice out and let the rules speak.
Beautifully illustrated; the art-to-text ratio is high, making the book primarily visual reference.
context: The DMG is famously digressive and encyclopedic. Gygax's prose ('the apparent disparity in armor class') is legendary. The book remains a touchstone of OSR-style D&D play.

question: The original D&D's three booklets (1974) were supplemented by Supplement I (Greyhawk, 1975), Supplement II (Blackmoor, 1975), Supplement III (Eldritch Wizardry, 1976), and Supplement IV (Gods, Demi-Gods & Heroes, 1976). What did Blackmoor add to D&D?
answer: Monk class, naval rules, hit locations; substantially expanded the game's scope.
choices: Monk class, naval rules, hit locations; substantially expanded the game's scope.
Thief class, critical hits, the world of Greyhawk; not Blackmoor (those are Greyhawk Supplement I).
Psionics, Druid as a class, demonic lore; not Blackmoor (those are Eldritch Wizardry).
Deities and clerical alignments; not Blackmoor (those are Gods, Demi-Gods & Heroes).
context: Blackmoor added Monk class (from Brian Blume), naval combat rules, hit locations, and disease rules. Each supplement added a class: Greyhawk (Thief), Blackmoor (Monk), Eldritch Wizardry (Druid again).

question: Supplement IV: Gods, Demigods & Heroes (1976) introduced deity statistics to D&D. The book gave game-mechanical stats (hit dice, AC, etc.) for deities from real-world mythologies. The 1980 expanded AD&D version added Cthulhu Mythos and Melnibonean deities. What happened to those entries?
answer: Removed in 1981 due to legal disputes with the H.P. Lovecraft and Michael Moorcock estates.
choices: Removed in 1981 due to legal disputes with the H.P. Lovecraft and Michael Moorcock estates.
Removed because of fan complaints about D&D's inclusion of horror mythology; not a legal dispute issue.
Removed because the deities were too powerful, breaking the game-balance; a design rather than legal decision.
Removed in 1986 after TSR's leadership change; an early Lorraine Williams-era editorial choice.
context: Chaosium (Call of Cthulhu RPG, 1981) and Moorcock (with Chaosium) demanded removal. The original Deities and Demigods (1980) is now a collector's item.

question: The Isle of Dread (Module X1, 1981) by David Zeb Cook and Tom Moldvay was the first Expert-level D&D module. The module is a sandbox-style hex-crawl through a lost-world island filled with dinosaurs. What inspired the module's setting?
answer: The Lost World by Arthur Conan Doyle (1912) and King Kong (1933); a pulp-era dinosaur-island trope.
choices: The Lost World by Arthur Conan Doyle (1912) and King Kong (1933); a pulp-era dinosaur-island trope.
The Jurassic Park novel by Michael Crichton (1990); too late for X1's 1981 publication.
The Land That Time Forgot by Edgar Rice Burroughs (1918); a real Burroughs influence but a different trope.
Tarzan stories by Burroughs; not X1's primary inspiration despite Burroughs's pulp influence.
context: Doyle's Lost World and King Kong are the pulp-era dinosaur-island inspirations. The Isle of Dread became a hugely popular sandbox module. It includes a famous taeko language gimmick.

question: X2: Castle Amber (1981) by Tom Moldvay is a memorable Expert-level D&D module set in a sinister castle inhabited by the cursed Amber family. The module draws heavily on the fiction of which Weird Tales-era writer?
answer: Clark Ashton Smith's Averoigne stories (1930s); Moldvay's love of Smith inspired Amber's haunted aesthetics.
choices: Clark Ashton Smith's Averoigne stories (1930s); Moldvay's love of Smith inspired Amber's haunted aesthetics.
H.P. Lovecraft's Dunwich and Innsmouth; not Moldvay's primary inspiration for Castle Amber.
Robert E. Howard's Conan; the pulp influence is broad but Howard isn't Castle Amber's primary inspiration.
Edgar Rice Burroughs's Pellucidar; not a Castle Amber inspiration despite Burroughs's broader influence.
context: Smith's Averoigne (medieval France) is the primary X2 inspiration. The Amber family's curse and the parallel dimension imagery come from Smith. X2 is widely considered Moldvay's masterpiece.

question: Tracy and Laura Hickman wrote Ravenloft (Module I6, 1983) after their car broke down on a long drive. The module features Strahd von Zarovich, a vampire lord. The Hickmans's design philosophy was famously articulated in a 1983 essay. What did they call it?
answer: The Hickman Revolution, emphasizing narrative-driven adventures over pure dungeon-crawling.
choices: The Hickman Revolution, emphasizing narrative-driven adventures over pure dungeon-crawling.
The Module Method, a step-by-step process for writing successful adventure modules at TSR.
The Quest System, a unified design framework that TSR used for all module development thereafter.
The Tracy-Laura System, an early playtesting structure for TSR adventure modules from 1983 onward.
context: The Hickman Revolution (or sometimes the Hickman Manifesto) emphasized narrative over dungeon-crawl. Their work on Dragonlance Chronicles (1984-85) was the apotheosis of this approach.

question: Dragonlance was created at TSR by a team including Tracy and Laura Hickman and Margaret Weis. The Hickmans came up with the original idea after their 1983 Ravenloft success. Margaret Weis joined to write the novels. Who else was on the original Dragonlance design team?
answer: Michael Williams, Roger E. Moore, Jeff Grubb, and Doug Niles; among the original Dragonlance writers.
choices: Michael Williams, Roger E. Moore, Jeff Grubb, and Doug Niles; among the original Dragonlance writers.
Gary Gygax himself; Gygax was actively involved in Dragonlance during his TSR tenure 1984-85.
Frank Mentzer, Ed Greenwood; both at TSR but not on the original Dragonlance design team.
Lorraine Williams; she was TSR's executive but not directly involved in Dragonlance design.
context: The Dragonlance design team included Michael Williams, Roger Moore, Jeff Grubb, and Doug Niles among many others. Gygax was not on the team; he had been pushed toward Hollywood by 1984.

question: TSR's Dark Sun campaign setting (1991) was a departure from typical D&D fantasy. The setting was a post-apocalyptic desert world called Athas, ruled by tyrannical Sorcerer-Kings. Magic in Athas was destructive. What was the iconic art on Dark Sun?
answer: Brom (Gerald Brom), whose painted style defined the setting's harsh, dark aesthetic.
choices: Brom (Gerald Brom), whose painted style defined the setting's harsh, dark aesthetic.
Larry Elmore, the Dragonlance and Forgotten Realms artist; Elmore did not lead Dark Sun art.
Jeff Easley, the Players Handbook 2nd-edition cover artist; not Dark Sun's primary illustrator.
Tony DiTerlizzi, the Planescape artist (1994 onward); not Dark Sun's primary illustrator.
context: Brom's Dark Sun art is iconic. His work on the setting (and later Demon Stone, Forgotten Realms) made him one of the most influential fantasy artists. DiTerlizzi did Planescape.

question: TSR's Planescape campaign setting (1994) was Gygax's planar cosmology made into an adventure setting. The setting's central city was Sigil, City of Doors, in the form of a torus. Who ruled Sigil?
answer: The Lady of Pain, an enigmatic deity whose presence in Sigil is the central mystery of the setting.
choices: The Lady of Pain, an enigmatic deity whose presence in Sigil is the central mystery of the setting.
Bahamut, the Platinum Dragon, the lawful-good dragon-deity of the chromatic-metallic system.
Vecna, the lich-deity; Vecna does not rule Sigil in Planescape, but is a major outer-planes power.
Asmodeus, the lord of the Nine Hells; he is a major figure in Planescape but does not rule Sigil.
context: The Lady of Pain rules Sigil. Her mysterious nature is central to Planescape. She slays anyone who tries to learn too much about her. Planescape: Torment (1999) is a celebrated computer-RPG adaptation.

question: TSR's Spelljammer campaign setting (1989) was D&D in space. Ships sailed between crystal spheres (planet-sized realms) through the phlogiston (the substance of space). The setting introduced many memorable space-creatures. What is the most-iconic Spelljammer race?
answer: Giff, the hippopotamus-faced humanoid mercenaries armed with primitive firearms (smokepowder).
choices: Giff, the hippopotamus-faced humanoid mercenaries armed with primitive firearms (smokepowder).
Neogi, who actually first appeared in Spelljammer (1989); but they're not the most-iconic race.
Beholders, who actually exist in many D&D settings; not primarily Spelljammer-related.
Mind Flayers, who actually exist in many D&D settings; not primarily Spelljammer-related.
context: Giff (in their World War I-style military uniforms) are the iconic Spelljammer race. Neogi (centipede-spider mind-slavers) are also Spelljammer originals. 5e revived Spelljammer in 2022.

question: TSR's Basic D&D (Moldvay 1981, Mentzer 1983) used Mystara as its default campaign setting. The world was developed from earlier Greyhawk and Blackmoor influences. Where in Mystara is the most-iconic starting location?
answer: Karameikos, the duchy on the southern coast of the Known World; the setting of Mentzer's Red Box adventures.
choices: Karameikos, the duchy on the southern coast of the Known World; the setting of Mentzer's Red Box adventures.
The Republic of Darokin, in the north; not Mystara's most-iconic starter setting in the Red Box.
Glantri, the magocracy in the mountains; not Mystara's most-iconic starter setting in the Basic D&D.
Alphatia, the magical empire across the sea; not Mystara's most-iconic Red Box setting.
context: Karameikos in Mystara is the default Red Box setting. The Gazetteer series (1987-93) detailed the Known World region by region. Mystara was demoted to a setting line as Forgotten Realms took priority.

question: TSR's Voyage of the Princess Ark was a Dragon Magazine series (1990-1993) by Bruce Heard, detailing exploration of Mystara from the perspective of a flying ship. The Princess Ark herself was a magical sailing vessel. Who was the Princess Ark's captain?
answer: Haldemar of Haaken, a wizard-prince exploring Mystara's borderlands and outer Known World regions.
choices: Haldemar of Haaken, a wizard-prince exploring Mystara's borderlands and outer Known World regions.
Halaster the Mad, the wizard of Undermountain; not from the Princess Ark series at all.
Manshoon of Zhentil Keep, the Forgotten Realms wizard; not from the Princess Ark series.
Mordenkainen of Greyhawk, the famous Greyhawk wizard; not from the Princess Ark series.
context: Captain Haldemar's Voyage of the Princess Ark was one of Dragon's most-beloved 1990s columns. Bruce Heard's Mystara worldbuilding was extensive. Mystara's deep lore came from the series.

question: The Kraken is a D&D monster derived from Norse and pop-culture mythology. The Kraken is a colossal squid-like sea creature. In D&D mythology, krakens are intelligent and ancient. Where in the AD&D Monster Manual does the Kraken appear?
answer: The original Monster Manual (1977) by Gygax; the kraken was one of the original monster bestiary entries.
choices: The original Monster Manual (1977) by Gygax; the kraken was one of the original monster bestiary entries.
Monster Manual II (1983); a later supplement that added many sea creatures including the kraken.
Fiend Folio (1981); the British-developed supplement that added the kraken in a UK edition.
AD&D 2e Monster Manual (1989); the kraken was a 2e addition rather than original AD&D.
context: The Kraken is in Monster Manual I (1977). The monster's intelligence and ancient nature are part of its D&D identity. Krakens have been recurring in D&D's planar / underwater adventures.

question: The Vampire is one of D&D's classic undead. Vampires in D&D have specific powers: level-drain (touch), regeneration, alternate forms (mist, wolf, bat), gaze-attack. They have specific vulnerabilities. What's the vampire's most-iconic vulnerability in classic D&D?
answer: Sunlight; vampires destroyed by direct sunlight within seconds; specifically prevents vampires from operating by day.
choices: Sunlight; vampires destroyed by direct sunlight within seconds; specifically prevents vampires from operating by day.
Garlic; vampires repelled by garlic but not destroyed; they can simply avoid garlic-laden areas if they wish.
Holy water; vampires destroyed by holy water though it has less area-effect than sunlight.
A wooden stake through the heart, but only if combined with decapitation and a mouthful of garlic afterward.
context: Sunlight is the vampire's primary classic vulnerability. Stakes alone only paralyze; decapitation kills. Vampires have been a core monster since OD&D (1974).

question: TSR licensed Fritz Leiber's Lankhmar setting (from his Fafhrd and Gray Mouser stories) as an official D&D campaign setting in 1985. The Lankhmar boxed set was a faithful adaptation of Leiber's city-state. What was unique about the Lankhmar setting?
answer: It explicitly portrayed the Thieves' Guild as a major political faction; Leiber's stories required this.
choices: It explicitly portrayed the Thieves' Guild as a major political faction; Leiber's stories required this.
It used a unique magic-system based on three schools (Black, White, Gray) drawn from Leiber's stories.
It allowed characters to play as deities; not at all true of the Lankhmar setting in D&D format.
It removed the magic-user class entirely; magic was supposed to be rare per Leiber's stories.
context: The Thieves' Guild's political prominence reflects Leiber's stories. The Sorcerers' Guild and Beggars' Guild are also important. Lankhmar's underground sewers and thief-culture became iconic.

question: Chaosium published the Call of Cthulhu RPG in 1981, the first major Lovecraft-themed RPG. The RPG was designed by Sandy Petersen. The game's setting is Lovecraft's mythos in the 1920s. Call of Cthulhu's gameplay differs sharply from D&D's. How?
answer: Heavy emphasis on investigation and sanity loss; combat is dangerous and often fatal for investigators.
choices: Heavy emphasis on investigation and sanity loss; combat is dangerous and often fatal for investigators.
Heavy emphasis on grinding through encounters; investigators gain levels and grow stronger over time.
Pure hack-and-slash style; investigators fight Mythos creatures with conventional combat skills.
Strategic-wargaming style; investigators are units in a Lovecraftian-themed military campaign system.
context: Call of Cthulhu's investigative-and-sanity emphasis is its signature. Petersen's later D&D contributions (Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters, 2014) confirm the cross-pollination.

question: Game Designers' Workshop published Traveller, the first major science-fiction RPG, in 1977. Designed by Marc W. Miller, Traveller was a contemporary of D&D in the early RPG era. What was Traveller's character-creation gimmick?
answer: Characters could die during character creation; the system simulates careers prior to starting play.
choices: Characters could die during character creation; the system simulates careers prior to starting play.
Characters were generated by class only; the system used D&D-style level progression rather than careers.
Characters used species selection; the system focused on aliens rather than human Imperial citizens.
Characters were tied to predetermined story arcs; the system used adventure-paths rather than sandbox play.
context: Traveller's death-during-character-generation is iconic. Players roll career terms; failing a survival roll can kill the character. The Imperium (third Imperium) is Traveller's default setting.

question: Hero Games published Champions in 1981. Designed by George MacDonald and Steve Peterson, Champions was the first major superhero RPG. The system became famous for its character-creation point-buy approach. What did Champions do differently from D&D?
answer: Players spent points to buy powers and abilities; no classes, no leveling — a 'point-buy' character system.
choices: Players spent points to buy powers and abilities; no classes, no leveling — a 'point-buy' character system.
Players rolled randomly for powers; an inverse of D&D's class-based but level-up randomness for stats.
Players chose from a fixed set of superhero templates (Batman, Spider-Man, Hulk); no original characters.
Players were assigned characters by the GM; the system was a fully-controlled narrative without player choice.
context: Champions's point-buy system was revolutionary. The system became the basis of HERO System, used for many other RPGs. Champions's influence extended to GURPS and other point-buy systems.

question: West End Games published Paranoia in 1984. The RPG is set in a darkly comedic dystopian future where players are Troubleshooters working for the omniscient Computer in Alpha Complex. The game has a famous design philosophy. What is it?
answer: The Computer is your friend; player characters are encouraged to betray each other for the Computer's amusement.
choices: The Computer is your friend; player characters are encouraged to betray each other for the Computer's amusement.
The Computer is your enemy; player characters band together against an oppressive AI overlord system.
The Computer is your servant; player characters command the AI and use it as a tool for resource management.
The Computer is invisible; player characters never interact with it directly throughout the entire game.
context: Paranoia's 'The Computer is your friend' is darkly satirical. The Computer's commands are often paradoxical, the players are clones (with 6 lives), and treachery is a core mechanic. The setting is hilariously bureaucratic.

question: TSR replaced the AD&D Monster Manual format in 1989 with the Monstrous Compendium. The new format was a loose-leaf binder system that allowed players to add new monster entries as expansions were released. The format was widely disliked. Why?
answer: Loose-leaf pages tore at the binding holes; players struggled to maintain alphabetical order of monsters.
choices: Loose-leaf pages tore at the binding holes; players struggled to maintain alphabetical order of monsters.
The binders were too small for the full monster count; players couldn't fit the complete bestiary.
The print quality was lower than the original Monster Manual; the loose pages used cheaper paper.
The system was too expensive; each Monstrous Compendium volume cost more than a hardcover MM.
context: Loose-leaf binder tears are well-attested. TSR returned to hardcover with Monstrous Manual (1993) and reverted permanently in 3e (2000). The format was a 2e-era experiment.

question: Wizards of the Coast (which had acquired TSR in 1997) released Dungeons & Dragons 3rd Edition in 2000. The 3e rules were a major overhaul: unified d20 mechanic, racial bonuses, feats, etc. Who led the 3e design team?
answer: Monte Cook, Jonathan Tweet, and Skip Williams; widely considered the lead design trio for D&D 3e.
choices: Monte Cook, Jonathan Tweet, and Skip Williams; widely considered the lead design trio for D&D 3e.
Gary Gygax himself; Gygax was not involved in 3e design and had been out of TSR since 1985.
Wolfgang Baur, Steve Winter, and Bruce Cordell; all are real D&D designers but not the 3e lead trio.
Mike Mearls, Greg Bilsland, and James Wyatt; all are real D&D designers but came later (4e onward).
context: Cook, Tweet, and Williams led 3e. Monte Cook was a notable figure in late TSR. Tweet had designed RuneQuest 3e (1984) and 7th Sea. Williams had been at TSR since the early 1990s.

question: AD&D 2nd Edition was released in 1989 by TSR under Zeb Cook's editorial direction. The 2e era was characterized by extensive setting development (Forgotten Realms, Dragonlance, Ravenloft, Dark Sun, Planescape, Spelljammer) and rule-system stability. When did 2e officially end?
answer: 2000, when Wizards of the Coast launched D&D 3rd Edition; 2e ran 11 years total at TSR.
choices: 2000, when Wizards of the Coast launched D&D 3rd Edition; 2e ran 11 years total at TSR.
1997, immediately when WotC bought TSR; the company hesitated 3 years before launching 3e.
1995, when AD&D 2.5e (the Player's Option books) was launched; 2e officially ended then.
2003, well after 3e's launch; 2e continued in parallel for 3 years before being formally retired.
context: 2e ran 1989-2000. WotC launched 3e in August 2000. The Player's Option books (1995-96) were an in-edition variant, not 2.5e formally. 2e's setting line was extensive and well-developed.

question: Gary Gygax's AD&D Dungeon Masters Guide (1979) included extensive tables for everything from random treasure to weather to magical-item construction. The book famously included one specific Appendix dedicated to player-character generation and lifestyle. What was Appendix P about?
answer: Appendix P: Inspirational and Educational Reading — Gygax's famous reading list of fantasy and pulp fiction.
choices: Appendix P: Inspirational and Educational Reading — Gygax's famous reading list of fantasy and pulp fiction.
Appendix P: Pole-arms — exhaustively detailed weapons table that became infamous for its complexity.
Appendix P: Psionics — psionic combat tables added to the AD&D 1e DMG in the original edition.
Appendix P: Pricing — extensive prices for tavern meals, equipment, and other mundane items in town.
context: Appendix N (Inspirational Reading) is the famous list. Gygax recommended Howard, Lovecraft, Burroughs, Vance, Leiber, Anderson, and others. The list defined the OSR's literary canon. Appendix P refers to pole-arms in some references.

question: Gygax's classic AD&D module series include the A-series (Slave Lords), G-series (Giants), D-series (Drow), Q1 (Demonweb), S-series (Solo / Special), and T-series (Temple of Elemental Evil). The chained giants-to-drow series became iconic. What is the chained series called?
answer: GDQ (G1-2-3 → D1-2-3 → Q1), the linked storyline by Gygax that takes characters from giant lairs to demon planes.
choices: GDQ (G1-2-3 → D1-2-3 → Q1), the linked storyline by Gygax that takes characters from giant lairs to demon planes.
GAS series, an alternate informal name; not actually used in TSR's official module designation system.
Slave Lords/Giants/Drow trilogy, a fan-name that combines three different module series at once.
Greyhawk Quest Series, an alternate official name for the entire combined module campaign.
context: GDQ is the standard fan term. The modules G1-G2-G3-D1-D2-D3-Q1 form a continuous storyline from giants on the surface to the drow Underdark to the demon planes. The series was reprinted as GDQ 1-7 (1986).

question: Dragonlance Chronicles was launched in November 1984 with the publication of Dragons of Autumn Twilight by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman. The novel was published alongside Module DL1: Dragons of Despair. What was unique about the Dragonlance multimedia approach?
answer: Modules and novels released simultaneously; cross-promotional and reflecting the same events in both formats.
choices: Modules and novels released simultaneously; cross-promotional and reflecting the same events in both formats.
Modules and novels released sequentially over several years; each novel was supplemented by a later module set.
Modules released without companion novels; the novel series came after the module success was assured.
Modules and novels were sold as bundled boxed sets; not actually the Dragonlance approach to publication.
context: The simultaneous launch of DL1 module and Dragons of Autumn Twilight was revolutionary. Dragonlance Chronicles became a phenomenon. Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman wrote 12 modules and 3 novels.

question: Dragon Magazine #1 was published in June 1976 as The Dragon (the article was dropped later). The first issue was a 32-page magazine and contained articles on Dungeons & Dragons. Who edited the first issue?
answer: Tim Kask, the first full-time editor of The Dragon, who served until 1979 before passing the torch to Mohan.
choices: Tim Kask, the first full-time editor of The Dragon, who served until 1979 before passing the torch to Mohan.
Kim Mohan, who actually took over as editor in 1979 and edited the magazine into the 1980s era.
Gary Gygax himself, who wrote many early Dragon articles but did not edit the magazine itself.
Brian Blume, the TSR co-founder; Blume was on the corporate side, not directly editing Dragon.
context: Tim Kask was Dragon's first editor (1976-1979). Kim Mohan took over in 1979. Roger E. Moore later edited. Gygax wrote many articles for Dragon, including his famous 'Sage Advice' column.

question: Dragon Magazine ran continuously from 1976 to 2007. Paizo Publishing took over publication from Wizards of the Coast in 2002 and continued until 2007. Dragon #359 was the final print issue. What replaced Dragon Magazine?
answer: Dragon and Dungeon both became digital-only PDF magazines under Wizards's online D&D Insider service.
choices: Dragon and Dungeon both became digital-only PDF magazines under Wizards's online D&D Insider service.
Dragon merged with Dungeon Magazine into a single combined Dragon+Dungeon publication.
Dragon was simply discontinued without a replacement; the digital era and forums killed magazine publishing.
Dragon was re-licensed to a new publisher; the magazine continued in print after Paizo gave it up.
context: Wizards moved Dragon and Dungeon to D&D Insider in 2007 as a digital subscription. Paizo's Pathfinder RPG (2009) became the spiritual successor to TSR-era D&D. Dragon-style content lived on.

question: TSR launched Dungeon Magazine in 1986 as a companion to Dragon Magazine, focused on adventures (modules) rather than rules articles. The magazine ran 150 issues. Who was Dungeon's longest-tenured editor?
answer: Roger E. Moore, who edited Dungeon from 1986-1993, the magazine's foundational period at TSR.
choices: Roger E. Moore, who edited Dungeon from 1986-1993, the magazine's foundational period at TSR.
Erik Mona, who edited Dungeon under Paizo Publishing's tenure (2003-2007) but for fewer years total.
Barbara G. Young, who edited Dungeon in 1989-1991 briefly before passing it to other editors.
Roger Slifer, who was a recurring Dungeon writer but did not serve as the primary editor.
context: Roger E. Moore edited Dungeon for 7+ years from its 1986 launch. Erik Mona later edited under Paizo. Dungeon published countless seminal modules, including some Hickman work and the City of the Spider Queen Ravenloft module.

question: TSR's A-series (Slave Lords) modules were published 1980-1981 as a connected adventure series. The A-series climax was in A3: Assault on the Aerie of the Slave Lords (1981). The slave lords were a council of slavers operating from a hidden island fortress. Who were the four named slave lords?
answer: Edralve, Eclavdra (drow priestess), Stalman Klim, and others; the slave lords had drow leadership.
choices: Edralve, Eclavdra (drow priestess), Stalman Klim, and others; the slave lords had drow leadership.
Eclavdra appears in D3, not the Slave Lords; the slave lords are different characters entirely.
Strahd von Zarovich, the Ravenloft vampire; Strahd is from I6 (1983), not the Slave Lords (1980-81).
Halaster Blackcloak, the Undermountain wizard; Halaster is from much later Forgotten Realms.
context: The slave lords are a council of named NPCs. Eclavdra appears in D3 (Vault of the Drow). Strahd is in I6 (Ravenloft 1983). Halaster is from Forgotten Realms Undermountain (1990s).

question: TSR's Module C1: The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan (1980) was the first official D&D tournament module. The module is a pyramid-temple adventure in a Meso-American-style jungle setting. The module was designed by Harold Johnson and Jeff R. Leason. What is the unusual structure of the module?
answer: Players start at the BOTTOM of the pyramid and ascend; reversing the typical dungeon-crawl direction.
choices: Players start at the BOTTOM of the pyramid and ascend; reversing the typical dungeon-crawl direction.
Players start at the TOP of the pyramid and descend; the standard dungeon-crawl direction.
Players can enter from multiple points and explore in any direction; an early sandbox-style module.
Players move through a strictly linear corridor with no exploration; a railroad rather than dungeon-crawl.
context: C1's bottom-to-top ascent is unusual. The Mesoamerican theme is also distinctive. The module was reprinted in Dungeons of Dread (2013), the Premium Edition of classic AD&D tournament modules.

question: TSR's Module C3: The Lost Island of Castanamir (1984) by Ken Rolston is a teleport-puzzle dungeon. The dungeon is the abandoned tower of a mage named Castanamir, full of magical traps and odd encounters. The module became famous for what design element?
answer: Random teleport effects, with players never quite knowing where they'll end up; deliberate disorientation.
choices: Random teleport effects, with players never quite knowing where they'll end up; deliberate disorientation.
Strict linear progression; the most-linear module TSR ever published, with no real player choice.
Open sandbox; the most-open module TSR ever published, with no central storyline.
Player-vs-player combat; the only TSR module that explicitly required players to fight each other.
context: C3's random teleport effects are its signature. Rolston later wrote Morrowind (Bethesda 2002) and Oblivion (2006), bringing some C3 sensibilities to those open-world games.

question: Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman's Dragonlance Chronicles trilogy was published 1984-1985. The three novels (Dragons of Autumn Twilight, Dragons of Winter Night, Dragons of Spring Dawning) introduced the Companions: Tanis Half-Elven, Caramon and Raistlin Majere, Sturm Brightblade, Tasslehoff Burrfoot, Flint Fireforge, Goldmoon, and Riverwind. What kind of company are they?
answer: An adventuring party that comes together to oppose the Dragon Highlords' invasion of Krynn.
choices: An adventuring party that comes together to oppose the Dragon Highlords' invasion of Krynn.
A noble military unit defending the Solamnic Knights' fortress from the Dragon Armies.
A merchant caravan traveling through Krynn during peacetime, before the war begins entirely.
A circus troupe with various performance skills, who reluctantly become adventurers in the war.
context: The Companions are an adventuring party of friends who reunite at the Inn of the Last Home. Their group dynamic and individual arcs drive the trilogy. Many characters appear in subsequent novels.

question: TSR's Spelljammer campaign setting (1989) used a space-fantasy hybrid. Ships sailed through the phlogiston (the interplanetary medium) and entered crystal spheres (planetary realms). What was the most-iconic Spelljammer creature?
answer: The Spelljamming Ship — ships designed for space travel; the Mantis-class, the Wasp-class, etc.
choices: The Spelljamming Ship — ships designed for space travel; the Mantis-class, the Wasp-class, etc.
The Beholder (in space); but Beholders pre-existed Spelljammer and are not its iconic creature.
The Mind Flayer (in space); but Mind Flayers pre-existed Spelljammer and are not its iconic creature.
The Dragon (in space); but dragons pre-existed Spelljammer and are not its iconic creature.
context: Spelljamming ships are the setting's iconic element. The Spelljammer captain (a wizard or psionic) uses a Spelljamming Helm to power the ship. 5e Spelljammer (2022) revived the setting.

question: TSR's Planescape (1994) was set in Sigil, the City of Doors, ruled by the Lady of Pain. The setting included 15 philosophical factions, each representing a different worldview. What were two of the most prominent factions?
answer: The Sensates (sensation-seekers) and the Athar (deity-skeptics); two of Planescape's signature factions.
choices: The Sensates (sensation-seekers) and the Athar (deity-skeptics); two of Planescape's signature factions.
The Sorcerers' Guild and the Thieves' Guild; from Lankhmar setting, not Planescape's actual factions.
The Knights of Solamnia and the Order of the Hammer; from Dragonlance, not Planescape's factions.
The Harpers and the Zhentarim; from Forgotten Realms, not Planescape's actual factions list.
context: Planescape's 15 factions (Sensates, Athar, Bleak Cabal, etc.) each had a philosophy. The Faction War (1998) was the setting's signature event. The Planescape: Torment computer game (1999) is famous.

question: Black Isle Studios developed Planescape: Torment for PC (released December 1999). The game starred the Nameless One, an immortal man who awakens with no memory in the Mortuary of Sigil. The game's writing was extraordinarily literary for an RPG. Who was the lead designer?
answer: Chris Avellone, who became one of CRPG's most celebrated writers; later led Fallout: New Vegas (2010).
choices: Chris Avellone, who became one of CRPG's most celebrated writers; later led Fallout: New Vegas (2010).
Sid Meier, the Civilization designer; not involved in Planescape: Torment design at all.
Brian Fargo, the Interplay founder who founded inXile in 2002; not the lead designer on Torment.
Tim Cain, the Fallout (1997) designer; not the lead designer on Planescape: Torment.
context: Chris Avellone led design on Planescape: Torment. The game won critical acclaim but sold modestly. Avellone later led Fallout: New Vegas (2010), Wasteland 2 (2014), Pillars of Eternity (2015).

question: Dark Sun (1991) introduced a unique magic-system to D&D. Magic in Athas was destructive — drawing on plant life and draining it. There were two ways to cast magic. What were the two ways?
answer: Preserver magic (sustainable, weaker) and Defiler magic (more powerful but destroys the surrounding plants).
choices: Preserver magic (sustainable, weaker) and Defiler magic (more powerful but destroys the surrounding plants).
Sun magic (during the day) and Shadow magic (at night); not the actual Dark Sun magic split.
Old magic (pre-apocalypse) and New magic (post-apocalypse); not the actual Dark Sun magic split.
Metal magic (using rare metals) and Bone magic (using bone); not the actual Dark Sun magic split.
context: Preserver vs. Defiler is the Dark Sun magic split. Preservers can become powerful but slowly; Defilers gain power instantly but destroy plant life. The choice is morally significant.

question: TSR's Kara-Tur and Oriental Adventures (1985) was edited by Gary Gygax and David Zeb Cook. The setting was an East-Asian-inspired fantasy region originally connected to the Forgotten Realms. What was the setting's primary cultural source?
answer: Imperial China (with elements of feudal Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Mongolia); a pan-East-Asian-fantasy blend.
choices: Imperial China (with elements of feudal Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Mongolia); a pan-East-Asian-fantasy blend.
Imperial Japan exclusively; the setting was strictly Japan-based without other Asian influences.
Imperial China exclusively; the setting was strictly China-based without other Asian influences.
Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan; the setting was strictly Mongol-based, not pan-Asian.
context: Kara-Tur draws on multiple East Asian cultures. The setting includes Shou Lung (China-like), Kozakura (Japan-like), Wa, Tabot, etc. Oriental Adventures rulebook was the gateway product.

question: TSR's Al-Qadim (1992) campaign setting was an Arabian-Nights-themed setting for AD&D. The setting is connected to the Forgotten Realms (the land of Zakhara, off the south coast of Faerun). Who designed Al-Qadim?
answer: Jeff Grubb (lead designer); the setting was Grubb's signature contribution to TSR's expanding-setting era.
choices: Jeff Grubb (lead designer); the setting was Grubb's signature contribution to TSR's expanding-setting era.
Ed Greenwood; not the designer of Al-Qadim despite his Forgotten Realms expertise.
Gary Gygax; not at TSR by 1992 when Al-Qadim was published.
Tracy Hickman; not the designer of Al-Qadim despite his TSR design experience.
context: Jeff Grubb designed Al-Qadim. The setting drew on Arabian Nights, the Rubaiyat, and other Middle-Eastern-fantasy sources. Al-Qadim ran several years with multiple supplements.

question: TSR's Maztica (1991) was an Aztec-inspired fantasy region connected to the Forgotten Realms. The setting is across the Trackless Sea, west of Faerun. The setting was based on actual Aztec/Inca/Maya history. Who designed Maztica?
answer: Douglas Niles, who also wrote much of Dragonlance and many other TSR-era novels.
choices: Douglas Niles, who also wrote much of Dragonlance and many other TSR-era novels.
Tracy Hickman; not the designer of Maztica despite his TSR design experience.
Ed Greenwood; not the designer of Maztica despite his Forgotten Realms expertise.
Jeff Grubb; not the designer of Maztica despite his Al-Qadim work.
context: Doug Niles designed Maztica. The setting included the Trilogy of the Empires (Maztica novel series). Niles is one of TSR's most prolific authors.

question: Wizards of the Coast's Eberron campaign setting was launched in 2004. The setting was the winner of a 'Fantasy Setting Search' competition; out of 11,000 submissions, Keith Baker's pitch won. The setting is what specific kind of fantasy?
answer: Pulp-adventure / magitech fantasy; airships, magical trains, noir-style cities, gritty action.
choices: Pulp-adventure / magitech fantasy; airships, magical trains, noir-style cities, gritty action.
Strict Tolkienian high-fantasy; the same template as Forgotten Realms and Dragonlance.
Hard-science-fiction in fantasy framing; the magic-system is fully scientifically detailed.
Space-fantasy; ships sail between worlds in the same Spelljammer-style format.
context: Eberron is a pulp-magitech setting. Airships, the Lightning Rail (magical train), warforged (sentient construct race), and other elements distinguish it. Keith Baker has continued working on it.

question: Tracy and Laura Hickman's Strahd von Zarovich (Module I6: Ravenloft, 1983) is one of D&D's most beloved villains. Strahd's backstory involves his family Castle Ravenloft, his brother Sergei, and a woman named Tatyana. Without spoiling specifics, what was Strahd's mortal profession?
answer: Conqueror-warlord; Strahd was the leader of his army's eastern campaign in his mortal years.
choices: Conqueror-warlord; Strahd was the leader of his army's eastern campaign in his mortal years.
Court mage of a king; Strahd was a wizard at the royal court before his transformation.
Roving knight-errant; Strahd was a chivalric wanderer before settling at Ravenloft Castle.
Religious crusader; Strahd led a religious-military campaign before his transformation.
context: Strahd was a warlord and conqueror in his mortal life. His backstory (later detailed in I10: House of Strahd and Curse of Strahd 5e) involves his family land of Barovia and his obsession with Tatyana.

question: TSR published Module I10: House of Strahd in 1990 as a remake of I6: Ravenloft (1983) updated for AD&D 2nd Edition. The remake incorporated 7 years of fan feedback and additional Tracy Hickman writing. What was added in the remake?
answer: More extensive Strahd backstory and tarokka card-reading mechanic for randomized treasure placement.
choices: More extensive Strahd backstory and tarokka card-reading mechanic for randomized treasure placement.
Removal of Strahd as the villain entirely; House of Strahd has a different vampire as primary antagonist.
Strict 1e mechanics; the remake actually used the original AD&D 1e rules, not 2e at all.
Module-specific spells exclusive to House of Strahd; not actually a feature of the 1990 remake.
context: The tarokka deck (a fortune-telling card mechanic) randomizes where Strahd's heirlooms hide. This made the module replayable. Curse of Strahd (2016) kept the tarokka.

question: Ed Greenwood's Forgotten Realms features the wizard Elminster Aumar as its signature NPC. Elminster lives in the village of Shadowdale in northern Faerun. His various Realms appearances span decades. What's Elminster's role in the meta-narrative of the setting?
answer: Greenwood's avatar; Elminster is the in-character source of the lore that Greenwood publishes in real life.
choices: Greenwood's avatar; Elminster is the in-character source of the lore that Greenwood publishes in real life.
A random NPC; Elminster has no special meta-narrative role beyond being a recurring character.
Greenwood's deceased mentor; Elminster is loosely based on a real-world figure who is not Greenwood himself.
A retcon character; Elminster was added later in Forgotten Realms's development to centralize lore in one NPC.
context: Elminster is Greenwood's literary avatar. Greenwood often writes as if Elminster has dictated the lore to him in real life. Volo, another NPC, plays a similar bardic-historian role.

question: R.A. Salvatore's Drizzt Do'Urden has assembled various traveling parties across his many novels. The Original Companions of the Hall — from the Icewind Dale trilogy and beyond — include Drizzt and five others. Who is the half-elf rogue (?) of the original Companions?
answer: Regis, a halfling rogue, who is actually not half-elf at all; Salvatore's Companions has no half-elf member.
choices: Regis, a halfling rogue, who is actually not half-elf at all; Salvatore's Companions has no half-elf member.
Catti-brie, a human warrior; not actually a half-elf rogue. The Companions has no half-elf.
Tanis Half-Elven; this is a Dragonlance character, not in Drizzt's Companions of the Hall.
Bruenor Battlehammer is a dwarf and not a half-elf; the Companions has no half-elf member.
context: The Companions are: Drizzt (drow), Bruenor (dwarf), Wulfgar (human barbarian), Catti-brie (human warrior/archer), Regis (halfling), Guenhwyvar (panther). No half-elf member.

question: Greyhawk's named spells (Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound, Bigby's Crushing Hand, Tenser's Floating Disc, etc.) honor Gygax's player characters. The spells became standard AD&D spells through the editions. What changed in 4e (2008) for the named spells?
answer: Named spells were either renamed to generic descriptive names or removed; Greyhawk references were de-emphasized.
choices: Named spells were either renamed to generic descriptive names or removed; Greyhawk references were de-emphasized.
Named spells were converted to feats; spells in 4e moved to powers, with named-spells becoming feats.
Named spells were stripped of their power and demoted to cantrips; not actually true of 4e.
Named spells were all removed entirely; 4e had no spells linked to Greyhawk NPCs.
context: 4e (2008) removed many named spells in favor of generic descriptions. Tenser's Floating Disc became 'Floating Disc' etc. 5e (2014) restored many named spells as a return to D&D's roots.

question: MTG's Lord of Atlantis (Alpha, 1993) is one of MTG's first 'lord'-type creatures — a creature that buffs all creatures of a specific type (Merfolk). Lord of Atlantis gives all Merfolk +1/+1 and Islandwalk. What was MTG's first 'lord'-type creature overall?
answer: Lord of Atlantis was indeed MTG's first lord-type creature in Alpha (1993).
choices: Lord of Atlantis was indeed MTG's first lord-type creature in Alpha (1993).
Goblin King, the Alpha 1993 red lord; predated Lord of Atlantis in alphabetical order on cards.
Zombie Master, the Alpha 1993 black lord; predated Lord of Atlantis in alphabetical order on cards.
Lord of the Pit, the Alpha 1993 black demon; not a lord-type creature (the Pit isn't a creature type).
context: All three (Lord of Atlantis, Goblin King, Zombie Master) are Alpha lords. Lord of the Pit is named with 'Lord' but isn't a lord-creature mechanically. The pattern continued in many sets afterward.

question: The 1980s Christian-right 'Satanic Panic' targeted D&D as occult. The 1985 Chick Tract 'Dark Dungeons' by Jack Chick depicted a teenage girl driven to suicide and witchcraft by playing D&D. The tract has become a meme and was even adapted into a 2014 short film. Who funded the 2014 film adaptation?
answer: Kickstarter funded by parodists JR Ralls and Chick Publications cooperated on the film as a humorous adaptation.
choices: Kickstarter funded by parodists JR Ralls and Chick Publications cooperated on the film as a humorous adaptation.
Chick Publications themselves; the company funded a literal adaptation of their own tract directly.
Hasbro; the D&D rights holder paid for the parody film to mock the 1980s panic.
A major Hollywood studio; the film was a commercial release rather than a Kickstarter parody.
context: JR Ralls's Kickstarter-funded Dark Dungeons (2014) was a parody. Chick Publications cooperated. The film is a darkly comedic look at the Satanic Panic.

question: 60 Minutes aired a segment on D&D and its alleged dangers in 1985. The segment featured Patricia Pulling of BADD and various concerned parents. The segment was a peak of D&D-related panic in the U.S. What was Gary Gygax's response?
answer: Gygax appeared in his own interview to defend D&D; he calmly explained the game's actual practices.
choices: Gygax appeared in his own interview to defend D&D; he calmly explained the game's actual practices.
Gygax refused to comment to 60 Minutes; he never spoke publicly about the Satanic Panic period.
Gygax wrote a fiery letter that 60 Minutes refused to air; he never appeared on the show himself.
Gygax left TSR before the show aired; his successors handled the public-relations response instead.
context: Gygax appeared on 60 Minutes to defend D&D. The Satanic Panic peaked in 1985-86. Gary Gygax was out of TSR by late 1985 (Williams takeover), but he had been the public face of D&D during the panic period.

question: When AD&D 2nd Edition launched in 1989, demons (Type IV-VI in 1e) were renamed Tanar'ri and devils (Baator) were renamed Baatezu. This avoided overtly Satanic terminology. When were the original 'demon' and 'devil' names restored in D&D?
answer: AD&D 2e Planescape's Faces of Evil supplement (1997); the panic had largely faded by then.
choices: AD&D 2e Planescape's Faces of Evil supplement (1997); the panic had largely faded by then.
AD&D 3rd Edition (2000); the new edition restored demons and devils in their original naming.
AD&D 2.5e Player's Option (1995); the half-edition restored some original AD&D 1e terminology.
AD&D 5th Edition (2014); the modern edition was the first to use demons and devils explicitly.
context: Planescape's Faces of Evil (1997) brought back demons and devils as the lower-planar fiends. AD&D 3e (2000) fully restored the original terminology. Modern D&D (5e) freely uses demons and devils.

question: Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel Mazes and Monsters fictionalized the James Egbert case and depicted RPGs as dangerously immersive. The 1982 made-for-TV movie starred Tom Hanks. The film became a touchstone of the Satanic Panic. What was the in-film name of the D&D-equivalent game?
answer: Mazes and Monsters itself; the in-film RPG game and the book/film both share the same title.

Dragons and Dungeons; an in-film RPG that was a different fictional name from the actual one.
context: The in-film game is called Mazes and Monsters. Jaffe's novel was a thinly-veiled D&D allegory. The 1982 TV film starred Hanks as the player who descends into RPG-induced psychosis.

question: James Dallas Egbert III disappeared from Michigan State University on August 15, 1979. The case became the basis for the Satanic Panic claims that D&D's escapism into 'steam tunnels' could lead to mental illness. What was Egbert's actual cause of disappearance?

context: Egbert had personal struggles (depression, drug use, sexual-orientation issues). He had attempted suicide in the steam tunnels before running away. He was found alive in 1979, then committed suicide in 1980 unrelated to D&D.

question: Original D&D (1974) by Gygax and Arneson had three booklets in a white box: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures. The booklets were approximately how many pages total?

context: Original D&D was approximately 100 pages total. The Holmes Basic (1977) was about 48 pages. The B/X Basic (1981) and BECMI (1983-86) added much more material in revised editions.

question: Gary Gygax's AD&D Dungeon Masters Guide (1979) was approximately 240 pages and dense with tables, rules, and Gygax's commentary. The book famously contained Appendix N — Gygax's recommended fantasy reading list. How many authors did Gygax list in Appendix N?
answer: About 30 authors, with novels and stories ranging from Robert E. Howard to Roger Zelazny.

context: Gygax's Appendix N lists about 30 authors. The OSR (Old-School Renaissance) treats Appendix N as a canonical reading list. Howard, Lovecraft, Burroughs, Vance, Leiber, Anderson, Moorcock, Tolkien, and Anderson are foundational.

question: Dragonlance Chronicles by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman ran 1984-1985 (three novels). The first novel, Dragons of Autumn Twilight, ends with the Companions completing a major quest in Pax Tharkas. What is the Pax Tharkas?
answer: A mountain fortress where the Dragon Highlords have enslaved hundreds of refugees.

A grand cathedral where the Companions seek refuge from the Dragon Armies.
A floating city where the dwarves of Krynn have retreated during the war.

context: Pax Tharkas is a mountain fortress in Chronicles. The Companions free the slaves there. The fortress reappears in later Dragonlance novels.

question: The Dragonlance Legends trilogy by Weis and Hickman was published 1986 (after the success of Chronicles). The trilogy focuses on the Majere twins, Caramon and Raistlin. What is the trilogy's central time-travel premise?
answer: Raistlin attempts to challenge the gods; the trilogy explores time-travel to the past via the Device of Time Journeying.
choices: Raistlin attempts to challenge the gods; the trilogy explores time-travel to the past via the Device of Time Journeying.
Caramon seeks to reform Krynn after the War of the Lance; the trilogy is non-time-travel.
The twins join a new generation of adventurers; the trilogy is set 50 years after Chronicles.
Tasslehoff and Tika lead a new quest; the trilogy doesn't feature the Majere twins centrally.
context: Legends's time-travel premise (Raistlin going to the past and Caramon following) is central. The Device of Time Journeying is the time-travel artifact. The trilogy: Time of the Twins, War of the Twins, Test of the Twins.

question: TSR's Module I7: Baltron's Beacon (1984) by Philip Meyers and Bruce Heard is an AD&D 1e adventure. The module is widely cited as one of the most-disliked TSR modules of its era. What was the issue?
answer: Excessive number of trap-rooms and 'gotcha' moments; the module felt like a deliberate killer-DM exercise.
choices: Excessive number of trap-rooms and 'gotcha' moments; the module felt like a deliberate killer-DM exercise.
Pure railroad without player choice; the most-linear AD&D module TSR ever published.
Excessive in-jokes and meta-humor; the module broke immersion repeatedly with player-character jokes.
Strict 1e mechanics that didn't work; the module's encounters had unbalanced math for AD&D 1e.
context: Baltron's Beacon's reputation for trap-rooms is well-attested in retro-RPG reviews. The module is widely considered weak by classic-D&D standards. It's a frequent cautionary example.

question: MTG Alpha was released on August 5, 1993, at Gen Con in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The set's launch was modest — 2.6 million cards in print. The set's price was very low by modern standards. What was the price of a booster pack at launch?
answer: $2.45 per 15-card booster pack; far below the modern booster pack pricing standard.
choices: $2.45 per 15-card booster pack; far below the modern booster pack pricing standard.
$3.95 per 15-card booster pack; closer to modern Standard booster pack pricing.
$1.45 per 15-card booster pack; below the actual 1993 launch price.
$4.95 per 15-card booster pack; above the actual 1993 launch price.
context: Alpha boosters were $2.45 retail. Starter decks were $7.95. Modern Standard boosters are $4-5. The Alpha price reflected the modest expectations Wizards had for the game.

question: MTG's Planeswalker card type was introduced in Lorwyn (October 2007). Before Planeswalker became a card type, Planeswalkers were lore-only entities in MTG's flavor text and storyline. What was the design challenge of making Planeswalkers a card type?
answer: Balancing their power level; Planeswalkers had to feel epic but not break the game's mechanics.
choices: Balancing their power level; Planeswalkers had to feel epic but not break the game's mechanics.
Balancing their color identity; Planeswalkers had to be multi-color but not break the color pie.
Balancing their casting cost; Planeswalkers had to feel expensive but still be reasonable.
Balancing their visual design; Planeswalkers had to be distinct from other card types visually.
context: Mark Rosewater has spoken extensively about the Planeswalker design challenge. The loyalty-counter mechanic and +/-/0 ability structure were innovative solutions. Planeswalkers have become central to MTG.

question: The Mind Flayer (Illithid) society is highly hierarchical. Common Mind Flayers (Standard Illithids) serve under Ulitharids (Mind Flayer subspecies with four additional tentacles) and Elder Brains (collective intelligences of brains floating in a brine pool). When did this hierarchy first appear in D&D?
answer: AD&D 1e Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth (S4, 1982); Gary Gygax developed the Illithid society details there.
choices: AD&D 1e Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth (S4, 1982); Gary Gygax developed the Illithid society details there.
AD&D 1e Monster Manual (1977); the Mind Flayer's social hierarchy was complete from the start.
AD&D 2e Forgotten Realms (1987); the hierarchy was a Forgotten Realms-specific lore addition.
AD&D 3e (2000); the hierarchy was added in the modern edition rather than the original AD&D era.
context: Illithid society was developed in AD&D 1e modules. The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth (1982) by Gygax detailed Illithid lore. The Elder Brain and Ulitharid hierarchy is foundational.

question: The Duergar (Gray Dwarves) are an evil dwarf subrace from the Underdark in D&D. They first appeared in the AD&D 1e Fiend Folio (1981). What is their distinctive special ability?
answer: Innate ability to enlarge and become invisible; psionic-related abilities not shared with regular dwarves.
choices: Innate ability to enlarge and become invisible; psionic-related abilities not shared with regular dwarves.
Innate ability to fly; not actually a Duergar racial trait in any edition of D&D.
Innate ability to breathe underwater; not actually a Duergar racial trait in any edition of D&D.
Innate ability to cast fireball; not actually a Duergar racial trait in any edition of D&D.
context: Duergar's innate enlarge-self and invisibility (often called Duergar's racial spells) are their signature. The 1981 Fiend Folio established the subrace. Modern editions have continued the tradition.

question: Drow first appeared briefly in Module G3 (1978) and were detailed in Module D3: Vault of the Drow (1978). The drow's matriarchal society is centered on the worship of Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders. Lolth's lower planar realm has a specific name. What?
answer: The Demonweb Pits, in the 66th layer of the Abyss; the setting of Module Q1 (1980).
choices: The Demonweb Pits, in the 66th layer of the Abyss; the setting of Module Q1 (1980).
The Underdark; this is a D&D setting concept, not Lolth's specific Abyssal layer.
Avernus, the first layer of Baator (the Nine Hells); not Lolth's realm — that's Tiamat's.
Lankhmar, a city setting in the official 1985 D&D Lankhmar boxed set; not a realm.
context: Lolth's Demonweb Pits is in the 66th layer of the Abyss. Q1: Queen of the Demonweb Pits (1980) is the climactic module of the GDQ series. Modern 5e adventures have revisited the Demonweb.

question: Ridley Scott's 1982 Blade Runner sees Deckard tracking renegade replicants through a rain-drenched Los Angeles in November 2019. Edward James Olmos plays Gaff, a cryptic police officer who folds small origami figures and leaves them where Deckard will find them — a chicken, a stick figure, a unicorn at the very end. The unicorn was added on set, reportedly because of an unrelated production detail involving Olmos and Scott. What was that detail?
answer: Olmos was an obsessive origami hobbyist who brought paper to set; Scott made the unicorn callback to Deckard's daydream
choices: Olmos was an obsessive origami hobbyist who brought paper to set; Scott made the unicorn callback to Deckard's daydream
Scott had storyboarded a horse but cut the daydream scene late, so Gaff's figure was changed at the last hour to match
Olmos refused to speak English on set, so Scott used origami as visual dialogue when subtitles felt clunky
Hampton Fancher had insisted on origami in the script; Scott resented this and minimized the figures wherever possible
context: Ridley Scott has variously confirmed the unicorn implies something about Deckard the audience is meant to wonder about for the rest of the film and beyond.

question: The Princess Bride opens in 1987 not on a castle or a duel but on a kid's bedroom — a sick boy, played by a young Fred Savage, lying in bed with a video game in his lap when his grandfather (Peter Falk) arrives to read him a story. Look carefully at the screen and the box on the bedspread: the game is a real, identifiable computer baseball title for the Commodore Amiga. Which game?
answer: Hardball II by Accolade — the box and on-screen play match the Amiga version released that same year
choices: Hardball II by Accolade — the box and on-screen play match the Amiga version released that same year
Earl Weaver Baseball by Electronic Arts — visible as the standard Amiga sim of the era on Savage's lap
RBI Baseball by Tengen — the unlicensed NES hit that crossed onto Amiga in a quiet 1987 release
Bases Loaded by Jaleco — the arcade port whose Amiga edition was on every kid's wish list in 1987
context: Director Rob Reiner is on record about the choice; the prop department insisted on a real Amiga title. The scene grounds the fairy tale in a real 1987 American kid's bedroom.

question: Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday in 1993's Tombstone delivers two of the most-quoted lines in modern Westerns: 'I'm your huckleberry' and 'You're a daisy if you do.' Audiences in 1993 mostly heard 'huckle bearer' and assumed a coffin reference. The screenwriter Kevin Jarre, an 1880s-slang obsessive, intended the older meaning. What did 'huckleberry' actually mean in frontier slang?
answer: It meant 'the right man for the job' or 'a willing partner' — Doc is accepting Ringo's challenge
choices: It meant 'the right man for the job' or 'a willing partner' — Doc is accepting Ringo's challenge
It meant 'a pallbearer' specifically for funerals — Doc is promising to bury Ringo himself
It meant 'a little brother' in trail-driving slang — Doc is calling Ringo beneath his station
It meant 'a sweetheart' in cattle-town pidgin — Doc is mocking Ringo with a feminine address
context: Mark Twain used 'huckleberry' the same way decades earlier. Kilmer studied 1880s diaries for the role and pushed for the older meaning over the coffin-reading Hollywood had grown up with.

question: John Milius's 1982 Conan the Barbarian opens not with dialogue but with a thundering orchestral piece — drums, brass, and a male chorus chanting in fake Latin behind the forging of a sword. The composer was Basil Poledouris, who later scored RoboCop and Starship Troopers. He recorded the score in Rome with a specific orchestra. Which one?
answer: The Orchestra di Santa Cecilia of Rome, conducted by Poledouris himself across three weeks of sessions
choices: The Orchestra di Santa Cecilia of Rome, conducted by Poledouris himself across three weeks of sessions
The London Symphony Orchestra at Abbey Road, the same venue used a year earlier for Raiders of the Lost Ark
The Berliner Philharmoniker under guest baton, a deal arranged through Universal's European distribution
The Vienna Philharmonic at the Musikverein, which Poledouris insisted on for the brass-heavy 'Anvil of Crom'
context: Poledouris said he wanted Roman heaviness — Carl Orff's Carmina Burana energy, but for a Cimmerian war horn. The 'Anvil of Crom' is now a fixture of trailer music.

question: Katsuhiro Otomo's 1988 anime Akira pushed celluloid animation to a level studios had not attempted: over 2,200 shots and 327 distinct colors, many created specifically for the film. Otomo also broke with anime convention by recording the voice acting first, then animating mouth movements to match. What was the standard Japanese practice at the time?
answer: Animators drew the lip flaps first to a loose timing chart; voice actors then matched the finished animation in dubbing
choices: Animators drew the lip flaps first to a loose timing chart; voice actors then matched the finished animation in dubbing
Animators and voice actors recorded in the same booth simultaneously; sync was approximate and corrected in editing
Voice actors were hired only after animation was complete; their performances were locked entirely to drawn lips
Voice was recorded to a final storyboard but never to animation; mouths were redrawn frame by frame after the fact
context: Otomo's pre-scoring approach is now standard in high-end anime and was used on Studio Ghibli's later work. It made Akira's dialogue feel uncannily physical compared to its peers.

question: Released as a 26-episode series in spring 1998 by Studio Sunrise, Cowboy Bebop was canceled mid-run on TV Tokyo due to violence complaints, then restored to its full count in syndication on WOWOW. Director Shinichiro Watanabe and composer Yoko Kanno's Seatbelts gave it the iconic 'Tank!' opening. When did the show first broadcast in the US, and on what channel?
answer: September 2001 on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim — its Saturday 9 PM slot helped define the new block
choices: September 2001 on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim — its Saturday 9 PM slot helped define the new block
January 2000 on Toonami pre-Adult Swim — running as the weeknight headliner against Dragon Ball Z
October 1999 on FOX Kids Saturday block in a heavily-edited dub airing alongside Digimon
August 2002 on Encore Action — a paid premium channel showing the uncensored Japanese DVD-rip version
context: The US premiere was September 2, 2001 — exactly nine days before September 11. Several episodes featuring terrorist plots were rescheduled in the aftermath.

question: Hideaki Anno's Neon Genesis Evangelion ran 26 episodes on TV Tokyo in 1995-1996. By the late episodes, Gainax had run out of money and time. The final two episodes are remembered by fans for an unusually abstract, low-animation, introspective approach unlike the mecha action of earlier weeks. What practical condition drove that approach?
answer: Gainax had nearly exhausted both budget and schedule; Anno leaned into static images and text cards by necessity
choices: Gainax had nearly exhausted both budget and schedule; Anno leaned into static images and text cards by necessity
Anno wanted those episodes hand-painted on glass plates, a slow technique that ate the schedule on its own
TV Tokyo censors had rejected the original action-heavy cuts; Gainax reshot the finale in two weeks of stills
The original animators had walked out over a pay dispute; replacement freelancers worked only from rough scripts
context: Anno later remade the ending as End of Evangelion (1997), a theatrical film. Whether necessity-as-virtue or vision-realized, the original 25-26 remain a permanent debate among fans.

question: Mamoru Oshii's 1995 anime Ghost in the Shell adapted Masamune Shirow's manga into a meditative cyberpunk feature for Production I.G. Five years later, the Wachowskis premiered The Matrix and openly cited Oshii's film as a direct influence. They reportedly handed a producer a tape of Ghost in the Shell and said: make it look like this. Who was that producer?
answer: Joel Silver, the Matrix producer the Wachowskis pitched with the Ghost in the Shell tape as their visual reference
choices: Joel Silver, the Matrix producer the Wachowskis pitched with the Ghost in the Shell tape as their visual reference
Jerry Bruckheimer, who passed on the Matrix pitch and later cited Ghost in the Shell as the reason he regretted it
Roland Emmerich, who briefly attached as producer before exiting; the tape stayed in Warner Bros. development
Lawrence Bender, who optioned the Matrix script through A Band Apart and screened the tape for the studio
context: The green-on-black cascading code, the bullet time, the cable-jack sockets in the necks — all of it traces back to Oshii's Production I.G. team.

question: The 1987 animated TMNT cartoon turned April O'Neil — a computer programmer in Eastman and Laird's original 1984 Mirage comic — into a Channel 6 news reporter in a bright yellow jumpsuit. The new look was a deliberate design choice by the cartoon's production crew. What was the practical animation reason given for the yellow jumpsuit?
answer: It read instantly on the smaller TVs of the era; one bold flat color cut animation cost and kept her visible in any scene
choices: It read instantly on the smaller TVs of the era; one bold flat color cut animation cost and kept her visible in any scene
It echoed Murphy Brown's wardrobe palette, signaling 'TV reporter' to younger viewers who didn't know the type
Eastman and Laird requested it specifically as a rights-distinguishing change from the comic's purple-clad April
Network notes demanded a single color outfit per main character to simplify the toy line's repaint patterns
context: April's yellow jumpsuit became iconic enough that the 1990 live-action film kept it, despite real reporters never dressing that way.

question: The 1985 Rankin/Bass cartoon ThunderCats featured Panthro, the team's gruff mechanic and master of the nunchucks, voiced by a respected stage actor with a busy parallel career. The same actor played Russell Huxtable, Cliff's father, on The Cosby Show during the cartoon's exact same run. Who?
answer: Earle Hyman — the Shakespearean stage actor who played both Panthro and Russell Huxtable on Cosby
choices: Earle Hyman — the Shakespearean stage actor who played both Panthro and Russell Huxtable on Cosby
