Bob McFadden — voice of Snarf and many Rankin/Bass second leads of the era, including some Saturday morning regulars
Lynne Lipton — voice of Cheetara and WilyKit, and a Carol Burnett Show veteran of the 1970s comedy circuit
context: Hyman trained at the Yale Drama School and toured Norway in Othello. He recorded ThunderCats sessions on Cosby breaks at NBC's New York studios.

question: The 1986 animated Transformers: The Movie has a famously bleak first act that traumatized a generation of children, killing off several Generation 1 characters in quick succession to clear shelf space for the 1986 toy line. Hasbro had ordered the cast purge for commercial reasons. What was the standing kid-show industry rule the film also openly broke?
answer: Network TV cartoons did not show on-screen character deaths; the theatrical PG release sidestepped that rule
choices: Network TV cartoons did not show on-screen character deaths; the theatrical PG release sidestepped that rule
Network TV cartoons did not allow swear words; the film's mild 'damn' counted as breaking the floor at the time
Network TV cartoons did not allow nightclub scenes; the Junkion bar sequence was the first in animation history
Network TV cartoons did not allow live-action footage; the film's framing prologue was a real-camera shoot
context: G.I. Joe: The Movie a year later toned its character casualties back after parent letters poured in. The 1986 Transformers movie remains a sui generis cultural moment.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's Castle in the Sky (1986) is often listed as a Studio Ghibli film, and Ghibli officially formed in June 1985 between Nausicaa and Totoro. But Castle in the Sky was greenlit before Ghibli's incorporation and produced under unusual circumstances. What was the actual production arrangement for Castle in the Sky?
answer: Tokuma Shoten funded it and assembled a temporary studio; Ghibli was incorporated specifically to make this film
choices: Tokuma Shoten funded it and assembled a temporary studio; Ghibli was incorporated specifically to make this film
Topcraft animated it the same way they did Nausicaa; Ghibli was a distribution-only banner over the film for marketing

It was independently funded by Miyazaki and Takahata personally; Ghibli incorporated after profits came in
context: The Ghibli incorporation paperwork lists Castle in the Sky as the founding production. Without that film, the studio as we know it would not have existed.

question: The 1964 Rankin/Bass Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer is one of the most-aired specials in American television history. Its 'Animagic' stop-motion was animated by a Japanese studio that had pioneered the technique decades earlier under a director whose work Arthur Rankin Jr. discovered through Soviet-era cultural exchanges. Whose studio?
answer: Tadahito Mochinaga's MOM Production in Tokyo — the puppet-animation pioneer Rankin found via Soviet-Japanese cultural ties
choices: Tadahito Mochinaga's MOM Production in Tokyo — the puppet-animation pioneer Rankin found via Soviet-Japanese cultural ties
Hiroshi Tabata's Tabata Production in Tokyo — primarily a hand-drawn studio that Rankin briefly contracted for the work
Toshio Suzuki's Topcraft in Tokyo — later known for Nausicaa, but with stop-motion experience under government contract
Hisashi Sakaguchi's Studio Zero in Tokyo — a manga-adjacent collective Rankin used in the late 1960s exclusively
context: Mochinaga had worked in Manchuria during the war, then directed Soviet stop-motion shorts in Moscow. His Tokyo team did Rudolph, Frosty, and most of the Rankin/Bass canon.

question: Tim Burton conceived The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993) as a poem in the early 1980s while at Disney. By the time the film entered production a decade later, Burton was making Batman Returns and Ed Wood. He produced and designed but did not direct. Who did?
answer: Henry Selick — the stop-motion specialist who later directed James and the Giant Peach and Coraline

Joe Ranft — the Pixar story veteran who consulted on Nightmare but was not credited as director
context: Selick's name is on the poster as director; Burton's is on it as producer and creator. The misconception that Burton directed it is one of the most stubborn in modern film fandom.

question: John Williams's Star Wars score, recorded in March 1977 before A New Hope's release, was performed not by the Los Angeles Philharmonic or a Hollywood studio orchestra but by a famous British ensemble at a specific London venue. The decision saved money and gave the score its big symphonic sound. Which orchestra and venue?
answer: The London Symphony Orchestra at Anvil Studios in Denham, where Williams recorded most of his 1970s-80s film work
choices: The London Symphony Orchestra at Anvil Studios in Denham, where Williams recorded most of his 1970s-80s film work
The Royal Philharmonic at Abbey Road Studio One, the same venue then used for Apocalypse Now's score
The BBC Symphony Orchestra at Maida Vale Studios, contracted through the BBC's commercial-recording arm
The Philharmonia Orchestra at CTS Studios in Wembley, where Williams later recorded the Indiana Jones sequels
context: Williams's LSO partnership ran through the prequels, returning across decades. The London symphonic sound IS the Star Wars sound; American studio orchestras have never quite matched it on the saga.

question: The climax of Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) ends with a sequence ILM artists later called 'the showstopper.' The melting-face and dissolving-skull effects on the German soldiers were practical, built in Stuart Freeborn's tradition: gelatin, latex, plaster molds. What ILM technique made the gelatin face appear to flow?
answer: Heat lamps melted a gelatin head while a high-speed camera filmed it; the footage was reversed and color-corrected
choices: Heat lamps melted a gelatin head while a high-speed camera filmed it; the footage was reversed and color-corrected
A wax head was filmed sublimating in vacuum chamber; the optical printer composited the shots over a still actor
A latex mask was filmed shrinking on a hot plate; reverse animation made it appear to grow then liquefy on cue
A puppeteered head with internal pumps released colored corn syrup; high-speed cameras smoothed the spray to liquid
context: The 1981 effect predates digital morphing by a decade. Director Steven Spielberg told ILM 'I want it to look like a Renaissance painting of damnation' — they delivered.

question: Back to the Future began principal photography in 1984 with a different actor playing Marty McFly. After about five weeks of shooting, director Robert Zemeckis and producer Steven Spielberg made the costly decision to recast and reshoot with Michael J. Fox, who became available when Family Ties accommodated his schedule. Who was the original Marty?
answer: Eric Stoltz — whose footage remains studio-locked except for brief flashes in the 2009 documentary
choices: Eric Stoltz — whose footage remains studio-locked except for brief flashes in the 2009 documentary
Corey Hart — at the height of his 'Sunglasses at Night' fame and briefly attached during pre-production
C. Thomas Howell — coming off The Outsiders and the closest second to Fox in the casting search
Anthony Michael Hall — coming off Sixteen Candles and offered the role before Stoltz signed on
context: The Stoltz footage exists in a Universal vault. Crispin Glover and Lea Thompson were already cast when the change happened; their early scenes were shot twice.

question: Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) features a now-iconic trail of candies leading Elliott to E.T. Spielberg's first choice for the brand was a longer-established American chocolate candy that flatly refused the product placement, citing a worry the alien was unappealing. Hershey's then said yes for a newer product. What was the brand that turned Spielberg down?
answer: Mars, makers of M&M's — who declined fearing E.T.'s appearance would associate their candy with something ugly

Nestle, makers of Smarties — who declined because Smarties were a UK-Canada brand without US grocery presence
Ferrero, makers of Tic Tacs — who declined because of a candy-vs-mint category concern, not appearance
Necco, makers of Necco Wafers — who declined because their candy didn't roll on the floor the way Spielberg wanted
context: Reese's Pieces sales reportedly tripled within two weeks of release. The story is now a classic case study in product placement marketing courses.

question: John McTiernan's Predator (1987) began production with a different alien design and a different actor inside the suit. The original suit was a slim, agile creature; the actor was a young Belgian martial artist who walked off set after disputes about the suit's heat and visibility. Stan Winston was then flown in for a complete redesign. Who was the original Predator?
answer: Jean-Claude Van Damme — fired or quit early in production over the suit's heat and the obscured fight choreography
choices: Jean-Claude Van Damme — fired or quit early in production over the suit's heat and the obscured fight choreography
Dolph Lundgren — briefly attached during early casting but never on set; the role went to a stunt performer
Bolo Yeung — the Bloodsport heavy who was the production's third choice after the original walk-off
Brian Thompson — the Cobra and Terminator villain whose Predator costume tests survive in the DVD extras
context: Stan Winston flew home, sketched a new design on a napkin during a long flight, and built the iconic mandibled Predator we know. Kevin Peter Hall, a seven-foot performer, wore the new suit.

question: James Cameron's Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) is remembered as a CGI watershed for the T-1000's liquid-metal transformations by ILM. But of roughly 300 effects shots in the finished film, only a fraction were digital. Most were Stan Winston practical effects: full-scale puppets, mirror tricks, prosthetic appliances. About how many shots were actually CGI?
answer: Roughly 40 CGI shots — fewer than 15% of the total; the rest were Winston's practical work and traditional effects
choices: Roughly 40 CGI shots — fewer than 15% of the total; the rest were Winston's practical work and traditional effects
Roughly 150 CGI shots — half the film; ILM rendered them on dedicated Silicon Graphics workstations for two years
Roughly 220 CGI shots — most of the T-1000 footage; only the actor close-ups used physical Robert Patrick
Roughly 280 CGI shots — almost the entire effects budget; only a handful of stunt-double shots were practical

question: Ridley Scott's Alien (1979) became a horror landmark partly because of the creature design. The xenomorph and its environment were built on the work of a Swiss surrealist painter whose 1976 book of biomechanical paintings Ron Cobb showed Scott. What was the book?
answer: Necronomicon by H. R. Giger — the 1977 collection containing the Necronom IV image that became the xenomorph
choices: Necronomicon by H. R. Giger — the 1977 collection containing the Necronom IV image that became the xenomorph

Dunecycle by John Schoenherr — the Hugo-winning Dune cover artist whose work shaped the Nostromo's interiors instead

question: Vangelis scored Blade Runner (1982) almost entirely on a single piece of equipment: a monstrous polyphonic analog synthesizer, expensive even in 1982, that Vangelis owned personally and brought to every session. The instrument's velocity-sensitive keyboard and aftertouch made the score's particular weeping textures possible. What synth?
answer: The Yamaha CS-80 — the eight-voice polyphonic synth Vangelis used on Chariots of Fire and Blade Runner alike
choices: The Yamaha CS-80 — the eight-voice polyphonic synth Vangelis used on Chariots of Fire and Blade Runner alike
The Moog Modular System 55 — the room-sized Moog that Wendy Carlos had used on Switched-On Bach in 1968

The Roland Jupiter-8 — the polyphonic Japanese synth Vangelis briefly owned but did not bring to Blade Runner

question: The Stay Puft Marshmallow Man's appearance late in Ghostbusters (1984) was a Dan Aykroyd improvisation during script revisions with Harold Ramis. Aykroyd had a specific image in mind from his Canadian childhood — a marshmallow brand mascot in advertising he'd seen and feared as a kid. What brand?
answer: The Campfire Marshmallows mascot — a chef-hatted figure in 1950s magazine ads Aykroyd had seen at his grandfather's

question: The 1984 Karate Kid earned one Academy Award nomination — not for Ralph Macchio, not for the famous crane kick, not for John Avildsen's direction. answer: Best Supporting Actor — Morita lost to Haing S. Ngor for The Killing Fields the same year

Best Actor — Morita lost to F. Murray Abraham for Amadeus in a tight five-nominee race
Best Original Screenplay — Robert Mark Kamen was credited but did not personally attend the ceremony
Best Original Song — 'You're the Best Around' was nominated despite the film opening late in the year

question: The 1989 film The Wizard, starring Fred Savage and Beau Bridges, is now infamous as a feature-length commercial for Nintendo. Its climax centers on a tournament finale where the protagonists play a Nintendo game North America had not yet seen. The film was Nintendo's marketing strategy for that game's US launch. Which game?

Tetris for NES — Nintendo's launch title for the 1989 holiday season after the rights battle with Atari

question: The original Dungeons & Dragons was published in January 1974 by Tactical Studies Rules (TSR) of Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. The first edition came as three small booklets in a brown wood-grain box. The booklets were Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and one more. What was the third booklet, and what was the original print run?
answer: Underworld & Wilderness Adventures; the first print run was approximately 1,000 sets, hand-assembled in Gygax's basement
choices: Underworld & Wilderness Adventures; the first print run was approximately 1,000 sets, hand-assembled in Gygax's basement
Combat & Encounters; the first print run was approximately 5,000 sets, professionally printed in Milwaukee
Rules & Procedures; the first print run was approximately 500 sets, hand-numbered for collectors
Spells & Saving Throws; the first print run was approximately 10,000 sets, printed for Origins Convention
context: The original 1974 D&D set sold out within a year. The system rapidly expanded with supplements (Greyhawk, Blackmoor, Eldritch Wizardry, Gods Demi-Gods & Heroes, Swords & Spells) before AD&D launched in 1977.

question: Advanced Dungeons & Dragons First Edition launched in 1977 with the Monster Manual, the first AD&D hardcover. The Player's Handbook and Dungeon Master's Guide followed. What years saw the publication of the Player's Handbook and Dungeon Master's Guide respectively?
answer: Player's Handbook in 1978; Dungeon Master's Guide in 1979 — completing the core trilogy in three years
choices: Player's Handbook in 1978; Dungeon Master's Guide in 1979 — completing the core trilogy in three years
Player's Handbook and Dungeon Master's Guide both in 1978 — simultaneous release of both core books
Player's Handbook in 1979; Dungeon Master's Guide in 1980 — completing the core trilogy in four years
Player's Handbook in 1977 alongside Monster Manual; Dungeon Master's Guide in 1979
context: The 1977-1979 AD&D core release defined the game for the next decade. The 1985 Unearthed Arcana expansion added the cavalier and barbarian classes and the dual-wielding rules.

question: Gary Gygax's home campaign setting, used for playtesting AD&D rules and adventures, was Greyhawk — based on the central continent of Oerik in the world of Oerth. Gygax originally ran the campaign from his home in Lake Geneva starting in 1972 (predating published D&D). The original Castle Greyhawk dungeon had a famous depth. How many levels deep was the original Castle Greyhawk?
answer: Approximately 13 levels deep — Gygax expanded the dungeon over years of weekly play with his children and friends
choices: Approximately 13 levels deep — Gygax expanded the dungeon over years of weekly play with his children and friends
Approximately 3 levels deep — modest scope for the playtest dungeon before publication formalized it
Approximately 100 levels deep — Gygax's reported maximum for the megadungeon at the campaign's peak
Approximately 50 levels deep — official AD&D published depth in the 1976 World of Greyhawk Folio
context: The original Castle Greyhawk dungeon was never fully published. Greyhawk Ruins (1990) and Castle Zagyg (Gygax's 2005 post-TSR project) attempted reconstructions but neither is the original Gygax dungeon.

question: Dave Arneson's Blackmoor campaign — set in his home in Minnesota — is the historical origin of the role-playing game. Arneson developed the Blackmoor campaign from his earlier Braunstein wargames starting around 1971, before any published rules existed. Arneson is credited as co-creator of D&D alongside Gygax. What was Arneson's specific innovation that distinguished Blackmoor from prior wargames?
answer: Individual character persistence and dungeon adventures with leveling progression — the proto-RPG framework
choices: Individual character persistence and dungeon adventures with leveling progression — the proto-RPG framework

Dice-based combat resolution — the d6 had been used in war games long before Blackmoor
Player vs. dungeon master dynamic — this was actually a Gygax innovation predating Blackmoor
context: Arneson and Gygax had a long legal dispute over royalties. Arneson sued TSR multiple times. The Blackmoor supplement (1975) was D&D's second expansion.

question: TSR Module B1, In Search of the Unknown (1979), was the introductory dungeon module included in the AD&D Basic Set. The module was designed as a teaching tool for new dungeon masters, with empty rooms for the DM to populate with their own contents. Who wrote Module B1?
answer: Mike Carr — TSR designer who also developed the introductory rules for Basic D&D
choices: Mike Carr — TSR designer who also developed the introductory rules for Basic D&D

Lawrence Schick — wrote the 1980 Module B2 Keep on the Borderlands rather than B1
context: B1 In Search of the Unknown was replaced in 1980 by B2 The Keep on the Borderlands as the Basic Set's intro module — B2 became one of the most-played D&D adventures ever printed.

question: TSR Module B2, The Keep on the Borderlands (1980), was the introductory adventure for the AD&D Basic Set and became one of the bestselling D&D modules ever — over 1.5 million copies. Gary Gygax wrote it personally. The module features two main areas: the Keep itself (a frontier outpost), and a sprawling dungeon area where monsters of different races coexist. What is the dungeon area called?
answer: The Caves of Chaos — a series of interconnected caves housing different humanoid monster tribes
choices: The Caves of Chaos — a series of interconnected caves housing different humanoid monster tribes

The Vault of the Drow — actually a Gygax module in the D series, not part of B2
The Ghost Tower of Inverness — actually an Allen Hammack tournament module, not part of B2
context: The Caves of Chaos's deliberate exposure to multiple monster types in conflict was a teaching device for new DMs to learn about monster ecology and politics.

question: Gary Gygax's Tomb of Horrors (Module S1, 1978) was designed for a tournament at Origins International Game Expo III in 1975 to test 'character killers' — players who relentlessly pushed for maximum power. The module became infamous for instant-death traps. What was the tournament's intent and the module's design philosophy?
answer: To test player skill and creativity over character power; with traps demanding clever solutions over combat
choices: To test player skill and creativity over character power; with traps demanding clever solutions over combat
To rank tournament players by survival time; the module had no exits and players competed for longest survival
To showcase Gygax's worldbuilding talent; the module was a one-shot setting reveal of the Vault of the Drow
To benchmark new dungeon master techniques; the module had no solo play possible and required four players
context: Tomb of Horrors was eventually published in 1978. The lich Acererak in the module became one of D&D's most famous villains. The module has been revised and republished multiple times since.

question: Gary Gygax's Expedition to the Barrier Peaks (Module S3, 1980) is famously a science-fantasy crossover module — a crashed spaceship the players explore in a high-fantasy setting. The module includes statistics for laser weapons, robots, and an android NPC. What was the historical origin of Barrier Peaks's science-fantasy elements?
answer: It was originally an Origins V 1976 tournament module before TSR commercially released it in 1980
choices: It was originally an Origins V 1976 tournament module before TSR commercially released it in 1980

It was a 1977 Gygax pitch for a successor to Greyhawk that was never published as a setting
It was a 1975 Gygax experiment to merge D&D with the Metamorphosis Alpha rules he was also developing
context: Metamorphosis Alpha (1976) is a separate Gygax science-fantasy RPG. Barrier Peaks introduced D&D players to the idea of crashed-spaceship-as-dungeon, a concept used in dozens of later modules.

question: Gary Gygax's Vault of the Drow (Module D3, 1978) is the third and most famous module in his Descent into the Depths of the Earth series. The 'D' series — D1, D2, D3 — introduced D&D to a new dungeon environment that became permanent in the setting. What environment?

The Elemental Planes — fire, water, earth, air planes, also not specifically underground
context: The D series formed a five-module campaign with G1-G3 (Giants) and Q1 (Queen of the Demonweb Pits). Lolth's debut and the foundation of Drow lore came from this series.

question: TSR Module Q1, Queen of the Demonweb Pits (1980), was the climactic adventure of Gygax's giant/drow campaign series (G-D-Q). The module was unique in that Gygax did not write it personally — he co-wrote it with another designer who later became one of TSR's signature art-directors. Who?

context: Sutherland's illustrations were a signature of 1970s-80s TSR products. His Cylinder of Misery cover for Q1 is one of D&D's most distinctive piece of art.

question: TSR Module I6, Ravenloft (October 1983), was written by Tracy and Laura Hickman. The module's villain Strahd von Zarovich, lord of Castle Ravenloft, became one of D&D's most famous antagonists. The Ravenloft module introduced something new to D&D in 1983 — a random tarot-card-like system that customizes Strahd's motivations and locations of key items. What was the system called?
answer: The Tarokka deck — a 54-card Vistani fortune-telling system that randomized Strahd's plot each session
choices: The Tarokka deck — a 54-card Vistani fortune-telling system that randomized Strahd's plot each session

The Strahd Compass — a multi-die roll system; actually a 1990 Ravenloft Hardcover addition
context: Ravenloft was groundbreaking horror gaming in 1983. The Hickmans went on to write Dragonlance the same year. Tracy Hickman became one of TSR's most influential designers of the 1980s.

question: The Dragonlance Chronicles (Dragons of Autumn Twilight, Dragons of Winter Night, Dragons of Spring Dawning) launched in 1984-85 as TSR's first major fiction crossover. The novels by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman were based on a 1984-85 campaign module series (DL1-DL14). What was the publishing rationale?

question: TSR launched the Forgotten Realms campaign setting in 1987 with the Grey Box, written primarily by Ed Greenwood and Jeff Grubb. Greenwood was an established freelance writer with a long history in Dragon Magazine. Where did Greenwood develop the Realms before TSR licensed it?

question: Elminster Aumar, Sage of Shadowdale, is the most famous wizard character in the Forgotten Realms setting, appearing in dozens of TSR/WotC novels (mostly by Ed Greenwood himself). question: R. A. Salvatore created the drow ranger Drizzt Do'Urden in his 1988 novel The Crystal Shard. Drizzt became one of the most popular D&D fiction characters and Salvatore's first novel. question: Drizzt's first novel (The Crystal Shard, 1988) introduced him as a secondary character. R. A. Salvatore's Drizzt-focused novel that established his backstory came two years later as the first of a prequel trilogy. What was the title and what was the trilogy?

question: TSR launched the Spelljammer campaign setting in 1989 — a high-fantasy D&D setting where wizards command flying ships through outer space. The setting introduced a new D&D concept: that adventurers could leave their home worlds and visit others. What was the in-fiction explanation for this novelty?

question: TSR's Planescape (1994) was a 2nd Edition Advanced Dungeons & Dragons campaign setting based on the AD&D planar cosmology (the Nine Hells, the Seven Heavens, the Elemental Planes, etc.). question: TSR's Dark Sun (1991) was a 2nd Edition campaign setting on the desert world of Athas — a brutal post-apocalyptic setting where psionics replaced traditional magic and the sun was dying. The visual style was distinct from any prior D&D setting. Who was Dark Sun's primary visual artist?

question: Magic: The Gathering's Alpha set released on August 5, 1993, from Wizards of the Coast in Seattle. The game was designed by Richard Garfield, then a mathematics graduate student. question: Magic's Alpha printing was a small experimental run of approximately 2.6 million cards in August 1993. The set sold out within weeks. question: The 'Power Nine' are nine of Magic's most powerful and valuable Alpha and Beta cards, named for their game-warping abilities. The cards have been banned in nearly all formats since the late 1990s but remain prized by collectors. What are the nine cards?

question: Magic's first expansion set, Arabian Nights, released in December 1993, four months after Alpha. question: Magic's second expansion, Antiquities (March 1994), focused on the artifact-magic side of the game's color pie. question: Magic's third expansion, Legends (June 1994), was the largest pre-1995 set with 310 cards. question: Magic's Alpha set (August 1993) contained 295 cards in the printed set, but only 116 unique cards including the basic lands. The set went through multiple printings within months. How did Alpha cards differ visually from later sets?

question: Richard Garfield has told the story of Magic's original conception in interviews. question: TSR sued multiple smaller game publishers throughout the 1980s and 1990s over various IP and trademark disputes. question: Tactical Studies Rules (TSR), Inc., the publisher of Dungeons & Dragons, was acquired by Wizards of the Coast in 1997, ending TSR's 24-year run as an independent publisher. The acquisition was driven by TSR's financial difficulties at the time. About what was the purchase price for TSR?

question: TSR was restructured in 1985 when Lorraine Williams — the sister of TSR's largest shareholder — took over the company from Gary Gygax. Gygax was forced out of the company he had co-founded in 1973. What was Williams's relationship to Brian Blume, TSR's then-largest shareholder?

question: TSR published two key D&D periodicals throughout most of its existence: Dragon Magazine (article-focused, from 1976) and Dungeon Magazine (adventure-focused, from 1986). Both continued under Wizards of the Coast. When did Dragon and Dungeon Magazines finally cease print publication?

question: Dragonlance Chronicles (Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman, 1984) was TSR's first major published novel. The novelization grew out of D&D module play at TSR offices. The Hickmans had a specific design goal for Dragonlance that distinguished it from prior fantasy. What was the goal?

question: TSR's Deities & Demigods (1980), AD&D's source book on the gods of various mythologies, originally included the Lovecraftian Cthulhu Mythos as a pantheon among the others. The 1980 first printing was unusual for one specific publishing reason. Why was the Cthulhu Mythos removed in subsequent printings?
answer: TSR did not have permission from Chaosium, which had recently acquired the Mythos game rights
choices: TSR did not have permission from Chaosium, which had recently acquired the Mythos game rights
TSR removed it due to player complaints about complexity; Lovecraft's gods were too statistically unusual for AD&D
TSR removed it because it conflicted with the Christian themes of other AD&D products that year
TSR removed it after the 1981 Pulse comic book lawsuit established Mythos rights with DC Comics
context: Chaosium had acquired Cthulhu Mythos rights through Lin Carter's estate. The original Deities & Demigods first printing is now a valuable collector's item.

question: Tom Moldvay's 1981 revision of Basic D&D used a different presentation than the 1977 Holmes version. Moldvay's edition came in a smaller box with simpler rules optimized for younger players. The Moldvay box's striking dragon-attacking-warriors cover by Erol Otus is now iconic. About how many copies of the Moldvay/Cook D&D Basic Set sold during its 1981-1983 print run?
answer: Approximately 750,000 copies of the Basic Set during its 1981-1983 print run
choices: Approximately 750,000 copies of the Basic Set during its 1981-1983 print run
Approximately 100,000 copies — disappointing sales that triggered the 1983 Mentzer revision
Approximately 3 million copies — exceptional sales that established D&D as a mass-market product
Approximately 50,000 copies — small print run for a niche hobby product
context: The Moldvay/Cook D&D Basic Set was a massive seller. Frank Mentzer's 1983 Red Box (and his Expert, Companion, Master, Immortals sets) followed and sold even more copies in the mid-1980s.

question: Frank Mentzer's 1983 revision of D&D Basic Set — the famous 'Red Box' edition — used a more dramatic painted cover by an artist who became one of TSR's signature illustrators of the 1980s. Who painted the iconic Red Box cover?
answer: Larry Elmore — Red Box cover painter; also illustrated Dragonlance Chronicles and many other TSR products
choices: Larry Elmore — Red Box cover painter; also illustrated Dragonlance Chronicles and many other TSR products
Jeff Easley — AD&D 1e core book artist; not the Red Box cover painter
Clyde Caldwell — Forgotten Realms and Ravenloft cover artist; not the Red Box cover painter
Bill Willingham — Fables comic writer; briefly worked at TSR as artist but not the Red Box cover
context: Elmore's Red Box cover shows a warrior fighting a dragon at a cave entrance. The painting is one of the most reproduced images in tabletop RPG history.

question: Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd Edition launched in 1989 with new core rulebooks. The 2nd Edition revision was prompted partly by the controversies of the 1980s 'Satanic Panic' moral crusade. Zeb Cook led the rules revision. What were the most significant rules changes from 1st to 2nd Edition?
answer: Removal of assassins, monks, and half-orcs (renamed to evil priests, etc.); simplified rules across the board
choices: Removal of assassins, monks, and half-orcs (renamed to evil priests, etc.); simplified rules across the board
Addition of the cleric class; the original AD&D had only fighter, magic-user, and thief — clerics were 2nd Edition new
Removal of all racial restrictions on classes; humans were the only playable race in 2nd Edition
Removal of all alignment system; 2nd Edition was alignment-free in its initial form
context: The Satanic Panic of the 1980s targeted D&D specifically through media campaigns. TSR's 2nd Edition removed material considered controversial. Demons were renamed 'tanar'ri' and devils were renamed 'baatezu.'

question: AD&D 2nd Edition (1989) responded to the Satanic Panic by renaming demons and devils with constructed Outer Planar terminology. The Lower Planes — D&D's hells and abysses — were rebranded with new race names. What were the new names?
answer: Tanar'ri replaced demons; baatezu replaced devils — both names invented for 2nd Edition's rebrand
choices: Tanar'ri replaced demons; baatezu replaced devils — both names invented for 2nd Edition's rebrand
Yugoloth replaced demons; lawful evil planar replaced devils — actually yugoloth referred to neutral evil instead
Daemon replaced demon; lawful daemon replaced devil — these names were not actually used in 2nd Edition
Modron replaced demon; modron replaced devil — modrons were actually lawful neutral planar beings
context: The renamed devils and demons made their TSR debut in the 1991 Monstrous Compendium Volume 8: Outer Planes Appendix. The terms persisted until 3rd Edition (2000) reintroduced 'devil' and 'demon' to D&D.

question: TSR's Ravenloft expanded from a single module (I6, 1983) to a full campaign setting in 1990 with the Realm of Terror box set, designed by Bruce Nesmith and Andria Hayday. The setting featured the Demiplane of Dread — a pocket dimension where evil characters become 'darklords' of their personal hells. Strahd was such a darklord. The setting introduced now-famous Ravenloft NPCs. Who is Dr. Rudolph van Richten?
answer: A scholarly monster hunter; the source of various Ravenloft guides published throughout the 1990s
choices: A scholarly monster hunter; the source of various Ravenloft guides published throughout the 1990s
A Ravenloft villain; one of the realm's darklords introduced in the 1990 box set
A Ravenloft deity; the realm's god of mortality introduced in the 1990 box set
A Ravenloft prophet; a Tarokka-card reader whose predictions guide players
context: Van Richten's Guide to the Vistani, to the Created, to Werebeasts, and many others were published throughout the 1990s. The character became one of Ravenloft's most beloved NPCs.

question: TSR's Player's Option series in 1995 attempted to add modular character creation rules to AD&D 2nd Edition: Skills & Powers, Combat & Tactics, Spells & Magic. The books were popular but heavily criticized for breaking existing balance. What was the most controversial Player's Option innovation?
answer: Class kits — pre-built variant class packages that overpowered base AD&D classes when stacked
choices: Class kits — pre-built variant class packages that overpowered base AD&D classes when stacked
Critical hit tables — replaced AD&D's traditional natural-20 rule with detailed limb-damage tables
Spell points — replaced spell slots with a points-based magic system that broke 2nd Edition balance
All-attribute skill checks — required every action to be tested against an attribute roll
context: The Player's Option series's modular approach was a precursor to 3rd Edition's character-build flexibility. TSR's financial collapse came shortly after.

question: D&D 3rd Edition launched in August 2000, the first edition after TSR's acquisition by Wizards of the Coast. The new edition included an unprecedented business innovation by WotC: a license that allowed other companies to publish d20-based games using D&D's core mechanics. What was the license called?
answer: The Open Game License (OGL) — released in 2000 alongside d20 SRD (System Reference Document)
choices: The Open Game License (OGL) — released in 2000 alongside d20 SRD (System Reference Document)
The Wizards Open License (WOL) — released in 2002 after the d20 boom had already begun
The Hasbro Open License (HOL) — actually released in 2003 by Hasbro after acquiring WotC
The Tabletop Open License (TOL) — actually released in 2005 by Wizards in response to community pressure
context: Paizo Publishing, which had taken over Dragon and Dungeon Magazines, used the OGL to publish its own d20 RPG. Pathfinder (2009) competed directly with D&D 4e and eventually outsold it.

question: Pathfinder, the d20-based RPG from Paizo Publishing, launched in 2009 as a competitor to D&D 4th Edition. Paizo had been publishing Dragon and Dungeon Magazines under license from Wizards from 2002, but Wizards reclaimed the magazines in 2007. Paizo's response was to create their own d20 RPG. What was Pathfinder's specific design philosophy relative to 4e?
answer: Stay close to 3.5e mechanics, expanding them rather than rebuilding from scratch as 4e had done
choices: Stay close to 3.5e mechanics, expanding them rather than rebuilding from scratch as 4e had done
Embrace the simpler MMO-influenced design of 4e, but with deeper customization options
Combine the simplicity of Basic D&D with the customization of GURPS, in a deliberate retro-design
Use a new dice system entirely (3d6 rather than d20) to differentiate from existing D&D-style games
context: Pathfinder 2nd Edition (2019) further refined the system. Paizo is now the second-largest tabletop RPG publisher in the US after Wizards of the Coast.

question: D&D 4th Edition (2008) was a significant design departure from 3.5e — moving the game toward simpler, more tactical, MMORPG-influenced mechanics with at-will/encounter/daily powers. The 4e launch was commercially successful initially but received a mixed critical reception. What design choice drew the most fan criticism?
answer: Removing the wizard-cleric-rogue-fighter distinction; all classes now had similar power-structure rules
choices: Removing the wizard-cleric-rogue-fighter distinction; all classes now had similar power-structure rules
Removing magic items entirely; the 4e system relied on inherent character bonuses rather than gear
Removing humans from the game; humans were classified as a specialty race in 4e
Removing the d20 entirely; 4e used 3d6 as its primary dice mechanic
context: Pathfinder rose to dominance during the 4e era partly by maintaining the 3.5e-style class distinctions. D&D 5e (2014) reversed many 4e design choices.

question: D&D 5th Edition launched in 2014 under lead designers Mike Mearls and Jeremy Crawford. The new edition aimed to recapture the lapsed D&D player base through a simplified, more accessible system. By approximately what year had 5e overtaken Pathfinder as the dominant RPG?
answer: By 2016-2017, 5e had clearly overtaken Pathfinder; the Stranger Things and Critical Role booms followed
choices: By 2016-2017, 5e had clearly overtaken Pathfinder; the Stranger Things and Critical Role booms followed
By 2020, with the pandemic boost to remote tabletop gaming; before then Pathfinder remained dominant
By 2014, immediately on release; 5e overtook Pathfinder before the year was out
By 2022, with the gaming industry's general post-pandemic boom; before then Pathfinder competed evenly
context: D&D 5e's success has been partly credited to Stranger Things (2016-) and the Critical Role livestream show. The pandemic year 2020 dramatically expanded the RPG market.

question: Before Dungeons & Dragons was published in 1974, Gary Gygax wrote a fantasy supplement to his medieval miniatures wargame Chainmail (1971). The Chainmail supplement introduced rules for fantastic creatures and magic — the missing link between traditional wargames and roleplaying. Who was Chainmail's co-author?
answer: Jeff Perren — co-authored Chainmail with Gary Gygax in 1971; widely cited as the first D&D-precursor rule set
choices: Jeff Perren — co-authored Chainmail with Gary Gygax in 1971; widely cited as the first D&D-precursor rule set
Dave Arneson — Gygax's eventual D&D co-creator, but did not co-author Chainmail itself
Mike Carr — TSR designer; not the co-author of Chainmail in 1971
Tim Kask — TSR editor; not the co-author of Chainmail in 1971
context: Chainmail's fantasy supplement included rules for dragons, dwarves, elves, and magic — the proto-D&D material. Arneson's Blackmoor campaign was developed using Chainmail before D&D existed.

question: The G1-G2-G3 Giants series modules (Steading of the Hill Giant Chief, Glacial Rift of the Frost Giant Jarl, Hall of the Fire Giant King) by Gary Gygax came before the D series (Descent into the Depths, Shrine of the Kuo-Toa, Vault of the Drow). The G-D-Q series formed a single mega-campaign. Approximately when were the G modules first published?
answer: 1978 — the G modules were the first tournament-derived modules published by TSR
choices: 1978 — the G modules were the first tournament-derived modules published by TSR
1980 — the G modules came after the D modules and immediately before Q1
1976 — the G modules predate published D&D and use Chainmail rules instead
1985 — the G modules came after the Unearthed Arcana expansion and use 2nd Edition rules
context: The G1-G3 modules were originally Origins tournament modules from 1978. Gary Gygax published them as TSR modules later that year and the next.

question: Unearthed Arcana (1985) was Gary Gygax's last major rules contribution to AD&D before being forced out of TSR. The book added new classes (cavalier, barbarian, thief-acrobat), new spells, new magic items, weapon specialization rules, and dual-wielding. What was the specific commercial reason for the rush to publish Unearthed Arcana?
answer: TSR was financially troubled in 1985; Gygax compiled the book in months to rush a major hit to market
choices: TSR was financially troubled in 1985; Gygax compiled the book in months to rush a major hit to market
Gygax was being pushed out and wanted to leave a final mark on AD&D before his departure
Random House had been demanding new D&D content as part of the publishing distribution agreement
TSR was rushing to release before D&D's 10th anniversary so the book could include retrospective material
context: Unearthed Arcana's quick assembly produced a famously buggy product. Many of its mechanics were later officially errata'd or revised in 2nd Edition.

question: Magic's Revised Edition launched in April 1994 as the third (post-Alpha, Beta, Unlimited) reprinting of the base set. Revised was the second white-bordered Magic set after Unlimited. Revised's print run was significantly larger than Unlimited's, reflecting the rapid expansion of the game. About how many cards were in Revised's total print run?
answer: Approximately 500 million cards across the Revised print run — vastly larger than any earlier set
choices: Approximately 500 million cards across the Revised print run — vastly larger than any earlier set
Approximately 50 million cards — comparable to Unlimited's run, just a continuation
Approximately 10 million cards — Revised was a small reprinting before the Chronicles reprint set
Approximately 5 billion cards — Revised was the largest print run of any TCG card ever
context: Revised was widely available throughout 1994-1995. Many adult collectors today own Revised Magic cards as their first introduction to the game.

question: Magic's Pro Tour — the professional competitive Magic circuit — launched in February 1996 in New York with the inaugural Pro Tour. The first Pro Tour winner became an immediate legend in competitive Magic. Who won the first Pro Tour?
answer: Michael Loconto — won Pro Tour New York 1996, the first ever Pro Tour championship
choices: Michael Loconto — won Pro Tour New York 1996, the first ever Pro Tour championship
Jon Finkel — the most famous Pro Tour winner; first won in 1998, not the inaugural event
Kai Budde — German Pro Tour player; first won in 1999, not the inaugural event
Bob Maher Jr. — won several Pro Tours; not the inaugural 1996 event
context: The Pro Tour ran from 1996 to 2018 as Magic's flagship competitive event. WotC has since restructured competitive Magic into the Magic Pro League and other formats.

question: Magic's first World Championships were held in 1994 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin (then home of Wizards of the Coast). The inaugural champion went on to be one of the early stars of competitive Magic. Who won the first Magic World Championship?
answer: Zak Dolan — a 17-year-old American player who won the inaugural 1994 Magic World Championship
choices: Zak Dolan — a 17-year-old American player who won the inaugural 1994 Magic World Championship
Olle Rade — a Swedish player; he won the third Magic World Championship in 1996, not the first
Tom Chanpheng — an Australian player; he won the second Magic World Championship in 1996
Jakub Slemr — a Czech player; he won the fourth Magic World Championship in 1997
context: The World Championships followed a different format than the Pro Tour. The two competitive events coexisted for decades.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's Spirited Away won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature at the 75th Academy Awards (2003), the first hand-drawn (and only the second non-English-language) film to win the category. The film became the highest-grossing Japanese film of all time on initial release. The Academy Award win followed an unusual road for an anime to mainstream Western recognition. Who personally championed Spirited Away's US distribution?
answer: John Lasseter — Pixar's creative head at the time, who personally championed Spirited Away's Disney distribution
choices: John Lasseter — Pixar's creative head at the time, who personally championed Spirited Away's Disney distribution
Steven Spielberg — never personally involved in Spirited Away's distribution; sometimes confused with Lasseter's role
George Lucas — never personally involved in Spirited Away's distribution despite Star Wars cross-marketing rumors
Brad Bird — Iron Giant and Incredibles director; admired Miyazaki but did not handle the US distribution
context: Lasseter is a longtime Miyazaki fan and visited Studio Ghibli multiple times. His personal advocacy helped Disney distribute Miyazaki films in North America in the 2000s.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke (1997) was a darker, more violent Studio Ghibli film than typical of the studio's family-friendly output. The film took four years to make and used hand-drawn animation alongside selective computer-generated imagery. The film grossed enormously in Japan, breaking previous Ghibli records. Approximately how long was Princess Mononoke's runtime?
answer: Approximately 134 minutes — one of the longest hand-drawn Ghibli films
choices: Approximately 134 minutes — one of the longest hand-drawn Ghibli films
Approximately 84 minutes — comparable to most Ghibli films which run 80-95 minutes typically
Approximately 180 minutes — too long for any Ghibli film actually released
Approximately 240 minutes — Princess Mononoke was originally a two-part film cut for theatrical release
context: Princess Mononoke's box office and the cult following it built abroad helped finance Spirited Away (2001). Mononoke is on most lists of essential 1990s anime films.

question: Hayao Miyazaki's My Neighbor Totoro (1988) had a difficult commercial path. The film's family-friendly fantasy was paired in theaters with Isao Takahata's Grave of the Fireflies, an intensely sad WWII drama. The double bill was Ghibli's commercial strategy. What was the studio's rationale for the pairing?
answer: Both films were short; the double feature gave Japanese theaters a full-length program with two Ghibli works at once
choices: Both films were short; the double feature gave Japanese theaters a full-length program with two Ghibli works at once
The studio wanted to test audience reaction; both films were considered risky and the pairing hedged the bet
Toho insisted on the pairing as a condition of distribution; the studio could not have released either film solo
Miyazaki and Takahata had a personal rivalry; the studio paired the films to settle which was more popular
context: Both films were under 90 minutes. The Totoro-Fireflies double bill is one of the most emotionally extreme pairings in cinema history.

question: Hirohiko Araki's JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3, Stardust Crusaders (1989-1992), follows Jotaro Kujo and his companions as they travel halfway around the world to confront a recurring villain in a specific city. Where does Stardust Crusaders's journey end?
answer: Cairo, Egypt — Jotaro's destination at the end of the 50-day journey
choices: Cairo, Egypt — Jotaro's destination at the end of the 50-day journey
Tokyo, Japan — the journey is a return-home from a different starting point
London, England — the journey passes through Europe before ending in Britain
Hong Kong — the journey was originally meant to end in China before Araki revised
context: Stardust Crusaders is widely considered one of the most influential anime series for its 'Stand battles' system. The Cairo setting reflects Araki's love of Egyptian iconography.

question: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba (manga 2016, anime 2019) became a global anime phenomenon thanks largely to the visual quality of its anime adaptation by a particular studio known for compositing-heavy production. Which studio handled the Demon Slayer anime?
answer: Ufotable — also produced the Fate/Zero, Fate/Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works, and other compositing-heavy anime
choices: Ufotable — also produced the Fate/Zero, Fate/Stay Night Unlimited Blade Works, and other compositing-heavy anime
Mappa — major studio for shonen anime but did not animate Demon Slayer; works on Jujutsu Kaisen and Attack on Titan final season
Madhouse — Black Lagoon, Death Note, One-Punch Man studio; did not animate Demon Slayer
Bones — My Hero Academia and Fullmetal Alchemist Brotherhood studio; did not animate Demon Slayer
context: Ufotable's elaborate digital compositing on Demon Slayer fight scenes set a new technical benchmark for TV anime in 2019-2020.

question: Katsuhiro Otomo's anime Akira (1988) required a specific technical innovation in its production for the time. The film used over 2,200 distinct shots and 327 separate colors created for it. Which production studio handled Akira?
answer: TMS Entertainment — handled Akira's production, also responsible for the Disney AKIRA-influenced contributions in later 80s American animation
choices: TMS Entertainment — handled Akira's production, also responsible for the Disney AKIRA-influenced contributions in later 80s American animation
Madhouse — major anime studio of the era; did not animate Akira despite being a TMS contemporary
Toei Animation — Japan's largest anime studio; did not animate Akira
Studio Pierrot — handled Naruto and Bleach; did not animate Akira despite working in the era
context: TMS Entertainment's Akira production budget reportedly reached 1.1 billion yen (~9 million USD in 1988), then a record for anime cinema.

question: The Simpsons aired its first full episode as a half-hour Christmas special on December 17, 1989: 'Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire,' written by Mimi Pond. The Simpsons had been short interstitial cartoons on The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. Approximately how many of these shorts aired before the first full episode?
answer: Approximately 48 Tracey Ullman Show shorts ran from April 1987 to April 1989 before the prime-time series began
choices: Approximately 48 Tracey Ullman Show shorts ran from April 1987 to April 1989 before the prime-time series began
Approximately 100 Tracey Ullman Show shorts ran from 1986 to 1989; double the actual amount
Approximately 10 Tracey Ullman Show shorts ran only in 1988; much fewer than actual
Approximately 200 Tracey Ullman Show shorts ran from 1986 to 1990; vastly more than actual
context: The Simpsons has run for over 30 seasons. The original Mimi Pond pilot script 'Family Therapy' was rewritten by James L. Brooks and Matt Groening before the Tracey Ullman Show transition.

question: Hideaki Anno's Neon Genesis Evangelion (1995-96) was produced by Gainax, the Tokyo studio Anno had co-founded with friends from college. Gainax had previously produced what is widely considered one of the first major anime to depict otaku culture itself. What was that earlier Gainax production?
answer: Otaku no Video (1991) — a Gainax OVA depicting young otaku culture; a key piece of 1990s anime culture
choices: Otaku no Video (1991) — a Gainax OVA depicting young otaku culture; a key piece of 1990s anime culture
Patlabor (1989) — the Mobile Police anime; produced by a different studio, not Gainax
Bubblegum Crisis (1987) — produced by ARTMIC, not Gainax; sometimes confused with Gainax productions
Akira (1988) — produced by TMS Entertainment, not Gainax
context: Gainax also produced Royal Space Force: The Wings of Honneamise (1987), one of the most acclaimed anime films of the decade. Anno's directorial work began at Gainax.

question: Watsuki Nobuhiro's Rurouni Kenshin manga (1994-1999) is set in a specific historical period of Japan — the early Meiji era, just after the Tokugawa shogunate had fallen. The Kyoto Arc of Rurouni Kenshin (manga volumes 7-18, anime episodes 28-62) follows protagonist Kenshin Himura confronting a recurring villain in Kyoto. Who is the central villain of the Kyoto Arc?
answer: Makoto Shishio — a fellow assassin from the Bakumatsu era whose burns and bandages mark his survival of betrayal
choices: Makoto Shishio — a fellow assassin from the Bakumatsu era whose burns and bandages mark his survival of betrayal
Hajime Saito — actually a recurring ally character in the Kyoto Arc, not the antagonist
Aoshi Shinomori — a Kyoto Arc supporting antagonist from earlier in the series, not the central villain
Soujirou Seta — Shishio's lieutenant; he plays a major role but is not the central antagonist
context: Watsuki researched the Meiji era extensively. The Kyoto Arc was adapted as a live-action film trilogy starting in 2012.

question: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (1984) was Steven Spielberg's sequel to Raiders of the Lost Ark. The film's intensely violent and gory content prompted a specific change to the US film rating system. What was the change, and what was the film's role in prompting it?
answer: The PG-13 rating was introduced in 1984 partly in response to Temple of Doom; the new rating bridged PG and R
choices: The PG-13 rating was introduced in 1984 partly in response to Temple of Doom; the new rating bridged PG and R
The R rating was introduced in 1984 specifically in response to Temple of Doom; the new rating restricted under-17
The NC-17 rating was introduced in 1984 in response to Temple of Doom; the new rating restricted adult content
The G rating was introduced in 1984 specifically to accommodate the post-Temple-of-Doom adult content
context: MPAA's PG-13 rating debuted with John Milius's Red Dawn (1984). Temple of Doom (released two months earlier) and Joe Dante's Gremlins (released the same week) were the cited triggers for the new rating.

question: Disney's Tron: Legacy (2010), directed by Joseph Kosinski, was a 28-year sequel to the 1982 original. The film's score was composed by an unusual choice — a French electronic music duo whose first major composing job was a feature film. Who scored Tron: Legacy?
answer: Daft Punk — Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo; their first major film score
choices: Daft Punk — Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo; their first major film score
Justice — French electronic duo, but did not score Tron: Legacy despite the era's resemblance
Air — French electronic duo who scored The Virgin Suicides (1999) but not Tron: Legacy
M83 — Anthony Gonzalez's French electronic act, who later scored Oblivion (2013)
context: Daft Punk's Tron: Legacy soundtrack with the London Symphony Orchestra became one of the most acclaimed film scores of the 2010s.

question: Dan Aykroyd's original 1983 script for Ghostbusters had a vastly more elaborate scope than the final 1984 film. Aykroyd had pitched a multi-team international ghost-fighting organization spanning multiple time periods. The script was rewritten by Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and director Ivan Reitman to bring it within budget. What was Aykroyd's original vision?
answer: A multi-team Ghost Smashers with international branches; supernatural threats and time travel were all in the script
choices: A multi-team Ghost Smashers with international branches; supernatural threats and time travel were all in the script
A serious horror film with no comedy; the Aykroyd original was a Lovecraftian horror project
A single-team Ghostbusters confined to New York City; the original was actually smaller than the released film
A musical Ghostbusters with original Aykroyd songs; the original was a musical comedy
context: Aykroyd had been deeply interested in spiritualism since childhood. His grandfather was a researcher into paranormal phenomena. The Aykroyd-Ramis collaboration became one of the most successful comedy pairings in Hollywood.

question: Ridley Scott's Blade Runner has been released in multiple versions. The original 1982 theatrical cut had a voiceover narration and a happy ending added by the studio. Scott's 1992 Director's Cut removed both and added a key scene. What scene did Scott add to the 1992 cut?
answer: Deckard's unicorn dream — the daydream that pairs with Gaff's origami unicorn at the end
choices: Deckard's unicorn dream — the daydream that pairs with Gaff's origami unicorn at the end
The Tyrell death scene — restored from the deleted footage in the 1982 theatrical cut
Roy Batty's tears in rain monologue — actually present in the 1982 theatrical cut
The opening crawl explaining replicants — actually present in the 1982 theatrical cut
context: The 2007 Final Cut is Scott's definitive version, with all his edits and effects. The Final Cut's release on Blu-ray became the reference version of the film.

question: Ridley Scott's Alien (1979) included a now-legendary scene in which the alien creature bursts from the chest of crew member Kane. The actor John Hurt played Kane. The scene was filmed with practical effects, with the actors not fully prepared for the magnitude of the splatter. What was the in-set reaction?
answer: Several cast members had genuine shock reactions; the day's filming continued without retakes
choices: Several cast members had genuine shock reactions; the day's filming continued without retakes
All cast members were briefed in advance; the reactions were entirely performed
Hurt and the other actors had walked through the scene multiple times; the reactions were strictly choreographed
The scene was filmed multiple times; the actors became inured to the splatter and the reactions are subdued
context: John Hurt's chest-burst was a single take. Veronica Cartwright's character Lambert had perhaps the most genuine reaction. The scene became one of the most-referenced single horror moments in cinema.

question: The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) was directed by Jim Sharman as a film adaptation of Richard O'Brien's 1973 stage musical The Rocky Horror Show. The film's initial theatrical release was a financial flop in 1975. The film became one of the longest-running theatrical phenomena in cinema history through its midnight-screening tradition. When did Rocky Horror's midnight-screening cult emerge?
answer: 1976 — at the Waverly Theater in New York's Greenwich Village; the model for the global cult
choices: 1976 — at the Waverly Theater in New York's Greenwich Village; the model for the global cult
1980 — after multiple regional theaters had already started the tradition individually
1975 — immediately on the film's first theatrical release; the cult was a launch phenomenon
1985 — after Rocky Horror's 10th anniversary re-release brought it back to theaters
context: Rocky Horror has been in continuous midnight rotation in major US cities since 1976. The cult's audience-participation rituals are entirely unique in mainstream cinema.

question: David Fincher's Fight Club (1999) was based on Chuck Palahniuk's 1996 debut novel. The film starred Brad Pitt and Edward Norton. The film was a commercial disappointment on its 1999 release but became a cult favorite on DVD in the early 2000s. The film's central narrative is famously about something the viewer is not meant to be told. What is the film's tagline-level setup, kept spoiler-free?
answer: Two strangers form an underground fighting club for white-collar men; the club grows into a movement
choices: Two strangers form an underground fighting club for white-collar men; the club grows into a movement
Two strangers meet in a support group for a disease neither has; they form a romantic relationship
A corporate worker discovers his neighbor is plotting a major corporate sabotage; both men work together
An accountant discovers a strange cult in his city; he is recruited and rises through its ranks
context: Fight Club's first rule (don't talk about Fight Club) and the central narrative reveal have become foundational pop-culture references. The film's themes of consumer alienation aged into prophecy.

question: The Wachowskis's The Matrix (1999) revolutionized Hollywood action cinema partly through its martial arts choreography. The film's fight scenes were designed by a specific Hong Kong choreographer brought to Hollywood specifically for the film. Who?
answer: Yuen Woo-ping — Hong Kong action choreographer who also did Crouching Tiger and the Matrix sequels
choices: Yuen Woo-ping — Hong Kong action choreographer who also did Crouching Tiger and the Matrix sequels
Sammo Hung — Hong Kong action choreographer; did not work on The Matrix despite similar period work

Donnie Yen — Hong Kong action star; not the Matrix choreographer despite Wachowski-Donnie Yen rumors

question: Hideaki Anno's End of Evangelion (1997) was a theatrical film that served as an alternate finale to the 1995-96 TV series, replacing the controversial episodes 25-26 with a longer, more elaborate ending. The film was made in response to fan reaction to the TV finale. What was the production studio?
answer: Gainax — produced both the original TV series and End of Evangelion, both directed by Anno

question: Hiromu Arakawa's manga Fullmetal Alchemist (2001-2010) was first adapted as a TV anime in 2003 by Studio Bones. The first anime diverged significantly from the manga because Arakawa had not yet completed her story. A second more faithful anime adaptation followed in 2009. question: Nintendo and Ape's EarthBound (1995, SNES) for North America was the sequel to Mother (1989, Famicom). The North American release came with an expensive cardboard box containing a Player's Guide, but sold poorly relative to expectations. Approximately how many copies did EarthBound sell in North America?
answer: Approximately 140,000 copies in North America; far below Nintendo's expectations of 250,000+

question: SNK's Neo Geo AES (Advanced Entertainment System), released in 1990, was a home console that ran the same hardware as the Neo Geo MVS arcade. The system was extraordinarily expensive at launch. Approximately what was the AES launch price for the console plus a single game?

Approximately 100 USD for the console plus 100 USD per game cartridge — far below the actual price
context: The Neo Geo AES was sold primarily through Sears stores in the early 1990s. The hardware's longevity was remarkable — SNK released new Neo Geo games into the early 2000s.

question: SNK's The King of Fighters '94, released for the Neo Geo MVS arcade in August 1994, debuted a 3-on-3 team battle system that became the franchise's defining mechanic. The series's most famous narrative arc — the 'Orochi Saga' — spanned multiple yearly KOF releases. Which KOF games make up the original Orochi Saga?

question: Raizing's Battle Garegga (1996) is a legendary arcade vertical shoot-em-up known for its extreme score competition and balance. The game's scoring system, including the 'rank' mechanic that adjusted difficulty based on player performance, became influential in subsequent shoot-em-ups. Mid 2010s — well after the actual Japanese arcade competition era
context: Battle Garegga's score tables included names that became arcade legends. CAVE's later shoot-em-ups (DoDonPachi, Mushihimesama) inherited Garegga's competitive scoring traditions.

question: Konami's Gradius (1985) was a horizontal scrolling shoot-em-up that defined the genre's options system — power-ups that orbit the player ship and add firepower. Gradius famously was also the first home of the 'Konami Code' (up up down down left right left right B A), entered for full power-up on the Famicom port. The Konami Code became one of the most famous cheat codes in gaming history. What did the code do in Gradius's home port?

choices: Granted the player all power-ups at once — Speed, Missile, Double, Laser, Option, and Shield

Activated the secret no-clip mode — the player ship became invulnerable
context: The Konami Code appeared in dozens of Konami games. Contra (1987) used it for 30 lives. The code has become a cultural reference and Easter egg in many non-Konami games and websites.

question: Konami's Contra (Nintendo NES port, 1988) is famous for the Konami Code variant that grants 30 lives — making the brutally hard arcade port survivable for home players. Contra has a specific two-player mode that allowed friend run-and-gun experiences. What were the two players' character names in Contra?

question: Super Mario Bros. 2 in North America (1988) was actually a reskinned port of a Japanese game called Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic (1987), a Fuji TV-promoted Mario-style platformer with different characters. The original Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 (Lost Levels, 1986) was considered too hard for Western audiences. Why did Nintendo choose to reskin Doki Doki Panic rather than localize the original SMB 2?

context: The original Japanese SMB 2 (Lost Levels) eventually came to North America in 1993's Super Mario All-Stars (SNES). The two SMB 2s are distinctly different games.

question: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (2015) was Kojima's last game with Konami before his departure from the company. The development was famously troubled, with reports of Konami restricting Kojima's resources during production. About when did Kojima formally leave Konami?

question: Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. Melee (2001, GameCube) was Masahiro Sakurai's second Smash Bros. release. Melee became the longest-running competitive title in the Smash Bros. franchise, with a serious tournament scene that lasted into the 2020s despite multiple later sequels. What is the most famous Melee tournament event?

question: Squaresoft's Xenogears (1998, PS1) was a notoriously ambitious JRPG with a sprawling story by Tetsuya Takahashi. The second disc of the game's two-disc release was widely criticized for replacing extensive gameplay with text-and-still-image storytelling. What is the in-universe explanation given for the unusual presentation?
answer: Takahashi has cited budget and time constraints; the storyboard was preserved but the gameplay had to be cut

context: Xenogears went on to spawn Xenosaga (Square, 2002) and Xenoblade Chronicles (Monolith Soft, 2010). Tetsuya Takahashi's storytelling ambitions defined a sub-genre of JRPG.

question: Fumito Ueda's Ico (2001, PS2) at Team Ico established the minimalist style that defined the studio. The game follows a young boy with horns who escapes a haunted castle while protecting a girl named Yorda. The game's design philosophy stripped away many conventional video game elements. An entirely diegetic HUD where dialogue choices appeared as physical objects in the game world
context: Ico's minimalism influenced many later games (Limbo, Inside, Journey). Fumito Ueda's design talks remain a foundation of game design education.

question: Fumito Ueda's Shadow of the Colossus (2005, PS2) is structured as 16 boss battles against giant beings called colossi. The game has no smaller enemies, no NPCs other than the player's mount (Agro) and the goal of saving a sleeping girl. The structure was a radical departure from contemporary action games. What is the typical playthrough length?
answer: Approximately 10-15 hours for a single playthrough; about 40 minutes per colossus on average

context: Shadow of the Colossus was remade in 2018 for PS4 with updated visuals. The original PS2 version remains the canonical artistic statement.

question: FromSoftware's Dark Souls (2011) was directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki — no relation to Hayao Miyazaki of Studio Ghibli. The game was a spiritual successor to FromSoftware's Demon's Souls (2009, PS3) and established the 'Soulslike' genre. What was Miyazaki's design ethos that defined Dark Souls?

context: Miyazaki's design has been hugely influential on the 2010s-2020s action game landscape. Elden Ring (2022) was Miyazaki's largest-scale work; Dark Souls established the template.

question: Interplay's Fallout (1997) was a post-apocalyptic isometric RPG developed by Black Isle Studios. The game's setting and style established a long-running franchise. Tim Cain was the project lead; Brian Fargo was Interplay's CEO. The Fallout setting drew on a specific older science fiction concept that anchored its retrofuturism. What concept?

question: Irrational Games's System Shock 2 (1999) was directed by Ken Levine in collaboration with Looking Glass Studios. The game was a precursor to BioShock (2007), with similar themes of cybernetic experimentation and a malevolent AI (SHODAN). What was System Shock 2's protagonist class system?

question: Blizzard's StarCraft (1998) introduced a three-faction RTS with the Terran (human), Protoss (alien psionic), and Zerg (alien hivemind) species. question: Blizzard's Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos (2002) introduced the hero unit system that became central to the multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) genre. A Warcraft III mod, Defense of the Ancients (DotA), began the entire MOBA genre. About when did DotA emerge as a mod?

question: Blizzard North's Diablo (1996) launched the action RPG dungeon-crawler genre. The game was set in a single town (Tristram) with a deep dungeon below the church. The character classes available at launch were three. What classes were available at Diablo's 1996 launch?

question: Sony Online Entertainment's EverQuest (1999) was one of the first commercially successful 3D MMORPGs, released a year before Asheron's Call and four years before World of Warcraft. question: Sony Online Entertainment's EverQuest: Ruins of Kunark (April 2000) was EverQuest's first expansion pack, introducing the continent of Kunark and the Iksar (lizardman) playable race. The expansion was notable for several design innovations. What was the most discussed Kunark addition?

question: FromSoftware's Elden Ring (February 2022) was directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki with worldbuilding by author George R. R. Martin. The game won Game Awards Game of the Year 2022. Martin's contribution was limited to a specific aspect of the game's lore. What did Martin write for Elden Ring?

question: Neil Gaiman's American Gods (2001 novel) won the Hugo, Nebula, and Bram Stoker Awards in 2002. The novel was loosely connected to Gaiman's Sandman comics universe, set in a world where myth and reality are blurred. The novel was developed from a specific 1990s idea Gaiman had. question: Alan Moore's Promethea (1999-2005), illustrated by J.H. Williams III, was a series for Moore's ABC (America's Best Comics) imprint at Wildstorm/DC. question: Frank Miller's 300 (Dark Horse, May-September 1998) was a five-issue limited series about the Battle of Thermopylae (480 BCE), where King Leonidas led 300 Spartans against the Persian invasion. question: Alan Moore's From Hell (1991-1998) — illustrated by Eddie Campbell — is a nine-volume graphic novel exploring the Jack the Ripper murders of 1888 London. question: Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's Watchmen (1986-1987) is set in an alternate 1985 where superheroes have existed since the 1940s. The setting includes specific divergences from real history. Who is the US President in Watchmen's 1985?

question: Alan Moore's V for Vendetta — illustrated primarily by David Lloyd — began in 1982 in the British Warrior magazine, then completed at DC after Warrior's closure. The series was set in a near-future totalitarian Britain. The story's central image — a Guy Fawkes mask worn by the protagonist V — became a real-world political icon decades later. context: Anonymous's adoption of the Guy Fawkes mask in 2008 onward made it a global protest icon. Moore has spoken about the irony of his fictional character becoming a real-world symbol.

question: Alan Moore and Melinda Gebbie's Lost Girls (Top Shelf, 2006) is a three-volume erotic graphic novel featuring three Victorian-era literary characters: Alice (Wonderland), Dorothy (Oz), and Wendy (Neverland). question: The Dark Phoenix Saga concluded in Uncanny X-Men #137 (September 1980), a story written by Chris Claremont and drawn by John Byrne. The issue was significant for several reasons in comics history. What made issue 137 a watershed in superhero comics?

question: Frederic Wertham's 1954 book Seduction of the Innocent argued that comic books contributed to juvenile delinquency. question: Marvel's Civil War (2006-2007) was a seven-issue event by writer Mark Millar and artist Steve McNiven. The crossover spanned many Marvel titles in the surrounding months. question: Grant Morrison's JLA (DC, 1997-2000) restarted the Justice League franchise with a 'Big Seven' lineup: Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Aquaman, Green Lantern (Kyle Rayner), Flash (Wally West), and Martian Manhunter. question: DC's first multiverse crossover came in The Flash #123 (September 1961), titled 'Flash of Two Worlds.' The story established Earth-1 (the modern Flash, Barry Allen) and Earth-2 (the Golden Age Flash, Jay Garrick). What was the immediate impact of the multiverse concept on DC continuity?

question: DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985), written by Marv Wolfman and illustrated by George Perez, was a 12-issue event series that consolidated DC's multiverse into a single Earth. question: The term 'Sasquatch' for the Pacific Northwest large humanoid cryptid was coined in 1929 by a Canadian schoolteacher who collected indigenous folklore. The teacher anglicized the term from a Salish language word meaning 'wild man.' Who was the teacher?

question: The term 'Bigfoot' (for the Pacific Northwest cryptid) was coined in 1958 in a newspaper article. question: The Patterson-Gimlin film (1967) has been alleged to be a costumed actor by various researchers over the decades. The most cited claim is that the subject is a man named Bob Heironimus in a custom-made gorilla suit. Who allegedly made the suit?

question: The Tatzelwurm is a small cryptid reported in the Alpine regions of Switzerland, Austria, Bavaria, and northern Italy since the medieval period. question: The Kraken — a mythological sea monster of Scandinavian folklore — gained scientific validation in the 19th century when a real giant cephalopod was confirmed by Western science. When was the giant squid first scientifically documented?

question: The okapi — a forest-dwelling relative of the giraffe — was a cryptid for centuries before scientific validation. Reports of a 'forest unicorn' in central Africa were dismissed by Western zoologists until specimens were obtained. When was the okapi first scientifically described?

context: Spurling was the stepson of Marmaduke Wetherell, a big-game hunter the Daily Mail had once humiliated. The hoax was Wetherell's revenge. Spurling confessed shortly before his death.

question: From November 1966 through November 1967, residents of Point Pleasant, West Virginia, reported sightings of a large winged creature with glowing red eyes. question: In 1587, English colonist Governor John White established a settlement on Roanoke Island in modern-day North Carolina. question: On November 24, 1971, a man calling himself Dan Cooper boarded Northwest Orient Flight 305 from Portland to Seattle. question: The Voynich Manuscript, held at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library since 1969, is a 240-page illustrated codex written in an unknown script with botanical, astronomical, and biological drawings. question: On July 2, 1937, Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the central Pacific during their attempted circumnavigation flight. question: Edgar Rice Burroughs (1875-1950) was 36 years old, broke, and a failed pencil-sharpener salesman when he sent his first novel to The All-Story magazine in 1912. The magazine bought it — about a Civil War veteran transported to Mars. What was the first published Burroughs novel?

context: Burroughs went on to write 27 Tarzan novels and 11 Mars-set John Carter novels. Disney adapted John Carter in 2012 to a famously disappointing reception — partly because the source material's age made it feel derivative.

question: Clark Ashton Smith (1893-1961), a third member of the Weird Tales triumvirate alongside Lovecraft and Howard, wrote prose poetry in pulps from his California home where he lived in deep poverty. Smith invented a fictional setting — Earth's final continent under a dying red sun, where black sorcery rules and the dead are coin. What was Smith's invented setting called?

context: Smith wrote all four settings — Zothique, Hyperborea, Averoigne, and Poseidonis — alongside dozens of poems. Jack Vance's Dying Earth (1950) acknowledged Zothique as inspiration; Wolfe and others followed.

question: The Shadow, the mysterious crime-fighter who 'knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men,' began as a radio narrator before he was a character. The Shadow's first appearance was on the radio in 1930, not in pulp magazines. What was the original show, and what role did the Shadow play?

context: Street and Smith bought a Shadow pulp series in 1931. Walter Gibson wrote 282 Shadow novels under the pseudonym Maxwell Grant from 1931 to 1949. Orson Welles voiced the Shadow on radio in 1937-1938.

question: The Doc Savage pulp series launched in 1933 from Street and Smith, the same publisher as The Shadow. The lead author, writing under the house name Kenneth Robeson, was a single ghostwriter for nearly all of the 181 published Doc Savage novels — a remarkable productivity feat in pulp history. Who was the real author of most Doc Savage novels?

question: Action Comics #1 (June 1938) introduced Superman to the world, kicking off the Golden Age of comics. The creators sold the rights to Detective Comics, Inc. (later DC) for an infamously small sum that would haunt them for decades. Who were the creators, and what did they reportedly receive for the rights?

Jerry Siegel and Stan Lee sold the Superman rights for $250 — combined as a Superman-and-Captain-America package
context: Siegel and Shuster sued repeatedly across the next decades to reclaim rights. They eventually received credit and a small annuity from Warner. Their case is the foundational injustice of comics history.

question: Detective Comics #27 (May 1939) introduced 'The Bat-Man' — a vigilante in a bat-cowl detective costume swinging through Gotham City. question: All-Star Comics #8 (December 1941) introduced Wonder Woman in a story written by William Moulton Marston, a Harvard-trained psychologist with an unusual day job that informed his comic-writing. context: Marston's polygraph and his Wonder Woman lasso of truth share the same conceptual origin. His unconventional household (a wife and a partner co-raising children) also informed Wonder Woman's all-female utopia.

question: Marvel's Fantastic Four #1 (November 1961), the start of the Silver Age of Marvel Comics, introduced the team of Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm, and Ben Grimm. question: Amazing Fantasy #15 (August 1962) introduced Peter Parker, the high-school student bitten by a radioactive spider. question: Wolverine's first full appearance was in Incredible Hulk #181 (November 1974), in a story by writer Len Wein and artist Herb Trimpe. question: MAD Magazine launched in October 1952 as a comic book from EC Comics, written and edited by Harvey Kurtzman. MAD became a 25-cent magazine in 1955, partly to escape the new Comics Code Authority. Who replaced Kurtzman as editor in 1956 and ran MAD for the next 28 years?
