Side-scrolling with depth layers; intended as a callback to Resident Evil's earliest pitch from 1994
context: RE4 went on to define a generation of action games — Gears of War, Uncharted, and dozens of imitators borrowed the over-the-shoulder template Mikami's team locked in.

question: Bungie's Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) launched alongside the original Xbox and helped Microsoft establish the console as a viable platform. The game's surprising history is that Halo was not originally pitched as an Xbox FPS; it began as a totally different genre on a different platform. What was Halo's original form?
answer: A real-time strategy game for Macintosh — revealed at Macworld 1999 before Microsoft acquired Bungie
choices: A real-time strategy game for Macintosh — revealed at Macworld 1999 before Microsoft acquired Bungie
A first-person shooter for Windows — revealed at E3 1999 before the Xbox platform existed publicly
A multiplayer-only space combat game for PS2 — revealed at Tokyo Game Show 1999 before publisher conflicts
A console RPG with FPS combat for Dreamcast — pitched to Sega in 1998 before the platform's commercial troubles
context: Microsoft bought Bungie in 2000 and pivoted Halo to Xbox FPS. The original RTS pitch survives in trailers from the 1999 Macworld event.

question: Bethesda Game Studios' The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind (2002, Xbox and PC) shifted away from the procedurally generated landscapes of Daggerfall (1996) to a single hand-crafted continent. The change was a watershed: where Daggerfall had 487,000 square miles of generated land, Morrowind's hand-built island is what size?
answer: About 10 square miles of hand-crafted terrain — Vvardenfell, the volcanic island in the inland sea of Morrowind
choices: About 10 square miles of hand-crafted terrain — Vvardenfell, the volcanic island in the inland sea of Morrowind
About 100 square miles of hand-crafted terrain — the entire province of Morrowind including its mainland
About 1,500 square miles of hand-crafted terrain — a full Daggerfall-comparable scale by manual craft
About 50 acres of hand-crafted terrain — a single city Bethesda expanded with procedural fill at the borders
context: Vvardenfell remains a fan-favorite Elder Scrolls setting. Morrowind's hand-crafted style became the template for Oblivion and Skyrim, even as their landmasses grew.

question: Markus 'Notch' Persson's Minecraft began as a 2009 indie project Persson released playably on the Java forum TIGSource. Minecraft openly took its core block-mining-and-building idea from a slightly earlier 2009 indie game by Zachary Barth. What was that earlier game?
answer: Infiniminer — Zachary Barth's 2009 multiplayer block game whose mining mechanic Notch openly drew on
choices: Infiniminer — Zachary Barth's 2009 multiplayer block game whose mining mechanic Notch openly drew on
Dwarf Fortress — Tarn Adams's ongoing procedural-fortress simulator, an inspiration but not a block-building peer
Crayon Physics — Petri Purho's 2009 indie physics puzzler, often cited alongside Minecraft as an early peer
World of Goo — 2D Boy's 2008 indie hit, sometimes confused with Minecraft's indie-success narrative
context: Notch later credited Infiniminer publicly. Microsoft acquired Mojang for 2.5 billion USD in 2014 — the largest indie-to-corporate sale in gaming history.

question: id Software's DOOM (1993) is remembered for many firsts in PC FPS history. One commercial decision shaped not only DOOM's success but the whole 1990s shareware ecosystem of bedroom PC gaming. What was id's distribution model for DOOM's first release?
answer: Free shareware episode 1, paid mail-order for episodes 2 and 3 — direct distribution bypassing retailers
choices: Free shareware episode 1, paid mail-order for episodes 2 and 3 — direct distribution bypassing retailers
Retail box only at Babbage's and Egghead Software — id's distribution agreement covered no mail order
Subscription PC magazine cover disc only — DOOM was shipped initially only on PC Gamer cover discs
Pre-internet BBS download only with paywall — id charged BBS sysops a license fee to host DOOM
context: id Software made millions through direct shareware-to-paid conversion. The model funded Wolfenstein 3D's expansion and DOOM II in 1994.

question: id Software's Quake (1996) advanced the 3D engine, introduced fully polygonal level geometry, and shipped with a score by an unusual choice — a then-rising American industrial musician. Who scored Quake, and how did the music differ from typical mid-90s FPS soundtracks?
answer: Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails — dark ambient industrial textures rather than the era's MIDI rock tracks
choices: Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails — dark ambient industrial textures rather than the era's MIDI rock tracks
Skinny Puppy's Cevin Key — industrial textures with vocal samples that Bethesda later removed from the GOG re-release
Bobby Prince — also did Wolfenstein 3D and DOOM; chose ambient drone for Quake's atmospheric departure
Tom Salta — composer on later Microsoft Flight Simulator; his Quake demo was rejected for too much melody
context: Reznor's nail-gun ammunition pickups are stamped with NIN logos — a deliberate Easter egg. The original CD audio Quake soundtrack was never legally re-released digitally.

question: Valve Software's Half-Life (1998) reset what mid-90s players expected from an FPS — scripted scenes, no cutscenes, environmental storytelling. The studio's two founders came from a specific corporate background that shaped Valve's culture. Where did Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington work before founding Valve in 1996?
answer: Microsoft — both were software engineers there in the early 1990s, leaving with Windows stock options
choices: Microsoft — both were software engineers there in the early 1990s, leaving with Windows stock options

id Software — both were briefly at id in 1995 before John Carmack let them leave to start a publisher
Lucasarts — both worked on the X-Wing series before crossing over to FPS development at Valve
context: Valve was funded partly by Microsoft stock cash-out. The studio's culture (flat hierarchy, peer-reviewed projects) has been documented in HR handbooks since.

question: Blizzard Entertainment's World of Warcraft (November 2004) launched the most successful MMORPG in history. The studio had recently shipped Warcraft III (2002). Before pivoting WoW's pre-production, Blizzard had been working on a different MMO entirely. What was the project they shelved?
answer: Starcraft: Ghost — a console action game; shelved partly so the team could focus on World of Warcraft
choices: Starcraft: Ghost — a console action game; shelved partly so the team could focus on World of Warcraft

Warcraft IV — already announced for 2003; shelved when WoW's pre-production showed more promise
Lost Vikings 3 — a 2004 platformer; canceled outright when half the team moved to WoW assets
context: WoW had a long beta and shipped on November 23, 2004. It peaked at over 12 million subscribers in 2010. Starcraft: Ghost was canceled in 2006 after years of development.

question: Nintendo's Game Boy launched in 1989 in North America with a single game packed in the box that became the single most important reason for many adults to buy the handheld. The choice of pack-in over Mario was a deliberate move by Nintendo of America's marketing team. What was the pack-in title?
answer: Tetris — bundled with the Game Boy at launch in North America, credited with the device's adult sales
choices: Tetris — bundled with the Game Boy at launch in North America, credited with the device's adult sales
Super Mario Land — bundled in Japan but not in North America at launch, where Tetris was packed in
Baseball — a Nintendo first-party title bundled in some markets but not the primary US pack-in
Alleyway — Mario's Game Boy brick-breaker; bundled in select Toys R Us territories but not nationwide
context: Henk Rogers's deal for Tetris's handheld rights and the bundle agreement are central to the 2023 Tetris film with Taron Egerton.

question: Nintendo's choice to ship the N64 (1996) on cartridges rather than CD-ROM is now widely seen as the strategic mistake that cost them Final Fantasy 7 and lost market dominance to Sony. The decision was rational at the time, however. What were the two main reasons Nintendo gave for sticking with cartridges?
answer: No load times, plus higher piracy resistance — Nintendo cited both repeatedly in 1995-96 press briefings
choices: No load times, plus higher piracy resistance — Nintendo cited both repeatedly in 1995-96 press briefings
Lower per-unit production cost, plus regional save-state simplicity — Nintendo's stated 1995 rationale
Higher polygon counts possible, plus pure CPU access bandwidth — Nintendo's engineering-focused 1996 reasoning
Memory-mapped peripheral expansion, plus battery-backed cartridge-save persistence — Nintendo's hardware-side reasoning
context: Cartridges did mean no load times. But the 32-64 MB cap was crippling: FF7 used three CDs and would have required a hundred N64 cartridges to ship.

question: Sega's Dreamcast (1999) had a critically successful 18-month run but was abandoned by Sega in January 2001 with no warning to retailers, third parties, or fans. The console hit specific commercial milestones before being discontinued. About how many Dreamcasts had shipped at end-of-life?
answer: About 10.6 million units worldwide — Sega exited the console hardware business permanently after this run
choices: About 10.6 million units worldwide — Sega exited the console hardware business permanently after this run
About 30 million units worldwide — comparable to the Sega Genesis's lifetime numbers in North America
About 5 million units worldwide — only the launch wave; Sega never reached its first sales milestone
About 50 million units worldwide — peaked at 60M and then collapsed when PS2 reached the same shelves
context: Sega became a third-party publisher after the Dreamcast. The console's library — Shenmue, Soulcalibur, Crazy Taxi, Jet Set Radio — remains a cult favorite.

question: Nintendo's Wii (2006) launched with a pack-in collection of motion-controlled mini-games that became the global system seller. The strategy of broadening the gaming audience beyond traditional gamers was given a specific name by Nintendo's senior leadership at the time. What was the name?
answer: Blue Ocean Strategy — adapted from W. Chan Kim's book; Iwata used it for the Wii's audience expansion
choices: Blue Ocean Strategy — adapted from W. Chan Kim's book; Iwata used it for the Wii's audience expansion
Yellow Sky Strategy — Iwata's own coinage; never named publicly though the documents leaked in 2017
Open Field Strategy — Sega's term, which Iwata's team borrowed unattributed in internal Wii planning
Greenfield Strategy — Microsoft's term; Iwata briefly used it in 2005 before reverting to Iwata's preferred phrasing
context: Satoru Iwata named the strategy publicly in 2005-2006 talks. The Wii eventually outsold the Xbox 360 and PS3 to become the seventh-generation winner.

question: Tetsuya Nomura's Kingdom Hearts (2002, PS2) brought together Square's Final Fantasy characters and Disney's animated film characters in a single action-RPG. The collaboration began with a chance elevator encounter between Square and Disney executives in Tokyo, and a Square pitch about a Mickey Mouse Square Enix game. Where was the chance meeting?
answer: An elevator in Disney's Tokyo office — Square's Shinji Hashimoto encountered a Disney executive in the lift
choices: An elevator in Disney's Tokyo office — Square's Shinji Hashimoto encountered a Disney executive in the lift
A Square Enix booth at Tokyo Game Show — a Disney executive wandered over and proposed cross-licensing
A Japanese restaurant near Tokyo Disneyland — Square's Nomura was dining when Disney executives joined
A Disney+ launch ceremony in Tokyo — Nomura's first contact with Disney's Japanese subsidiary
context: Hashimoto and Nomura have told versions of this story in interviews. Kingdom Hearts has since become a sprawling cross-media franchise.

question: Namco's Ridge Racer (1993) launched in arcades with a smooth racing experience built on a hardware trick that earlier Namco titles couldn't pull off. The trick used the rotation matrix of a polygon environment around the player car, rather than rendering the surroundings traditionally. What was the technique called?
answer: Texture mapping on the System 22 hardware — the first arcade board to support real-time perspective-corrected textures
choices: Texture mapping on the System 22 hardware — the first arcade board to support real-time perspective-corrected textures
Sprite-scaling with Yu Suzuki's Super Scaler Z80 technology — borrowed from Sega's competing arcade lineup
Polygon mode-7 wraparound — Namco's borrowing of SNES Mode 7 graphics chip technology to arcade
Vector-line rendering with on-the-fly shading — a callback to the 1979 Asteroids vector hardware
context: The Namco System 22 board powered Ridge Racer and later Time Crisis. Texture-mapped polygons were a 1993 arcade revolution; home consoles took two more years to match it.

question: Capcom's Vampire Savior (1997), the third arcade Darkstalkers game, refined Vampire Hunter's monster-themed roster with new characters including Jedah Dohma and Q-Bee. The game introduced a distinct round structure unlike Street Fighter II's. What was the round structure?
answer: Single round to KO with damage carrying between rounds; one health bar across the whole match
choices: Single round to KO with damage carrying between rounds; one health bar across the whole match
Best two of three rounds with a permanent loser-bonus; the loser gained meter for the next round
Single round to a 99-second timer with damage scaling up over time; round ends at clock or KO
Three rounds with stage transitions between each; each stage gave a different combat-stat modifier
context: Vampire Savior's round structure influenced later Capcom fighters. Morrigan, Jedah, and Felicia remain fan-favorite Capcom mascots well beyond the Darkstalkers series itself.

question: Neversoft's Tony Hawk's Pro Skater (1999, PS1) introduced video game players to street skateboarding through real-world skater rosters, real spots, and real skate culture. The first game's level set drew heavily from one specific California city's iconic real skating locations. Which?
answer: San Francisco — including the Embarcadero plaza and Hubba Hideout, real spots in 1990s skate culture
choices: San Francisco — including the Embarcadero plaza and Hubba Hideout, real spots in 1990s skate culture

San Diego — including the Mission Beach boardwalk and downtown plazas, real spots from Hawk's youth
context: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1+2 (2020) remaster includes the original 1999 spots. The Embarcadero plaza in real San Francisco was a 1990s pilgrimage site for skaters.

question: Fumito Ueda's Shadow of the Colossus (2005, PS2) at Team Ico is a minimal-narrative game built around boss fights against giant beings the player must climb. The game's predecessor at Team Ico, also directed by Ueda, established his minimalist style. What was that earlier game?
answer: Ico (2001, PS2) — Ueda's prior Team Ico release; about a boy escaping a castle with a girl named Yorda

Panzer Dragoon (1995, Saturn) — Ueda was a Sega AM team member before Team Ico; this is contested fan lore
The Last Guardian (2016, PS4) — actually Ueda's next game after Shadow of the Colossus, not his earlier
context: Ueda's Team Ico made three games: Ico, Shadow of the Colossus, and The Last Guardian. Each took longer than the last. His style is now an entire reference category in design talks.

question: Valve's Team Fortress 2 (2007) shipped as part of The Orange Box collection — itself a remarkable package release of five games. The other four games in The Orange Box were three Half-Life products and one Valve experimental project. What was the experimental Orange Box release?
answer: Portal — Valve's puzzle game built from the Narbacular Drop student project, debuted with TF2 in The Orange Box

Day of Defeat: Source — Valve's WWII shooter, sometimes confused with The Orange Box but actually a separate release
Left 4 Dead — Valve's cooperative zombie shooter, actually released in 2008 after The Orange Box
context: The Orange Box's value-per-dollar was a 2007 benchmark. Portal, TF2, and Half-Life 2 Episode Two all came in one box.

question: Keita Takahashi's Katamari Damacy (2004, PS2) — about rolling up household objects into a giant ball — began as a project Takahashi pitched while still a student at a Japanese art university. Namco bought the pitch and let the student finish school while developing the game. Where did Takahashi study?
answer: Musashino Art University in Tokyo — Takahashi's sculpture-major art school during Katamari Damacy's pitch

question: Hideki Kamiya's Okami (2006, PS2) at Clover Studio used a brush-stroke 'Celestial Brush' mechanic to combat and traverse an Edo-period stylized Japan. Clover Studio was Capcom's experimental subsidiary founded in 2004. What was Clover's commercial fate after Okami's reception?

question: ASCII Corporation's RPG Maker series, released in Japan as RPG Tsukuru since 1988, had an unauthorized fan-translated PC version pirated and circulated on early 2000s English-language sites. question: 2D Boy's World of Goo (2008) was a watershed indie game made by a two-person team: Kyle Gabler (formerly at EA's Maxis) and Ron Carmel (formerly at EA's Sims division). The studio shipped on Wii via WiiWare, PC via direct download, and Steam. About how long did the two-person team take to make World of Goo?
answer: About two years — between Gabler's 2006 prototype Tower of Goo and the 2008 retail release on multiple platforms
choices: About two years — between Gabler's 2006 prototype Tower of Goo and the 2008 retail release on multiple platforms

About five years — Gabler's prototype dates to 2003, predating Carmel's involvement by two years
About four months — a Global Game Jam derivative of Tower of Goo that 2D Boy polished and shipped quickly
context: World of Goo's commercial success on WiiWare and Steam helped legitimize the indie distribution model that would lead to Steam Greenlight, the Humble Bundle, and the wider 2010s indie boom.

question: Jonathan Blow's Braid (2008) was an Xbox Live Arcade indie release with time-rewind mechanics, painterly 2D art by David Hellman, and music licensed from existing indie classical-folk artists. Each world in Braid had a distinct time mechanic; one specific world's mechanic made it stand out as a thinking-game classic. Which mechanic?
answer: World 3 introduced an item that, when carried, became immune to the time-rewind of other game objects
choices: World 3 introduced an item that, when carried, became immune to the time-rewind of other game objects
World 2 introduced a parallel-world split mechanic, with two simultaneous game-state instances on screen
World 4 introduced a permanent fast-forward mechanic, accelerating game time independently of player input
World 5 introduced a global-pause mechanic, freezing all non-player objects until the player touched them
context: Braid sold 55,000 copies on Xbox Live Arcade in its first week. Blow's later The Witness (2016) built on Braid's puzzle-as-philosophy approach.

question: Tarn and Zach Adams's Dwarf Fortress (2006 alpha) began as a freeware text-based fortress-management game and has been in continuous development for nearly two decades, including a 2022 Steam release with graphical tiles. The game's core procedural-world depth is extreme. About how many years of fortress simulation does Dwarf Fortress generate per world by default?
answer: About 200 to 1,000 years of pre-history before the player even starts; configurable up to 10,000+ years

About 25 years of pre-history by default; longer histories require fortress dwarves to die and be reborn
context: Dwarf Fortress's procedural histories track every legend, mountain hall, and noble. Tarn Adams's commitment to the project is one of indie gaming's longest-running case studies.

question: Derek Yu's Spelunky was first released as a freeware PC game in 2008 with simple pixel art. A remake for Xbox Live Arcade in 2012 added new sprites by Yu, online co-op, and full 16:9 HD presentation. The Spelunky design borrowed structurally from a famous predecessor genre. What genre?
answer: Roguelike — Spelunky combined platformer mechanics with roguelike permadeath and procedural levels
choices: Roguelike — Spelunky combined platformer mechanics with roguelike permadeath and procedural levels

Metroidvania — Spelunky borrowed from Castlevania and Metroid for its level-interconnection design
Tower defense — Spelunky's enemy placement borrowed from defense games of the early flash era
context: Spelunky 2 (2020) deepened the formula. Yu's design talks on Spelunky's procedural generation are required reading in indie circles.

question: The first commercially successful pinball machine — by some measures, the first machine many Americans would recognize as 'pinball' — was a coin-operated tabletop game without flippers. It hit American taverns in 1931 and sold around 50,000 units in seven months despite the Depression. What was the machine called?
answer: Baffle Ball — D. Gottlieb's 1931 pinball machine, often called the first commercially successful pinball
choices: Baffle Ball — D. Gottlieb's 1931 pinball machine, often called the first commercially successful pinball
Bingo — a 1932 Mills Industries release that briefly held the title before Gottlieb's machine reclaimed it
Whiffle Board — Automatic Industries's 1931 release, technically older but commercially behind Baffle Ball
Ballyhoo — Bally's 1932 release, often credited as the first pinball but actually the second-mover
context: Baffle Ball had no flippers — flippers came in 1947 with Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty. Pinball as we know it grew from this Chicago Depression-era invention.

question: Atari's E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial (1982) for the 2600 became the most famous bad video game in American history, partly due to a legend about millions of unsold cartridges being buried in a New Mexico landfill. The story was treated as urban legend for over 30 years — until it was excavated in 2014. What did the dig find?
answer: Hundreds of crushed and mangled E.T. cartridges, plus other unsold Atari stock — partially confirming the legend
choices: Hundreds of crushed and mangled E.T. cartridges, plus other unsold Atari stock — partially confirming the legend
Mostly Pac-Man and Asteroids cartridges; only a single broken E.T. cartridge in the dig pit, debunking the legend
An entire warehouse of pristine cartridges underneath the dirt — proving the legend in full intact form
Nothing except trash from local restaurants; the landfill had never received Atari materials, refuting the legend
context: The 2014 excavation in Alamogordo, NM produced the documentary Atari: Game Over. Some recovered cartridges sold to collectors for hundreds of dollars each.

question: Atari's Asteroids (1979) was the first commercial arcade game to ask players who scored well to type their initials onto a permanent high-score table. Lyle Rains and Ed Logg's game shipped on vector display hardware to give it the crisp white lines older raster displays couldn't render. What was the maximum displayed score before rollover?
answer: 99,990 — the score rolls over to zero after this point but the game continues with no maximum lives

999,990 — the score rolls over after this; the rollover screen makes the high-score table show negative
9,999,990 — the score never rolls over within human play; the cabinet has no maximum
999,999 — the score caps here rather than rolling, ending the run for the rest of the game
context: Asteroids's high-score initials are now standard in arcade history. Logg also designed Centipede; Atari's vector hardware ran a series of classic games into the early 1980s.

question: Williams Electronics's Defender (1981), designed by Eugene Jarvis, is famous for being controllable only by a hand-on-stick, hand-on-buttons split — six buttons plus a joystick for the four directions. Defender innovated a now-common arcade game feature that was not in Pac-Man or Donkey Kong. What feature?
answer: Mini-map overhead radar — Defender showed the entire scrolling-stage map at the top of the screen
choices: Mini-map overhead radar — Defender showed the entire scrolling-stage map at the top of the screen

Continuous music looping — Defender had no music; the silence was Jarvis's deliberate design choice
Adjustable lives — Defender shipped with a coin-operator menu allowing 2 to 7 starting lives
context: Defender's radar became standard in 1980s arcade games. The Williams team's Robotron 2084 (1982) extended Jarvis's eight-button design with twin joysticks.

question: Atari's Tempest (1981), designed by Dave Theurer, was a vector-graphics arcade game played on a rotating-knob-controlled tube. Tempest's level structure had a specific twist that distinguished it from Asteroids or Defender. What was Tempest's level structure?
answer: 16 distinct level shapes (circle, square, V, W, etc.); each level cycles through with increasing difficulty
choices: 16 distinct level shapes (circle, square, V, W, etc.); each level cycles through with increasing difficulty
100 procedurally generated tubes; level designs were random with a fixed difficulty curve across the set

12 colors of tubes; the level structure was color-based with no shape variation across the set
context: Tempest's 16 level shapes became iconic. Jeff Minter (Llamasoft) later made Tempest 2000, an Atari Jaguar remake that pushed the original's vector aesthetic into hyperkinetic form.

question: Williams Electronics's Joust (1982), designed by John Newcomer, was one of the first arcade games to support two-player simultaneous cooperation. Both players ride flying ostriches and joust enemy buzzards by hitting them from above. The two-player twist on the cabinet was meaningful. What was novel about Joust's two-player mode?
answer: Two players could either cooperate against waves or attack each other for points — first co-op-vs-compete arcade

Two players faced off in a permanent versus mode; cooperation was patched in later but never the original release
context: Joust's social dynamic — cooperate or compete — became a coffee-shop legend. The Williams hardware team's collaborations continued into the late 1980s.

question: Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar's Robotron: 2084 (1982) introduced the twin-stick shooter genre with a simple control scheme: one joystick to move, one joystick to shoot. The inspiration for the move-and-shoot-with-separate-sticks idea came from a specific pre-1982 game that influenced Jarvis. What game?

Combat (1977) by Atari — the 2600 pack-in tank game that established the move-and-shoot pattern
context: Berzerk's eight-direction shooting led to Jarvis's twin-stick refinement. Robotron 2084 sold 23,000 cabinets and is widely considered the apex of early-80s arcade shooters.

question: Kentaro Miura's manga Berserk began serialization in 1989 in Hakusensha's Young Animal magazine. It was first animated as a 1997 TV series at OLM Studio. A second, more divisive adaptation came in 2012-2013 as a film trilogy by a different Tokyo studio known for its hand-drawn auteur shorts and theatrical work — the same studio behind Mind Game and Mutafukaz. question: The 2020 film Demon Slayer: Mugen Train, directed by Haruo Sotozaki at Ufotable, broke the all-time Japanese box-office record on its release in the middle of the pandemic. The film it dethroned had held the record for almost twenty years and was itself an animated film by a beloved director. Which film?
answer: Spirited Away (2001) by Hayao Miyazaki — held the all-time Japan box-office record from 2001 until October 2020
choices: Spirited Away (2001) by Hayao Miyazaki — held the all-time Japan box-office record from 2001 until October 2020
